affected_groups.explanation: Survey recipients are subject to the increased criminal penalty and new civil penalties for failing to complete and return the survey.

affected_groups.group: Covered water users in regional water planning areas or municipalities with a projected water shortage
affected_groups.explanation: These users are subject to an additional $2,500 civil penalty for each week of noncompliance.

affected_groups.group: People providing survey information regarding windmills used for domestic and livestock purposes
affected_groups.explanation: The amended provisions, including the new penalties, do not apply to this survey information.

major_effects.label: Higher misdemeanor classification
major_effects.explanation: Changes the offense for failing to complete and return a survey from a Class C to a Class A misdemeanor.

major_effects.label: Weekly civil penalties
major_effects.explanation: Imposes escalating weekly penalties of $5,000 for the first week, $10,000 for the second, and $15,000 for each subsequent week; covered users in projected-shortage areas also owe an additional $2,500 per week. These provisions exclude survey information regarding domestic and livestock windmills.

major_effects.label: State suits to recover penalties
major_effects.explanation: Requires the attorney general to institute a suit to recover civil penalties when requested by the executive administrator or the board.

agencies.name: Texas Water Development Board
agencies.explanation: The board is given a role in requesting a suit to recover the new civil penalties; the Water Code definition identifies the board as the Texas Water Development Board.

agencies.name: Office of the Attorney General
agencies.explanation: The attorney general must bring a state suit to recover the civil penalties when requested by the executive administrator or the board.

HB365.summary: The bill requires the Texas Commission on Law Enforcement to collect and maintain specified incident-based data, develop standard-format and data-quality policies, review those policies periodically, and publish accessible data and a glossary, subject to public-information disclosure limits. It also requires a study and recommendations on data quality, redundant requirements, and the feasibility of collecting broader encounter data, with a report due by January 1, 2029; the study provision expires September 1, 2029.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill changes how law-enforcement incident data is standardized, maintained, and made available, and studies possible data about officer encounters.
The bill adds ongoing data-management, policy-review, publication, and study-reporting duties for the commission.

locations.name: Texas
locations.explanation: The requirements concern the statewide Texas Commission on Law Enforcement and incident data submitted by law enforcement agencies.

affected_groups.group: Law enforcement agencies submitting incident-based reports
affected_groups.explanation: The commission's new standard-format guidelines and data-quality policies concern the reports these agencies submit.

affected_groups.group: Members of the public and academic researchers
affected_groups.explanation: The bill provides for public access to releasable incident data and seeks data quality sufficient to support academic research.

major_effects.label: Incident-data standards and quality review
major_effects.explanation: Requires standard-format submission guidelines and data-quality policies, with periodic review and revision; it does not replace the underlying reporting requirements referenced in existing law.

major_effects.label: Public access to releasable data
major_effects.explanation: Requires accessible electronic publication of the incident-based data, except information not subject to disclosure under Chapter 552, and publication of a glossary.

major_effects.label: Study and recommendations
major_effects.explanation: Requires a study and recommendations, reported by January 1, 2029, including whether broader officer-encounter data collection is feasible; it does not itself require that additional data to be collected.

agencies.name: Texas Commission on Law Enforcement
agencies.explanation: The commission is assigned the data collection, policy-development, publication, review, and study duties.

agencies.name: Texas Department of Public Safety
agencies.explanation: The department is expressly named as a participant in the required consultation for developing the submission guidelines and data-quality policies.

HB366.summary: HB 366 would require municipalities with populations above 100,000 to grant or deny building-permit applications for housing developments allocated low-income housing tax credits within half the time allowed for other residential permit applications. If a municipality has an accelerated residential permitting process, applicants for those projects could use it; the measure applies only to municipal building permits and does not affect zoning.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes municipal building-permit review for qualifying affordable housing projects.
Imposes permit-review requirements on qualifying municipalities.

locations.name: Municipalities with populations over 100,000
locations.explanation: The permitting requirements apply only in municipalities above this population threshold.

affected_groups.group: Municipalities with populations over 100,000
affected_groups.explanation: These municipalities would have to decide qualifying permit applications within a shortened review period and allow use of an accelerated process if they have one.

affected_groups.group: Applicants for housing projects allocated low-income housing tax credits
affected_groups.explanation: Their building-permit applications would receive the shortened review period and, where available, access to the municipality’s accelerated process.

major_effects.label: Expedited municipal building-permit review
major_effects.explanation: For covered projects in municipalities with populations over 100,000, permit decisions must be made within half the usual municipal period; applicants may use an accelerated review process if the municipality has adopted one. The requirement concerns municipal building permits only and does not affect zoning.

HB367.summary: The bill would limit liability for sport shooting range sponsors and compensated instructors when required warnings are posted and an injury results from inherent range risks or participant negligence. The protection would not cover specified reckless or intentional conduct or certain known latent hazards without a warning, and the bill would require warning signs at shooting areas and warning language in written participant contracts.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill changes liability and warning requirements concerning firearm activities and injuries at sport shooting ranges.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The bill amends Texas law governing sport shooting ranges, with no geographic limitation stated.

affected_groups.group: Sport shooting range sponsors and compensated instructors
affected_groups.explanation: They would receive the conditional liability protection and have warning-language obligations for written participant contracts.

affected_groups.group: Sport shooting range owners and owners of property where a range operates
affected_groups.explanation: Range owners would have to post and maintain warning signs; the liability provisions also cover sponsors and professionals in specified circumstances.

affected_groups.group: Sport shooting range participants and people bringing injury claims
affected_groups.explanation: The bill defines participant injuries broadly and limits when claims for those injuries may be brought against covered sponsors or professionals.

major_effects.label: Conditional liability limitation
major_effects.explanation: Subject to subsection (b)’s exceptions, a sponsor or professional would not be liable if the required warning is posted and the injury is proximately caused by an inherent activity risk or a participant’s or another participant’s negligence. The protection does not apply to specified reckless or intentional misconduct.

major_effects.label: Exceptions to liability protection
major_effects.explanation: The limitation would not apply to injuries caused by specified reckless or intentional conduct, or by a known or reasonably knowable latent dangerous property condition for which no warning was provided.

major_effects.label: Required participant warnings
major_effects.explanation: For the liability limitation to apply, range owners must post and maintain the prescribed sign by each designated shooting area, and sponsors or professionals must include the prescribed language in applicable written contracts.

HB368.summary: For covered outside-counsel contracts entered into on or after the Act’s effective date, the Comptroller must approve the contract for it to be valid; if approval is denied, the Attorney General must provide the legal services in the manner required by law. The bill also establishes invoice certification and limited Comptroller review before payment, and requires the attorney or law firm to pay an administrative fee.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes state contracting and oversight procedures for outside counsel retained by the Attorney General.
Adds prepayment review of covered legal-service invoices and a fee payable to the Comptroller.

affected_groups.group: Attorneys and law firms providing outside legal services to the Attorney General
affected_groups.explanation: Their covered contracts require Comptroller approval, their invoices are subject to the new process, and they must pay an administrative fee when entering into a contract to provide legal services to the Attorney General.

major_effects.label: Comptroller approval of outside-counsel contracts
major_effects.explanation: Covered contracts require Comptroller approval to be valid; if approval is denied, the Attorney General must provide the services in the manner required by law.

major_effects.label: Invoice certification and review
major_effects.explanation: The Attorney General must certify specified invoice information and submit invoices for review; the Comptroller’s review is limited to whether the services fall within the contract term and scope for payment eligibility.

major_effects.label: Administrative fee
major_effects.explanation: An attorney or law firm must pay the Comptroller an administrative fee when entering into a covered contract.

agencies.name: Office of the Attorney General
agencies.explanation: The office must seek Comptroller approval for covered contracts, provide specified invoice certifications, and provide the services itself if contract approval is denied.

agencies.name: Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts
agencies.explanation: The Comptroller must approve covered contracts and review invoices for specified payment eligibility criteria, and receives the administrative fee when an attorney or law firm enters into a contract to provide legal services to the Attorney General.

HB369.summary: The bill would authorize specified personal cannabis use by adults age 21 or older and create a state licensing and regulatory framework for commercial cannabis operations. It would limit local governments’ ability to prohibit or unreasonably restrict authorized operations while allowing certain local regulations and providing assistance payments to qualifying municipalities and counties. It would impose cannabis sales taxes, allocate the proceeds among specified state and local purposes, and make sales to people under 21 a criminal offense.

policy_tags.explanation: Creates licenses, operating requirements, and state rules for cannabis growers, establishments, transporters, and testing facilities.
Authorizes specified conduct that otherwise could trigger legal action and creates misdemeanor offenses for selling or giving cannabis to people under 21.
Imposes additional taxes on cannabis sales, with different rates for sales to consumers and sales from growers to establishments.
Directs cannabis tax proceeds to state accounts, qualifying local governments, and the permanent school fund.
Allocates the remainder of cannabis tax proceeds to the permanent school fund.
Directs a share of cannabis tax proceeds to an account limited to chemical dependency prevention, treatment, and rehabilitation.
Limits local restrictions on authorized cannabis operations, permits specified local regulations, and provides assistance payments to qualifying municipalities and counties.
Protects a residential tenant’s ability under a lease to possess cannabis and consume it by means other than smoking on the premises.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The bill creates a statewide regulatory and tax framework for cannabis sales and operations in Texas.

affected_groups.group: Adults age 21 or older
affected_groups.explanation: Would be authorized to use, possess, process, transport, or transfer cannabis products to another adult without remuneration, subject to the amount specified by commission rule.

affected_groups.group: Cannabis businesses and their workers
affected_groups.explanation: Growers, establishments, transporters, and testing facilities would need licenses and would be subject to operating requirements; employees dispensing cannabis would need registration.

affected_groups.group: People under 21
affected_groups.explanation: Would be barred from cannabis establishments and cannabis consumption businesses, and sales or transfers of cannabis to them would be prohibited and punishable.

affected_groups.group: Municipalities and counties with cannabis establishments
affected_groups.explanation: Would have limited authority to restrict authorized operations and could receive state assistance payments for regulation and oversight costs, subject to the account’s available funds.

affected_groups.group: Residential tenants and property owners
affected_groups.explanation: Would be affected by a property owner’s general authority to prohibit or restrict cannabis activity on property they own, occupy, or manage, except that a residential tenant may not be prohibited from possessing cannabis, cannabis products, or related paraphernalia, or from consuming cannabis by means other than smoking on the premises.

major_effects.label: Adult-use and licensed commercial framework
major_effects.explanation: Would authorize specified personal conduct by adults subject to limits and conditions, including use, possession, and transport of no more than 2 ounces of cannabis, with no more than 15 grams of that amount in concentrate form, and cultivation for personal use of no more than 12 plants in an enclosed area equipped with locks or other security devices that restrict access. It would also create licensed commercial roles for cultivation, sales, transport, and testing.

major_effects.label: Protections for authorized conduct and residential tenants
major_effects.explanation: Would protect a person from legal action solely due to conduct authorized under Section 491.0051 or 491.0052, and prevent prohibiting residential tenants from specified cannabis possession and non-smoking consumption.

major_effects.label: State standards for cannabis operations and products
major_effects.explanation: Would require rules covering grower and establishment regulation, testing, packaging and labeling, and secure transport.

major_effects.label: Limits and permissions for local regulation
major_effects.explanation: Would bar political subdivisions from prohibiting or unreasonably restricting authorized cannabis operations while allowing consistent local rules on hours, location, business manner, and the number of certain licensees.

major_effects.label: New cannabis sales taxes
major_effects.explanation: Would impose 20 percent tax on establishment-to-consumer sales and 15 percent tax on grower-to-establishment sales, in addition to Chapter 151 taxes; the new tax does not apply to low-THC cannabis regulated under Chapter 487.

major_effects.label: Allocation of tax proceeds and local assistance
major_effects.explanation: Would allocate tax proceeds among local oversight, chemical dependency services, veterans’ assistance, and the permanent school fund. Local payments would be limited to qualifying local governments and may be reduced if account funds are insufficient.

major_effects.label: Criminal penalties for sales to people under 21
major_effects.explanation: Would make selling or giving cannabis to a person under 21, or to someone intending to deliver it to a person under 21, an offense. The offense would be a Class A misdemeanor if the recipient was under 18 and a Class B misdemeanor if the recipient was 18 to under 21.

major_effects.label: Sales and program oversight reports
major_effects.explanation: Would require monthly sales reports from cannabis establishments to the comptroller and an annual licensing and regulation report from the executive director to the governor.

agencies.name: Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation
agencies.explanation: Would administer the new chapter, issue licenses, and handle related licensing and enforcement functions. The requirement to begin licensing the listed entities by November 1, 2028, is conditioned on applicants having met all approval requirements.

agencies.name: Texas Commission of Licensing and Regulation
agencies.explanation: Would adopt rules for administering and enforcing the chapter. The bill names the commission, but the supplied canonical registry has no matching entry.

agencies.name: Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts
agencies.explanation: Would administer the local-share account, review local payment applications, and handle tax-proceeds deposits; cannabis establishments would also send it monthly sales reports.

agencies.name: Texas Department of Public Safety
agencies.explanation: Would receive notice when a license is suspended or revoked, and the public safety director may seize or seal specified cannabis-related property. The bill also adds license applicants to the criminal-history information provisions.

HB370.summary: The bill makes certain people eligible for nondisclosure orders after dismissal and discharge from misdemeanor deferred adjudication, subject to offense exclusions, a 180-day waiting period, and other statutory conditions. For dismissals and discharges on or after January 1, 2030, the Department of Public Safety must identify qualifying people and notify the court, which must issue an order; people with qualifying dismissals and discharges on or after January 1, 1993, may also request a department determination or present evidence to the court, and eligible people may not be charged a fee for the order. The bill also requires criminal-history records to indicate whether a specified affirmative finding was filed.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes eligibility and procedures for orders restricting public disclosure of criminal-history information after deferred adjudication.

locations.name: Texas
locations.explanation: The bill changes Texas statutes and applies to qualifying cases handled by courts under those statutes statewide.

affected_groups.group: People with qualifying misdemeanor deferred-adjudication cases
affected_groups.explanation: People may qualify after dismissal and discharge if they meet the bill's offense, timing, and other statutory conditions.

affected_groups.group: Courts and clerks handling deferred-adjudication cases
affected_groups.explanation: The applicable court receives notice through its clerk and must issue an order after receiving qualifying notice.

affected_groups.group: Criminal justice agencies
affected_groups.explanation: An order prohibits these agencies from publicly disclosing criminal-history information related to the covered offense.

major_effects.label: Eligibility for nondisclosure orders
major_effects.explanation: Creates entitlement to an order for qualifying misdemeanor deferred-adjudication cases, subject to offense exclusions, the waiting period, and the other listed requirements.

major_effects.label: Department screening and court-issued orders
major_effects.explanation: Requires monthly identification and notice for qualifying dismissals and discharges on or after January 1, 2030; the court must issue an order after receiving notice. A person may also request a department determination or present evidence directly to the court.

major_effects.label: Criminal-history record detail
major_effects.explanation: Requires the computerized criminal-history system to record whether a specified affirmative finding was filed in a deferred-adjudication case.

major_effects.label: No fee for eligible orders
major_effects.explanation: A person entitled to an order under this section may not be required to pay a fee relating to its issuance.

agencies.name: Texas Department of Public Safety
agencies.explanation: The department must review computerized criminal-history records, identify qualifying people, and send notices; Section 5 names the Department of Public Safety in connection with these notice provisions.

agencies.name: Office of Court Administration of the Texas Judicial System
agencies.explanation: The office prescribes the manner for department notices and must confer with the Department of Public Safety about notice content.

HB371.summary: HB 371 would require a political subdivision to adopt two conditional budgets for a fiscal year beginning in a tax year when it adopts an ad valorem tax rate above its voter-approval rate: one assuming voters approve the adopted rate and one assuming they approve the voter-approval rate. It would also revise tax notices and ballots so voters in covered elections choose between those rates, and tie the resulting tax rate and related corrected bills or refunds to the rate approved; the changes apply to relevant fiscal and tax years beginning on or after the Act's effective date.

policy_tags.explanation: Requires qualifying political subdivisions to adopt two contingent budgets when they adopt a tax rate above the voter-approval rate.
Changes property-tax rate approval procedures and the tax rate that applies after covered elections.
Revises required election notices and ballots to allow voters in covered elections to approve either the adopted rate or the voter-approval rate.
Changes school-district tax-rate election procedures; it does not make broader changes to school programs.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The provisions apply to qualifying political subdivisions across the state, not to a named locality.

affected_groups.group: Political subdivisions, including counties, municipalities, school districts, and special purpose districts
affected_groups.explanation: Their governing bodies must adopt the conditional budgets when the bill's tax-rate condition applies.

affected_groups.group: Registered voters in affected taxing units
affected_groups.explanation: Voters choose between the adopted tax rate and the voter-approval tax rate in covered elections.

affected_groups.group: Property owners and taxpayers in affected taxing units
affected_groups.explanation: Their tax bills may be corrected and taxes refunded if voters approve the voter-approval rate after bills were issued or paid.

major_effects.label: Two conditional budgets
major_effects.explanation: For an applicable fiscal year, the governing body must adopt one budget contingent on approval of the adopted rate and another contingent on approval of the voter-approval rate; ordinary budget preparation, notice, and hearing provisions apply to both.

major_effects.label: Tax-rate election notices and ballots
major_effects.explanation: In covered elections, required notices and ballots present the adopted rate and the voter-approval rate as alternatives for voters to approve.

major_effects.label: Tax rates and post-election adjustments
major_effects.explanation: The rate approved by a majority becomes the current-year rate. If voters approve the voter-approval rate after tax bills have been mailed, corrected bills are required, and taxpayers who overpaid may receive refunds under the stated conditions.

HB372.summary: The bill would require a taxing unit’s collector to apply a property owner’s payment to taxes before penalties or interest, unless the owner gives written instructions otherwise. It would cap the total penalties and interest a person owes on a delinquent tax at $500; the payment-application rule applies only to payments received on or after the Act’s effective date.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes how property tax payments are applied and caps penalties and interest owed on delinquent taxes.
Assigns a payment-application duty to collectors of taxing units, including local taxing entities.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The bill amends the Texas Tax Code and establishes a general rule for taxing units rather than limiting the changes to a particular place.

affected_groups.group: Property owners making tax payments
affected_groups.explanation: Their payments would be applied to tax due before penalties or interest unless they provide written instructions otherwise.

affected_groups.group: People liable for delinquent taxes
affected_groups.explanation: Their total liability for penalties and interest on a delinquent tax would be capped at $500.

affected_groups.group: Taxing units and their tax collectors
affected_groups.explanation: Collectors must apply payments to tax before penalties or interest, unless the property owner provides written instructions for a different application.

major_effects.label: Tax payment application priority
major_effects.explanation: Requires payments to be applied to tax due before penalties or interest, unless the property owner provides written instructions for a different application.

major_effects.label: Cap on delinquent-tax penalties and interest
major_effects.explanation: Limits the total penalties and interest a person is liable for on a delinquent tax to $500.

HB373.summary: The bill would require the department to issue specialty license plates for active or former members of the United States Naval Construction Battalions, with specified Seabees wording and logo. It would also add these plates to the list of plates whose emblem may be included on certain other plates, subject to the existing rules.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill creates a specialty motor-vehicle license plate and changes which plate emblems may be included on certain other plates.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The bill establishes a Texas specialty license plate; it does not limit issuance to a particular locality.

affected_groups.group: Active or former members of the United States Naval Construction Battalions
affected_groups.explanation: They would be eligible for the newly specified specialty plates.

affected_groups.group: People entitled to plates under the provisions listed in Transportation Code Section 504.202(e-1)
affected_groups.explanation: Under the existing rules, they may request the emblem of another plate to which they are entitled; the bill adds the new Seabees plate to that list.

major_effects.label: Create Seabees specialty plates
major_effects.explanation: The department would issue specialty plates for active or former members of the Naval Construction Battalions, with the specified wording and Navy Seabee logo.

major_effects.label: Add Seabees plate to emblem options
major_effects.explanation: The new plate is added to the list of plates whose emblem may be included on certain other plates, subject to the existing limits and request process.

agencies.name: Texas Department of Motor Vehicles
agencies.explanation: Chapter 504 defines “Department” as the Texas Department of Motor Vehicles, and the bill assigns it the specialty license plate issuance duty.

HB374.summary: For agreements entered into on or after September 1, 2027, a governmental entity may agree with a private entity to restrict disclosure of information about a data center project only if the entity and agreement comply with the chapter. The agreement must expire no later than two years after execution and is not effective until approved by a majority vote at a public meeting that includes an opportunity for public testimony.

policy_tags.explanation: Sets conditions for governmental entities entering confidentiality agreements concerning data center projects meeting the bill's definition.
Imposes meeting, notice, and agreement requirements on local governments that enter covered agreements.
Creates public meeting, notice, complaint, and enforcement procedures for governmental entities.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The requirements apply to the bill-defined state agency and local government classes across Texas.

affected_groups.group: Local governments
affected_groups.explanation: Municipalities, counties, special-purpose districts or authorities, and other political subdivisions must follow the requirements if they enter covered agreements.

affected_groups.group: State agencies and institutions of higher education
affected_groups.explanation: These entities are included in the bill's definition of state agency and are subject to the requirements for covered agreements.

affected_groups.group: Private entities seeking confidentiality for data center projects
affected_groups.explanation: Their agreements with governmental entities may restrict disclosure only if the chapter's requirements are met.

affected_groups.group: Members of the public
affected_groups.explanation: The public receives advance meeting notice and an opportunity to testify, and a person may file a sworn complaint alleging a violation.

major_effects.label: Limits on data center nondisclosure agreements
major_effects.explanation: Covered agreements must expire within two years and are ineffective unless approved by a majority vote at a public meeting with an opportunity for public testimony.

major_effects.label: Public notice before approval
major_effects.explanation: Requires advance notice in the applicable publication channels and a plain-language summary explaining the agreement and why it is considered necessary.

major_effects.label: Attorney general enforcement
major_effects.explanation: After determining a complaint is valid, the attorney general must bring an action to invalidate the agreement, compel compliance, and recover any applicable civil penalty.

major_effects.label: Civil penalty for intentional violations
major_effects.explanation: A governmental entity found by a court to have intentionally violated the chapter may be penalized up to $1,000 per violation; each day is a separate violation.

agencies.name: Office of the Attorney General
agencies.explanation: The attorney general receives complaints and must bring an enforcement action when a complaint is determined to be valid.

agencies.name: State agency
agencies.explanation: The bill-defined class of state agencies, including institutions of higher education, is subject to the chapter when entering covered agreements; the source does not identify individual agencies.

HB375.summary: HB 375 would define “regulatory tax” and require the Legislature and Texas Legislative Council to identify state taxes as taxes in new laws, while correcting existing references only when otherwise amending the law. It would also require state agencies to use that terminology in rules and other materials, correcting existing references when those materials are amended, and require the Chapter 325 commission to consider and recommend statutory revisions during agency reviews.

policy_tags.explanation: Creates statutory terminology requirements for identifying state taxes, including regulatory taxes; it does not change tax rates or amounts.
Assigns terminology duties to state institutions and adds a consideration-and-recommendation duty to agency reviews under Chapter 325.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The requirements apply to state laws and state agencies across Texas, without a narrower geographic limitation.

affected_groups.group: State agencies and covered institutions
affected_groups.explanation: A state agency may not identify a state tax as another type of charge when proposing or adopting its rules, reference materials, publications, or electronic media. It must correct an incorrectly identified reference when amending those materials.

affected_groups.group: Texas Legislature and Texas Legislative Council
affected_groups.explanation: They are directed to use tax terminology in new legislation and to correct existing references when otherwise amending the relevant law.

affected_groups.group: Taxpayers and readers of state materials
affected_groups.explanation: They are the intended beneficiaries of clearer identification of state taxes; the bill does not itself change tax amounts.

major_effects.label: Tax terminology requirements
major_effects.explanation: Requires accurate identification of state taxes in new legislation and agency materials; existing references are corrected only when the relevant law or material is otherwise amended.

major_effects.label: Agency-review recommendations
major_effects.explanation: Requires the Chapter 325 commission, as part of its review of a state agency, to consider and recommend statutory revisions for correct tax terminology.

agencies.name: Texas Legislative Council
agencies.explanation: The bill expressly directs the Council, along with the Legislature, to use the required terminology in legislation.

agencies.name: Sunset Advisory Commission
agencies.explanation: The bill assigns the commission a duty in agency reviews under Government Code Chapter 325, but does not name it in this text.

HB376.summary: The bill replaces average daily attendance with average enrollment as the measure used across public school finance, setting the basic calculation as the average number of students enrolled during the school year and requiring the estimate to use enrollment counts from the last Fridays of October and March. It also shifts related school funding formulas, program counts, and eligibility measures to enrollment; this changes the basis for calculating amounts but does not guarantee a uniform increase or decrease in funding.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes the enrollment measure used across public school finance, school programs, and related eligibility calculations.
Changes the student-count basis used in state school aid and other public education funding formulas.
Changes the enrollment-based benchmark used to calculate money transferred to participating children's education accounts.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The changes apply to the statewide public school finance system rather than to a particular locality.

affected_groups.group: School districts and open-enrollment charter schools
affected_groups.explanation: For qualifying school districts and open-enrollment charter schools, the commissioner adjusts average enrollment under Section 48.005, replacing average daily attendance.

affected_groups.group: Students participating in education-assistance programs
affected_groups.explanation: The enrollment-based funding benchmark used for money transferred to participating children's accounts changes.

affected_groups.group: Adult education program participants
affected_groups.explanation: The share of instructional days for which a student is counted is based on the portion of the school year the student is enrolled, rather than a 100 percent attendance rate.

major_effects.label: Use average enrollment in school-finance calculations
major_effects.explanation: Replaces average daily attendance with average enrollment across state aid and related school-finance formulas; the change does not itself guarantee that a district's funding rises or falls.

major_effects.label: Set enrollment calculation and data inputs
major_effects.explanation: Requires rules for calculating average enrollment, including use of district enrollment counts from the last Fridays of October and March.

major_effects.label: Rebase education-assistance account amounts
major_effects.explanation: Uses average enrollment, rather than average daily attendance, in the statewide per-student funding benchmark for transfers to participating children's accounts.

major_effects.label: Count adult education students by enrollment duration
major_effects.explanation: Sets the portion of instructional days counted according to how much of the school year a student is enrolled, with no count for enrollment under 10 percent of the year.

agencies.name: commissioner/agency (Education Code)
agencies.explanation: The bill assigns enrollment-calculation rulemaking to the commissioner and requires the agency to use specified enrollment counts. The excerpt does not verify the canonical identity of these generic references.

agencies.name: Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts
agencies.explanation: A child's participation may end when the child is counted toward a district's or charter school's average enrollment for Foundation School Program funding, affecting the program's eligibility determinations administered under the subchapter.

HB377.summary: HB 377 would extend a handgun license through the 90th day after its printed expiration date if the holder submits the specified renewal materials no later than 10 days before expiration. The department would promptly provide a receipt, and the holder would be treated as having an unexpired license for specified Penal Code and other state-law purposes during the extension only while carrying both the receipt and expired license; the change applies only to licenses expiring on or after the Act's effective date.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes the validity period and proof requirements for a license to carry a handgun.
Defines when an extended license is treated as unexpired for purposes including specified Penal Code chapters.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The bill concerns state handgun licenses and their status under state law.

affected_groups.group: Handgun license holders who submit renewal materials on time
affected_groups.explanation: They may receive an extension if they submit the specified renewal materials by the statutory cutoff.

affected_groups.group: Handgun carriers relying on an extended license
affected_groups.explanation: For the specified legal purposes, they are treated as holding an unexpired license during the extension only while carrying both the receipt and expired license.

major_effects.label: Conditional license-expiration extension
major_effects.explanation: A license is extended through the 90th day after its printed expiration date if the holder submits the specified renewal materials by the stated cutoff.

major_effects.label: Receipt and recognition during extension
major_effects.explanation: The department must provide a receipt; the holder is treated as having an unexpired license for specified legal purposes only while carrying both the receipt and expired license.

agencies.name: Texas Department of Public Safety
agencies.explanation: Section 411.001 defines “Department” as the Department of Public Safety of the State of Texas, and the bill requires the department to provide the license holder a receipt.

HB378.summary: The bill would require the Health and Human Services Commission, working with a nonprofit veterans organization, to operate a grant pilot providing at least 250 veterans diagnosed with PTSD—including treatment-resistant PTSD—with personalized treatment protocols administered at home and subject to specified treatment goals and medication exclusions. The commission would adopt rules and report participation and effectiveness by October 1, 2032; the pilot and chapter would expire September 1, 2033.

policy_tags.explanation: Creates a pilot to provide personalized treatment protocols to veterans with PTSD.
Creates a state-administered grant program, to be operated using available resources; the bill does not specify a dedicated appropriation.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The bill establishes a state-administered pilot and specifies no narrower geographic service area.

affected_groups.group: Veterans diagnosed with PTSD, including treatment-resistant PTSD
affected_groups.explanation: They are the intended recipients of the pilot's personalized treatment protocols.

affected_groups.group: Nonprofit veterans organizations
affected_groups.explanation: The commission must operate the pilot in cooperation with a nonprofit veterans organization.

affected_groups.group: Grant recipients providing treatment protocols
affected_groups.explanation: Grant awards must be made under contracts with recipients providing the protocols.

major_effects.label: Veterans PTSD treatment pilot
major_effects.explanation: Creates a time-limited pilot to provide personalized, at-home treatment protocols to at least 250 veterans with PTSD, including treatment-resistant PTSD, subject to specified treatment goals and exclusions.

major_effects.label: Grant awards
major_effects.explanation: Authorizes grants under recipient contracts and permits the commission to accept gifts, grants, and donations; the program must operate using available resources.

major_effects.label: Implementing rules
major_effects.explanation: Requires the executive commissioner to adopt rules to implement the chapter.

major_effects.label: Pilot results report
major_effects.explanation: Requires a report on the number of veterans served and an evaluation of the pilot's effectiveness.

agencies.name: Health and Human Services Commission
agencies.explanation: The commission is assigned operation of the pilot, grant administration, and reporting; the executive commissioner must adopt implementing rules.

HB379.summary: The bill would require senior retirement communities to maintain emergency plans that provide a properly sized, temperature-controlled refuge during power outages and notify the local fire marshal of an outage lasting more than 12 hours. It would also require annual fire-marshal inspections, allow local governments to enforce violations as fire-code violations, and expressly include senior retirement community facilities in the purpose of the Texas backup-power package subchapter.

policy_tags.explanation: Creates emergency preparedness, power-outage refuge, inspection, and fire-code enforcement requirements for senior retirement communities.
Imposes operational standards and recurring inspections on senior retirement communities.
Assigns inspection functions to local fire marshals and authorizes municipalities, counties, and emergency services districts to enforce violations.
Expressly includes senior retirement community facilities in the purpose of the subchapter addressing Texas backup-power packages.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The requirements apply to senior retirement communities across Texas, without limiting them to a particular locality.

affected_groups.group: Senior retirement communities and their residents
affected_groups.explanation: Communities must implement outage plans, provide refuge space, maintain refuge temperatures, and undergo annual inspections; residents are the beneficiaries of refuge provisions.

affected_groups.group: Local fire marshals, municipalities, counties, and emergency services districts
affected_groups.explanation: Local fire marshals receive outage notices and conduct inspections; specified local governments may impose penalties or other enforcement actions.

major_effects.label: Emergency plans and refuge standards
major_effects.explanation: Plans must provide at least 15 square feet of refuge space per resident during a power outage, maintain refuge temperatures between 68 and 82 degrees Fahrenheit, and provide notice to the local fire marshal after an unplanned service interruption or loss lasting more than 12 hours.

major_effects.label: Annual inspections and corrective actions
major_effects.explanation: Communities must request and submit to an inspection at least annually; fire marshals review emergency power arrangements, document deficiencies, issue correction orders, and conduct necessary follow-up inspections.

major_effects.label: Local enforcement
major_effects.explanation: A municipality, county, or emergency services district may impose a penalty or other enforcement action as if the community violated the applicable fire code.

major_effects.label: Backup-power program purpose
major_effects.explanation: The subchapter's stated purpose would expressly include facilities operated by senior retirement communities; this amendment does not itself guarantee funding to a facility.

HB380.summary: HB 380 separates intent to violate or abuse a person sexually into a distinct aggravated-kidnapping provision, Penal Code Section 20.04(a)(7), while leaving bodily-injury intent in subsection (a)(4). It updates cross-references in community-supervision, sex-offense classification, criminal-history, parole, and sentencing provisions to use the new subsection; the community-supervision restriction applies only when the victim was younger than 14. The changes apply only to offenses committed on or after the Act’s effective date.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill revises an aggravated-kidnapping offense provision and updates related community-supervision, offense-classification, and sentencing cross-references.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The bill amends Texas Penal Code and criminal-procedure provisions that apply statewide.

affected_groups.group: People accused of aggravated kidnapping involving intent to violate or abuse the person sexually
affected_groups.explanation: Their conduct is assigned a distinct aggravated-kidnapping subsection.

affected_groups.group: Defendants convicted under Section 20.04(a)(7) when the victim was younger than 14
affected_groups.explanation: They are ineligible for jury-recommended community supervision under the specified provision.

affected_groups.group: People with qualifying aggravated-kidnapping convictions
affected_groups.explanation: Their convictions are referenced in related sex-offender, reportable-conviction, sexually violent offense, and sentencing provisions.

major_effects.label: Separate aggravated-kidnapping provision
major_effects.explanation: Intent to violate or abuse the person sexually becomes a distinct subsection, separate from the bodily-injury intent provision.

major_effects.label: Community-supervision eligibility
major_effects.explanation: A conviction under Section 20.04(a)(7) bars eligibility under the specified provision only if the victim was younger than 14.

major_effects.label: Related offense classifications and sentencing references
major_effects.explanation: The bill updates references to aggravated kidnapping in sex-offender and reportable-conviction definitions and in the repeat-offender life-imprisonment provision.

major_effects.label: Victim-age criminal-history information
major_effects.explanation: The existing requirement to include victim age in the computerized criminal history system is updated to reference arrests or charges under Section 20.04(a)(7).

agencies.name: Texas Department of Criminal Justice
agencies.explanation: The bill updates the offense cross-reference in a provision requiring life imprisonment in TDCJ for specified current and prior convictions, so the new aggravated-kidnapping subsection is reflected in that sentencing provision.

HB382.summary: HB 382 would add a municipally owned utility acting as a retail public utility in a defense community to the entities eligible for grants under the subchapter. The bill expands who may receive grants; it does not itself award a grant.

policy_tags.explanation: Expands grant eligibility to include a municipally owned utility in a defense community.
Broadens the class of entities eligible to receive grants under the subchapter.

locations.name: Defense communities
locations.explanation: The newly eligible utility must be located in a defense community; the bill does not identify a particular community.

affected_groups.group: Municipally owned utilities acting as retail public utilities in defense communities
affected_groups.explanation: These utilities would become eligible for grants under the subchapter.

major_effects.label: Expanded grant eligibility
major_effects.explanation: Adds qualifying municipally owned utilities in defense communities to the entities eligible for grants.

HB383.summary: Beginning with the 2027–2028 school year, school districts would be prohibited from providing student instruction on Veterans Day, extending the existing Memorial Day prohibition. If making up instructional minutes lost to specified closures would require instruction on either day, the commissioner would have to approve fewer minutes than normally required.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes when school districts may provide student instruction and how instructional minutes may be made up.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The restriction applies to school districts as a class, without a narrower geographic limitation in the bill.

affected_groups.group: Public school districts
affected_groups.explanation: Districts would be barred from providing instruction on Veterans Day and could need to adjust make-up instruction plans.

affected_groups.group: Students in public school districts
affected_groups.explanation: Students would not receive instruction on Veterans Day under the proposed prohibition.

major_effects.label: Veterans Day instruction prohibition
major_effects.explanation: Adds Veterans Day to the days on which a school district may not provide student instruction.

major_effects.label: Make-up instruction approval
major_effects.explanation: When making up minutes lost to specified closures would require instruction on Memorial Day or Veterans Day, the commissioner must approve fewer than the otherwise required minutes.

agencies.name: commissioner
agencies.explanation: The bill extends the condition under which the commissioner must approve fewer instructional minutes; the source does not identify the commissioner's office or canonical agency.

HB384.summary: The bill would require vendors bidding on state agency contracts involving the release of personally identifiable information to verify that they will not monetize that information. Agencies could not contract without the verification and would have to terminate a vendor after a final finding of violation; vendors could also face procurement restrictions and civil penalties. These rules would apply only to contracts whose bid request or other expression of interest is made public on or after the Act’s effective date.

policy_tags.explanation: Creates restrictions on vendors' use and monetization of personally identifiable information obtained through state agency contracts.
Changes state agency contracting requirements and consequences for violations.
Imposes verification, procurement eligibility restrictions, and potential civil liability on vendors.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The requirements apply to the defined class of state agencies, without a narrower geographic limitation.

affected_groups.group: State agencies
affected_groups.explanation: Must require vendor verification and terminate contracts following a final determination of violation.

affected_groups.group: Vendors and their subcontractors
affected_groups.explanation: Bidders and covered subcontractors are subject to the verification requirement and potential contract, procurement, and penalty consequences.

affected_groups.group: Individuals whose personally identifiable information is released to vendors
affected_groups.explanation: Their information is covered by the restrictions on sale, compensated sharing, licensing, or other monetization.

affected_groups.group: Individuals younger than 18
affected_groups.explanation: Violations involving their personally identifiable information carry a higher civil penalty.

major_effects.label: Bid verification requirement
major_effects.explanation: A vendor bidding on a contract for release of personally identifiable information must verify that it will not monetize information obtained under the contract.

major_effects.label: Agency contracting duties
major_effects.explanation: Agencies may not contract without the required verification and must terminate the contract after a final determination that the vendor violated the section.

major_effects.label: Vendor procurement restrictions
major_effects.explanation: A vendor found in violation may not respond to or receive a state agency contract for one year; the comptroller may also impose additional one-year debarment periods through the referenced procedures.

major_effects.label: Civil penalties
major_effects.explanation: A vendor found in violation is liable for $7,500 per violation, or $10,000 when the information concerns an individual younger than 18; the attorney general may sue to recover the penalty.

agencies.name: state agency
agencies.explanation: The bill-defined class of state agencies would have to enforce the bid verification requirement and terminate a contract after a final determination of violation; the term covers multiple branches and institutions, not one registry entity.

agencies.name: Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts
agencies.explanation: The comptroller may determine an additional one-year period of vendor debarment under the referenced procedures.

agencies.name: Office of the Attorney General
agencies.explanation: The attorney general may bring an action to recover a civil penalty and may recover fees and costs.

HB385.summary: HB 385 would shorten juvenile detention orders from a maximum of 10 to five working days; subsequent orders would generally be capped at five days, or seven days in a county without a certified juvenile detention facility, down from 15. It would require the Texas Juvenile Justice Department to study time in detention and intervals between hearings, then report findings and recommendations with specified breakdowns by December 1, 2028, without personally identifying children.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes the permitted duration of detention orders in juvenile court proceedings and requires a study of juvenile detention.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The detention study covers children held in facilities under the cited Texas Family Code provision, with results broken down by county.

affected_groups.group: Children detained in juvenile facilities
affected_groups.explanation: The bill would shorten the maximum detention-order period from 10 to five working days generally, and from 15 to seven working days in counties without a certified juvenile detention facility.

affected_groups.group: Counties without a certified juvenile detention facility
affected_groups.explanation: Subsequent detention orders in these counties would have a seven-working-day maximum instead of 15.

affected_groups.group: Juvenile courts
affected_groups.explanation: Courts entering detention orders would be subject to the shorter maximum durations.

major_effects.label: Shorter juvenile detention-order limits
major_effects.explanation: The maximum duration would decrease from 10 to five working days generally; subsequent orders would be limited to seven days, rather than 15, in counties without a certified juvenile detention facility.

major_effects.label: Juvenile detention study and report
major_effects.explanation: The department must study time detained and time between hearings, report findings and recommendations by December 1, 2028, provide specified breakdowns, and ensure collected information does not personally identify a child.

agencies.name: Texas Juvenile Justice Department
agencies.explanation: The bill defines the department as the Texas Juvenile Justice Department and assigns it the study and reporting duties.

HB386.summary: HB 386 would require covered health benefit plans, including specified basic coverage plans, to cover medically necessary treatment for a pediatric neuroinflammatory disorder when a suitably trained physician diagnoses the condition and the treating physician prescribes and documents the treatment. It would restrict certain denial or delay grounds, limit cost-sharing and repeat preauthorization for the same treatment during the applicable 12-month period, and require annual reporting on denials and appeals. These requirements apply only to plans delivered, issued for delivery, or renewed on or after January 1, 2028.

policy_tags.explanation: Creates a health-plan coverage requirement for treatment of a defined pediatric disorder and related services.
Imposes coverage, approval, cost-sharing, and data-submission requirements on health benefit plan issuers.

locations.name: Texas
locations.explanation: The bill amends the Texas Insurance Code and applies to covered plans governed by its provisions.

affected_groups.group: Children under 18 with a pediatric neuroinflammatory disorder
affected_groups.explanation: Their medically necessary treatment may qualify for coverage under the bill's diagnostic and documentation conditions.

affected_groups.group: Enrollees in covered health benefit plans
affected_groups.explanation: Enrollees may receive coverage for qualifying treatment and related administration and monitoring costs.

affected_groups.group: Health benefit plan issuers
affected_groups.explanation: Issuers must provide qualifying coverage, comply with limits on denials and cost-sharing, and may be required to submit data.

major_effects.label: Coverage for pediatric neuroinflammatory disorder treatment
major_effects.explanation: Covered plans must cover qualifying prescribed treatment, including listed therapies and associated administration and ancillary services, when the specified diagnosis and documentation conditions are met.

major_effects.label: Limits on denials, cost-sharing, and repeat preauthorization
major_effects.explanation: Issuers may not deny or delay approval on the listed sole grounds; cost-sharing cannot exceed that for other services in the same benefit tier, and separate doses or courses of the same treatment do not alone require additional preauthorization during the applicable 12-month period.

major_effects.label: Annual reporting on denials and appeals
major_effects.explanation: The department must collect data on denials and appeals of denials and submit an annual summary to the legislature; it may require issuers to provide data.

agencies.name: the department
agencies.explanation: The bill assigns the department data-collection and annual reporting duties, but the supplied text does not identify the department's formal name.

HB387.summary: The bill would abolish the death penalty: a person convicted of a capital felony would receive life imprisonment if the offense was committed before age 18, and life without parole if it was committed at age 18 or older. It also revises capital-case sentencing, jury procedures, and county indigent-defense appointment requirements. The changes would apply to criminal actions pending, on appeal, or begun on or after the effective date, including actions based on earlier offenses, but would not affect final convictions already in place.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes criminal penalties and the trial, jury, sentencing, and indigent-defense procedures applicable to criminal cases.
Removes county indigent-defense appointment procedures' requirement to follow the special appointment standards for capital cases in which the death penalty is sought.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The criminal-law changes apply to covered criminal actions across Texas.

affected_groups.group: People convicted of capital felonies
affected_groups.explanation: Their sentence would depend on whether they committed the offense before age 18 or at age 18 or older.

affected_groups.group: Defendants and prospective jurors in criminal cases
affected_groups.explanation: The bill revises jury waiver and other procedures for criminal trials, including capital-felony trials.

affected_groups.group: County indigent-defense appointment systems
affected_groups.explanation: County procedures would no longer have the specified requirement to comply with special appointment standards for capital cases in which the death penalty is sought.

major_effects.label: Death penalty abolished
major_effects.explanation: Capital-felony sentences would be life imprisonment for offenses committed before age 18 and life without parole for offenses committed at age 18 or older. The bill also replaces the death option for the offense addressed in Government Code Section 557.012(b) with imprisonment.

major_effects.label: Criminal trial and jury procedures
major_effects.explanation: Revises jury waiver, jury selection, and punishment-assessment procedures, replacing procedures tied to capital cases in which the state sought death.

major_effects.label: County indigent-defense appointment requirements
major_effects.explanation: Removes the specified county-procedure requirements for appointments in capital cases in which the death penalty is sought.

agencies.name: Texas Department of Criminal Justice
agencies.explanation: The bill specifies that capital-felony sentences are imprisonment in TDCJ, with the term determined by the person's age when the offense was committed.

agencies.name: Texas Judicial Branch
agencies.explanation: The bill changes criminal-case jury waiver and punishment procedures administered by Texas trial courts.

HB388.summary: The bill would require day-care centers, group day-care homes, and family homes to report capacity and enrollment information to the Texas Workforce Commission monthly and after changes. The commission would publish age-group-specific information, including available openings, on its child-care availability portal, and the executive commissioner of the Health and Human Services Commission would adopt implementation rules.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The submission requirement applies to each covered day-care center, group day-care home, and family home under Texas law.

affected_groups.group: Day-care centers, group day-care homes, and family homes
affected_groups.explanation: These facilities must report capacity and enrollment data and provide updates when capacity or enrollment changes.

affected_groups.group: Parents seeking child-care openings
affected_groups.explanation: The portal information is intended to help parents locate facilities in their geographic region with available openings.

major_effects.label: Capacity and enrollment reporting
major_effects.explanation: Covered facilities must submit age-disaggregated capacity and enrollment information monthly and notify the commission after changes.

major_effects.label: Publication of child-care availability information
major_effects.explanation: The Texas Workforce Commission must include the submitted information on its child-care availability portal, including available enrollment positions.

major_effects.label: Implementation rules
major_effects.explanation: The executive commissioner of the Health and Human Services Commission must adopt rules necessary to implement the new reporting section.

agencies.name: Texas Workforce Commission
agencies.explanation: The commission must receive capacity and enrollment information, publish it on its child-care availability portal, and receive updates after changes.

agencies.name: Health and Human Services Commission
agencies.explanation: The commission's executive commissioner is directed to adopt rules implementing the new reporting provision.

HB389.summary: HB 389 would require HHSC to provide Medicaid medical assistance to women of reproductive age, expressly including those ages 19–49, who apply and whose household income is no more than 133% of the federal poverty level, but only when federal matching funds are available. HHSC’s executive commissioner would adopt implementing rules and take steps to expand eligibility; the new criteria would apply to initial eligibility determinations and recertifications made on or after implementation, regardless of when the person applied.

policy_tags.explanation: Expands eligibility for medical assistance under Chapter 32, subject to income, application, age, and federal matching-funds conditions.
Changes access to publicly funded medical assistance for qualifying women.

locations.name: Statewide, Texas
locations.explanation: The eligibility provision applies to qualifying women in the state.

affected_groups.group: Women of reproductive age who meet the income and application criteria
affected_groups.explanation: They could qualify for medical assistance if federal matching money is available; the bill expressly includes women ages 19 through 49.

major_effects.label: Expanded Medicaid eligibility
major_effects.explanation: Requires medical assistance for qualifying women of reproductive age who apply and meet the income limit, only when federal matching money is available.

major_effects.label: Implementation rules
major_effects.explanation: Directs the executive commissioner to adopt rules to implement the eligibility expansion.

major_effects.label: Conditional federal authorization process
major_effects.explanation: If a state agency determines a federal waiver or authorization is necessary before implementation, it must request it and may delay implementation until it is granted.

agencies.name: Health and Human Services Commission
agencies.explanation: The commission must provide the assistance and its executive commissioner must adopt rules and take implementation actions.

HB390.summary: Except as provided by Subsection (c), the bill would require a rapid and effective method that renders livestock or poultry insensible to pain before specified handling or cutting when slaughtered for human consumption. Subsection (c) includes an exception for poultry slaughtered solely for personal consumption by the individual performing the slaughter or members of that individual's household.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill sets a slaughter-method requirement for livestock and poultry.
The requirement regulates the method used by persons slaughtering livestock or poultry for human consumption, subject to the poultry exceptions.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The bill adds a requirement to Texas law governing covered slaughter statewide.

affected_groups.group: Persons who slaughter livestock or poultry for human consumption
affected_groups.explanation: They would be required to use a humane method, except where the stated poultry exemptions apply.

affected_groups.group: People slaughtering poultry for noncommercial, personal, or household use
affected_groups.explanation: These poultry slaughter situations are excluded from the requirement.

major_effects.label: Humane slaughter method required
major_effects.explanation: Covered slaughter of livestock or poultry for human consumption must use a rapid and effective method to render the animal insensible to pain before specified handling or cutting; the stated poultry exceptions remain.

HB391.summary: The bill requires the Texas Department of Criminal Justice to adopt a policy requiring correctional officers at department-operated or contracted facilities to wear body cameras during their shifts and keep them activated while performing their duties. The department must adopt the policy by January 1, 2028.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill changes camera requirements for correctional officers performing their duties at correctional facilities.
The bill requires body-camera equipment and activation during correctional officers' work; it does not establish separate recording, retention, or access rules.

affected_groups.group: Correctional officers at facilities operated by or under contract with the Texas Department of Criminal Justice
affected_groups.explanation: They must be equipped with a body camera during their shifts and keep it activated while performing their duties.

affected_groups.group: People at covered correctional facilities who may be recorded
affected_groups.explanation: They may be captured by cameras that officers must keep activated while performing their duties.

major_effects.label: Required body-camera policy
major_effects.explanation: Requires the department to adopt a policy mandating that covered correctional officers wear cameras during shifts and keep them activated while performing their duties.

agencies.name: Texas Department of Criminal Justice
agencies.explanation: The department must adopt the required body-camera policy.

HB392.summary: The bill would let a local entity or campus police department prohibit employees and others under its control from assisting or cooperating with a federal immigration officer in matters regarding activities at a place of worship or domestic violence shelter. It revises the existing exception to include domestic violence shelters.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes when local entities and campus police departments may prohibit cooperation with federal immigration officers.
Authorizes local entities and campus police departments to prohibit specified cooperation.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The authorization applies generally to local entities and campus police departments under Texas law, without limiting it to a named jurisdiction.

affected_groups.group: Local entities and campus police departments
affected_groups.explanation: These bodies may prohibit the specified assistance or cooperation.

affected_groups.group: Employees and others under the direction or control of local entities or campus police departments
affected_groups.explanation: They may be subject to a prohibition on cooperation concerning activities at the specified locations.

affected_groups.group: Federal immigration officers
affected_groups.explanation: Their requests for cooperation concerning activities at the specified locations could be affected if a covered entity or department adopts a prohibition.

major_effects.label: Permitted noncooperation concerning shelter activities
major_effects.explanation: A local entity or campus police department may prohibit covered persons from assisting or cooperating with federal immigration officers in matters regarding activities at a domestic violence shelter; the bill permits, but does not require, such a prohibition.

HB394.summary: Beginning with the 2028–2029 school year, the bill would move the default first day of instruction to the first Monday in September, while preserving an exception for year-round districts and a limited early-start option for qualifying campuses in districts with at least 190,000 students. It would also bar local innovation plans adopted or renewed on or after the Act’s effective date from exempting a district from the first-day requirement.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes public school instructional-calendar requirements and the limits on local innovation plans.
Restricts school districts’ scheduling discretion and their ability to use local innovation plans to obtain an exemption.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The requirements apply generally to school districts, subject to the stated exceptions.

affected_groups.group: Texas school districts and their boards of trustees
affected_groups.explanation: Districts must follow the revised start-date rule, and their local innovation plans cannot exempt them from it when the plan is adopted or renewed on or after the effective date.

affected_groups.group: Public school students, including students at qualifying campuses
affected_groups.explanation: The calendar rule sets when instruction may begin; the limited early-start option requires a majority of students at each relevant campus to be educationally disadvantaged.

major_effects.label: Changes the default school-year start date
major_effects.explanation: Moves the general earliest start date from the fourth Monday in August to the first Monday in September. Year-round systems may start earlier; districts with enrollment of at least 190,000 may start on or after the third Monday in August at a campus or no more than 20 percent of campuses if the other statutory conditions are met, including locally funded additional instructional time.

major_effects.label: Limits local innovation plan exemptions
major_effects.explanation: Adds the first-day-of-instruction requirements to the provisions from which a district may not be exempted through a local innovation plan. This plan-related change applies only to plans adopted or renewed on or after the Act’s effective date.

HB395.summary: Subject to Section 53.0231, the bill would limit when licensing authorities may deny, suspend, revoke, or disqualify a person from an occupational license or examination because of a conviction, including for renewal: generally, the person must apply within five years of the later of conviction or release from confinement, or have a later qualifying offense, while specified offenses allow action at any time. Authorities would have to support conviction-related decisions under a preponderance-of-the-evidence standard and bear that burden in appeals; these decision rules apply to covered actions and proceedings beginning January 1, 2028. The bill would also require applicant notices and annual reports to the Legislature and the public on applications, denials, and criminal-history evaluation letter requests.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill changes conviction-based eligibility for occupational licenses and licensing examinations, including renewals.
The bill changes licensing authorities' standards and procedures for occupational licensing decisions and reporting.

locations.name: Texas
locations.explanation: The provisions apply across the state to licensing authorities covered by Chapter 53.

affected_groups.group: People with criminal convictions who seek, hold, or renew occupational licenses or seek licensing examinations
affected_groups.explanation: Their eligibility may be assessed under the bill's revised conviction-related criteria and evidentiary standards.

affected_groups.group: Applicants denied because of a conviction or placement on deferred adjudication community supervision
affected_groups.explanation: Their denial counts would be included in licensing authorities' records and annual reports.

affected_groups.group: Licensing authorities subject to Chapter 53
affected_groups.explanation: They would have notice and reporting duties. For actions under Section 53.021, a licensing authority may determine that a conviction relates to the occupation’s duties and responsibilities only if it finds by a preponderance of the evidence, after considering the listed factors, that those factors support the determination.

major_effects.label: Conviction-based licensing eligibility
major_effects.explanation: Adds timing and offense-based conditions for conviction-related licensing actions, including disqualification from renewal. Specified offenses allow action at any time; the five-year rule and later-offense condition apply to other covered grounds.

major_effects.label: Decision and appeal evidentiary standards
major_effects.explanation: A licensing authority may not take an action authorized by Section 53.021 unless it finds by a preponderance of the evidence that consideration of the listed factors supports taking that action. In an administrative appeal or judicial review, the licensing authority bears the burden of proving the required grounds and support for its decision.

major_effects.label: Applicant notices
major_effects.explanation: Covered authorities must put information about conviction-based disqualification, relevant decision factors, and the evaluation-letter process on license applications and their websites.

major_effects.label: Annual licensing reports
major_effects.explanation: Covered authorities must maintain counts of applications and outcomes, including conviction- or deferred-adjudication-related denials and evaluation-letter requests, and submit and publish an annual report.

agencies.name: Licensing authorities subject to Chapter 53, Occupations Code
agencies.explanation: The bill directly assigns notice, recordkeeping, and reporting duties to covered licensing authorities and changes their licensing decision standards. The text does not identify which individual authorities are included.

HB396.summary: The bill would generally increase the written notice before a landlord files a forcible-detainer suit from three to 14 days for tenants under written or oral rental agreements and tenants at will or by sufferance; the parties could agree to a longer, but not shorter, notice period. A landlord terminating a lease under Property Code Section 91.003 could still file beginning on the third day after giving notice, and the changes would apply only to suits where notice to vacate is given on or after the Act's effective date.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes notice requirements for landlords seeking possession of rental property through an eviction suit.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The bill amends the Texas Property Code and establishes a generally applicable state rule.

affected_groups.group: Tenants facing eviction
affected_groups.explanation: Tenants under written or oral rental agreements and tenants at will or by sufferance receive the longer general notice period, subject to the stated exception.

affected_groups.group: Landlords seeking eviction
affected_groups.explanation: Landlords generally must give at least 14 days’ written notice before filing, unless the parties contracted for a longer notice period in a written lease or agreement. For a termination under Section 91.003, the landlord may file on or after the third day after giving notice.

major_effects.label: Longer general eviction notice
major_effects.explanation: Raises the general written notice period from three to 14 days for the specified tenants before a forcible-detainer suit may be filed; the parties may agree to a longer period, but not a shorter one.

major_effects.label: Section 91.003 filing exception
major_effects.explanation: When a landlord terminates a lease as provided by Section 91.003, the landlord may file a forcible-detainer suit on or after the third day after giving notice rather than waiting under the general 14-day rule.

HB397.summary: HB 397 would require merchants selling stored value cards to prominently display a conspicuous sign warning consumers about stored value card fraud and advising potential victims what steps to take. The attorney general would adopt and publish a model sign, but merchants could use another sign that meets the requirements.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill creates a consumer-warning display requirement for merchants selling stored value cards.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The merchant sign requirement is established in the Texas Business & Commerce Code and is not limited to a particular place.

affected_groups.group: Merchants who sell stored value cards
affected_groups.explanation: They would have to display a conspicuous fraud-warning sign at their businesses.

affected_groups.group: Consumers who may be targets of stored value card fraud
