affected_groups.explanation: They would see a warning and advice about steps to take if they believe they may be victims of fraud.

major_effects.label: Merchant warning-sign requirement
major_effects.explanation: Covered merchants would have to prominently display a visible sign warning about stored value card fraud and advising potential victims.

major_effects.label: Optional model sign
major_effects.explanation: The attorney general would adopt and publish a model sign; merchants could use a different sign that satisfies the requirements.

agencies.name: Office of the Attorney General
agencies.explanation: The bill directs the attorney general to adopt and publish a model sign for merchants to use optionally.

HB398.summary: For a child placed with a relative or other designated caregiver by the department, the bill makes the caregiver eligible to receive the child’s support rights and benefits, including monthly benefits and SSI, and requires the department to pass them through. It also makes an exception to the general assignment of a child’s support rights to the state for this pass-through.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes the department’s administration of support rights and benefits for children in its placements by requiring pass-through to caregivers.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The change applies to covered placements under the Texas Family Code; no narrower geographic area is specified.

affected_groups.group: Relatives and other designated caregivers of children placed by the department
affected_groups.explanation: They become eligible to receive the child’s support rights and benefits.

affected_groups.group: Children placed with relatives or other designated caregivers by the department
affected_groups.explanation: Their support rights and benefits are to be passed through to the caregiver on their behalf.

major_effects.label: Caregiver eligibility for child benefits
major_effects.explanation: Makes a relative or other designated caregiver eligible to receive support and benefits, including monthly benefits, for a child placed with that person by the department.

major_effects.label: Pass-through of support rights and benefit payments
major_effects.explanation: Requires the department to pass through the child’s support rights and payments for the child, including SSI; the general assignment of support rights to the state is subject to this exception.

agencies.name: the department
agencies.explanation: The bill directly requires the department to pass through support rights and benefits. The supplied text uses a generic term, so its canonical agency identity is not verified.

HB399.summary: HB 399 would make a public school liable for an on-campus homicide causing the death of an enrolled student if the school was grossly negligent or reckless, or engaged in intentional misconduct, in providing campus security. The new liability rule would apply only to acts or omissions occurring on or after the Act’s effective date.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill changes the civil liability rules applicable to public schools when a student is killed on campus.
The liability rule may apply to locally operated public-school entities, including school districts, to the extent they are included in “public school.”
The new liability rule concerns school-campus security and a homicide causing a student's death.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The bill amends the Texas Civil Practice and Remedies Code and applies to public schools within its scope.

affected_groups.group: Public schools and their operators
affected_groups.explanation: They may face civil liability for a qualifying student homicide on campus; the text does not expressly identify which kinds of public schools are covered.

affected_groups.group: Students enrolled in public schools
affected_groups.explanation: The liability rule concerns a homicide causing the death of an enrolled student on the school's campus.

major_effects.label: Civil liability for campus homicide
major_effects.explanation: A public school is liable when gross negligence, recklessness, or intentional misconduct in providing campus security is connected to an on-campus homicide causing the death of an enrolled student. The rule applies only to acts or omissions on or after the Act's effective date.

HB401.summary: The bill would require a school district or open-enrollment charter school to provide a halal option in any breakfast or lunch program when a student or the student’s parent or other person in parental relation requests one. The requirement would apply beginning with the 2027–2028 school year.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill changes meal options that public school districts and open-enrollment charter schools must provide in their breakfast and lunch programs.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The requirement applies to school districts and open-enrollment charter schools across the state.

affected_groups.group: Students and parents or other persons in parental relation requesting a halal meal option
affected_groups.explanation: A request by one of these people triggers the school's duty to provide the option.

affected_groups.group: School districts and open-enrollment charter schools
affected_groups.explanation: These schools must provide the requested option in their breakfast and lunch programs.

major_effects.label: Requested halal meal option
major_effects.explanation: Requires a halal option in any district or charter school breakfast or lunch program when requested by a student or a person in parental relation.

HB402.summary: HB 402 would expand acceptable photo identification for voting in Texas to include qualifying tribal identification documents, photo IDs issued by in-state public or private institutions of higher education, and photo IDs issued by Texas state agencies. It also changes the wording for existing forms of identification to specify that they are issued to the voter.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill changes which photo identification documents are acceptable for voting.

locations.name: Texas statewide
locations.explanation: The bill amends the state’s voting identification requirements.

affected_groups.group: Texas voters
affected_groups.explanation: Voters may use additional qualifying forms of photo identification.

affected_groups.group: Tribal organizations and federally recognized tribes located in Texas
affected_groups.explanation: Their qualifying identification cards or documents would be acceptable for voting if they meet the bill’s listed requirements.

affected_groups.group: Public and private institutions of higher education located in Texas
affected_groups.explanation: Their photo IDs would be acceptable for voting.

affected_groups.group: Texas state agencies
affected_groups.explanation: Photo IDs they issue would be acceptable for voting; the bill does not assign them a new issuance duty.

major_effects.label: Expands acceptable voter photo identification
major_effects.explanation: Adds qualifying tribal documents with the voter’s photograph and address, photo IDs from in-state higher education institutions, and photo IDs from Texas state agencies.

HB403.summary: HB 403 would make the Government Code §552.108(a)(2) and (b)(2) exceptions inapplicable to covered records when a person described or depicted other than a peace officer is deceased or incapacitated, or everyone described or depicted consents. For certain alleged-misconduct documents in police officers’ personnel files, it removes the exception from disclosure requirements when a person described or depicted other than the officer is deceased or incapacitated. A governmental body’s release to a deceased or incapacitated person’s family member does not waive future claims that the information is excepted from disclosure.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes the application of public-information disclosure exceptions and the effect of certain disclosures by governmental bodies.
Changes the restriction on local fire or police department personnel-file disclosures, with a new allowance for certain police misconduct information.
The bill changes access to records concerning alleged police officer misconduct.
The bill changes when sensitive law-enforcement records may be disclosed based on the status or consent of people described or depicted in them.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The bill amends Texas Government Code and Local Government Code provisions applicable to covered governmental bodies and local departments across the state; it names no particular place.

affected_groups.group: People described or depicted in covered records
affected_groups.explanation: Their death or incapacity, or consent by everyone described or depicted, can affect whether specified disclosure exceptions apply.

affected_groups.group: Family members of deceased or incapacitated people
affected_groups.explanation: A governmental body's release of covered information to them does not waive future claims that the information is excepted from disclosure.

affected_groups.group: Police officers and local police departments
affected_groups.explanation: The bill concerns alleged-misconduct documents in police officers’ personnel files and qualifies the department's restriction on releasing those records.

affected_groups.group: People requesting covered records
affected_groups.explanation: The changes affect when covered records may be released in response to information requests.

major_effects.label: Conditional access to covered records
major_effects.explanation: The specified §552.108 exceptions would not apply to covered records when a person described or depicted other than a peace officer is deceased or incapacitated, or when everyone described or depicted consents. For alleged-misconduct documents in a police officer’s personnel file, the provision applies when a person described or depicted other than the officer is deceased or incapacitated.

major_effects.label: Police department personnel-file release rule
major_effects.explanation: The restriction on department-file releases is qualified to permit release of information about alleged police misconduct when §552.108 permits it.

major_effects.label: No waiver from certain family disclosures
major_effects.explanation: Releasing covered information to a deceased or incapacitated person's family member does not waive the governmental body's ability to assert a disclosure exception later.

HB404.summary: HB 404 would establish annual cost-of-living adjustments for service-retirement, disability-retirement, and death benefits under the Teacher Retirement System of Texas, using any annual increase in CPI-W as the adjustment rate. Trustees could pay an increase only if they find the system actuarially sound and able to pay; if available money cannot cover the full adjustment while maintaining actuarial soundness, they must use the largest supportable rate. The changes apply only to benefits paid by the system on or after January 1, 2028.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill could increase benefit payments from the state retirement system, subject to actuarial soundness and available funds.

affected_groups.group: Recipients of Teacher Retirement System service-retirement, disability-retirement, and death benefits
affected_groups.explanation: Their benefits may be increased through the annual adjustment, subject to the system's actuarial soundness and available funds.

major_effects.label: Inflation-linked benefit adjustments
major_effects.explanation: Trustees would set an annual adjustment based on CPI-W and increase benefits accordingly, but may pay an increase only when the system is actuarially sound and has money available; if funds are insufficient for the full adjustment, they must use the largest rate supportable while maintaining actuarial soundness.

agencies.name: Teacher Retirement System of Texas
agencies.explanation: The bill changes benefits paid by the named system and assigns the board of trustees annual rate-setting and benefit-adjustment duties.

HB405.summary: HB 405 would require a person using an AI-based dynamic pricing model to set the price of a good to disclose that use to each consumer. The disclosure would need to describe the model and its use of AI, and be provided at the point of sale or acknowledged before an online purchase; a violation would be an actionable deceptive trade practice.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill creates a consumer disclosure obligation for qualifying dynamic pricing practices and makes violations actionable as deceptive trade practices.
The disclosure duty specifically applies when the pricing model uses an artificial intelligence system.

locations.name: Texas
locations.explanation: The chapter applies to retailers conducting business in Texas.

affected_groups.group: Retailers and other persons using AI-based dynamic pricing to set prices of goods
affected_groups.explanation: They would have to disclose use of the model to each consumer.

affected_groups.group: Consumers purchasing goods
affected_groups.explanation: They would receive the disclosure at a physical point of sale or acknowledge it before completing an online purchase.

major_effects.label: Disclosure of AI-based dynamic pricing
major_effects.explanation: A person using an AI-based dynamic pricing model for a good would need to provide each consumer a clear, conspicuous description of the model and how it uses AI, with the method of delivery depending on whether the sale is in person or online.

major_effects.label: Deceptive-trade-practice actionability
major_effects.explanation: A violation of the new chapter would be classified as a deceptive trade practice and actionable under the referenced subchapter.

HB406.summary: HB 406 would add optional veteran identification to voter-registration and driver/ID applications, provide a veteran indication on qualifying voter certificates, and create paths for the Texas Veterans Commission to connect veterans with services. Voter registrars would compile veteran applicants’ addresses and, if provided, telephone numbers for transmission to the Commission; driver/ID applicants who identify as veterans would receive a services information sheet and could be contacted by the Commission. The voter-form change applies to forms distributed on or after September 1, 2027; the driver/ID changes apply to applications issued or renewed on or after the Act’s effective date.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes voter-registration applications, voter certificates, registrar duties, and information available through voter-registration records.
Adds confidentiality protections for veteran status in voter-registration information and for information shared through the driver/ID process.
Requires voter registrars, including county election officials, to compile veteran-applicant information.
Changes the driver’s-license and personal-identification-certificate application process to include an optional veteran-status indication and related services information.

locations.name: Texas (statewide)
locations.explanation: The changes apply to voter-registration and driver/ID application processes under state law, rather than to a specified locality.

affected_groups.group: Voter-registration applicants and voters who report qualifying military service
affected_groups.explanation: May optionally identify qualifying service on an application; those who do may receive a veteran indication on their voter registration certificate.

affected_groups.group: Voter registrars and county election officials
affected_groups.explanation: Must compile a list of registration applications indicating qualifying military service, including residence addresses and any provided telephone numbers.

affected_groups.group: Veterans applying for driver’s licenses or personal identification certificates
affected_groups.explanation: May voluntarily identify as veterans during specified license or ID applications and receive information about state veterans services.

major_effects.label: Veteran identification on voter forms and certificates
major_effects.explanation: Adds an optional service-status response to voter-registration forms and a “veteran” indication to certificates when the voter reports qualifying service. The form change applies only to applications distributed on or after September 1, 2027.

major_effects.label: Veteran-applicant information transfer
major_effects.explanation: Requires registrars to compile veteran-applicant information for transmission to the Texas Veterans Commission under procedures adopted by the Secretary of State.

major_effects.label: Confidentiality of veteran status
major_effects.explanation: Makes veteran status in voter-registration information confidential and bars its website posting; information received through the driver/ID process is also confidential and not subject to public disclosure under Chapter 552.

major_effects.label: Veterans-services outreach through driver/ID applications
major_effects.explanation: For applicants who voluntarily identify as veterans, creates a process for providing a state-services information sheet and sharing specified information confidentially with the Texas Veterans Commission, which may contact them. Applies to license/ID applications issued or renewed on or after the Act’s effective date.

agencies.name: Texas Secretary of State
agencies.explanation: Must adopt procedures for transmitting veteran-applicant information collected by registrars to the Texas Veterans Commission.

agencies.name: Texas Veterans Commission
agencies.explanation: Would receive veteran-status information and may contact individuals to connect them with veterans services.

agencies.name: Texas Department of Public Safety
agencies.explanation: Transportation Code Section 521.001 defines “Department” as the Department of Public Safety, and Section 521.011 assigns the department duties concerning veteran status information and sharing it with the Texas Veterans Commission.

HB407.summary: HB 407 would remove Confederate Heroes Day from the Texas state-holiday list and add the first Tuesday after the first Monday in November of even-numbered years as a state holiday. The change is scheduled to take effect September 1, 2027.

policy_tags.explanation: Adds the general-election-day formula for even-numbered years to the state-holiday list.
Changes the statutory schedule of Texas state holidays.

locations.name: Texas
locations.explanation: The bill changes the list of state holidays.

affected_groups.group: Texas state employees
affected_groups.explanation: The changed state-holiday schedule may affect state employees whose holidays are governed by this list.

major_effects.label: Changes the state-holiday schedule
major_effects.explanation: Removes Confederate Heroes Day and adds the November general-election-day date in even-numbered years.

HB408.summary: The bill would repeal sales-and-use-tax exemptions for gas and electricity used by qualifying data centers and large data center projects, along with related provisions. Applications pending on the effective date would be denied, but projects certified before then could keep their existing exemption until its term expires, subject to the limits in prior law.

policy_tags.explanation: Repeals data-center-specific sales-and-use-tax exemptions.
Changes the exemption and certification framework specifically for qualifying data centers and large data center projects.
Changes the application of sales-tax exemptions to taxes imposed by municipalities and revises related provisions for taxes authorized under Chapters 321 and 323.
Repeals a targeted tax benefit available to qualifying data center projects.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The bill amends statewide Texas sales-and-use-tax provisions and addresses taxes imposed under municipal and other local tax chapters.

affected_groups.group: Operators and developers of qualifying data centers and large data center projects
affected_groups.explanation: They would lose the data-center-specific exemption for new or not-yet-certified projects; applications still pending on the effective date would be denied.

affected_groups.group: Operators of data centers and large data center projects certified before the effective date
affected_groups.explanation: They may continue receiving the applicable exemption through its existing term, subject to the limitations in the former law.

affected_groups.group: Municipal taxing jurisdictions
affected_groups.explanation: The bill changes whether the data-center-related energy use falls within exemptions applicable to municipal taxes.

major_effects.label: Repeals data-center energy-use tax exemptions
major_effects.explanation: Removes the specific exemption for gas and electricity used directly by qualifying data centers and large data center projects, and repeals the related certification provisions.

major_effects.label: Ends pending certifications but preserves existing exemptions temporarily
major_effects.explanation: Applications pending on the effective date are denied; projects certified before that date may continue receiving the applicable exemption until its existing term expires, subject to prior-law limitations.

agencies.name: Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts
agencies.explanation: The bill ends the certification pathway for new projects and expressly bars approval of applications pending on the effective date; previously certified projects retain their exemptions for the specified remaining term.

HB409.summary: The bill would let a school district employee use available state-minimum personal leave for compensation on a school holiday when the employee otherwise would not be paid, capped at two such days per year. This applies only to employees who are not exempt from federal overtime provisions and whose pay is not annualized, beginning with the 2027–2028 school year.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes a personal-leave rule for school district employees in the Education Code.
Creates a limited paid-leave entitlement for qualifying school district employees.
The new paid-leave rule applies to school district employees and affects school districts as employers.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The bill applies generally to qualifying school district employees across Texas.

affected_groups.group: School district employees who are not exempt from federal overtime provisions and whose pay is not annualized
affected_groups.explanation: These employees may use up to two available personal-leave days for compensation on otherwise unpaid school holidays.

affected_groups.group: School districts
affected_groups.explanation: School districts are affected as employers administering the new employee leave entitlement.

major_effects.label: Paid leave use on school holidays
major_effects.explanation: Qualifying employees may use available personal leave for compensation on otherwise unpaid school holidays, limited to two days per year.

HB410.summary: The bill would require each law enforcement agency to adopt and post a policy limiting facial coverings during officers’ duties, subject to specified exceptions, with a process for challenging a policy and seeking a court order. Beginning January 1, 2028, knowing covered use would be a Class C misdemeanor, and specified civil claims arising from use in violation of the law would bar official immunity and provide prevailing claimants the greater of actual damages or $10,000.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill limits when law enforcement officers may wear identity-obscuring coverings while performing their duties.
The bill creates a criminal offense for specified knowing use of facial coverings by law enforcement officers and related persons.
For specified claims arising from facial-covering use in violation of the law, the bill bars official immunity and provides a minimum damages remedy.
Political subdivisions may submit written challenges to agency policy compliance, and law enforcement agencies must adopt the required policies.

locations.name: Texas
locations.explanation: The policy-adoption requirement applies to each law enforcement agency in the state.

affected_groups.group: Law enforcement agencies
affected_groups.explanation: Agencies must adopt and post policies limiting facial coverings during officers’ duties.

affected_groups.group: Peace officers and persons acting for out-of-state or federal law enforcement
affected_groups.explanation: They are subject to the offense provision, with specified exceptions and a defense for conduct complying with the employing agency’s policy.

affected_groups.group: Claimants bringing specified civil actions against peace officers
affected_groups.explanation: Claimants in covered actions arising from facial-covering use in violation of the law receive the stated immunity and damages provisions.

affected_groups.group: Members of the public and political subdivisions
affected_groups.explanation: Either may submit a written challenge to an agency policy’s compliance with the bill.

major_effects.label: Agency facial-covering policies
major_effects.explanation: Agencies must adopt and post policies restricting use to specified circumstances. A policy is presumed compliant unless a written challenge is found accurate; it remains in effect unless a court orders amendment by writ of mandamus.

major_effects.label: Criminal offense for knowing covered use
major_effects.explanation: Knowing use during official duties is a Class C misdemeanor, subject to listed exceptions; there is also a defense when the use complied with the agency policy.

major_effects.label: Civil liability in specified actions
major_effects.explanation: For the listed actions arising from an officer’s conduct while wearing a facial covering in violation of the law, official immunity is unavailable and a prevailing claimant may recover the greater of actual damages or $10,000.

agencies.name: law enforcement agency
agencies.explanation: The bill directly requires each law enforcement agency to adopt and post a facial-covering policy. It does not identify particular state agency bodies by name.

HB411.summary: The bill applies to law enforcement agencies operating in counties with populations over 500,000 and requires them to adopt a written policy for injuries or deaths caused by a peace officer, whether on or off duty. The policy must require the officer to submit a bodily specimen within six hours to assess blood alcohol content and the presence of controlled substances.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill requires a post-incident drug and alcohol testing policy for certain law enforcement agencies and peace officers.

locations.name: Counties with populations of more than 500,000
locations.explanation: The bill limits coverage to agencies operating in counties above this population threshold; it names no particular county.

affected_groups.group: Law enforcement agencies operating in counties with populations over 500,000
affected_groups.explanation: These agencies must adopt the written testing policy.

affected_groups.group: Peace officers who cause a serious bodily injury or death
affected_groups.explanation: The required policy must require these officers to submit a specimen, whether the incident occurs on or off duty.

major_effects.label: Post-incident testing policy
major_effects.explanation: Covered agencies must adopt a written policy requiring a peace officer who causes a covered injury or death to provide a bodily specimen within six hours for assessment of alcohol and controlled substances.

agencies.name: law enforcement agency
agencies.explanation: The bill directly requires each agency within the specified scope to adopt the policy. The bill incorporates the term's meaning from Article 2B.0053, but that definition is not supplied, so specific agency identities cannot be resolved.

HB412.summary: HB 412 would limit certificate-of-obligation issuers to municipalities and counties, excluding hospital districts, and narrow the public works eligible for financing to an enumerated set that includes certain public-safety facilities. It would remove historic-structure restoration as an authorized purpose, reduce the maximum maturity from 40 to 30 years, lower protest-petition thresholds to 2 percent of registered voters, and apply the changes only to certificates issued on or after the Act's effective date.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes which local governments may issue certificates of obligation, which projects qualify, and the related maturity and protest-petition rules.
Revises which public-safety facilities may qualify as public works for certificate financing, including first-responder training facilities.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The provisions concern municipalities and counties generally, rather than a named locality or limited geographic area.

affected_groups.group: Municipalities and counties
affected_groups.explanation: Municipalities and counties remain defined as issuers. The bill reduces the maximum certificate maturity from 40 to 30 years and changes the protest petition threshold from five percent of qualified voters to two percent of registered voters; a qualifying protest requires election approval before issuance.

affected_groups.group: Hospital districts
affected_groups.explanation: Hospital districts would no longer be included in the definition of issuer for these certificate provisions.

affected_groups.group: Registered voters of municipalities and counties
affected_groups.explanation: A smaller share of registered voters could petition against issuance and trigger an election process.

major_effects.label: Issuer and eligible public works
major_effects.explanation: Removes hospital districts from the issuer definition and revises eligible project categories, including removing the utility and water-project, flood-control, and judicial-facility categories and specifying eligible police, fire, first-responder training, jail, or juvenile detention facilities.

major_effects.label: Demolition purpose
major_effects.explanation: Retains certificates for demolishing dangerous structures but removes restoration of historic structures as an authorized purpose.

major_effects.label: Shorter maximum maturity
major_effects.explanation: Reduces the maximum certificate maturity from 40 years to 30 years.

major_effects.label: Lower protest-petition thresholds
major_effects.explanation: Sets the protest threshold at two percent of registered voters for issuance protests and refinancing-certificate protests.

major_effects.label: Prospective application
major_effects.explanation: The changes apply only to certificates issued on or after the Act's effective date; earlier certificates remain governed by prior law.

HB413.summary: HB 413 would let governing boards of public institutions of higher education offer senior citizens up to 12 credit hours per semester or summer term without tuition, increasing the current limit from six hours. The benefit would remain optional and available only when space is available.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill expands the potential tuition-free course benefit for senior citizens at public institutions of higher education.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The change applies to institutions of higher education covered by Texas law, rather than to a named locality.

affected_groups.group: Senior citizens seeking credit courses at public institutions of higher education
affected_groups.explanation: They could receive a tuition-free enrollment benefit for up to 12 hours, subject to the institution's choice and available space.

affected_groups.group: Governing boards of institutions of higher education
affected_groups.explanation: Boards retain discretion whether to offer the benefit, with a higher maximum credit-hour limit.

major_effects.label: Higher limit for optional tuition-free enrollment
major_effects.explanation: A governing board may allow a senior citizen to take up to 12 credit hours without tuition each semester or summer term, rather than six; the benefit remains discretionary and depends on available space.

HB414.summary: The bill would require the Texas Department of Criminal Justice to install and maintain high-quality security cameras in common areas of its facilities, positioned to eliminate blind spots. It excludes areas where inmates have a reasonable expectation of privacy, and the department would not have to comply until September 1, 2029.

policy_tags.explanation: Creates a security-camera requirement for common areas of facilities operated by the state corrections department.

locations.name: Common areas of facilities operated by the Texas Department of Criminal Justice
locations.explanation: The camera requirement applies to these areas, subject to the privacy exception.

affected_groups.group: Inmates in department-operated facilities
affected_groups.explanation: Their common areas would be camera-monitored, while areas where they have a reasonable expectation of privacy are excluded.

affected_groups.group: Operators of Texas Department of Criminal Justice facilities
affected_groups.explanation: They would be responsible for installing and maintaining cameras that meet the bill's requirements.

major_effects.label: Security cameras in facility common areas
major_effects.explanation: Requires cameras in each covered common area, with high-quality video and positioning that eliminates blind spots; areas where inmates have a reasonable expectation of privacy are excluded. Compliance is not required until September 1, 2029.

agencies.name: Texas Department of Criminal Justice
agencies.explanation: The bill directly requires the department to install and maintain cameras in common areas of its facilities.

HB415.summary: The bill would bar an institution of higher education from disciplining a student for academic dishonesty unless it determines beyond a reasonable doubt that the student committed the alleged misconduct. The requirement would apply beginning with the 2027–2028 academic year.

policy_tags.explanation: Sets an evidentiary standard for academic-dishonesty discipline at institutions of higher education.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The requirement applies to qualifying institutions of higher education across Texas.

affected_groups.group: Students accused of academic dishonesty
affected_groups.explanation: Their institutions could discipline them for the alleged misconduct only after making the specified finding.

affected_groups.group: Institutions of higher education
affected_groups.explanation: Institutions of higher education may not take disciplinary action for academic dishonesty unless they determine beyond a reasonable doubt that the student engaged in the alleged misconduct.

major_effects.label: Higher evidentiary standard for academic-dishonesty discipline
major_effects.explanation: An institution could not impose discipline for academic dishonesty unless it determines beyond a reasonable doubt that the student engaged in the alleged misconduct.

agencies.name: Institution of higher education
agencies.explanation: The bill directly restricts when an institution of higher education may discipline a student. It does not identify a particular system or campus, and the registry provides no matching institution-wide entry.

HB416.summary: HB 416 would prohibit state agencies from using artificial intelligence systems to conduct employee performance reviews or make employment-related decisions, including hiring, promotion, demotion, and termination. It would also bar state agency employees from entering information that is confidential and not subject to disclosure under Chapter 552 or other law into an AI system.

policy_tags.explanation: Restricts state agency use of AI systems and bars employees from entering certain confidential information into them.
Changes how state agencies may conduct employee reviews and make employment decisions.
Imposes restrictions on state agency operations and employee use of AI systems.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The bill applies generally to state agencies and their employees across the state.

affected_groups.group: State agencies
affected_groups.explanation: Their use of AI systems for employee reviews and employment decisions would be restricted.

affected_groups.group: State agency employees
affected_groups.explanation: State agency employees may not enter information into an AI system if it is confidential and not subject to disclosure under Chapter 552 or other law.

major_effects.label: Limits AI use in employment decisions
major_effects.explanation: State agencies could not use AI systems for employee performance reviews or employment-related decisions.

major_effects.label: Restricts input of confidential information
major_effects.explanation: State agency employees could not enter information that is confidential and not subject to disclosure under Chapter 552 or other law into an AI system.

agencies.name: state agency
agencies.explanation: The bill directly restricts state agencies, but does not identify particular agencies or establish a verified canonical identity for the general term.

HB417.summary: HB 417 would establish the Rita Littlefield Chronic Kidney Disease Centralized Resource Center within HHSC, including a registry through which patients and family members can register for clinical-trial information based on a patient’s disease stage. HHSC would provide centralized kidney-disease information and resources online in English and Spanish.

policy_tags.explanation: Creates a kidney-disease information and resource program, including a clinical-trials registry and treatment-related resources.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The bill establishes a centralized HHSC resource for general access and does not limit it to a particular geographic area.

affected_groups.group: People with chronic kidney disease or related illnesses
affected_groups.explanation: They would be able to access disease information, prevention and treatment resources, and stage-based clinical-trial information.

affected_groups.group: Patients' family members
affected_groups.explanation: Family members may register to receive educational information about clinical trials and opportunities.

affected_groups.group: Health care providers treating kidney disease
affected_groups.explanation: The center would aggregate professional resources and continuing education opportunities for these providers.

major_effects.label: Centralized kidney-disease resource center and registry
major_effects.explanation: Establishes a resource center for kidney-disease information and resources, including a registry for stage-based clinical-trial information.

major_effects.label: Bilingual online resources
major_effects.explanation: Requires the information and resources to be available in English and Spanish and published on the commission's website.

major_effects.label: Optional outside contributions
major_effects.explanation: Authorizes the commission to solicit and accept gifts, grants, and donations to implement the chapter.

agencies.name: Health and Human Services Commission
agencies.explanation: The center is established within the named commission, which is assigned its administration and resource-publication duties.

HB418.summary: HB 418 would allow state senators and state representatives, in addition to students and faculty or staff members at institutions of higher education, to submit written complaints to the Texas Higher Education Coordinating Board Office of the Ombudsman. A complainant must have reason to believe an institution violated a provision listed in Education Code Section 61.031(c) and provide the required contact information, specific statute, and supporting facts.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes who may submit complaints about covered compliance at institutions of higher education.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The bill changes the complaint process of a state higher education office for covered institutions, without limiting it to a named locality.

affected_groups.group: State senators and state representatives
affected_groups.explanation: They would be newly eligible to submit qualifying written complaints.

major_effects.label: Expands eligible complainants
major_effects.explanation: Adds state senators and state representatives to those who may submit a written complaint when they have reason to believe a covered institution failed to comply with a listed provision.

agencies.name: Texas Higher Education Coordinating Board Office of the Ombudsman
agencies.explanation: The bill expands the categories of people who may submit written complaints to the named office.

HB419.summary: HB 419 would move fine arts from the enrichment curriculum to the foundation curriculum that K–12 school districts must offer. It retains the one-credit fine arts requirement in the foundation high school program and would apply beginning with the 2027–2028 school year.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes the required curriculum for public schools by placing fine arts in the foundation curriculum.
Imposes a curriculum duty on school districts, which are local public entities.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The curriculum change applies to school districts offering kindergarten through grade 12 across Texas.

affected_groups.group: Texas public school districts offering kindergarten through grade 12
affected_groups.explanation: They would have to include fine arts in the foundation curriculum they offer.

affected_groups.group: Public school students
affected_groups.explanation: Students would encounter fine arts as part of the foundation curriculum; the bill retains a one-credit fine arts requirement in the foundation high school program.

major_effects.label: Fine arts moved into foundation curriculum
major_effects.explanation: Districts would offer fine arts as part of the required foundation curriculum rather than as an enrichment subject. The bill retains the one-credit fine arts requirement in the foundation high school program.

agencies.name: State Board of Education
agencies.explanation: The bill changes the curriculum categories and references used in the Board's existing curriculum rule framework, including the fine arts credit requirement.

HB420.summary: HB 420 would establish a family health aide program for eligible STAR Kids recipients receiving private duty nursing at home, allowing a participating parent, guardian, or family member to provide nursing services if licensed, employed by the recipient’s provider agency, and working under a nurse’s delegation and supervision. The commission would administer licensing, training, screening, and a provider reimbursement floor, and must implement the program by September 1, 2028; an agency may delay a provision if it determines that a necessary federal waiver or authorization is pending.

policy_tags.explanation: Creates a licensed family aide role to provide supervised home nursing services to eligible recipients.
Limits program eligibility to recipients enrolled in STAR Kids and eligible for private duty nursing under Texas Health Steps.
Creates an occupational license, training requirements, and employment conditions for family health aides.
Requires reimbursement for licensed health aide services at a specified minimum rate.

locations.name: Texas statewide
locations.explanation: The reimbursement requirement applies to the program’s services at rates specified for this state.

affected_groups.group: STAR Kids recipients eligible for private duty nursing
affected_groups.explanation: Eligible recipients may receive services from a participating family health aide, and the commission must screen for eligibility and notify a representative about potential program availability.

affected_groups.group: Parents, legal guardians, and family members of eligible recipients
affected_groups.explanation: They may elect to participate, but must meet the program’s licensing and employment conditions to provide aide services.

affected_groups.group: Home and community support services agencies and private duty nurses
affected_groups.explanation: Agencies may employ licensed aides and receive reimbursement for their services; nurses delegate and supervise the aide’s permitted services.

major_effects.label: Family health aide program
major_effects.explanation: Creates a program for eligible family members to assist with private duty nursing services in the home, subject to program conditions.

major_effects.label: Aide licensing and oversight
major_effects.explanation: Requires a license and commission-approved qualifications and training; creates a registry and licensing complaint and investigation procedures.

major_effects.label: Provider reimbursement
major_effects.explanation: Requires agency reimbursement at no less than the specified Medicare visit-rate floor, with reimbursement also subject to the stated enhanced certified nursing assistant rate.

major_effects.label: Recipient screening and notice
major_effects.explanation: Requires the commission to add program eligibility criteria to STAR Kids assessment tools and notify a recipient’s parent or legally authorized representative about potential availability.

agencies.name: the commission
agencies.explanation: The bill assigns the commission program administration, eligibility screening, licensing, training, registry, outreach, and reimbursement duties. Its canonical agency identity is not established by the supplied text.

agencies.name: Texas Board of Nursing
agencies.explanation: The Board is assigned a consultation role in program development and in adoption of licensing rules; its rules also govern delegation of nursing tasks.

HB421.summary: Before a covered criminal hearing or proceeding begins, the judge must inform the state and defense attorneys about procedures available under Article 38.071 for taking testimony from a child under 13 who may testify about an offense listed in that article. The requirement applies only to proceedings that commence on or after the Act’s effective date; earlier-started proceedings remain governed by prior law.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill adds a prehearing duty in covered criminal proceedings concerning testimony by a child witness.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The bill amends the Texas Code of Criminal Procedure with a rule for covered criminal proceedings, rather than limiting the rule to a particular place.

affected_groups.group: Judges presiding over covered criminal hearings or proceedings
affected_groups.explanation: They must inform both attorneys about the available procedures for taking the child's testimony.

affected_groups.group: Attorneys representing the state and defendants
affected_groups.explanation: They must be informed before the covered hearing or proceeding begins.

affected_groups.group: Children younger than 13 who may testify about a listed offense
affected_groups.explanation: The judge’s information duty concerns available procedures for taking their testimony; the bill does not itself change those procedures.

major_effects.label: Prehearing notice about child-testimony procedures
major_effects.explanation: Before a covered proceeding begins, the judge must inform state and defense attorneys about procedures available under Article 38.071 for taking the child’s testimony. This applies only to proceedings commencing on or after the effective date.

agencies.name: judge
agencies.explanation: The bill directly assigns the judge a new duty, but does not identify the court or judicial body to which the judge belongs.

HB422.summary: The bill would extend a handgun license through the 90th day after its printed expiration date if the holder submits the required renewal materials by mail or online at least 10 days before that date. The department would send a receipt, and the holder would be treated as having an unexpired license during the extension only while carrying both the receipt and the expired license; the change would apply only to licenses expiring on or after the Act’s effective date.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill changes the duration and proof of a handgun license for a person carrying a handgun.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The bill addresses the status of a license under Texas law.

affected_groups.group: Handgun license holders submitting renewal materials
affected_groups.explanation: Eligible holders could receive an extension if they submit the required renewal materials by the specified time and carry both the receipt and expired license during the extension.

major_effects.label: Conditional license-expiration extension
major_effects.explanation: A license would remain extended through the 90th day after its printed expiration date if the holder submits the renewal materials by the 10th day before expiration.

major_effects.label: Receipt and temporary recognition as unexpired
major_effects.explanation: The department would provide a receipt; during the extension, the license would be considered unexpired for the stated legal purposes only when the holder carries both the receipt and expired license.

agencies.name: Texas Department of Public Safety
agencies.explanation: Chapter 411 defines “Department” as the Department of Public Safety of the State of Texas, and the bill requires the department to provide the license holder a receipt.

HB423.summary: HB 423 would let a political subdivision satisfy a legal newspaper-notice requirement using specified alternative media it determines has greater circulation than the area’s most-circulated newspaper, after a public meeting, while also posting the notice on its own and the comptroller’s websites. The comptroller could require newspaper notice if the circulation condition is not met and may waive website posting when internet access is limited if the subdivision adds notice to a public agenda board; the bill also requires reporting about alternative notice methods and a biennial comptroller report.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes how political subdivisions may provide legally required public notice and adds related meeting and reporting duties.
Assigns the comptroller publication, reporting, and rulemaking duties for the alternative-notice framework.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The notice option applies to political subdivisions generally rather than to a named locality.

affected_groups.group: Political subdivisions
affected_groups.explanation: They may use qualifying alternative notice methods and must follow the bill’s meeting, publication, and reporting requirements when doing so.

affected_groups.group: Newspapers and alternative-media providers
affected_groups.explanation: Newspapers may be displaced for qualifying notices, while listed alternative media may be used for those notices.

affected_groups.group: People seeking public notices
affected_groups.explanation: They may encounter required notices through alternative media and online publication, with additional agenda-board notice required if the comptroller waives website posting.

major_effects.label: Alternative notice methods
major_effects.explanation: Allows a political subdivision to substitute authorized media for newspaper publication when it demonstrates greater circulation at a public meeting; website posting is also required unless waived under the limited-internet-access provision.

major_effects.label: Notice-method reporting
major_effects.explanation: Requires subdivisions using alternative media to submit method and circulation information, and requires a biennial report comparing notice methods.

major_effects.label: Administrative rules
major_effects.explanation: Authorizes the comptroller to adopt rules to administer the new subchapter.

agencies.name: Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts
agencies.explanation: The comptroller must promptly publish certain notices on its Internet website after receipt, unless it requires notice by newspaper or waives the requirement. It must prepare and submit a report, and may require newspaper notice, grant a waiver, authorize additional media, and adopt rules.

HB424.summary: HB 424 would require agreements under Government Code Section 753.051 to prohibit a sheriff and specified sheriff’s-department personnel and contractors from targeting a child for federal immigration-law enforcement while the child is in or on a child protected area. The bill defines enforcement to include investigating or monitoring suspected violators, and applies the requirement only to agreements entered into or renewed on or after the Act’s effective date; it does not prohibit all immigration enforcement at those places.

policy_tags.explanation: Restricts targeting a child for federal immigration-law enforcement in child protected areas under covered sheriff agreements.
Sets a required term in agreements involving sheriffs and imposes a restriction on sheriffs and sheriff’s-department personnel or contractors.
Provides a specific protection against targeting children for immigration-law enforcement while they are in defined protected areas.

locations.name: Child protected areas
locations.explanation: The bill defines these premises to include specified places where children gather or receive services.

affected_groups.group: Children in child protected areas who may be targeted for federal immigration-law enforcement
affected_groups.explanation: Covered agreements must prohibit targeting a child for such enforcement while the child is in or on a child protected area.

affected_groups.group: Sheriffs and sheriff’s-department officers, employees, and applicable contractors
affected_groups.explanation: The bill requires the agreement to prohibit these parties from targeting a child in a protected area.

major_effects.label: Restriction on targeting children in protected areas
major_effects.explanation: Requires covered agreements to prohibit sheriffs and specified department personnel or contractors from targeting a child for federal immigration-law enforcement while the child is in or on a child protected area.

HB425.summary: The bill would require a qualifying volunteer fire department that receives county money on or after the Act's effective date to report in writing to the county commissioners court how it used the money, with reports due annually until the money is fully spent. The county would have to publish each report on its website.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill imposes reporting and online publication duties involving county funding and county commissioners courts.
The reporting requirement applies to qualifying associations organized to provide and actively providing firefighting services.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The requirements apply to qualifying volunteer fire departments receiving money from a county and counties receiving their reports, without limiting the provisions to a named area.

affected_groups.group: Qualifying volunteer fire departments receiving county money
affected_groups.explanation: These departments must report how they used the county money annually until it is fully spent.

affected_groups.group: Counties and county commissioners courts
affected_groups.explanation: Commissioners courts receive the reports, and counties must publish them online.

major_effects.label: County-funding use reports and publication
major_effects.explanation: Qualifying volunteer fire departments must report how county money was used annually until it is fully spent; the county must publish each report on its website. The requirement applies only to money received on or after the Act's effective date.

HB426.summary: Beginning with the 2027-2028 school year, qualifying school districts and open-enrollment charter schools must provide a halal option for any breakfast or lunch program when a student or the student’s parent or guardian requests one. The requirement applies only to schools located wholly or partly in a county with a population of at least 2.1 million or an adjacent county.

policy_tags.explanation: Adds a meal-option requirement for certain public schools’ breakfast and lunch programs.
Imposes a new duty on qualifying school districts, which are local governmental entities.

locations.name: Counties with a population of 2.1 million or more and counties adjacent to them
locations.explanation: The bill applies to a district or charter school located wholly or partly in a county meeting either geographic criterion.

affected_groups.group: Students, and their parents or persons standing in parental relation
affected_groups.explanation: They may request the halal option for a student’s breakfast or lunch.

affected_groups.group: Qualifying school districts and open-enrollment charter schools
affected_groups.explanation: They must provide the requested option if they provide a breakfast or lunch program and are within the bill’s geographic scope.

major_effects.label: On-request halal meal option
major_effects.explanation: Requires covered districts and charter schools to provide a halal option in any breakfast or lunch program when requested by a student or the student’s parent or person standing in parental relation.

HB427.summary: HB427 would broaden an election-related offense from creating and distributing a deepfake video to creating or modifying specified artificially generated media, including images, audio, video, radio broadcasts, and written text, with intent to deceive and intent to injure a candidate or influence an election. It would exempt political advertising that is satire or parody, advertising a listed media entity is paid to publish or broadcast, and qualifying bona fide news coverage that includes the specified disclosure.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes the scope of an offense tied to influencing an election and distribution within 30 days of an election.
Expands the conduct that can constitute the specified criminal offense.
The offense definition would cover media created or modified using generative AI or other computer software.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The bill amends a Texas Election Code provision and states no narrower geographic limitation.

affected_groups.group: People who create artificially generated media and cause it to be published or distributed
affected_groups.explanation: Their conduct may fall within the expanded offense when the stated intent and timing conditions are met.

affected_groups.group: Candidates
affected_groups.explanation: The offense continues to cover conduct intended to injure a candidate.

affected_groups.group: Broadcasters, publishers, and online platforms
affected_groups.explanation: The bill names these entities in exclusions for paid publication or broadcast and certain disclosed bona fide news coverage.

major_effects.label: Broader election-related offense
major_effects.explanation: Expands the media covered by the offense beyond deepfake videos to specified artificially generated media, while retaining the intent requirements and the requirement that it be published or distributed within 30 days of an election.

major_effects.label: Exceptions for specified political advertising and news coverage
major_effects.explanation: The offense does not apply to political advertising that is satire or parody, advertising a listed media entity is paid to publish or broadcast, or specified bona fide news coverage when it includes the required disclosure.

HB428.summary: The bill would let a legislator request an unannounced inspection of a covered permanent concrete plant on behalf of a district resident who is eligible to be affected and submits a written complaint. The Texas Commission on Environmental Quality would prioritize responding to the request and provide specified information; a priority response does not require the commission to conduct an inspection, and a denial would require an explanation within 90 days.

policy_tags.explanation: Creates an inspection-request process for certain permitted concrete plants, an environmental regulatory matter.
Adds a process and response duties for the commission when a legislator submits a qualifying inspection request.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The process is available to legislators statewide for plants meeting the bill's criteria.

locations.name: The requesting legislator's district
locations.explanation: The person on whose behalf the request is made must permanently reside in the legislator's district.

affected_groups.group: Legislators
affected_groups.explanation: A legislator may submit a qualifying inspection request on behalf of a constituent.

affected_groups.group: District residents who may be affected by a covered concrete plant
affected_groups.explanation: A resident must live in the member's district, qualify as a person who may be affected, and submit a written complaint to the member.

affected_groups.group: Operators of covered permanent concrete plants
affected_groups.explanation: Their plants may be the subject of a legislator-requested unannounced inspection.

major_effects.label: Legislator-requested inspection process
major_effects.explanation: Allows a legislator to request an unannounced inspection for a qualifying constituent and requires the commission to prioritize its response, but does not require an inspection to occur.

major_effects.label: Request records and notices
major_effects.explanation: Requires the commission to maintain a file and provide specified policies, procedures, and notice to the legislator and complainant; if it denies the request, it must explain why within 90 days.

agencies.name: Texas Commission on Environmental Quality
agencies.explanation: The bill assigns the commission duties to prioritize qualifying requests, maintain a request file, provide specified information, and explain denials.

HB429.summary: HB 429 would exempt specified personal information about current or former State Office of Administrative Hearings administrative law judges from public disclosure, including whether they have family members, regardless of compliance with specified opt-out provisions. It would also add those judges to the groups covered by Section 552.1175 of the Government Code and Section 25.025 of the Tax Code. The changes apply only to requests received on or after the Act's effective date; earlier requests remain governed by prior law.

policy_tags.explanation: Expands confidentiality protections for covered judges' personal and family-related information.
Changes public-information disclosure rules for the specified information.
The change to disclosure rules applies to requests received by governmental bodies, including local bodies handling covered information.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The changes apply to covered information requests received by governmental bodies or officers under Texas law.

affected_groups.group: Current and former administrative law judges for the State Office of Administrative Hearings
affected_groups.explanation: Their specified personal information receives expanded confidentiality protections.

affected_groups.group: Governmental bodies and officers responding to information requests
affected_groups.explanation: They apply the updated exceptions to disclosure for covered information.

major_effects.label: Expanded confidentiality for personal information
major_effects.explanation: Creates a public-disclosure exception for covered judges' specified home and identifying information and information revealing whether they have family members, regardless of compliance with Sections 552.024 or 552.1175.

major_effects.label: Adds judges to groups covered by existing protections
major_effects.explanation: Extends coverage under Section 552.1175 of the Government Code and Section 25.025 of the Tax Code to current and former administrative law judges for the office.

agencies.name: State Office of Administrative Hearings
agencies.explanation: Current and former administrative law judges of the named office are the individuals receiving the expanded confidentiality protections; the bill does not assign the office a separate administrative duty.

HB430.summary: HB 430 would establish a Department of State Health Services-administered emergency medical services personnel retention benefit program in coordination with the Employees Retirement System of Texas. Eligible Texas-resident EMTs, advanced EMTs, and licensed paramedics with at least 30 qualifying years of service would receive lifetime life and health coverage, with the department paying the premiums.

policy_tags.explanation: Establishes life insurance and health benefit coverage for qualifying EMS personnel, with coverage depending in part on Medicare eligibility.
Requires the department to pay coverage premiums and use money appropriated or otherwise available to administer the program and provide benefits.
Creates a long-service benefit program expressly intended to incentivize retention of EMS personnel.

locations.name: Texas
locations.explanation: The benefit program concerns Texas residents who apply for benefits.

affected_groups.group: Long-serving emergency medical technicians, advanced emergency medical technicians, and licensed paramedics
affected_groups.explanation: These personnel may qualify if they meet the service and Texas-residency requirements; service may be as an employee or volunteer and requires at least 1,000 hours in a year.

major_effects.label: Creates lifetime EMS personnel benefits
major_effects.explanation: Establishes a retention program providing lifetime life and health coverage, including a $100,000 life-insurance death benefit.

major_effects.label: Sets service, credential, and residency criteria
major_effects.explanation: Eligibility requires a specified EMS license or certification, at least 30 years of service, and Texas residency when applying.

major_effects.label: Requires the department to pay premiums
major_effects.explanation: The department must pay insurance premiums for eligible individuals' life and health coverage, using money appropriated or otherwise available for the purpose.

major_effects.label: Requires implementation rules
major_effects.explanation: The HHSC executive commissioner must adopt rules necessary to implement the program.

agencies.name: Department of State Health Services
agencies.explanation: Must establish and administer the program, determine eligibility, provide coverage, and pay premiums.

agencies.name: Employees Retirement System of Texas
agencies.explanation: Its board of trustees is identified in the bill and must coordinate with the department to establish and administer the program.

agencies.name: Health and Human Services Commission
agencies.explanation: The HHSC executive commissioner must adopt rules necessary to implement the bill.

HB431.summary: For automobile insurance claims involving property damage or bodily or psychological injury for which an insurer may be liable, HB 431 would prohibit oral releases and make a release exchanged for consideration unenforceable unless it is a separate written agreement. These rules would apply only to contracts entered into on or after January 1, 2028; earlier contracts remain governed by prior law.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill regulates how automobile insurers and other parties may release covered claims.

locations.name: Texas
locations.explanation: The chapter applies to insurers writing automobile insurance in this state.

affected_groups.group: Claimants, including insureds making first-party claims and people with property-damage or injury claims
affected_groups.explanation: Their covered claims could not be released orally under the bill.

affected_groups.group: Personal and commercial automobile insurers
affected_groups.explanation: Insurers writing automobile insurance in Texas are subject to the release restriction.

major_effects.label: Written agreements required for covered releases
major_effects.explanation: For covered claims, parties may not enter an oral release; a release exchanged for consideration is unenforceable unless the contract is a separate written agreement.

major_effects.label: Prospective application
major_effects.explanation: The changes apply only to contracts entered into on or after January 1, 2028; earlier contracts remain governed by prior law.

HB432.summary: HB 432 would require school district boards, before ordering a campus closure or consolidation, to hold at least three public-comment meetings, post an impact statement for each affected campus, and notify district parents and employees. A board could not vote at those required meetings, and the closure or consolidation vote would have to be recorded and separate; the requirements would not apply to emergency or commissioner-ordered closures. The requirements would apply to closures or consolidations ordered on or after the Act’s effective date.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill establishes procedures for school district campus closures and consolidations.
The bill imposes new procedural duties on school district governing boards, which are local public bodies.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The requirements apply generally to school district campus closures or consolidations under the Education Code, rather than to a specified locality.

affected_groups.group: School district boards and school districts
affected_groups.explanation: Boards would have to complete the new public process before ordering a covered closure or consolidation.

affected_groups.group: Parents and persons standing in parental relation to district students, and district employees
affected_groups.explanation: These groups would receive advance notice of each required meeting.

affected_groups.group: Students at campuses proposed for closure or consolidation
affected_groups.explanation: The impact statement must address matters including receiving-campus capacity, transportation, walkability, and affected student programs.

major_effects.label: Campus impact statements
major_effects.explanation: District boards would post an impact statement for each campus proposed for closure or consolidation, covering specified operational, financial, and student impacts.

major_effects.label: Public process and advance notice
major_effects.explanation: Boards would hold at least three open meetings with public comment, with at least two at or near the affected campus when practicable, and give parents and employees advance notice.

major_effects.label: Limits on closure and consolidation votes
major_effects.explanation: The board could not vote on the closure or consolidation at a meeting required by the bill; the vote must be recorded and may not be combined with another vote.

HB433.summary: The bill would replace the mockingbird with the golden-cheeked warbler as Texas’s state bird. It changes the state-symbol designation and does not add an agency duty or program.

locations.name: Texas statewide
locations.explanation: The designation is for the state bird of Texas.

major_effects.label: State-symbol designation
major_effects.explanation: Changes the bird designated as the state bird from the mockingbird to the golden-cheeked warbler.

HB434.summary: HB 434 would create a temporary 10-member task force to evaluate housing needs of LGBTQ+ senior citizens, including people who may need long-term care, and develop potential housing solutions. The task force would report its findings and recommendations to state officials and the Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs by September 1, 2028, and would expire on December 1, 2028.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill creates a housing-focused study and solution-development task force for LGBTQ+ senior citizens; it does not itself require housing construction or change housing eligibility or standards.
The bill establishes a temporary task force, specifies its membership and duties, and requires it to report to state officials.

locations.name: Texas
locations.explanation: The task force is established through state-level appointments and reports to state officials and a Texas state agency.

affected_groups.group: LGBTQ+ senior citizens, including those who may need long-term care
affected_groups.explanation: They are the population whose housing needs the task force will assess, including needs related to transition into long-term care facilities.

major_effects.label: Temporary housing-needs task force
major_effects.explanation: Creates a 10-member task force to evaluate the specified population's housing needs and develop potential solutions.

major_effects.label: Findings and recommendations report
major_effects.explanation: Requires a written report summarizing the evaluation and proposing potential housing solutions, including any legislative recommendations.

agencies.name: Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs
agencies.explanation: The department is a required recipient of the task force's written report. The bill also allows, but does not require, an appointee to represent the department.

HB435.summary: The bill would require water districts subject to Chapters 36, 49, or 60 of the Water Code, if any part of the district is in a county with at least 125,000 people, to record qualifying regularly scheduled open meetings in audio and video and post archived copies online. Districts with no part in such a county would instead have to make audio recordings of qualifying meetings and post archived copies online.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill changes open-meeting recording and online-publication duties for covered water districts.
It imposes new meeting-recording and access duties on qualifying water districts.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The requirements apply to qualifying Water Code districts across the state, with the recording format determined by the population of counties where each district is located.

affected_groups.group: Water districts subject to Chapters 36, 49, or 60 of the Water Code
affected_groups.explanation: Covered districts would have recording and online-archiving duties, with audio and video required when any part of the district is in a county with a population of at least 125,000, and audio only otherwise.

affected_groups.group: People seeking online access to water-district meeting recordings
affected_groups.explanation: Archived recordings of the covered meetings would be made available on the Internet.

major_effects.label: Recording requirements
major_effects.explanation: Covered districts would record qualifying regularly scheduled open meetings: audio and video for districts with any part in a county of at least 125,000 people, and audio for districts with no part in such a county. The requirement excludes work sessions and special called meetings.

major_effects.label: Online access to archived recordings
major_effects.explanation: Districts would make archived copies of the recordings required by the bill available on the Internet.

HB436.summary: HB 436 would cap the annual percentage rate at 36% for deferred presentment transactions, except that a restriction or limitation under another law prevails if it results in a lower total cost. It would also cap the annual percentage rate for consumer-credit extensions obtained or facilitated by a credit services organization; that rate calculation includes interest, lender charges, and other consideration received by the organization or its representative. A transaction violating either cap would be void and unenforceable, and a lender entering a noncompliant deferred presentment transaction would commit a Class A misdemeanor. The provisions apply only to credit made on or after the effective date, with a refinance treated as made on the date of the credit being refinanced.

policy_tags.explanation: Sets maximum rates and charge-calculation rules for specified credit transactions and services.
Creates a Class A misdemeanor for a lender entering a deferred presentment transaction that violates the rate restriction.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The bill establishes generally applicable Texas Finance Code rules and specifies no narrower geographic area.

affected_groups.group: Borrowers in deferred presentment transactions
affected_groups.explanation: Would receive the protection of a 36% annual percentage rate ceiling, except that a restriction or limitation under another law prevails if it results in a lower total cost.

affected_groups.group: Consumers obtaining credit through credit services organizations
affected_groups.explanation: Would receive a 36% rate ceiling on credit obtained or facilitated by a credit services organization.

affected_groups.group: Lenders and credit services organizations
affected_groups.explanation: Would be subject to the applicable rate restrictions; lenders face a misdemeanor consequence for violating the deferred presentment restriction.

major_effects.label: 36% APR ceilings
major_effects.explanation: Caps the annual percentage rate for deferred presentment transactions and for consumer-credit extensions obtained or facilitated by a credit services organization; the latter calculation includes charges and other consideration received by the organization or its representative.

major_effects.label: Noncompliant transactions void
major_effects.explanation: Transactions violating either rate restriction would be void and unenforceable.

major_effects.label: Misdemeanor for noncompliant deferred presentment lending
major_effects.explanation: A lender entering a deferred presentment transaction in violation of the cap would commit a Class A misdemeanor.

HB437.summary: The bill expands the period for the election-related deep-fake video offense: a person with intent to injure a candidate or influence an election commits the offense by creating a deep fake video and causing it to be published or distributed within 90 days of an election, rather than 30 days. The change applies only to offenses committed on or after the Act’s effective date; earlier offenses remain governed by prior law.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes the period tied to an election during which creating and distributing a deep fake video can constitute an offense.
Expands the time period covered by an existing criminal offense.

locations.name: Statewide in Texas
locations.explanation: The bill amends the Texas Election Code without limiting the change to a particular locality.

affected_groups.group: People who create and cause deep fake videos to be published or distributed
affected_groups.explanation: Their conduct may fall within the offense for a longer period around an election, when the specified intent is present.

affected_groups.group: Candidates
affected_groups.explanation: The offense includes conduct undertaken with intent to injure a candidate.

major_effects.label: Expanded election-related deep fake offense window
major_effects.explanation: Extends from 30 to 90 days the period around an election in which the specified creation and publication or distribution of a deep fake video can constitute the offense. The amendment applies only to offenses committed on or after the effective date.
