policy_tags.explanation: Creates oversight requirements for state agencies’ use of AI, including AI actions that risk substantial harm to confidential information.
Requires agency policies and procedures for specified AI decisions and assigns the Department of Information Resources rulemaking duties.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The requirements apply to qualifying state agencies, without limiting them to a particular geographic area.

affected_groups.group: State agencies that deploy or use artificial intelligence systems
affected_groups.explanation: These agencies must establish and maintain oversight policies and implement interim safeguards before they are required to comply with the adopted rules.

affected_groups.group: State employees and officers providing human oversight
affected_groups.explanation: Oversight personnel must meet minimum standards and have training, relevant information, and authority to intervene in AI decisions or actions.

affected_groups.group: Individuals and others affected by covered AI decisions or actions
affected_groups.explanation: They may be affected when an AI system controls a consequential decision or presents a reasonably foreseeable risk of substantial harm to health, safety, property, infrastructure, or confidential information.

major_effects.label: Agency human-oversight policies
major_effects.explanation: Qualifying agencies must maintain policies and procedures for meaningful human oversight of covered AI decisions and actions.

major_effects.label: Minimum oversight standards
major_effects.explanation: The Department of Information Resources must establish minimum standards, including standards for oversight timing and documentation; the required oversight must be proportionate to the nature and risk of the covered decision or action.

major_effects.label: Interim safeguards during the transition
major_effects.explanation: Agencies need not comply with the adopted rules until the 90th day after adoption, but must implement appropriate interim safeguards until they are required to comply.

agencies.name: Department of Information Resources
agencies.explanation: The bill assigns the department responsibility for adopting minimum standards for human oversight, including standards on timing and documentation.

HB475.summary: Beginning with the 2027–2028 school year, when the agency conducts a monitoring-system inspection of a residential or day placement facility that contracts with a school district, it must consider whether therapeutic educational services align with medical standards and best practices for the student’s disability and whether facility employees have completed and follow crisis prevention and intervention training. The bill adds these inspection considerations; it does not require an inspection in every case.

policy_tags.explanation: Adds considerations to inspections of facilities providing services to students with disabilities under school district contracts.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The provision applies to covered facilities with school district contracts and does not limit its reach to a named place or defined region.

affected_groups.group: Students with disabilities placed in residential or day placement facilities
affected_groups.explanation: Their therapeutic educational services are among the matters considered during a covered inspection.

affected_groups.group: School districts that contract with residential or day placement facilities
affected_groups.explanation: Facilities contracted by school districts are covered by the added inspection considerations.

affected_groups.group: Residential and day placement facilities and their employees
affected_groups.explanation: A covered inspection considers whether facility employees have completed and adhere to crisis prevention and intervention training.

major_effects.label: Additional inspection considerations
major_effects.explanation: When the agency conducts an inspection under the existing monitoring system, it must consider educational-service alignment with medical standards and best practices, and facility employees’ crisis prevention and intervention training; the bill does not itself require an inspection in every case.

agencies.name: Texas Education Agency
agencies.explanation: Chapter 29 describes the agency as the state education agency responsible for special education. The proposed Section 29.0101 adds inspection considerations for residential and day placement facilities to the monitoring system developed under Section 29.010.

HB476.summary: HB 476 would make knowingly disseminating information that connects a voter to the voter’s individual ballot selections in violation of the right to a secret ballot an offense, except as provided by Subsection (b) or (c). The offense would be a third-degree felony, subject to exceptions for election officials acting lawfully, court or tribunal authority, and voter permission. A court could order consecutive confinement sentences in specified cases involving related offenses and use of the disseminated information.

policy_tags.explanation: Creates a criminal offense concerning disclosure of information linking voters to their ballot selections.
Creates a felony offense and authorizes possible consecutive confinement sentences in specified cases.
Criminalizes certain disclosures of personally identifiable voter information.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The proposed Election Code offense applies statewide in Texas.

affected_groups.group: Voters
affected_groups.explanation: Their ballot selections are protected from specified disclosure without permission or other stated authority.

affected_groups.group: People who disseminate voter information
affected_groups.explanation: A person who knowingly makes the specified disclosure may face the new felony offense, subject to exceptions.

affected_groups.group: Election officials
affected_groups.explanation: An election official handling or disclosing voter information in the lawful discharge of official duties is excepted from prosecution under this section.

major_effects.label: Felony for specified voter-information disclosure
major_effects.explanation: Creates a third-degree felony for knowingly connecting a voter to the voter’s ballot selections through dissemination, subject to the stated exceptions.

major_effects.label: Possible consecutive sentences
major_effects.explanation: Allows a court to order confinement sentences to run consecutively when the person is also found guilty of qualifying additional offenses arising from the same criminal episode and use of the information.

HB477.summary: The bill would make a murder capital murder when the actor’s conduct is motivated by the political affiliation, association, belief, or ideology of the actor or victim. It would provide that a mistake of fact is not a defense to that charge and allow motivation to be established through statements, actions, or other objective factors.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill expands the circumstances in which murder is classified and prosecuted as capital murder and specifies a defense and evidence rule.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The bill amends the Texas Penal Code, with no narrower geographic limitation stated.

affected_groups.group: People accused of murder motivated by the political affiliation, association, belief, or ideology of the actor or victim
affected_groups.explanation: Their alleged conduct could qualify as capital murder under the new provision.

affected_groups.group: People targeted for their political affiliation, association, belief, or ideology
affected_groups.explanation: Their murder could meet the new political-motivation criterion for capital murder.

major_effects.label: Adds politically motivated murder to capital murder
major_effects.explanation: A murder meeting the political-motivation criterion would qualify as capital murder, exposing the accused to capital-murder prosecution and punishment.

major_effects.label: Sets rules for motive and mistake of fact
major_effects.explanation: A mistake of fact that gave rise to the specified motivation is not a defense, and motivation may be shown through statements, actions, or other objective factors.

HB478.summary: HB 478 would require municipalities and counties to establish emergency-services capacity assessment procedures for proposed operation or substantial expansion of large custodial facilities—facilities designed or used to keep 250 or more people in continuous custody or supervision. A facility could operate or expand only if the responsible local entity finds sufficient capacity or the operator enters and complies with an agreement addressing identified deficiencies; temporary facilities established in connection with a declared disaster are exempt. Procedures would be due by December 1, 2027, but compliance would not be required before January 1, 2028.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill assigns municipalities and counties responsibility for establishing local assessment procedures and allows them to enforce the chapter.
The assessment process concerns local fire protection and emergency medical services capacity.
The bill makes assessment approval or compliance with a mitigation agreement a condition for operating or substantially expanding a covered facility.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The implementation requirement applies to each municipality and county in Texas.

locations.name: Areas within municipalities and unincorporated county areas
locations.explanation: Assessment procedures apply to facilities in municipal areas or county unincorporated areas, as applicable.

affected_groups.group: Municipalities and counties
affected_groups.explanation: They must establish assessment procedures and may seek equitable relief against a person who violates the chapter.

affected_groups.group: People proposing to operate or substantially expand large custodial facilities
affected_groups.explanation: They must obtain an assessment and satisfy the capacity or mitigation-agreement condition before operating or expanding.

affected_groups.group: Local entities responsible for fire protection and emergency medical services
affected_groups.explanation: The entity performing an assessment must determine whether capacity is sufficient and identify specific deficiencies when it is not.

major_effects.label: Local emergency-services assessment procedures
major_effects.explanation: Municipalities and counties must create procedures for assessments that evaluate service capacity, identify deficiencies, provide public notice, and allow for disputes. Temporary facilities established in connection with a declared disaster must be exempt.

major_effects.label: Operating and expansion conditions
major_effects.explanation: A person may operate or substantially expand a covered facility only after a finding of sufficient emergency-services capacity or by entering into and complying with an agreement to mitigate identified deficiencies. A municipality or county may not prohibit operation or expansion when the person satisfies either condition.

major_effects.label: Local enforcement
major_effects.explanation: A municipality or county may bring an action for appropriate equitable relief against a person who violates the chapter.

HB479.summary: HB 479 would allow a person convicted of a felony to qualify and register to vote if the person is not currently incarcerated for that offense, replacing the requirement to complete the sentence or have the voting disability lifted. Other voter qualifications, including age, citizenship, mental-capacity requirements, and residency, would remain.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill changes voter qualifications and eligibility for voter registration after a felony conviction.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The voter-registration eligibility change applies to registration in Texas.

affected_groups.group: People convicted of felonies who are not currently incarcerated for the offense
affected_groups.explanation: They could qualify and register to vote without first completing parole, supervision, or probation, subject to the other voter qualifications.

major_effects.label: Voter eligibility after felony conviction
major_effects.explanation: A felony conviction would bar qualification and registration only while the person is currently incarcerated for that offense, replacing the requirement to complete the sentence or have the voting disability lifted.

agencies.name: Texas Secretary of State
agencies.explanation: The change to statewide voter-registration eligibility is relevant to statewide election administration, though the bill does not name the office or assign it a distinct duty.

HB480.summary: The bill would create a state fund, a seven-member board, and a grant program for county fairs and local rodeos. Grants would support facilities, event programs, personnel, and public health and safety; recipients and the board would have specified reporting duties.

policy_tags.explanation: Creates grants intended to promote livestock and agricultural programs, including local youth agricultural programs.
The grant program includes educating the public about livestock and agricultural programs as a stated public purpose.
Establishes a dedicated fund for the grant program, with specified sources and restricted uses; the bill does not itself appropriate a specific amount.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The program concerns Texas livestock and agricultural programs and appointments representing different regions of the state.

affected_groups.group: County fairs and local rodeos
affected_groups.explanation: They may apply for grants and, if awarded, must submit the applicable report specified by the bill.

affected_groups.group: County livestock programs and local youth agricultural programs
affected_groups.explanation: Grant applicants must specify how funds would benefit these programs within the county.

major_effects.label: Creates a board and grant program
major_effects.explanation: Establishes a board to administer grants to county fairs and local rodeos for facilities, events, personnel, and public health and safety.

major_effects.label: Creates a dedicated grant fund
major_effects.explanation: The fund may receive legislative transfers, gifts or grants, and investment interest, and may be used only for program implementation and administration. Disbursements without appropriation are limited to the chapter and its rules.

major_effects.label: Requires grant and program reports
major_effects.explanation: Awarded applicants must submit a report: those with budgets greater than $10 million must report economic impact, while those with budgets less than $10 million must report community economic-development needs. Neither report category expressly covers a budget of exactly $10 million; the excerpt does not specify what report, if any, applies to that case. The board must also submit a biennial report to legislators.

agencies.name: Texas Livestock and Rodeo Education and Continuation Board
agencies.explanation: The bill creates the board and assigns it responsibility for administering the grant program, adopting rules, employing staff, and reporting.

agencies.name: Office of the Governor
agencies.explanation: The bill places fund administration within the Office of the Governor; the supplied registry has no matching entry.

HB481.summary: HB481 would let a voter voting by mail because of absence from the county of residence choose on the application to receive balloting materials electronically. The marked ballot would still have to be returned by mail or common or contract carrier; the bill also requires procedures from the Secretary of State and confidentiality protections for the email address used to request the materials.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes the application and ballot-delivery and return procedures for a category of voters voting early by mail.
Creates an electronic transmission option for ballot materials and protects the request email address from public disclosure.
Assigns early voting clerks duties related to receiving returned ballots and protecting voters' email addresses.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The bill amends Texas Election Code procedures without limiting them to a particular locality.

affected_groups.group: Voters voting by mail because they are absent from their county of residence
affected_groups.explanation: They may choose to receive balloting materials electronically, but must return the marked ballot by mail or common or contract carrier.

affected_groups.group: Early voting clerks
affected_groups.explanation: They must ensure that email addresses provided for electronic ballot requests are excluded from public disclosure and receive returned ballots.

major_effects.label: Electronic delivery of balloting materials
major_effects.explanation: Eligible voters absent from their county of residence may elect electronic receipt of the balloting materials; the marked ballot must still be returned physically by mail or common or contract carrier.

major_effects.label: Confidentiality of request email addresses
major_effects.explanation: Email addresses used to request electronic balloting materials are confidential and must be excluded from public disclosure.

major_effects.label: Implementation procedures
major_effects.explanation: The Secretary of State must prescribe procedures to implement electronic transmission of the balloting materials.

agencies.name: Texas Secretary of State
agencies.explanation: Directly tasked with prescribing implementation procedures and authorizing other electronic transmission methods in writing.

HB482.summary: HB 482 would require social media platforms operating in Texas and covered by the referenced Business & Commerce Code provision to display a warning each time a user opens the platform. The warning would include mental-health resources, a statement about personal-data use and social media’s addictive nature, and require user acknowledgment before use; the Health and Human Services Commission’s executive commissioner would adopt rules by January 1, 2028, and platforms would not have to comply before April 1, 2028.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill requires covered social media platforms to display a statement about personal-data use and to require acknowledgment before users can operate the platform.
The bill imposes a warning-display and user-acknowledgment requirement on covered social media platform operators.

locations.name: Texas
locations.explanation: The platform requirement applies to covered platforms operating in the state.

affected_groups.group: Operators of social media platforms covered by the referenced Business & Commerce Code provision
affected_groups.explanation: Covered operators would have to display the warning and prevent platform use until a user verifies understanding.

affected_groups.group: Users of covered social media platforms, including minors
affected_groups.explanation: Users would see the warning whenever they open the platform and must verify they understand it before operating the platform; the warning concerns minors’ social media use and mental health.

major_effects.label: Required platform warning and acknowledgment
major_effects.explanation: Covered platforms operating in Texas would display a warning with mental-health resources, personal-data and addictive-use statements, and require user acknowledgment before use. Compliance is not required before April 1, 2028.

major_effects.label: Warning-label rules
major_effects.explanation: The Health and Human Services Commission’s executive commissioner would adopt evidence-based rules on the warning’s form and content by January 1, 2028.

agencies.name: Health and Human Services Commission
agencies.explanation: The commission’s executive commissioner is assigned to adopt evidence-based rules for the warning label.

HB483.summary: The bill would prohibit a toll project entity from collecting tolls for use of a toll project located in an area designated by a state-of-disaster declaration. The prohibition would apply only while the declaration is in effect.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill changes toll collection rules for toll projects during a declared disaster.

locations.name: Area designated by the state-of-disaster executive order or proclamation
locations.explanation: The prohibition is limited to toll projects located within the area designated in the disaster declaration.

affected_groups.group: Toll project entities
affected_groups.explanation: These entities would be prohibited from collecting tolls on covered projects while the disaster declaration is in effect.

affected_groups.group: Users of toll projects in designated disaster areas
affected_groups.explanation: They would not be charged tolls for use of covered projects during the period the declaration is in effect.

major_effects.label: Temporary toll collection suspension
major_effects.explanation: Toll project entities could not collect tolls for projects in the designated disaster area while the declaration remains in effect.

HB484.summary: The bill would make brine minerals real property owned by the land’s mineral-estate owner by default, unless a binding instrument provides otherwise, and make that owner responsible for protecting other owners’ correlative rights. It would revise Water Code definitions related to brine mining and Class V injection wells, while excluding groundwater, surface water, oil and gas waste, and oil and gas from the new definition of brine, and require the Railroad Commission to adopt rules that include operator reporting requirements.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes the default ownership of brine minerals as real property within a landowner’s mineral estate, subject to binding instruments.
Changes Water Code definitions governing brine mining and injection wells, including limits on what counts as brine.
Expands the activities covered by brine-mining regulation and requires rules establishing reporting requirements for production- and injection-well operators.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The bill establishes generally applicable state-law rules concerning land, brine mining, and related wells.

affected_groups.group: Owners of mineral estates
affected_groups.explanation: Their ownership and responsibility for protecting other owners’ correlative rights would be specified for brine minerals, subject to binding instruments.

affected_groups.group: Brine production and injection well operators
affected_groups.explanation: They would be covered by rules the Railroad Commission must adopt, including rules establishing reporting requirements.

major_effects.label: Default ownership of brine minerals
major_effects.explanation: Makes the mineral-estate owner the default owner of brine minerals below the land as real property, unless a binding instrument provides otherwise, and assigns responsibility for protecting other owners’ correlative rights.

major_effects.label: Revised brine and brine-mining definitions
major_effects.explanation: Defines brine to include contained particles and solutes but exclude specified groundwater, surface water, oil-and-gas waste, and oil-and-gas categories; broadens brine mining and Class V injection-well definitions to cover extraction of brine minerals and related substances.

major_effects.label: Brine-mining rules and operator reporting
major_effects.explanation: Requires the Railroad Commission to adopt rules to administer and regulate brine mining, including rules establishing reporting requirements for operators of brine production and injection wells.

agencies.name: Railroad Commission of Texas
agencies.explanation: The bill directs the Railroad Commission to adopt rules administering and regulating brine mining, including rules that establish operator reporting requirements.

HB485.summary: HB 485 would require the Texas Department of Transportation, when constructing highway projects, to coordinate with local flood control authorities and add stormwater outfalls or other appropriate flood-control measures. In adding measures, TxDOT would have to consider existing, proposed, and expected roadways reasonably near the project.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes flood-control requirements for TxDOT highway projects.
Requires flood-control and stormwater measures as part of highway projects.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The requirements apply to the department's highway projects, without limiting them to a particular place.

affected_groups.group: Communities near TxDOT highway projects
affected_groups.explanation: They may be affected by the added flood-control measures intended to minimize flooding impacts.

major_effects.label: Flood-control measures in highway projects
major_effects.explanation: Requires TxDOT to add stormwater outfalls and other appropriate flood-control measures, considering roadways reasonably near the project.

agencies.name: Texas Department of Transportation
agencies.explanation: The bill identifies TxDOT and assigns it the highway-project flood-control requirements.

HB486.summary: The bill would allow a person to collect a wild animal or bird killed in an unintentional motor vehicle collision on a public road or right-of-way for human consumption, if it is fit to eat and collection follows applicable commission rules. The commission could set additional collection requirements and limit which species or classes may be collected.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill changes rules governing collection of wild animals and birds.

locations.name: Public roads and rights-of-way
locations.explanation: The collection provision applies to wildlife killed in a collision on a public road or right-of-way.

affected_groups.group: People collecting wildlife for human consumption
affected_groups.explanation: They could collect qualifying animals or birds killed in an unintentional motor vehicle collision, subject to the bill’s conditions and applicable rules.

affected_groups.group: Wild animals and birds killed in unintentional motor vehicle collisions
affected_groups.explanation: The bill makes eligible animals and birds collectable for human consumption if they are in edible condition and other requirements are met.

major_effects.label: Allows collection of qualifying collision-killed wildlife
major_effects.explanation: A person may collect qualifying wildlife for human consumption if it is in edible condition and collection complies with applicable commission rules.

major_effects.label: Authorizes collection rules and species limits
major_effects.explanation: The commission may establish additional procedures and requirements and limit the species or classes that may be collected.

agencies.name: commission
agencies.explanation: The bill expressly gives the “commission” rulemaking authority, but the supplied sources do not identify which canonical state body that term means.

HB487.summary: The bill would allow an emergency response official to send an emergency geofencing message directing automated motor vehicles under an authorization to leave or avoid an identified area. The authorization holder would have to direct those vehicles accordingly within two minutes and provide the official with necessary message information within 30 business days after notice of the official’s intent to begin issuing messages; messages must state an initial duration, which an official may extend when necessary.

policy_tags.explanation: Creates emergency routing requirements for automated motor vehicles operating under an authorization.
Empowers emergency response officials to direct automated vehicles away from an area during an emergency.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The bill adds a provision to the Texas Transportation Code without limiting it to a particular place in Texas.

affected_groups.group: Authorization holders for automated motor vehicles
affected_groups.explanation: They would have to direct vehicles under their authorization to leave or avoid an identified area and provide information needed for emergency messaging.

affected_groups.group: Emergency response officials
affected_groups.explanation: They could issue emergency geofencing messages and, when necessary, extend the avoidance duration.

major_effects.label: Emergency geofencing authority and response
major_effects.explanation: Emergency response officials could issue messages directing vehicles to leave or avoid an area; authorization holders would have to transmit the directive within two minutes. The message must set an initial duration, which officials may extend when necessary.

major_effects.label: Emergency-message readiness
major_effects.explanation: After receiving notice that an official intends to begin issuing messages, an authorization holder would have to provide the information needed to issue, receive, and respond to them within 30 business days.

HB488.summary: HB 488 would amend Texas public-information law to expressly include an arrested person's name, charged offense, home address, and telephone number among basic information about an arrested person, an arrest, or a crime. It would require governmental bodies to promptly release requested basic information unless they seek to withhold it under another provision of the chapter, regardless of whether they request an attorney general decision about other responsive information.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill changes public-information disclosure duties for governmental bodies.

locations.name: Texas statewide
locations.explanation: The bill amends a provision of the Texas Government Code governing public information.

affected_groups.group: People requesting public information
affected_groups.explanation: Requesters would receive prompt release of basic information unless the governmental body seeks to withhold it under another provision of the chapter.

affected_groups.group: People who are arrested
affected_groups.explanation: Their names, charged offenses, home addresses, and telephone numbers are expressly included in basic information subject to the release rule.

major_effects.label: Prompt release of basic information
major_effects.explanation: Governmental bodies must promptly release requested basic information unless they seek to withhold it under another provision of the chapter; this applies regardless of an attorney general decision request concerning other information.

agencies.name: governmental body
agencies.explanation: The bill directly assigns the release duty to governmental bodies as a general statutory class; it does not name a specific state agency.

HB489.summary: HB 489 would direct the Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts to administer a rebate program for rental households, supported by a special fund outside the state general revenue fund. A household would qualify only if it paid rent to the same landlord for all 12 calendar months of the year for which it applies and submits an application by a comptroller-set date; payments would be up to 10% of rent paid in the previous tax year, with total annual payments capped at half the fund balance. Landlords would have to file comptroller-prescribed certificates of rent paid.

policy_tags.explanation: Creates a rebate program designated as property tax relief, though it does not change property tax liability or assessment.
Establishes a state fund and authorizes its money to be appropriated for program administration and rebate payments.
Creates rent-based rebates for residential rental households and requires landlords to report rent paid.

locations.name: Texas
locations.explanation: The bill establishes a state-administered rebate program for eligible rental households without limiting it to a specific area.

affected_groups.group: Rental households
affected_groups.explanation: May apply for rebates if they meet the same-landlord, 12-month rent-payment condition and other application requirements.

affected_groups.group: Landlords
affected_groups.explanation: Must file certificates reporting the rent each rental household paid in the previous tax year.

major_effects.label: Rental-household rebate program
major_effects.explanation: Directs the comptroller to administer a program providing rebates to eligible rental households.

major_effects.label: Special state fund
major_effects.explanation: Creates a fund outside general revenue; money may be appropriated only for administering the program and making rebates, and annual payments are capped at half the fund balance.

major_effects.label: Rebate eligibility and amount
major_effects.explanation: Subject to Subsections (d)-(f), a rental household may receive a payment of up to 10% of rent paid during the previous tax year. The conditions include paying rent to the same landlord for all 12 calendar months of the year and applying by the comptroller-set date using the prescribed form.

major_effects.label: Landlord rent certificates
major_effects.explanation: Requires landlords to file certificates with the comptroller reporting each rental household's rent for the previous tax year.

agencies.name: Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts
agencies.explanation: Must administer the rebate program and fund, make payments, and prescribe forms and the application date.

HB490.summary: HB 490 would extend the term of a county ethics commission chair from six months to one year. The change would apply only to chairs selected on or after the Act’s effective date; earlier selections would remain governed by the prior law.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill changes the term of a chair serving on a county ethics commission.

locations.name: Texas
locations.explanation: The bill addresses county ethics commissions without limiting the change to a particular county.

affected_groups.group: County ethics commission chairs
affected_groups.explanation: Chairs selected on or after the effective date would serve one-year terms; prior selections remain under the former law.

major_effects.label: Extends chair term
major_effects.explanation: Changes the county ethics commission chair’s term from six months to one year for chairs selected on or after the effective date.

HB491.summary: The bill changes quantity limits for emergency refills of insulin and insulin-related equipment or supplies. An insulin refill may exceed a 30-day supply only if the smallest commercially available package exceeds that amount; pharmacists may dispense multiple packages if their total does not exceed 30 days. Equipment or supplies are limited to the smallest commercially available package necessary for a 30-day supply.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes quantity limits for emergency refills of insulin and related equipment or supplies.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The bill amends Texas law and applies to emergency refills under that law statewide.

affected_groups.group: People seeking emergency refills of insulin
affected_groups.explanation: The bill changes the amount of insulin that may be dispensed in an emergency refill.

affected_groups.group: Pharmacists
affected_groups.explanation: The bill expressly allows pharmacists to dispense multiple insulin packages for an emergency refill when the total is no more than a 30-day supply.

affected_groups.group: People seeking emergency refills of insulin-related equipment or supplies
affected_groups.explanation: The bill sets the refill limit by reference to the smallest commercially available package necessary for a 30-day supply.

major_effects.label: Emergency refill quantity limits
major_effects.explanation: Changes the permitted package quantities for emergency insulin refills, including an exception when the smallest commercially available package exceeds 30 days and permission to use multiple packages totaling no more than 30 days. For insulin-related equipment or supplies, sets the limit at the smallest commercially available package necessary for a 30-day supply.

HB492.summary: Beginning with the 2027–28 school year, school districts and open-enrollment charter schools would be limited in how they use school-provided devices during instructional time, with exceptions for educational calculators in math and participation in hybrid or virtual courses. The bill directs the agency to adopt device and software standards addressing student data, parental consent, online safety, and required filtering. For bonds issued on or after September 1, 2027, school bond proceeds could not fund acquisition or updates of electronic devices for a student's exclusive use.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes student use of school-provided devices, requirements for school technology, and school bond authority.
Requires standards addressing student data collection, parental consent for software use, and filtering of school-provided devices.
Imposes duties on school districts and limits bond authority exercised by school district governing bodies and certain local entities acting for districts.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The amendments apply to school districts and open-enrollment charter schools under statewide Education Code provisions.

affected_groups.group: Students using school-provided electronic devices
affected_groups.explanation: Their device use during instructional time would be limited, subject to exceptions for math calculators and hybrid or virtual participation.

affected_groups.group: Parents of students using school devices or software
affected_groups.explanation: They would receive consent protections for most student software use and resources about cybersecurity and online safety.

affected_groups.group: School districts, open-enrollment charter schools, and local entities issuing district bonds
affected_groups.explanation: Schools would have device-related standards and filtering requirements, while certain entities' authority to issue bonds for student devices would be restricted.

major_effects.label: Device and software standards
major_effects.explanation: Requires the agency to adopt standards that minimize student data collection and require direct, informed parental consent for software use, except for applications necessary to administer specified assessments. Standards must also require filtering on devices provided to students.

major_effects.label: Limits on instructional-time device use
major_effects.explanation: Restricts instructional-time use of school-provided devices to specified technology-related instruction and bars their use for foundation-curriculum instruction; the restrictions do not apply to educational calculators in math courses or devices used to attend hybrid or virtual classes.

major_effects.label: Restriction on bond-financed student devices
major_effects.explanation: For bonds issued on or after September 1, 2027, the specified school-bond authority may not be used to acquire or update a device for a student's exclusive use.

agencies.name: Texas Education Agency
agencies.explanation: The bill directs the agency to adopt standards for permissible devices and software. The source does not identify the agency's canonical name.

HB493.summary: The bill expands eligibility for optional tuition-exemption scholarships at public institutions of higher education to include Texas residents who are highest-ranking graduates of U.S. Department of Defense-operated high schools, while retaining eligibility for highest-ranking graduates of accredited Texas high schools. The exemption covers both semesters of the first regular session after graduation; an institution president may approve an exemption for any one of the first four regular sessions when individual circumstances warrant, and the changes apply beginning with the 2027–2028 academic year.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes eligibility for tuition-exemption scholarships at public institutions of higher education.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: Eligibility includes graduates of accredited high schools in Texas and, for Department of Defense-operated high schools, Texas residents.

affected_groups.group: Texas residents who are highest-ranking graduates of U.S. Department of Defense-operated high schools
affected_groups.explanation: The bill adds these graduates to the students who may qualify for the tuition exemption.

affected_groups.group: Highest-ranking graduates of accredited Texas high schools
affected_groups.explanation: They remain eligible under the amended provision.

affected_groups.group: Public institutions of higher education
affected_groups.explanation: Their governing boards may issue the scholarships that provide the tuition exemption.

major_effects.label: Expanded eligibility for tuition exemptions
major_effects.explanation: Adds Texas-resident highest-ranking graduates of Department of Defense-operated high schools to those who may receive an optional exemption; the existing category of highest-ranking graduates of accredited Texas high schools remains eligible.

major_effects.label: Timing and discretionary exception retained
major_effects.explanation: The exemption generally covers both semesters of the first regular session after graduation, but may be granted for any one of the first four regular sessions when the institution president considers the individual circumstances to merit it.

HB494.summary: For first-time freshman admissions, general academic teaching institutions must consider an appropriate standardized test along with one or more listed socioeconomic indicators or factors. Graduate and professional programs at those institutions and medical or dental units must consider an appropriate test, but may not use it as the sole consideration or as the primary reason to end consideration; they must compare scores with applicants from similar socioeconomic backgrounds when those backgrounds can be properly identified. These admissions changes apply beginning with the 2028 fall semester, with an exception for English-proficiency tests used for students who graduated from a foreign institution of higher education.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes standardized-test consideration requirements for undergraduate, graduate, and professional admissions at specified public higher education institutions and units.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The admissions requirements apply to each institution within the specified Texas statutory categories, rather than to a named place or limited geographic area.

affected_groups.group: First-time freshman applicants to general academic teaching institutions
affected_groups.explanation: Their standardized-test performance and listed socioeconomic indicators or factors must be considered in admissions decisions.

affected_groups.group: Applicants to graduate or professional programs at general academic teaching institutions and medical or dental units
affected_groups.explanation: Their test performance must be considered, subject to limits on its use and a socioeconomic-background comparison when backgrounds can be properly identified.

major_effects.label: Undergraduate admissions test consideration
major_effects.explanation: Requires each general academic teaching institution to consider an appropriate standardized test in first-time freshman admissions, in addition to considering one or more listed socioeconomic indicators or factors.

major_effects.label: Graduate and professional admissions test consideration
major_effects.explanation: Requires consideration of an appropriate standardized test, bars its use as the sole criterion or primary criterion to end consideration, and requires comparison with similarly situated applicants when their backgrounds can be properly identified. The requirement does not apply to specified English-proficiency tests.

major_effects.label: Admissions applicability begins in fall 2028
major_effects.explanation: The amendments apply beginning with admissions for the 2028 fall semester; earlier academic periods remain governed by prior law.

HB495.summary: For municipal utility districts wholly or partly in a county bordering Mexico that contains a municipality with more than 500,000 people, the bill generally requires directors to be at least 18, a resident citizen of Texas, and a qualified voter in the district. A nonvoter may serve if fewer than 50 percent of the district’s retail water or sewer connections are residential and no qualified-voter candidate filed for each board position by the specified deadline. The new rule applies to members elected or appointed on or after the effective date; current members may finish their terms and may be reelected or reappointed if they meet the new qualifications.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes qualifications for directors of municipal utility districts in the specified counties.
Changes who may serve as a director by imposing a district-voter qualification, subject to an exception tied to candidate filings.

locations.name: Counties bordering the United Mexican States that contain a municipality with a population over 500,000
locations.explanation: The new qualification rule applies to districts wholly or partly located in counties meeting both criteria.

affected_groups.group: Prospective directors and candidates for municipal utility district boards in the covered counties
affected_groups.explanation: They generally must be qualified voters in the district, with a limited exception for nonvoters.

affected_groups.group: Municipal utility districts in the covered counties with fewer than 50 percent residential retail water or sewer connections
affected_groups.explanation: These districts may use the nonvoter exception if no qualified-voter candidate files for every board position by the stated deadline.

major_effects.label: Director qualifications in covered districts
major_effects.explanation: Directors generally must be qualified voters in the district and meet the referenced age and Texas-residency requirements. A nonvoter may serve only if fewer than half of the district’s retail water or sewer connections are residential and no qualified-voter candidate filed for each board position by the specified deadline.

major_effects.label: Prospective application and incumbent transition
major_effects.explanation: The new rule applies to members elected or appointed on or after the effective date. Members already serving may complete their terms and may be reelected or reappointed if they meet the new qualifications.

HB496.summary: HB 496 would create a franchise-tax credit for taxable entities operating licensed child-care centers, each certified as a provider in the Texas Rising Star Program. The credit would be based on additional salaries associated with center-capacity increases, with the percentage rising from 50% to 75% to 100% as the increase reaches the specified thresholds.

policy_tags.explanation: Creates a franchise-tax credit for eligible child-care center operators.

locations.name: Texas
locations.explanation: The bill describes the intended increase in child-care availability statewide.

affected_groups.group: Taxable entities operating licensed child-care centers, including members of affiliated groups filing a combined report
affected_groups.explanation: These entities may qualify for and claim the credit if they meet the program and capacity conditions.

affected_groups.group: Children and families seeking child care in Texas
affected_groups.explanation: They are intended to benefit from increased child-care availability, though the credit is provided to taxable entities.

major_effects.label: Franchise-tax credit for increased child-care capacity
major_effects.explanation: Provides a credit based on additional salaries associated with capacity increases of at least 25%, with higher credit percentages for larger increases. The credit cannot exceed franchise tax due after other applicable credits.

major_effects.label: Eligibility and capacity conditions
major_effects.explanation: Requires each operated center to be licensed, certified, or registered by the Department of Family and Protective Services and certified in Texas Rising Star. Combined-report groups use a test based on at least half of their locations; a credit may continue on the next two reports only if the capacity increase is maintained.

major_effects.label: Credit application with tax report
major_effects.explanation: Requires an entity to apply on or with the report for which it claims the credit and provide information requested to determine eligibility.

major_effects.label: Implementation rules
major_effects.explanation: Requires the comptroller to adopt rules to implement and administer the credit.

agencies.name: Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts
agencies.explanation: Must prescribe the credit application process and adopt rules to implement and administer the credit.

agencies.name: Department of Family and Protective Services
agencies.explanation: The department's licensing, certification, or registration status is part of the definition of an eligible child-care center; the bill assigns it no new duty.

HB497.summary: HB 497 would require covered health benefit plans, including county employee plans and local-government risk-pool coverage, to cover treatment of qualifying employed or volunteer first responders’ injuries without excluding care because the injury may be work-related or workers’ compensation-eligible. After an initial workers’ compensation denial, the health plan would pay the provider; if the carrier later accepts the claim, it would reimburse the plan and the responder for copayments or deductibles. The requirements would apply to plans delivered, issued, or renewed on or after January 1, 2028, and the Division of Workers’ Compensation would study the changes and report to the Legislature.

policy_tags.explanation: Requires covered health benefit plans to cover treatment of qualifying first responders’ injuries and establishes how treatment claims are paid.
Changes how workers’ compensation carriers reimburse health plans and injured first responders for work-related injury treatment.
Expressly applies the coverage requirements to county employee group health benefits and health and accident coverage provided by local-government risk pools.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The provisions address qualifying plans and first responders across Texas, including those employed by or volunteering for political subdivisions of the state.

affected_groups.group: Qualifying employed and volunteer first responders
affected_groups.explanation: Their injury treatment may not be excluded from covered health benefit plans solely because the injury is work-related or may be compensable under workers’ compensation.

affected_groups.group: Health benefit plan issuers
affected_groups.explanation: Covered issuers must pay providers after the required initial workers’ compensation denial and may later receive reimbursement from the carrier.

affected_groups.group: Workers’ compensation insurance carriers
affected_groups.explanation: A carrier that later accepts a denied first responder claim must reimburse the health plan and the responder’s copayments or deductibles.

affected_groups.group: County and local-government health benefit plans
affected_groups.explanation: The bill expressly includes county employee group health benefits and coverage provided by local-government risk pools.

major_effects.label: Required coverage for first-responder injuries
major_effects.explanation: Covered plans may not exclude injury treatment because the injury was or may have been sustained in the course and scope of first-responder employment; this includes volunteer services.

major_effects.label: Interim payment and reimbursement
major_effects.explanation: After an initial workers’ compensation denial, the plan pays the provider regardless of the final compensability decision. If the carrier later accepts the claim, it reimburses the plan and the responder’s copayment or deductible; the carrier’s reimbursement to the insurer is based on the actual amount paid for treatment.

major_effects.label: Study and report to the Legislature
major_effects.explanation: The Division of Workers’ Compensation must study the changes, including plan efficiency and geographic areas where coverage was successful, and report its findings and recommendations to the Legislature.

agencies.name: Texas Department of Insurance
agencies.explanation: Its Division of Workers’ Compensation is assigned a study and legislative-reporting duty.

HB498.summary: HB 498 would allow a local-option election in an area where off-premise liquor sales are already legal to prohibit or approve Sunday sales of liquor for off-premise consumption. Where Sunday sales are approved, package stores could sell from 10 a.m. to 9 p.m., wholesalers could sell to retailers anytime Sunday, and local distributors could sell to retailers from 5 a.m. to 9 p.m.

policy_tags.explanation: Creates a local-option election on Sunday off-premise liquor sales and specifies the ballot issue.
Changes when specified liquor permit holders may sell or deliver liquor on Sunday in areas approving those sales.

locations.name: Areas where off-premise liquor sales are legalized, subject to approval of Sunday sales by local-option election
locations.explanation: The election option is available where off-premise liquor sales are already legal; the Sunday sale permissions apply only where voters approve them.

affected_groups.group: Voters in areas where off-premise liquor sales are legalized
affected_groups.explanation: They may vote to prohibit or legalize Sunday off-premise liquor sales.

affected_groups.group: Package store permit holders, liquor wholesalers, and local distributors
affected_groups.explanation: In areas approving Sunday sales, the bill permits Sunday sales or deliveries by these permit holders within specified hours or, for wholesalers, at any time Sunday.

major_effects.label: Local-option election on Sunday liquor sales
major_effects.explanation: Allows a local-option election in areas where off-premise liquor sales are already legal and specifies the ballot issue.

major_effects.label: Sunday sale and delivery permissions
major_effects.explanation: In areas approving Sunday sales, authorizes Sunday sales by package stores and Sunday sales to retailers by wholesalers and local distributors, with different hours for each.

HB499.summary: HB 499 would expressly require proceedings under Article 15.17 to be public, alongside proceedings and trials in all courts. It would apply only to criminal proceedings commencing on or after its effective date; earlier proceedings would remain governed by prior law.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill changes the public-trial requirement for criminal proceedings.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The public-proceedings requirement applies to proceedings and trials in all courts under the Texas Code of Criminal Procedure.

affected_groups.group: People participating in or observing criminal proceedings
affected_groups.explanation: The bill would make the specified proceedings public.

affected_groups.group: Courts
affected_groups.explanation: Courts would be subject to the public-proceedings requirement.

major_effects.label: Public access to criminal proceedings
major_effects.explanation: Would expressly include Article 15.17 proceedings in the requirement that proceedings and trials in all courts be public.

agencies.name: all courts
agencies.explanation: The bill directly applies a public-proceedings requirement to courts, but it does not identify a particular court or canonical state body.

HB501.summary: The bill requires the comptroller to apply taxpayer payments to tax due before penalties or interest, unless the taxpayer gives written instructions for a different application. It changes delinquent-tax and tax-report penalties to a five-percent penalty unless another law provides a lower amount, and limits penalties imposed for failure to pay a tax or file a report when due to the amounts specified in the applicable subsections.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes how tax payments are applied and limits penalties for delinquent taxes and tax reports.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The bill amends Texas Tax Code provisions governing tax payments and penalties statewide.

affected_groups.group: Taxpayers who owe taxes or must file tax reports
affected_groups.explanation: Their payments may be applied to tax before penalties or interest, and penalties for late payment or filing are limited as specified.

major_effects.label: Tax-payment application
major_effects.explanation: Payments must go to tax due before penalties or interest unless the taxpayer gives written instructions for another application.

major_effects.label: Delinquent-tax and report penalties
major_effects.explanation: Sets a five-percent penalty unless another law provides a lower amount and limits the penalty to the applicable amounts in the specified subsections.

agencies.name: Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts
agencies.explanation: The bill directly directs the comptroller how to apply taxpayer payments.

HB502.summary: HB 502 directs the Railroad Commission of Texas to study whether abandoned or inactive oil and gas wells in Bexar County could feasibly be converted to geothermal energy production, including costs, potential uses, environmental and groundwater impacts, and possible pilot-program recommendations. The Commission must submit its findings and recommendations to the Legislature by December 1, 2028; the bill recommends but does not establish a pilot program, and the Act expires January 1, 2029.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill requires a feasibility study focused on converting oil and gas wells to geothermal energy production.

locations.name: Bexar County
locations.explanation: The study is specifically about wells located in Bexar County.

affected_groups.group: Owners or operators of abandoned or inactive oil and gas wells in Bexar County
affected_groups.explanation: The study considers ownership and liability concerns related to converting the wells; the bill does not impose new duties on owners or operators.

major_effects.label: Geothermal feasibility study
major_effects.explanation: Requires an assessment of well suitability, conversion costs, potential uses, impacts, barriers, and recommendations, including options for a possible pilot program.

major_effects.label: Report to the Legislature
major_effects.explanation: Requires the Commission to submit a written report of study findings and recommendations by December 1, 2028.

agencies.name: Railroad Commission of Texas
agencies.explanation: The Act defines the Commission as the Railroad Commission of Texas and assigns it the study and reporting duties.

HB503.summary: HB 503 would require the Commission on State Emergency Communications to establish and administer grants for nonprofit organizations, regional planning commissions, and emergency communication districts providing emergency communications services, including 9-1-1, to end users in Texas. The commission would set grant application, eligibility, selection, use-approval, and accountability procedures, and could accept gifts, grants, and donations to administer and finance the program.

policy_tags.explanation: The grant program supports emergency communications services, including 9-1-1 service.
The bill creates a grant program funded from money appropriated or otherwise available and permits the commission to accept additional funding.
Regional planning commissions and emergency communication districts are expressly eligible for assistance through the grant program.

locations.name: Texas
locations.explanation: The program concerns emergency communications services for end users in this state.

affected_groups.group: Nonprofit organizations, regional planning commissions, and emergency communication districts
affected_groups.explanation: These entities may receive grants to assist with providing emergency communications services.

affected_groups.group: End users of emergency communications services in Texas
affected_groups.explanation: They are the in-state beneficiaries of services supported by the grants.

major_effects.label: Emergency communications grants
major_effects.explanation: Requires the commission to establish and administer grants to assist eligible entities in providing emergency communications services, including 9-1-1.

major_effects.label: Grant procedures and controls
major_effects.explanation: Requires rules for applications, eligibility and selection, approval of grant-money use, and recipient accountability.

major_effects.label: Program funding sources
major_effects.explanation: The program may use money appropriated or otherwise available for it, and the commission may accept gifts, grants, or donations to administer and finance it.

agencies.name: Commission on State Emergency Communications
agencies.explanation: The bill assigns the commission responsibility for administering the program and establishing its rules. Section 2 identifies the commission as the Commission on State Emergency Communications; no canonical registry entry is supported by the supplied vocabulary.

HB504.summary: The bill would require the Texas Secretary of State to publish two public online databases covering elections and candidates or officeholders for partisan offices, mayors, city governing bodies, and independent school district trustee boards. Counties, political parties, cities, school districts, and other listed election authorities would submit or forward specified information, including public contact details; an officeholder’s name, office, and party affiliation would remain posted while the person holds office.

policy_tags.explanation: Creates public databases and information-submission requirements for specified elections, candidates, and officeholders.
Requires online publication of databases that include candidates’ and officeholders’ public contact information.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The candidate and officeholder database covers the specified offices in this state.

affected_groups.group: Candidates and officeholders for covered offices
affected_groups.explanation: Their election, office, and specified public contact information would be included in the public database.

affected_groups.group: Counties and political parties
affected_groups.explanation: They must provide election or candidate information to the Secretary of State, and counties forward information received from political subdivisions.

affected_groups.group: Cities, school districts, and other political subdivisions
affected_groups.explanation: They must provide covered election and candidate information to the county where they are located.

affected_groups.group: Members of the public
affected_groups.explanation: They would be able to view the election and candidate or officeholder databases on the Secretary of State’s public website.

major_effects.label: Public election and candidate databases
major_effects.explanation: Requires the Secretary of State to publish election information and information about covered candidates and officeholders online.

major_effects.label: Election and candidate information submissions
major_effects.explanation: Requires listed election authorities and political subdivisions to provide specified information, with counties forwarding information they receive.

major_effects.label: Implementation rules
major_effects.explanation: Directs the Secretary of State to adopt rules as necessary to implement the database requirements.

agencies.name: Texas Secretary of State
agencies.explanation: The Secretary of State must publish the databases and adopt rules to implement them.

HB505.summary: HB505 would remove the requirement that an actor be of the opposite sex from the victim to qualify for the age-proximity affirmative defense to indecency with a child; the defense’s other requirements would remain. The change would apply to covered offenses and pending criminal actions, but would not affect final convictions.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill changes eligibility for an affirmative defense to a criminal offense.

locations.name: Texas
locations.explanation: The bill amends Texas Penal Code provisions with statewide application.

affected_groups.group: People prosecuted for indecency with a child who may qualify for the affirmative defense
affected_groups.explanation: Actors meeting the defense’s age and other requirements would no longer be excluded solely because they are not the opposite sex from the victim.

major_effects.label: Affirmative-defense eligibility
major_effects.explanation: Removes the opposite-sex condition from the age-proximity affirmative defense; the age limit and other defense requirements remain.

major_effects.label: Application to pending cases
major_effects.explanation: The change would apply to offenses committed on or after the effective date and pending criminal actions, but not final convictions.

HB506.summary: The bill would allow representatives of specified institutions, as defined by TCEQ rules, and people residing within 440 yards of a proposed concrete plant to request a public hearing; it removes the former requirement that nearby residents be residing in a permanent residence. The change would apply only to permit applications submitted on or after the effective date of TCEQ’s rules; earlier applications would remain governed by prior law.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes eligibility to request a public hearing in connection with a concrete-plant permit.

locations.name: Statewide, Texas
locations.explanation: The change governs TCEQ permit hearings across the state.

locations.name: Area within 440 yards of a proposed plant
locations.explanation: The bill identifies proximity to the proposed plant as a geographic limit on resident hearing-request eligibility.

affected_groups.group: Representatives of schools, places of worship, licensed day-care centers, hospitals, and medical facilities, and people residing within 440 yards of a proposed plant
affected_groups.explanation: These people may request a hearing as persons who may be affected; TCEQ rules will establish which institutional representatives qualify.

affected_groups.group: Applicants for covered permits to construct concrete plants
affected_groups.explanation: Expanded hearing-request eligibility may affect hearings on their permit applications, but only for applications submitted after the rules take effect.

major_effects.label: Expanded hearing-request eligibility
major_effects.explanation: Adds qualifying representatives of specified institutions and removes the permanent-residence requirement for nearby residents. The change applies only to permit applications submitted on or after the effective date of the rules.

major_effects.label: Rules defining qualifying representatives
major_effects.explanation: Requires TCEQ to establish by rule who qualifies as a representative of the listed institutions.

agencies.name: Texas Commission on Environmental Quality
agencies.explanation: TCEQ is directly required to adopt rules establishing who qualifies as a representative of the listed institutions.

HB507.summary: HB 507 would bar state agencies and political subdivisions from requiring employees or independent contractors to test for cannabinoids or have a negative cannabinoid test as a condition of employment or contract, and from prohibiting specified low-THC cannabis or consumable hemp use. The chapter would not apply to covered peace officers or employees subject to federal DOT drug-testing rules; it would also restrict inquiries about employees’ use, provide legal remedies and waive governmental immunity to the extent of those remedies. The bill applies only to administration of a covered policy or drug test on or after its effective date.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes employment and contracting conditions by restricting cannabinoid testing requirements and certain restrictions on employee and contractor conduct.
The restrictions and related duties apply to political subdivisions of Texas as well as state agencies.
Regulates drug-testing, prescription-drug, and privacy policies of state agencies.
Adds a restriction on asking employees about low-THC cannabis or hemp use and requires compliance with relevant privacy laws.

locations.name: Texas
locations.explanation: The provisions apply to state agencies and political subdivisions of this state.

affected_groups.group: Employees and independent contractors of state agencies and political subdivisions
affected_groups.explanation: Their covered employers or contracting entities would be restricted from requiring cannabinoid testing or specified negative test results as a condition of employment or contract. The chapter excludes covered peace officers and employees subject to federal DOT testing rules.

affected_groups.group: Employees using low-THC cannabis or consumable hemp products
affected_groups.explanation: Employers and contracting entities could not prohibit the specified use as a condition of employment or contract; the low-THC cannabis provision is limited to use in accordance with the cited law.

affected_groups.group: State agencies and political subdivisions as employers and contracting entities
affected_groups.explanation: They would need to conform covered policies and could face claims and relief for violations.

major_effects.label: Limits on testing and employment policies
major_effects.explanation: Prohibits covered public employers from requiring cannabinoid screening or negative results and from prohibiting the specified low-THC cannabis or consumable hemp use as a condition of employment or contract. The chapter’s exceptions apply.

major_effects.label: Medical-use privacy
major_effects.explanation: Prohibits covered public entities from questioning employees about low-THC cannabis or hemp use and requires compliance with relevant state and federal privacy laws.

major_effects.label: Claims, relief, and immunity waiver
major_effects.explanation: Allows a person to assert actual or threatened violations in judicial or administrative proceedings and seek specified relief without first exhausting administrative remedies; waives sovereign or governmental immunity to the extent of liability for that relief.

agencies.name: state agency
agencies.explanation: The bill directly restricts state agencies’ employment and contracting policies and imposes a privacy-related duty, but identifies no particular agency.

HB508.summary: The bill would let vehicle registration applicants voluntarily indicate that they may transport a person with a disability, and require the registration department to send the related vehicle registration information—but not the type of disability—to the Department of Public Safety (DPS). DPS would add the information to the Texas Law Enforcement Telecommunications System to alert a peace officer during a traffic stop; the information would be confidential, and a visible plate marking could not be issued without the person's consent. The bill also restricts disclosure by system contractors and limits renewal of certain existing contracts unless they include the required nondisclosure prohibition.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes vehicle registration applications and the handling of registration information.
Creates limits on the sharing, disclosure, and system access of sensitive information about people with disabilities.
Requires a system that can alert peace officers during traffic stops that a vehicle operator may be transporting a person with a disability.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The registration and DPS system provisions apply statewide; the bill specifies no narrower geographic area.

affected_groups.group: Vehicle owners who may transport a person with a disability
affected_groups.explanation: May voluntarily make the registration indication and are covered by the information and visible-marking protections.

affected_groups.group: People with disabilities who may be transported
affected_groups.explanation: Their possible presence may be signaled to an officer, while information about the type of disability is restricted.

affected_groups.group: Peace officers making traffic stops
affected_groups.explanation: May receive an alert that the vehicle operator may be transporting a person with a disability.

affected_groups.group: Persons with contractual access to the Texas Law Enforcement Telecommunications System
affected_groups.explanation: Access to this information is conditioned on a contract prohibiting its disclosure to people outside the contract.

major_effects.label: Voluntary disability-transport indication
major_effects.explanation: Registration applications must allow applicants to voluntarily indicate that they may transport a person with a disability; the department may request a personal attestation.

major_effects.label: Traffic-stop alert system
major_effects.explanation: DPS must include the received registration information in the state law-enforcement telecommunications system so an officer making a traffic stop can be alerted.

major_effects.label: Confidentiality and disclosure limits
major_effects.explanation: Restricts disclosure of disability-related information, subject to the exception in Subsection (e); limits what DPS makes available through the system to covered contract users, bars a visible plate marking without consent, and requires a nondisclosure term in covered system-access contracts. Certain existing contracts may continue only for their current term and may not be renewed unless the renewed contract includes the required prohibition.

agencies.name: Texas Department of Public Safety
agencies.explanation: Must establish the alert system and receive registration information. Information may be made available to a person accessing the system under contract only if the contract prohibits disclosure to a person not subject to the contract.

agencies.name: Texas Department of Motor Vehicles
agencies.explanation: The bill assigns the registration application, information-transfer, and confidentiality duties to “the department,” but the supplied text does not verify the entity's canonical identity.

HB509.summary: The bill would require providers of covered subscription services to disclose contract terms and cancellation procedures, offer cancellation by the method used to sign up, and give advance renewal notice for certain contracts lasting at least 12 months; insurance offerings and specified insurance coverage are excluded. It would bar private suits under the chapter while allowing the attorney general to seek civil penalties, injunctions, and restitution if a provider fails to cure an initial violation after notice or commits a further violation after curing. The requirements would apply only to contracts entered into or renewed on or after the Act’s effective date.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill would impose contract disclosure, renewal-notice, and cancellation requirements on businesses providing covered subscription services.
The bill would assign the attorney general notice, enforcement, and litigation functions for violations.

locations.name: Texas
locations.explanation: The bill provides for state enforcement and restitution for affected consumers who reside in Texas.

locations.name: Travis County
locations.explanation: A civil enforcement action may be brought in district court in Travis County.

locations.name: A county in which any part of the violation occurs
locations.explanation: The bill also allows an enforcement action in a county where any part of the violation occurs.

affected_groups.group: Consumers who enter into covered subscription service contracts
affected_groups.explanation: Consumers would receive contract and cancellation disclosures, additional notice for certain automatic renewals, and multiple cancellation methods, subject to Subsections (b) and (c).

affected_groups.group: Businesses providing subscription services to consumers
affected_groups.explanation: Covered service providers would have new disclosure, renewal-notice, and cancellation duties and could face civil penalties for violations.

major_effects.label: Subscription disclosures and cancellation
major_effects.explanation: Providers would have to disclose the contract’s nature and cancellation procedure, provide multiple cancellation methods including the signup method, and give advance notice for automatic renewal of qualifying longer-term contracts.

major_effects.label: Civil penalties and consumer remedies
major_effects.explanation: After a provider fails to cure an initial violation following notice, or commits a violation after curing and certifying the initial violation, the state may seek penalties; the attorney general may also seek injunctions or restitution. The bill bars private causes of action under the chapter and the referenced deceptive-trade-practices subchapter.

agencies.name: Office of the Attorney General
agencies.explanation: The attorney general must provide notice before bringing an action for an initial violation and may bring actions to recover penalties, obtain injunctions, or seek restitution.

HB510.summary: The bill would require developers who know or reasonably should know their AI system will be used in a high-risk way to provide and test human oversight mechanisms, and would require deployers of high-risk systems to maintain controls that let an authorized person intervene. Violations would be subject to Attorney General enforcement under Subchapter C; the Attorney General could seek temporary injunctive relief before notice only when continued operation presents an immediate and substantial risk of serious harm. The bill also protects good-faith reporters from retaliation.

policy_tags.explanation: Regulates high-risk artificial intelligence systems, including systems that could threaten information-system security or confidential information.
Creates compliance obligations for covered AI developers and deployers.
The covered systems include those capable of actions presenting a reasonably foreseeable risk of substantial harm to individuals' health or safety.
Prohibits covered developers and deployers from taking adverse personnel action against certain good-faith reporters and helpers.
Assigns the Department of Information Resources a technical consultation role in Attorney General evaluations of compliance.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The bill establishes generally applicable Texas requirements for covered developers and deployers; no narrower geographic area is specified.

affected_groups.group: Developers of AI systems intended for high-risk use
affected_groups.explanation: Covered when they know or reasonably should know their system will be used as a high-risk system.

affected_groups.group: Deployers and operators of high-risk AI systems
affected_groups.explanation: Covered when they deploy or operate a high-risk AI system and must implement and maintain oversight controls.

affected_groups.group: Authorized human operators
affected_groups.explanation: Operators designated by deployers must have the training, authority, and technical access needed to monitor and intervene in system actions.
