affected_groups.explanation: They may commit the new offense if they use another person's breath specimen and then drive without first providing their own.

affected_groups.group: People who provide breath specimens for another person's ignition-interlock device
affected_groups.explanation: They may commit the new offense if they knowingly provide a specimen while knowing the restricted driver intends to drive without providing their own.

major_effects.label: Creates ignition-interlock breath-specimen offenses
major_effects.explanation: Creates offenses for a restricted driver who uses another person's specimen and then drives without providing their own, and for a person who knowingly assists with that conduct.

major_effects.label: Sets offense classifications and penalties
major_effects.explanation: The driver's offense is generally a Class A misdemeanor, elevated to a third-degree felony in specified circumstances; the assisting offense is generally a Class C misdemeanor, elevated to a Class A misdemeanor for a prior conviction under that subsection.

HB812.summary: The bill would require licensed nursing facilities to maintain 72 hours of emergency power in a resident-support area, plus a separately powered area when the facility has an installed unit locking device; facilities would generally have to comply by September 1, 2028, and may seek one-year extensions, including up to two additional extensions. Landlords of multiunit complexes with more than 50 units, where at least 75 percent of units have an authorized resident age 55 or older, would have to provide a 72-hour emergency-power area; they are not required to comply before September 1, 2028. The bill also requires annual nursing-facility generator inspections and provides for civil penalties of up to $5,000 per violation for landlords, with each continuing day treated as a separate violation.

policy_tags.explanation: Adds emergency-power requirements and annual generator inspections for licensed nursing facilities.
Requires landlords of specified multiunit complexes to provide emergency power for older authorized residents.
Authorizes a county prosecuting attorney to bring an action to recover civil penalties and related expenses.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The requirements apply to covered Texas nursing facilities and multiunit complexes, without limiting them to a named locality.

locations.name: County in which the violation occurs
locations.explanation: The county where a violation occurs determines which county prosecuting attorney may bring a penalty action.

affected_groups.group: Nursing facility operators
affected_groups.explanation: Must equip facilities with the required emergency power and fuel, subject to the stated compliance timeline and possible extensions.

affected_groups.group: Nursing facility residents
affected_groups.explanation: Would have access to designated emergency-powered areas during an outage, including an additional powered area in facilities with an installed unit locking device.

affected_groups.group: Landlords of qualifying multiunit complexes
affected_groups.explanation: Must provide an operational generator or comparable power source and fuel for a qualifying resident-support area.

affected_groups.group: Authorized residents age 55 or older in qualifying multiunit complexes
affected_groups.explanation: The emergency-powered area must be sized and appropriate for their needs.

affected_groups.group: County prosecuting attorneys
affected_groups.explanation: May bring actions to recover the landlord civil penalty and reasonable enforcement expenses.

major_effects.label: Nursing-facility emergency power
major_effects.explanation: Requires 72-hour emergency power in a resident-support area and, for facilities with an installed unit locking device, an additional separately powered area. Compliance is generally due by September 1, 2028; facilities may request one-year extensions, with no more than two additional one-year extensions.

major_effects.label: Emergency power at qualifying multiunit complexes
major_effects.explanation: Requires a 72-hour emergency-power area at complexes with more than 50 units where at least 75 percent of units meet the bill's age-55 occupancy threshold. Landlords are not required to comply before September 1, 2028.

major_effects.label: Nursing-facility inspections and checklist
major_effects.explanation: Requires annual inspections of nursing-facility emergency power sources and a rule-prescribed inspection checklist.

major_effects.label: Civil penalties for landlord violations
major_effects.explanation: A landlord may be liable for up to $5,000 for each violation; each day a violation continues is a separate violation. The attorney general or the county prosecuting attorney may bring the recovery action.

agencies.name: Health and Human Services Commission
agencies.explanation: The executive commissioner is expressly assigned rulemaking to implement the nursing-facility requirements, including the inspection checklist.

agencies.name: Office of the Attorney General
agencies.explanation: May bring an action to recover the civil penalty and related expenses for a landlord's violation.

HB813.summary: The bill would expand the definition of bullying to include targeting a student because of specified actual or perceived characteristics, and would expressly include artificial-intelligence applications among tools used for cyberbullying. It would require school districts to use more detailed investigation procedures and provide individualized supportive measures, and would expand incident reporting; the changes apply beginning with the 2027-2028 school year.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes public-school bullying definitions, district policies, investigations, student supports, and reporting.
Adds specified actual or perceived characteristics as a basis that can make conduct bullying.
Assigns school districts new policy, reporting, investigation, and student-support duties.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The requirements apply to each school district and covered open-enrollment charter school in Texas.

affected_groups.group: Students impacted by bullying, including alleged victims, students alleged to have engaged in bullying, and witnesses
affected_groups.explanation: They are covered by investigation procedures and individualized supportive measures.

affected_groups.group: School districts and open-enrollment charter schools
affected_groups.explanation: Districts must revise policies and provide supports; districts and charter schools are subject to expanded incident reporting.

affected_groups.group: School district employees
affected_groups.explanation: Employees must report qualifying bullying information they witness or receive in the course and scope of employment.

major_effects.label: Expanded bullying definitions
major_effects.explanation: Adds targeting based on specified actual or perceived characteristics as a bullying criterion and expressly includes AI applications among electronic communication tools for cyberbullying.

major_effects.label: District investigation procedures
major_effects.explanation: Requires notice, opportunities to provide information and review findings, an investigative report, and an appeal opportunity for impacted students.

major_effects.label: Individualized student supports
major_effects.explanation: Requires districts to provide nonpunitive, individualized supportive measures designed to protect safety and preserve access to education; they must be free and provided regardless of whether a student participates in an investigation.

major_effects.label: Bullying reporting requirements
major_effects.explanation: Adds employee reporting duties and requires annual campus-level incident counts to distinguish cyberbullying and incidents based on specified actual or perceived characteristics.

major_effects.label: Minimum standards
major_effects.explanation: Requires the Texas Education Agency to adopt or revise minimum standards for district bullying policies.

agencies.name: Texas Education Agency
agencies.explanation: Must adopt or revise minimum standards for school district bullying policies to comply with the bill.

HB814.summary: HB 814 would create civil liability for a person whose conduct constitutes the existing offense of female genital mutilation, allowing the victim to sue for resulting damages. A prevailing claimant could recover compensatory and exemplary damages, plus reasonable attorney’s fees and costs; the change would apply only to causes of action accruing on or after the Act’s effective date.

policy_tags.explanation: Adds a civil remedy for victims of female genital mutilation.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The bill amends Texas law and establishes a remedy under state law.

affected_groups.group: Victims of female genital mutilation
affected_groups.explanation: May bring an action for damages resulting from the mutilation.

affected_groups.group: People whose conduct constitutes the female genital mutilation offense
affected_groups.explanation: Would be subject to civil liability to the victim.

major_effects.label: Victim civil remedy
major_effects.explanation: Creates a civil claim against a person whose conduct constitutes the existing offense, for damages resulting from the mutilation.

major_effects.label: Recoverable damages and costs
major_effects.explanation: A prevailing claimant may recover compensatory and exemplary damages, as well as reasonable attorney’s fees and costs.

HB815.summary: The bill would authorize a municipality or county to invest up to $10 million of its own money or money under its control in Bitcoin or another cryptocurrency. The authorization would apply statewide.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill changes the investment authority of municipalities and counties.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The authorization applies generally to municipalities and counties in Texas.

affected_groups.group: Municipalities
affected_groups.explanation: Municipalities could invest up to $10 million of their money or money under their control in Bitcoin or another cryptocurrency.

affected_groups.group: Counties
affected_groups.explanation: Counties could invest up to $10 million of their money or money under their control in Bitcoin or another cryptocurrency.

major_effects.label: Cryptocurrency investment authority
major_effects.explanation: Would permit each municipality or county to invest up to $10 million of its own or controlled funds in Bitcoin or another cryptocurrency.

HB817.summary: The bill would require state officials and agencies to use “the people's money” when referring in covered official documents, publications, or notices to money held by the state or its officials or agencies that may be used only for a state public purpose, subject to the section's exceptions. One stated exception is for documents or publications concerning agency rules that must rely on statutory or constitutional phrasing for legal clarity.

policy_tags.explanation: Establishes a terminology requirement for state officials and agencies in qualifying official documents, publications, and notices.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The requirement concerns state-held money and documents issued by state officials or agencies.

affected_groups.group: State officials and state agencies
affected_groups.explanation: State officials and state agencies must use the specified phrase for covered references, subject to the section's exceptions. One stated exception is for documents or publications concerning agency rules that must use statutory or constitutional phrasing for legal clarity.

major_effects.label: Required terminology in state documents
major_effects.explanation: Requires “the people's money” in covered references to qualifying state-held money, with specified exceptions.

agencies.name: state agency
agencies.explanation: The bill directly imposes the terminology requirement on a state agency when it makes a covered reference, subject to the section's exceptions, including the stated exception for certain agency-rule materials needed for legal clarity.

HB818.summary: HB 818 would prohibit Texas governmental entities from entering agreements for civil immigration detention, renewing or extending them, or making specified increases to their term or capacity; it would also bar public money or property from being used for certain detention-facility purposes. State agencies could not provide financial assistance, including tax benefits, for those purposes. Agreements already in effect could continue until they expire under their terms, but the chapter would apply only to agreements entered into, renewed, extended, or modified on or after September 1, 2027.

policy_tags.explanation: Restricts governmental agreements and resources used for civil immigration detention, while distinguishing that detention from criminal custody.
The prohibitions cover political subdivisions, and the bill expressly addresses local entities' compliance.
Bars use of public money and state financial assistance, including grants and loans, for specified detention-facility purposes.
A state agency may not award a tax benefit for the specified detention-facility purposes.
Sets restrictions on governmental entities' agreements and use of controlled property, and authorizes the Attorney General to seek compliance by injunction.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The chapter covers state governmental bodies and political subdivisions of Texas.

affected_groups.group: State agencies and political subdivisions
affected_groups.explanation: These entities would face restrictions on detention agreements and use of public resources; state agencies would also be barred from awarding specified financial assistance.

affected_groups.group: People who may be held in civil immigration detention
affected_groups.explanation: The limits concern governmental arrangements for holding people in civil immigration detention; the bill does not prohibit criminal custody or federally operated detention at facilities that are not subject to a detention agreement.

major_effects.label: Restricts detention agreements
major_effects.explanation: Governmental entities could not enter detention agreements, renew or extend them, or make specified term or capacity increases. Existing agreements could run through their contractual expiration but could not be renewed, extended, or modified as specified.

major_effects.label: Restricts public resources and financial assistance
major_effects.explanation: Prohibits public spending or provision of controlled real property for specified detention-facility purposes and bars state financial assistance for those purposes.

major_effects.label: Authorizes injunctive enforcement
major_effects.explanation: The Attorney General may bring an action seeking an injunction to compel compliance.

agencies.name: Office of the Attorney General
agencies.explanation: The Attorney General is authorized to bring an action for injunctive relief to compel compliance.

agencies.name: state agency
agencies.explanation: The bill directly prohibits a state agency from awarding specified financial assistance; the source does not identify particular agencies by name.

HB819.summary: HB 819 would require counties and municipalities to use all defined surplus revenue from the preceding fiscal year for current-year property-tax relief that reduces property owners’ bills. It would also set a formula-based limit on local property-tax rates, with an exception when adopting a lower rate would impair a contract for previously pledged debt. The Comptroller would publish the inflation rate used in the calculations; the bill refers to an unidentified “board” to determine population growth.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill requires local surplus revenue to provide property-tax relief and limits county and municipal tax rates under a formula, subject to a debt-related exception.
The bill assigns revenue-use and tax-rate requirements to counties and municipalities and requires a designated local officer or employee to calculate and submit the rate.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The provisions apply to counties and municipalities generally, without limiting their application to a named place.

affected_groups.group: Counties and municipalities
affected_groups.explanation: Local governments must use defined surplus revenue for tax relief and comply with the new tax-rate limit, subject to the debt-related exception.

affected_groups.group: Property owners
affected_groups.explanation: The required local relief must reduce the ad valorem taxes property owners would otherwise pay.

major_effects.label: Surplus revenue required for property-tax relief
major_effects.explanation: Counties and municipalities must use all preceding-fiscal-year surplus revenue, defined by comparing receipts with the adopted budget adjusted for population growth and inflation, for current-year relief that lowers property owners’ tax bills.

major_effects.label: Formula-based local tax-rate limit
major_effects.explanation: A county or municipality may not adopt a rate above the formula limit, which uses prior-year receipts adjusted for population growth and inflation, estimated non-ad-valorem receipts, and current taxable value. A higher rate is allowed only where taxes were pledged for debt before adoption and a rate at or below the formula limit would impair the debt contract.

agencies.name: Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts
agencies.explanation: The Comptroller must determine and publish the state inflation rate used by the new provisions.

agencies.name: the board
agencies.explanation: The new definitions assign this body the determination of the state population growth rate, but the bill does not identify the body or establish that it is a particular state agency.

HB820.summary: The bill repeals the Texas Quantum Initiative. Any money appropriated to the initiative would instead go to the Texas Education Agency for the state fiscal biennium beginning September 1, 2027, to reduce the state compression percentage to the lowest possible percentage.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill repeals the Texas Quantum Initiative, a technology-focused initiative.
The bill directs initiative appropriations to the Texas Education Agency to reduce the state compression percentage under the Education Code.
The bill redirects money appropriated to the initiative to the Texas Education Agency for a specified state fiscal biennium.

locations.explanation: The funding direction concerns a state fiscal biennium and the state compression percentage.

affected_groups.group: Texas public school districts
affected_groups.explanation: The redirected funding is intended to reduce the state compression percentage under the Education Code, affecting state school-funding calculations.

major_effects.label: Repeal of the Texas Quantum Initiative
major_effects.explanation: Repeals the statutory subchapter governing the initiative.

major_effects.label: Redirects initiative appropriations to education funding
major_effects.explanation: Any money appropriated to the initiative is redirected to the Texas Education Agency for the biennium beginning September 1, 2027, to reduce the state compression percentage to the lowest possible percentage.

agencies.name: Texas Education Agency
agencies.explanation: The bill directs appropriated money to the agency for the specified state fiscal biennium.

HB821.summary: HB 821 would repeal Government Code Chapter 483, which established the Texas Advanced Nuclear Energy Office. It would require the comptroller to transfer any money appropriated to that office to the Texas Education Agency for the state fiscal biennium beginning September 1, 2027, to reduce the state compression percentage to the lowest possible percentage.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill repeals the statutory chapter for the Texas Advanced Nuclear Energy Office.
It redirects money appropriated to the office to the Texas Education Agency for a specified state fiscal biennium.
The transferred money is directed to reduce the state compression percentage under the Education Code.
The bill repeals the chapter associated with a named state office.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The bill concerns a state office and state-level funding, with no narrower geographic area specified.

affected_groups.group: Texas public education system
affected_groups.explanation: The transferred money is directed toward reducing the state compression percentage under the Education Code.

affected_groups.group: Texas advanced nuclear energy sector
affected_groups.explanation: The bill repeals the chapter associated with the Texas Advanced Nuclear Energy Office.

major_effects.label: Repeal of the Texas Advanced Nuclear Energy Office chapter
major_effects.explanation: Repeals Government Code Chapter 483, the chapter identified in the bill as added to establish the office.

major_effects.label: Transfer appropriated money to the Texas Education Agency
major_effects.explanation: The comptroller must transfer any money appropriated to the office to the agency for the state fiscal biennium beginning September 1, 2027, to reduce the state compression percentage to the lowest possible percentage.

agencies.name: Texas Advanced Nuclear Energy Office
agencies.explanation: The bill repeals the Government Code chapter associated with this named office; no canonical registry identity is supported by the supplied vocabulary.

agencies.name: Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts
agencies.explanation: The comptroller is assigned the transfer of appropriated money.

agencies.name: Texas Education Agency
agencies.explanation: The agency is designated to receive the transferred money for the stated school-finance purpose.

HB822.summary: HB 822 would repeal Subtitle E of Chapter 101A of the Health and Safety Code, the statutory framework associated with the Dementia Prevention and Research Institute of Texas. If voters approve the specified constitutional amendment, the comptroller would transfer any money appropriated to the institute to the Texas Education Agency to reduce the state compression percentage as far as possible; without voter approval, the Act has no effect.

policy_tags.explanation: Repeals the statutory framework for an institute devoted to dementia prevention and research.
Directs the transferred money to the Texas Education Agency for a change to the state compression percentage under the Education Code.
The transfer is directed toward reducing the state compression percentage, and the referenced constitutional amendment describes a related transfer for property tax relief.
Redirects any money appropriated to the institute to the Texas Education Agency, subject to the voter-approval condition.
Repeals the statutory subtitle associated with a named state institute.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The repeal and state-agency funding direction are statewide in scope.

affected_groups.group: People affected by dementia, Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and related disorders
affected_groups.explanation: The statutory framework being repealed concerns an institute associated with research, prevention, and treatment of these disorders.

affected_groups.group: School districts and property taxpayers
affected_groups.explanation: The transferred money is directed to reducing the state compression percentage, and the referenced constitutional amendment describes the related purpose as property tax relief.

major_effects.label: Repeal of institute framework
major_effects.explanation: Repeals Subtitle E of Title 2, Chapter 101A of the Health and Safety Code, as effective December 1, 2025.

major_effects.label: Redirects appropriated institute money
major_effects.explanation: Directs the comptroller to transfer any money appropriated to the institute to the Texas Education Agency for reducing the state compression percentage.

major_effects.label: Voter-approval condition
major_effects.explanation: The Act takes effect only if voters approve the specified constitutional amendment; otherwise it has no effect.

agencies.name: Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts
agencies.explanation: The comptroller is assigned the duty to transfer the specified appropriated money if the Act takes effect.

agencies.name: Texas Education Agency
agencies.explanation: The agency is the recipient of the transferred money, which is to be used to reduce the state compression percentage.

agencies.name: Dementia Prevention and Research Institute of Texas
agencies.explanation: The bill repeals the statutory subtitle associated with the institute and redirects any money appropriated to it; its precise status as a state body is not established in the supplied text.

HB823.summary: Licensing authorities must review each occupational regulation against a necessity-and-tailoring standard, repeal or modify regulations they are authorized to change if they fail that standard, or recommend legislative action if they are not; they must report their actions and recommendations. A person may petition an authority and may seek an injunction in district court when a regulation burdens entry into an occupation, subject to the bill’s evidentiary tests.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill establishes standards and review procedures for occupational regulations governing entry into licensed professions.
The review considers worker opportunities, and the bill provides a path to challenge regulations that burden occupational entry.
Political-subdivision licensing authorities are included in the bill’s definition and are subject to its review requirements when they issue covered authorizations.
The bill creates a comprehensive review, possible regulatory-reform, and reporting process for licensing authorities.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The review requirements apply to licensing authorities covered by the bill across Texas.

locations.name: Travis County
locations.explanation: The bill permits an injunction action in district court in Travis County.

locations.name: Any county in which the regulation is enforced
locations.explanation: The bill also permits an injunction action in a county where the challenged regulation is enforced.

affected_groups.group: State and political-subdivision licensing authorities
affected_groups.explanation: They must review covered occupational regulations and report to the legislature on actions taken and recommendations made under subsection (b).

affected_groups.group: People seeking to enter licensed occupations
affected_groups.explanation: They may petition for repeal or modification and seek injunctive relief when a regulation burdens entry, subject to the bill’s standards.

affected_groups.group: Licensed professions and businesses subject to occupational regulations
affected_groups.explanation: Their applicable occupational regulations are subject to review and potential repeal or modification.

major_effects.label: Review and potential reform of occupational regulations
major_effects.explanation: Authorities must review covered regulations; if a regulation fails the bill’s policy standard, they must repeal or modify it when authorized, or recommend legislative action when they are not authorized to do so.

major_effects.label: Legislative report on review actions
major_effects.explanation: Authorities must report actions taken and recommendations made as part of the review process.

major_effects.label: Petition and injunction process
major_effects.explanation: A person may petition for repeal or modification and seek an injunction; relief depends on the court’s findings under the necessity, tailoring, and less-restrictive-alternative tests, and a prevailing plaintiff receives reasonable fees and costs.

agencies.name: licensing authorities
agencies.explanation: The bill directly assigns review, possible repeal or modification, recommendation, and reporting duties to licensing authorities. This is a broad defined class that includes state entities and political-subdivision entities, not one identifiable canonical agency.

HB825.summary: The bill would require the property-tax-increase statement on the ballot proposition governed by Education Code Section 45.003(b) to appear in bold red text, in 72-point font. The change would apply only to elections ordered on or after the Act’s effective date.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill changes a ballot-proposition rule in the Education Code for the provision identified as Section 45.003(b-1).
The bill changes the required presentation of a statement on a ballot proposition.
The required ballot statement warns that the proposition is a property tax increase; the bill changes its formatting, not the tax amount.
The bill changes a ballot requirement under the Education Code provision identified as Section 45.003(b-1), affecting the relevant local school-district election process.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The bill applies to qualifying elections under the cited state-law provision, without limiting the change to a particular place.

affected_groups.group: Voters in elections using the affected ballot proposition
affected_groups.explanation: These voters would see the property-tax-increase statement in the specified formatting.

affected_groups.group: School districts conducting elections under Education Code Section 45.003(b)
affected_groups.explanation: The bill changes the required presentation of the ballot proposition in the cited Education Code provision.

major_effects.label: Formats a property-tax-increase ballot statement
major_effects.explanation: Requires the specified statement to appear in bold red, 72-point font on the relevant ballot proposition.

major_effects.label: Limits applicability to later-ordered elections
major_effects.explanation: The change applies only to elections ordered on or after the Act’s effective date.

HB826.summary: The bill would cap taxpayer-funded salaries for state officers and employees, and for officers and employees of political subdivisions, at the amount set for the governor in the applicable appropriations act. It would apply beginning with the state fiscal biennium starting September 1, 2027, and only to salary agreements or employment contracts entered into on or after the effective date; earlier agreements remain governed by prior law.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes compensation limits for state and political-subdivision officers and employees.
Sets a salary limit for officers and employees of counties, municipalities, districts, and other political subdivisions.
Limits taxpayer-funded salary payments by the state and political subdivisions.
Establishes a compensation limit applicable to state personnel and political-subdivision personnel.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The limits apply to state personnel and personnel of political subdivisions throughout Texas.

affected_groups.group: State officers and employees
affected_groups.explanation: Their taxpayer-funded salaries would be subject to the governor-linked cap for qualifying agreements or contracts.

affected_groups.group: Officers and employees of political subdivisions
affected_groups.explanation: The cap would cover personnel of counties, municipalities, special districts, school districts, junior college districts, and other political subdivisions.

major_effects.label: Cap on taxpayer-funded public salaries
major_effects.explanation: Limits covered salaries to the amount set for the governor in the applicable appropriations act. The new limits apply only to salary agreements or employment contracts entered into on or after the effective date.

HB827.summary: HB 827 would require the attorney general to establish a forfeiture case-tracking system and searchable public database, with law enforcement agencies and attorneys representing the state reporting seizure, case, disposition, and expenditure information subject to specified exceptions and privacy limits. It would require annual summaries and publication of specified audits, authorize fees and certain uses of forfeiture proceeds, and impose penalties and temporary restrictions on using proceeds or property when required expenditure reports are not submitted. The proposed changes apply only to state fiscal years beginning on or after January 1, 2028.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes reporting, public disclosure, and handling of property and proceeds from criminal asset-forfeiture proceedings.
Creates a searchable online database and limits the personal and property-identifying information that may be disclosed through it.
Assigns new tracking, audit, reporting, publication, and enforcement duties to state officials and reporting entities.
Changes permitted uses of forfeiture proceeds, authorizes an attorney general fee, and directs collected civil penalties to the general revenue fund.
Local law enforcement agencies may have reporting and penalty-related duties, and governmental immunity of political subdivisions is waived to the extent of the specified civil penalty liability.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The changes govern forfeiture activity under the Texas Code of Criminal Procedure and apply by state fiscal year, without limiting the provisions to a named locality.

affected_groups.group: State and local law enforcement agencies and attorneys representing the state
affected_groups.explanation: Must submit specified seizure and expenditure information. A law enforcement agency or attorney representing the state is subject to a civil penalty only if it violates the reporting requirement.

affected_groups.group: Owners and interest holders of seized property
affected_groups.explanation: Information about claims, case outcomes, and property disposition may be collected and published, while specified personal and property-identifying information is excluded.

affected_groups.group: Legislators and the public
affected_groups.explanation: A legislator may request a state auditor's audit, and the bill provides for public access to the database, specified audits, and the attorney general's annual report.

major_effects.label: Forfeiture tracking system and public database
major_effects.explanation: Requires the attorney general to create and maintain a system for seizure and forfeiture data and a searchable public database, subject to specified disclosure exclusions.

major_effects.label: Forfeiture and expenditure reporting
major_effects.explanation: When property is seized or forfeited under this chapter or under an agreement with the federal government, the bill requires reporting on seizures, cases, dispositions, and expenditures, plus an annual attorney general report; some seizure data is excepted, and identifying information is excluded from the public website.

major_effects.label: Legislator-requested state audit
major_effects.explanation: Requires the state auditor to perform an audit described in existing law upon request of a legislator, with no more than one audit per year under this new provision; specified audits must be submitted to the attorney general and published.

major_effects.label: Fees and permitted uses of forfeiture proceeds
major_effects.explanation: Allows specified forfeiture proceeds to pay the attorney general's fee and costs of compiling or submitting required reports; the attorney general may charge a reasonable fee for system and website costs.

major_effects.label: Consequences for missing expenditure reports
major_effects.explanation: A reporting violation is subject to a civil penalty. Until the required report is submitted, the attorney representing the state may not disburse funds to a noncompliant agency, and the agency or attorney may not expend proceeds or use covered property.

major_effects.label: Limits on public disclosure of identifying information
major_effects.explanation: Bars requiring or publishing specified personal information about owners and other individuals, as well as addresses and identifying numbers for seized or forfeited property.

agencies.name: Office of the Attorney General
agencies.explanation: The attorney general must establish and maintain the tracking system and public database, receive reports, publish information, and may charge a fee.

agencies.name: state auditor
agencies.explanation: Must perform an audit on a legislator's request, subject to the one-audit-per-year limit in this provision, and submit specified completed audits to the attorney general.

agencies.name: state or local law enforcement agencies
agencies.explanation: The generic category includes state agencies directly assigned seizure and expenditure reporting duties; reporting violations can also trigger penalties and restrictions on using forfeiture proceeds or property. The bill does not identify particular state agencies.

HB828.summary: The bill would bar a political subdivision from submitting a general obligation bond proposition for a purpose voters rejected within the preceding five years. The restriction would apply only to propositions for which the election was ordered on or after the Act’s effective date.

policy_tags.explanation: Limits political subdivisions’ authority to propose certain general obligation bond issuances.
Restricts when a bond proposition may be submitted to voters following a failed vote.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The restriction applies to political subdivisions without limiting its reach to a particular place.

affected_groups.group: Political subdivisions
affected_groups.explanation: Their authority to resubmit certain general obligation bond propositions is limited.

affected_groups.group: Voters
affected_groups.explanation: They would not be asked to vote on a proposition for the same purpose within five years after rejecting it.

major_effects.label: Limits repeat bond propositions
major_effects.explanation: A political subdivision may not submit a bond proposition for the same purpose within five years after voters rejected a prior proposition.

major_effects.label: Prospective application
major_effects.explanation: The restriction applies only when the election was ordered on or after the Act’s effective date.

HB829.summary: HB 829 would repeal Subchapter T of the Government Code, ending authority to enter new taxable-value-limitation agreements under the Texas Jobs, Energy, Technology, and Innovation Act. Agreements made before the Act's effective date would continue under the prior version of the subchapter, and related provisions would continue to recognize them.

policy_tags.explanation: Repealing the program ends future taxable-value-limitation agreements, while agreements made before the effective date remain in force.
The repealed incentive framework linked taxable-value limitations to attracting major investment and regional economic development.
The repeal ends the ability to use Subchapter T for new school-district reinvestment-zone designations and taxable-value limitations.
The bill repeals the incentive framework as it applies to clean-energy project agreements, while preserving agreements made before the effective date.

locations.name: Texas
locations.explanation: The bill changes a statewide Texas statutory program; it identifies no specific locality.

affected_groups.group: Businesses and project owners seeking new taxable-value limitations
affected_groups.explanation: They would no longer be able to enter new agreements under Subchapter T.

affected_groups.group: Parties to existing Subchapter T agreements
affected_groups.explanation: Agreements entered before the Act's effective date would continue under the prior law.

affected_groups.group: School districts
affected_groups.explanation: The repeal removes the Subchapter T basis for new school-district designations and agreements, while related provisions continue to address existing agreements.

major_effects.label: Repeal of Subchapter T
major_effects.explanation: The bill repeals the incentive subchapter, ending authority for new agreements under it; agreements made before the effective date remain in force under the prior law.

major_effects.label: Taxable-value limitation incentives
major_effects.explanation: New Subchapter T taxable-value limitations would no longer be available, but the bill preserves limitations under agreements entered before its effective date.

agencies.name: Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts
agencies.explanation: The bill amends the statutory restriction on the Comptroller's issuance of a credit to retain its application to agreements under the repealed subchapter; this concerns administration of legacy agreements, not a new incentive program.

HB830.summary: The bill would prohibit an officer or employee of a political subdivision from knowingly spending or authorizing public funds for a communication about an election measure resulting from official action by that subdivision, except notice required under Election Code Chapter 4. A violation would be a Class A misdemeanor, and the change would apply only to uses of funds or resources on or after the Act's effective date.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes rules on political-advertising and measure-related communications funded by political subdivisions.
Restricts how political subdivision officers and employees may use or authorize the use of public funds.
Makes a violation of the expanded prohibition an offense punishable as a Class A misdemeanor.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The restriction applies to political subdivisions under Texas law, rather than to a specifically named place.

affected_groups.group: Officers and employees of political subdivisions
affected_groups.explanation: They may not knowingly spend or authorize public funds for the specified communications.

affected_groups.group: Political subdivisions
affected_groups.explanation: Their public funds are subject to the new restriction for communications about certain election measures.

major_effects.label: Restricts public funding of measure-related communications
major_effects.explanation: Prohibits the specified use of public funds for communications about a measure submitted at an election following official action by the political subdivision, except required Chapter 4 notice.

major_effects.label: Class A misdemeanor
major_effects.explanation: A person who violates the prohibition commits a Class A misdemeanor.

HB831.summary: HB 831 would prohibit a state agency, as defined by Government Code §2062.001, from adopting or using a form that asks an individual to provide race or ethnicity. The bill would take effect September 1, 2027.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill would restrict forms state agencies may adopt or use.
The restriction concerns state-agency collection of individuals' race or ethnicity information.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The prohibition applies to state agencies generally across Texas.

affected_groups.group: Individuals asked to provide race or ethnicity on state agency forms
affected_groups.explanation: They would no longer be asked or required to provide that information on forms covered by the bill.

affected_groups.group: Texas state agencies
affected_groups.explanation: They would be prohibited from adopting or using forms that request or require an individual's race or ethnicity.

major_effects.label: Prohibition on race and ethnicity questions in agency forms
major_effects.explanation: State agencies could not adopt or use forms asking individuals to provide race or ethnicity.

agencies.name: state agency
agencies.explanation: The bill directly prohibits state agencies from adopting or using covered forms; the cited definition determines which entities are included, and no canonical identity is specified.

HB833.summary: HB 833 would prohibit a school district from contracting with or distributing public funds to a qualifying nonprofit association or organization for training, insurance or risk-pool participation, buy-board goods or supplies, or investment or professional services. The restriction would apply only to contracts entered into on or after the Act's effective date; earlier contracts would remain governed by prior law.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill changes school districts' authority to procure specified goods and services.
The bill restricts school districts' contracting and use of public funds.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The prohibition applies to school districts statewide.

affected_groups.group: School districts
affected_groups.explanation: Districts would be barred from contracting with or using public funds for specified purchases from qualifying nonprofits.

affected_groups.group: Nonprofit associations or organizations that primarily represent political subdivisions and employ an individual required to register as a lobbyist
affected_groups.explanation: These organizations would be barred as providers for the specified training, insurance or risk-pool participation, goods or supplies, and services.

major_effects.label: School-district procurement prohibition
major_effects.explanation: Limits school districts' ability to contract with or distribute public funds to qualifying nonprofits for training, insurance or risk-pool participation, buy-board goods or supplies, and investment or professional services.

HB835.summary: HB 835 would require voter registration applicants who lack the specified DPS license or identification number and Social Security number to provide a listed citizenship-confirming document. It would also narrow the acceptable photo-ID rules for certain DPS-issued IDs and require added documents for federal postcard applications and ballots returned under that chapter; election materials could be sent by airmail or by electronic transmission of an application image under Secretary of State procedures.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill changes voter-registration documentation, acceptable photo identification, and procedures for federal postcard applications and related ballots.

locations.name: Statewide in Texas
locations.explanation: The bill amends Texas Election Code provisions governing voter registration and voting procedures, with statewide relevance.

locations.name: Foreign addresses
locations.explanation: Federal postcard applicants must submit a document showing the applicant's foreign address.

affected_groups.group: Voter registration applicants without the specified DPS identification number and Social Security number
affected_groups.explanation: These applicants would have to provide a listed document confirming citizenship status.

affected_groups.group: Voters presenting DPS-issued identification
affected_groups.explanation: The bill changes the expiration period for specified DPS-issued photo IDs and excludes certain driver's licenses from the acceptable forms.

affected_groups.group: Federal postcard applicants and voters returning ballots under that chapter
affected_groups.explanation: Applicants must provide specified identity and foreign-address documents and an affidavit; returned ballots must include the required materials.

major_effects.label: Citizenship documentation for voter registration
major_effects.explanation: Applicants without the specified DPS number and Social Security number must submit a document listed in Section 63.0101(a) that confirms citizenship status.

major_effects.label: Acceptable photo identification
major_effects.explanation: Specified DPS-issued IDs must be unexpired or have expired no more than one year before presentation; a driver's license is excluded only if it is subject to one of the listed Transportation Code provisions.

major_effects.label: Federal postcard application and ballot materials
major_effects.explanation: Federal postcard applications must include a passport or military-ID photocopy, foreign-address documentation, and a signed affidavit; ballots returned under the chapter must include those materials.

major_effects.label: Ballot-material transmission options
major_effects.explanation: Balloting materials may be sent by airmail or provided through electronic transmission of an application image under procedures prescribed by the Secretary of State.

agencies.name: Texas Department of Public Safety
agencies.explanation: The bill changes the election-document rules for specified IDs issued by the Department, including their expiration window and the types of driver's licenses accepted.

agencies.name: Texas Secretary of State
agencies.explanation: The Secretary of State must provide early voting clerks compliance instructions and prescribe procedures for electronic transmission of an application image.

HB836.summary: The bill would require covered state agency actions—including rules, employment practices, communications, benefits, contracts, and curricula—to treat people and entities equally regardless of race, color, or national origin. It would deem any agency action that promotes the doctrine of diversity, equity, and inclusion to be prohibited discrimination and null and void from the outset.

policy_tags.explanation: Establishes an equal-treatment and nondiscrimination requirement based on race, color, and national origin for state agency actions.
Restricts state agency rules, policies, practices, communications, and other actions.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The requirements apply across the covered state agencies rather than to a named local area.

affected_groups.group: People and entities subject to state agency actions
affected_groups.explanation: They would be covered by the equal-treatment requirement in agency actions.

affected_groups.group: State agency employees and employment applicants
affected_groups.explanation: State agency employment practices are expressly subject to the bill's requirements.

major_effects.label: Equal treatment in state agency actions
major_effects.explanation: Requires covered agency actions to treat people and entities equally and not discriminate on the basis of race, color, or national origin.

major_effects.label: Invalidation of DEI-promoting agency actions
major_effects.explanation: Deems agency actions promoting the specified doctrine to be prohibited discrimination and null and void from the outset.

agencies.name: state agencies
agencies.explanation: The bill directly imposes requirements on all covered state agency actions; the cross-referenced statutory definition is not supplied, so specific entities cannot be identified.

HB838.summary: The bill would remove the separate gift-law exception for reportable gifts, awards, or mementos to legislative or executive branch members, while retaining the exception for qualifying items worth less than $50. It would revise spending prohibitions for registered lobbyists, including lowering the award-or-memento limit from $500 to $50 and applying the $500 entertainment and gift limits to a series of expenditures. It would also exclude certain Chapter 305 expenditure limits from annual inflation adjustments and require the Texas Ethics Commission to reverse specified earlier adjustments.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill changes lobbyist spending restrictions, public-servant gift-law exceptions, and the Texas Ethics Commission's threshold-adjustment duties.

locations.name: Statewide, Texas
locations.explanation: The bill amends Texas state statutes governing public servants, lobbyists, and the Texas Ethics Commission.

affected_groups.group: Registered lobbyists and people acting on their behalf with their consent or ratification
affected_groups.explanation: Except as provided by Section 305.025, their permitted expenditures for specified gifts, entertainment, awards, and other covered items would be changed.

affected_groups.group: Public servants, including legislative and executive branch members
affected_groups.explanation: The bill narrows an exception to the gift-offense provisions that applies to certain reportable gifts to legislative or executive branch members.

major_effects.label: Narrows gift-law exceptions
major_effects.explanation: Removes the separate exception for reportable gifts, awards, or mementos to legislative or executive branch members; the existing exception for qualifying items worth less than $50 remains.

major_effects.label: Revises lobbyist expenditure restrictions
major_effects.explanation: Changes the entertainment and gift limits to apply to a series of expenditures exceeding $500 in a calendar year, lowers the award-or-memento limit to $50, and caps certain other covered expenditures at $50.

major_effects.label: Exempts certain expenditure limits from annual inflation adjustments
major_effects.explanation: The Commission's annual threshold adjustment requirement would not apply to a law providing an expenditure limit for a person required to register under Chapter 305.

major_effects.label: Requires reversal of qualifying prior adjustments
major_effects.explanation: The Texas Ethics Commission must adopt rules to reverse earlier adjustments that would not have been made under the bill's change.

agencies.name: Texas Ethics Commission
agencies.explanation: The bill excludes certain Chapter 305 expenditure limits from annual inflation adjustments and directs the Commission to adopt rules reversing qualifying prior adjustments.

HB839.summary: HB 839 would bar a governmental agency or public official from adopting or enforcing a measure that burdens an individual's right to earn a living unless it is necessary to protect public health, safety, or welfare, is the least restrictive means, and less restrictive alternatives cannot achieve that interest without unnecessarily restricting entry. It would create remedies for people harmed by a violation and allow the violation to be raised as a defense in proceedings enforcing the measure.

policy_tags.explanation: Sets a substantive test for governmental restrictions on entry into a business, profession, occupation, or trade.
Creates protections and legal remedies for an individual's right to earn a living.
The restrictions apply to political subdivisions and their agencies, which may also face claims under the bill.
Constrains governmental agencies and public officials' authority to adopt or enforce measures and waives immunity to the extent of liability created.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The bill applies to state laws and to governmental agencies that include political subdivisions across Texas.

affected_groups.group: Individuals hindered from entering a regulated business, profession, occupation, or trade
affected_groups.explanation: People whose entry is hindered by a covered measure may bring an action if they intend to engage in the activity; they need not first apply for or obtain the relevant license or certification.

affected_groups.group: State and local governmental agencies and public officials
affected_groups.explanation: Their covered restrictions would be subject to the new test, and agencies or officials could be sued to the extent specified by the bill.

major_effects.label: Test for restrictions on earning a living
major_effects.explanation: A covered measure may burden the right to earn a living only if the agency or official demonstrates the measure is necessary to protect public health, safety, or welfare, is the least restrictive means, and less restrictive alternatives cannot achieve the interest without unnecessarily restricting entry.

major_effects.label: Private claims, remedies, and immunity waiver
major_effects.explanation: An aggrieved person may sue over a violation or threatened violation and may receive equitable relief, nominal damages, and reasonable fees and costs. Governmental and official immunity are waived only to the extent of liability created by the claim provision.

major_effects.label: Defense in enforcement proceedings
major_effects.explanation: A person whose right to earn a living is burdened in violation of the new standard may assert the violation as a defense in a judicial or administrative proceeding enforcing the measure.

major_effects.label: Broad applicability
major_effects.explanation: The chapter applies to laws adopted by governmental agencies regardless of when adopted and to state laws unless expressly exempted by reference to the chapter. The new claim and defense provisions have separate prospective application rules.

agencies.name: Governmental agency
agencies.explanation: The bill defines this as a broad class that includes the state, political subdivisions, and their agencies, and directly prohibits the class from adopting or enforcing covered measures. The bill does not identify a particular state body for canonical registry mapping.

HB840.summary: For an executive head of a state agency governed by a governing body and employees reporting directly to that head, the bill sets a 10-year service limit and requires a performance review by the fifth anniversary, with a decision whether to terminate employment. These changes apply only to contracts entered into on or after the Act’s effective date; earlier contracts remain governed by prior law.

policy_tags.explanation: Establishes service limits and performance-review duties for certain state agency leadership positions.
Changes employment duration and review requirements for covered agency executives and their direct reports.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The provisions concern qualifying Texas state agencies, without limiting their application to a particular place.

affected_groups.group: Executive heads of state agencies governed by a governing body
affected_groups.explanation: Their service is limited to 10 years, and their agency's governing body must review their performance by the fifth anniversary and determine whether to terminate employment.

affected_groups.group: Employees reporting directly to those executive heads
affected_groups.explanation: Their service is limited to 10 years, and the executive head must review their performance by the fifth anniversary and determine whether to terminate employment.

major_effects.label: 10-year service limit
major_effects.explanation: An individual may not serve more than 10 years as a covered agency executive head or in a position reporting directly to that head.

major_effects.label: Fifth-anniversary performance review
major_effects.explanation: By the fifth anniversary of employment, the governing body or executive head, as applicable, must review performance and determine whether to terminate employment.

agencies.name: State agency governed by a governing body
agencies.explanation: The bill directly limits service in covered agency positions and assigns the agency's governing body a performance-review and termination-determination duty. The bill does not identify particular agencies.

HB841.summary: The bill would require at least 60 percent of voters in an election to approve the issuance of a political subdivision’s general obligation bonds. The requirement applies only to bonds authorized by the subdivision’s governing body on or after the Act’s effective date.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes the voter-approval condition for political subdivisions to issue general obligation bonds.
Raises the required share of votes in favor at an election authorizing local general obligation bonds.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The requirement applies to political subdivisions generally, without limiting its reach to a particular place.

affected_groups.group: Political subdivisions and their governing bodies
affected_groups.explanation: A political subdivision may not issue general obligation bonds authorized on or after the effective date unless at least 60 percent of voters at the authorizing election vote in favor.

affected_groups.group: Voters in elections authorizing political-subdivision bonds
affected_groups.explanation: Their votes determine whether the required supermajority for bond issuance is reached.

major_effects.label: Supermajority approval for local bonds
major_effects.explanation: A political subdivision could not issue general obligation bonds unless at least 60 percent of voters at the authorizing election vote in favor; this applies only to bonds authorized by its governing body on or after the effective date.

HB842.summary: HB 842 would bar a public library, including a public school library, from using public money to join the American Library Association, take part in its events, or otherwise support it. The restriction would apply to spending on or after the effective date, except funds required to be spent under a contract entered into before that date.

policy_tags.explanation: The restriction expressly applies to public school libraries and limits their use of public funds.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The restriction is framed for covered public libraries under Texas law and is not limited to a named geographic area.

affected_groups.group: Public libraries, including public school libraries
affected_groups.explanation: These libraries would be prohibited from using public money for the specified forms of support for the American Library Association.

affected_groups.group: American Library Association
affected_groups.explanation: The prohibition would restrict covered libraries from using public money to support the association.

major_effects.label: Restricts public-library spending on the association
major_effects.explanation: Covered libraries could not use public money for membership, participation in the association's events, or other direct or indirect financial support. The restriction applies to spending on or after the effective date, except funds required under a preexisting contract.

HB843.summary: HB843 would establish an independent Legislative Economic Analysis Unit and board to review state agency rules, identify major rules under specified economic, competition, employment, investment, productivity, innovation, or social and cultural impact criteria, and publish analyses. The unit would also prepare an analysis of a grant or other financial benefit only if the lieutenant governor or speaker requests it. For agency rules adopted on or after the Act takes effect, a rule determined to be major would expire on the specified July 1 unless the legislature validates it by general law before then; an agency could not adopt the same or substantially the same rule after it expires.

policy_tags.explanation: Creates a legislative agency and board and assigns them rule-review and analysis duties.
Changes the process and duration of state agency rules classified as major, including a restriction on adopting an expired major rule again.
Requires the legislature to appropriate enough funding for the unit's operations and authorizes reimbursement of board members' necessary expenses.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The provisions apply to state agencies generally, rather than to a particular named place.

affected_groups.group: State agencies
affected_groups.explanation: Agencies must submit adopted rules, and rules classified as major face an expiration date and re-adoption restriction.

affected_groups.group: People, businesses, and industries affected by state agency rules
affected_groups.explanation: Rules classified as major would be subject to legislative validation or expiration, affecting those subject to the rules.

affected_groups.group: Legislators
affected_groups.explanation: The lieutenant governor and speaker appoint board members and the chief economist; the board also adopts procedures for legislative consideration of major-rule validation bills.

major_effects.label: Creates a legislative analysis unit and board
major_effects.explanation: Establishes the unit as an independent legislative agency, creates its governing board, and assigns rule and grant analysis functions.

major_effects.label: Requires operational appropriation
major_effects.explanation: Requires the legislature to appropriate an amount sufficient to fund the unit's operations.

major_effects.label: Requires rule submissions and public analysis
major_effects.explanation: Agencies must submit adopted rules; the unit must publish major-rule determinations and impact analyses. Grant impact analyses are prepared only on request of the lieutenant governor or speaker.

major_effects.label: Major-rule expiration and re-adoption restriction
major_effects.explanation: For rules adopted on or after the Act takes effect, a rule determined major expires on July 1 of the following odd-numbered year unless validated by general law before expiration; the agency may not adopt the same or substantially the same rule after it expires.

agencies.name: Legislative Economic Analysis Unit
agencies.explanation: The bill establishes the unit as an independent legislative agency and assigns it rule-review, determination, and analysis duties.

agencies.name: Legislative Economic Analysis Unit Board
agencies.explanation: The bill creates the board, gives it responsibility for procedures concerning legislative consideration of major rules, and assigns it a role in setting the chief economist's salary.

agencies.name: State agencies
agencies.explanation: Each state agency must submit its adopted rules, and rules determined to be major are subject to expiration and a limit on re-adoption.

agencies.name: Texas Legislative Council
agencies.explanation: The unit must request that the Council draft a bill to validate a rule it determines to be major.

HB844.summary: The bill would require school districts to publish proposed budgets in line-item form and adopted budgets in line-item form, keeping adopted budgets online for three years. It would also require municipal proposed budgets to be available in line-item form and, when a municipality has a website, require proposed and adopted budgets posted there in line-item form.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes budget publication requirements for school districts.
Changes municipal budget availability and website publication requirements.
Sets public budget disclosure and record-publication requirements for school districts and municipalities.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The requirements apply to school districts and municipalities under Texas law, without identifying a narrower geographic area.

affected_groups.group: Texas school districts
affected_groups.explanation: Must publish proposed and adopted budgets in line-item form, with adopted budgets kept online for three years.

affected_groups.group: Texas municipalities
affected_groups.explanation: Must make proposed budgets available in line-item form and, if maintaining a website, publish proposed and adopted budgets there in line-item form.

affected_groups.group: People seeking access to municipal budgets
affected_groups.explanation: May inspect municipal proposed budgets made available in line-item form.

major_effects.label: School district budget publication
major_effects.explanation: Requires proposed budgets to be published in line-item form and adopted budgets to be posted in line-item form and maintained online for three years.

major_effects.label: Municipal budget publication
major_effects.explanation: Requires proposed municipal budgets to be available in line-item form and, if the municipality has a website, requires proposed and adopted budgets to be posted there in line-item form.

HB847.summary: The bill would allow a law enforcement agency to use an automatic license plate reader only as authorized by a warrant or court order, and would limit resulting images and data to investigations of violent offenses. It would require prompt destruction unless the data concerns a vehicle involved in such an offense or investigation, or registered to a person involved, and would bar agreements to provide the data for other purposes. Agencies using the systems would adopt and annually publish a use policy and a report on scans, including scans used in investigations leading to arrest or prosecution.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill would restrict collection-derived data use, retention, and disclosure from automatic license plate readers.
The bill would condition law-enforcement use of plate readers on legal authorization and limit data use to investigations of violent offenses.
The bill changes rules governing a law enforcement agency's investigative use of automatic license plate readers.

locations.name: Texas statewide
locations.explanation: The bill adds a generally applicable provision to the Texas Transportation Code for covered law enforcement agencies.

affected_groups.group: Law enforcement agencies using automatic license plate readers
affected_groups.explanation: They would face restrictions on use and disclosure, destruction requirements, and policy and public reporting duties.

affected_groups.group: People whose vehicle plate images or related data are collected
affected_groups.explanation: Their data would be limited to investigating a qualifying violent offense and generally must be destroyed promptly after collection, unless it is from a vehicle involved in such an offense or an ongoing investigation of one.

major_effects.label: Warrant or court order required
major_effects.explanation: A law enforcement agency could use an automatic license plate reader only as authorized by a warrant or court order.

major_effects.label: Limits on plate-reader data use, retention, and disclosure
major_effects.explanation: Data use would be limited to violent-offense investigations, with prompt destruction required unless a stated vehicle or person-related exception applies; disclosure agreements would be barred except for a purpose authorized by the section.

major_effects.label: Agency policy and annual public reporting
major_effects.explanation: Agencies using the systems would adopt a use policy, annually report scan counts and specified investigative outcomes, and publish the policy and report online.

agencies.name: law enforcement agency
agencies.explanation: The bill directly restricts use of automatic license plate readers by law enforcement agencies and imposes policy and reporting duties on agencies that use them. The source does not identify which state entities fall within this generic term.

HB848.summary: HB 848 would add an Election Code rule barring a person who contributes to a political committee supporting a bond issuance from receiving money from proceeds connected with that bond, including contract payments. The restriction would apply only to contributions made on or after the Act's effective date.

policy_tags.explanation: Adds an Election Code restriction connecting contributions to committees that support a bond with eligibility to receive that bond's proceeds.
Restricts who may receive money from bond proceeds, including payments for goods or services.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The bill amends the Texas Election Code and states no narrower geographic limit.

affected_groups.group: People who contribute to political committees supporting a bond issuance and seek payments from that bond's proceeds
affected_groups.explanation: Such contributors would be barred from receiving any connected bond proceeds, including contract payments, for contributions made on or after the effective date.

major_effects.label: Restriction on receiving bond proceeds
major_effects.explanation: A person who makes a qualifying contribution may not receive money from proceeds connected with that bond, including payment under a goods-or-services contract; the restriction applies only to contributions made on or after the effective date.

HB850.summary: HB 850 would make children of active-duty members of foreign military forces stationed in Texas eligible for enrollment in a free prekindergarten class under Education Code Section 29.153, if they are at least three years old. The change applies beginning with the 2027–2028 school year.

policy_tags.explanation: Expands eligibility for enrollment in a public prekindergarten program.

locations.name: Texas
locations.explanation: Eligibility covers qualifying children whose foreign military member parent is stationed in Texas.

affected_groups.group: Children of active-duty members of foreign military forces stationed in Texas
affected_groups.explanation: Children in this group who are at least three years old become eligible for enrollment in the specified prekindergarten program.

major_effects.label: Expands prekindergarten eligibility
major_effects.explanation: Adds children of active-duty foreign military members stationed in Texas to the eligible group, subject to the existing minimum age requirement.

HB852.summary: HB 852 would, except as provided by subsection (b), require covered health care providers to conduct forensic medical examinations for consenting victims of alleged intimate partner violence or qualifying strangulation assault, with different timing and referral conditions for minors and adults. It would allow eligible providers and sexual assault nurse examiners to seek reimbursement, add victims’ right to information about that payment, and apply only to criminally injurious conduct occurring on or after the Act’s effective date.

policy_tags.explanation: Creates examination duties and reimbursement provisions for covered health care providers and sexual assault nurse examiners.
Changes crime-victim rights and requires law enforcement referrals for forensic examinations under specified circumstances.
Adds forensic examinations under the new subchapter as a reimbursable use of the fund.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The provisions establish generally applicable requirements under the Texas Code of Criminal Procedure and do not identify a narrower geographic area.

affected_groups.group: Victims of alleged intimate partner violence or strangulation assault
affected_groups.explanation: Consenting minor victims may receive examinations regardless of when they arrive at the provider, subject to the stated consent conditions. Other conditions may apply to non-minor victims. Victims may not be required to participate in an investigation or prosecution or pay for the examination.

affected_groups.group: Covered health care providers and sexual assault nurse examiners
affected_groups.explanation: Covered providers have examination or referral responsibilities, and providers and examiners may seek reimbursement for qualifying examinations.

affected_groups.group: Law enforcement agencies
affected_groups.explanation: Agencies must refer victims in specified cases and may refer certain adults who report after the 120-hour period when an examination may further an investigation or prosecution.

major_effects.label: Examination access and referrals
major_effects.explanation: Covered providers must examine consenting minors regardless of arrival time and consenting adults who arrive within 120 hours, or later if referred by law enforcement or a clinician after a preliminary evaluation. Law enforcement referrals are mandatory for reports within 120 hours and for minors regardless of when reported; examinations may be performed only by a sexual assault nurse examiner.

major_effects.label: Victim information and examination protections
major_effects.explanation: Victims gain a right to information about payment for these examinations and cannot be required to participate in an investigation or prosecution, or to pay for the examination.

major_effects.label: Reimbursement for examinations
major_effects.explanation: On application, providers or sexual assault nurse examiners may receive compensation for reasonable examination costs. A provider is not entitled to reimbursement unless the examination was performed on the provider’s premises by a sexual assault nurse examiner.

agencies.name: Office of the Attorney General
agencies.explanation: Receives reimbursement applications, prescribes their form and manner, and may provide application-process training.

HB853.summary: The bill would raise the Foundation School Program basic allotment amount used in the statutory formulas from $6,160 to $7,075. Beginning with the 2028–2029 school year, it would adjust the basic allotment annually for inflation based on the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes the basic allotment paid to school districts through the Foundation School Program.
Increases the formula amount used to determine state education allotments and provides for annual inflation adjustments.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The allotment applies to school districts under the statewide Foundation School Program.

affected_groups.group: School districts
affected_groups.explanation: A school district is entitled to an allotment for each student in average daily attendance, subject to adjustment under Subsection (a-1). The formula amount increases to $7,075, and beginning with the 2028–2029 school year the allotment is adjusted annually for inflation.

affected_groups.group: Students counted in average daily attendance
affected_groups.explanation: The basic allotment formula is calculated for each student in average daily attendance, subject to the stated exclusions.

major_effects.label: Increase and inflation adjustment to basic allotment
major_effects.explanation: Raises the basic allotment formula amount to $7,075 and, beginning in 2028–2029, adjusts the allotment annually by the specified inflation rate.

agencies.name: Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts
agencies.explanation: The bill assigns the comptroller responsibility for determining the inflation rate used in the annual allotment adjustment.

HB855.summary: The bill would require the Health and Human Services Commission to provide Medicaid medical assistance to applicants for whom federal matching funds are available, for eligibility determinations or recertifications made on or after January 1, 2028. It would require rules and an annual report on the expansion’s effects, including coverage, health care costs, and hospital charity and uncompensated care; implementation may be delayed if a necessary federal waiver or authorization is identified. The bill would take effect only if voters approve the specified constitutional amendment; otherwise, it would have no effect.

policy_tags.explanation: Expands eligibility for Medicaid medical assistance, subject to federal matching funds and the bill’s conditions.
Changes access to medical assistance and requires evaluation of health coverage and care costs.
The expansion requires the state to provide medical assistance to additional eligible applicants, and the required annual report includes state health care costs.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The eligibility and reporting provisions concern the Texas medical assistance program and individuals in the state.

affected_groups.group: Individuals applying for medical assistance who qualify for available federal matching funds
affected_groups.explanation: They would receive medical assistance if voters approve the specified constitutional amendment. The provision applies to initial eligibility determinations or recertifications made on or after January 1, 2028, regardless of when the individual applied.

affected_groups.group: Hospitals
affected_groups.explanation: The annual report must assess how the expansion affects hospital charity and uncompensated care costs.
