major_effects.label: Limits on the confidential-information exception
major_effects.explanation: Specifies that this exception does not encompass listed privileges or other exceptions to disclosure; it does not itself remove those separate protections.

major_effects.label: Prompt release and missed-deadline disclosure rules
major_effects.explanation: Requires prompt release of basic information unless another provision permits withholding, regardless of whether the governmental body requests an attorney general decision about other requested information. The missed-deadline disclosure rule is subject to Subsection (b).

major_effects.label: County clerk copy fees
major_effects.explanation: Requires county clerks providing nonpaper copies of maintained records to charge fees under Section 552.262 and repeals Section 552.231.

HB906.summary: HB 906 would let a public-information requestor require a governmental body to participate in alternative dispute resolution when the body has issued a specified written statement or requested an attorney general decision and the requestor disagrees with its determination or assertion. The requestor must give notice within 180 days; if the parties cannot agree on an impartial third party, the State Office of Administrative Hearings conducts the procedure at no cost to them, without affecting existing deadlines or duties. The State Office must adopt implementing rules, and the new procedure applies only to requests received on or after January 1, 2028.

policy_tags.explanation: Creates a dispute-resolution process for public-information requests and assigns implementation duties to a state administrative office.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The new procedure applies to covered public-information requests under Texas law, with no narrower geographic limitation stated.

affected_groups.group: Public-information requestors
affected_groups.explanation: Eligible requestors may initiate the dispute procedure when the specified disagreement conditions are met.

affected_groups.group: Governmental bodies receiving covered requests
affected_groups.explanation: A governmental body receiving a qualifying notice must participate in the procedure.

major_effects.label: Requestor-initiated dispute resolution
major_effects.explanation: Creates an alternative dispute resolution process that a requestor may require under specified conditions; a governmental body receiving notice must participate. The new process does not alter existing chapter deadlines or duties.

major_effects.label: Implementation rules
major_effects.explanation: Requires the State Office of Administrative Hearings to adopt rules to implement the procedure.

agencies.name: State Office of Administrative Hearings
agencies.explanation: The bill assigns the office implementing rulemaking and requires it to conduct the procedure at no cost to the parties when they cannot agree on an impartial third party. No canonical registry identity is established by the supplied material.

HB907.summary: The bill would require attorneys assisting public officials or governmental bodies with Open Meetings Act or Public Information Act responsibilities to complete the applicable training within 10 days; a governmental body generally could not compensate an attorney for training time unless the attorney is its employee. A public official could still designate a public information coordinator to administer responsibilities, but that designation would not satisfy the official’s own training duty; the coordinator would retain a separate training requirement. Transition rules give attorneys already assisting on the effective date until October 1, 2027, and officials who previously relied on a coordinator to complete their training until January 1, 2028.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes training and compliance requirements under the state’s open meetings and public information laws.
The training rules apply to public officials and governmental bodies subject to these chapters, including local governmental bodies.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The amendments govern responsibilities under chapters of the Texas Government Code without limiting them to a particular place.

affected_groups.group: Attorneys assisting public officials, public information coordinators, or governmental bodies
affected_groups.explanation: They would have to complete the applicable training within 10 days of being employed or engaged to assist.

affected_groups.group: Public officials
affected_groups.explanation: A public official could no longer rely on a coordinator to satisfy the official’s own Public Information Act training requirement.

affected_groups.group: Public information coordinators
affected_groups.explanation: Coordinators would retain their own training requirement after assuming their duties.

major_effects.label: Training requirement for assisting attorneys
major_effects.explanation: Attorneys assisting with Chapter 551 or 552 responsibilities would have to complete the relevant training within 10 days; governmental bodies generally could not compensate them for training time unless they are employees.

major_effects.label: Public official’s own training duty
major_effects.explanation: A public information coordinator may administer responsibilities and must complete training, but the designation does not discharge the public official’s own duty to comply with the training section.

major_effects.label: Transition training deadlines
major_effects.explanation: Attorneys already assisting on the effective date have until October 1, 2027, to complete the applicable training; officials who previously relied on a coordinator have until January 1, 2028, to complete theirs.

HB908.summary: The bill would require a governmental body holding an open meeting to let members of the public address non-agenda items before or during consideration of agenda items. The body could limit the number of speakers, but not to fewer than five.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes public-comment procedures for governmental bodies holding open meetings.
The requirement applies to local governmental bodies when they conduct open meetings.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The bill amends Texas law and sets a meeting procedure for governmental bodies without limiting it to a particular place.

affected_groups.group: Members of the public who want to address a governmental body about a non-agenda item
affected_groups.explanation: They would receive an opportunity to address the body before or during consideration of agenda items.

affected_groups.group: Governmental bodies holding open meetings, including local governmental bodies
affected_groups.explanation: They would have to allow non-agenda public comment, subject to a speaker limit of at least five people.

major_effects.label: Opportunity for non-agenda public comment
major_effects.explanation: Requires an opportunity to address non-agenda items before or during consideration of agenda items; any limit on speakers must allow at least five.

HB909.summary: Beginning with the 2027–2028 school year, each school district and open-enrollment charter school must provide age- and grade-appropriate cyber-safety instruction annually to students in every grade; districts and schools may choose the instructional format. The instruction may cover topics such as account security, online fraud, cyberbullying, responsible use of social media and artificial intelligence, and recognizing misinformation. The Texas Education Agency must develop and make optional instructional resources available, and schools must comply with applicable student privacy laws without being required to use particular software, applications, or AI technology.

policy_tags.explanation: Requires annual cyber-safety instruction for public school students and directs the state education agency to develop optional instructional resources.
The required instruction addresses online safety, personal information, cyber threats, and responsible use of digital technologies.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The instruction requirement applies to each school district and open-enrollment charter school, without limiting the requirement to a particular area.

affected_groups.group: Public school students
affected_groups.explanation: Students in every grade level must receive annual age- and grade-appropriate cyber-safety instruction.

affected_groups.group: School districts and open-enrollment charter schools
affected_groups.explanation: They must provide the instruction, while retaining discretion over the instructional format.

affected_groups.group: Parents and persons standing in parental relation to students
affected_groups.explanation: Schools may provide them with agency-available cyber-safety materials for promoting safe technology use at home.

major_effects.label: Annual cyber-safety instruction
major_effects.explanation: Requires districts and open-enrollment charter schools to provide age- and grade-appropriate instruction each year; the listed topics are examples the instruction may include.

major_effects.label: State-provided instructional resources
major_effects.explanation: Directs the Texas Education Agency to develop model lessons and professional-development materials and make them available to schools at no cost; the resources are optional for schools to use.

agencies.name: Texas Education Agency
agencies.explanation: The bill specifically directs the agency to develop and make available model instructional and professional-development resources.

HB910.summary: The bill would require a pilot program allowing defendants in state jail felony facilities to work remotely for private-sector employers. The department would set eligibility requirements, including education and conduct requirements for defendants and criteria for employers; the board would adopt rules, and the department would report on the program’s effectiveness by December 1, 2028. The section would expire September 1, 2029.

policy_tags.explanation: Creates a work pilot for defendants in state jail felony facilities.
Establishes a program for remote private-sector employment and sets eligibility requirements for participating employers and defendants.

locations.name: State jail felony facilities
locations.explanation: The pilot applies to defendants in these facilities; no specific facility or locality is named.

affected_groups.group: Defendants in state jail felony facilities
affected_groups.explanation: They may be eligible to participate in the remote-work pilot, subject to requirements that include education and conduct conditions.

affected_groups.group: Prospective private-sector employers
affected_groups.explanation: The department must set eligibility requirements for prospective employers participating in the pilot.

major_effects.label: Remote-work pilot
major_effects.explanation: Requires the department to establish and administer a pilot for remote private-sector work by defendants in state jail felony facilities.

major_effects.label: Participation requirements
major_effects.explanation: Requires eligibility requirements for defendants and prospective employers, including education and good-behavior requirements for defendants.

major_effects.label: Program rules
major_effects.explanation: Directs the board to adopt rules necessary to administer the pilot.

major_effects.label: Program evaluation report
major_effects.explanation: Requires the department to report on the pilot’s effectiveness to specified state officials and legislative committees.

agencies.name: the department
agencies.explanation: The bill assigns the department responsibility for establishing and administering the pilot, setting eligibility requirements, and reporting; the supplied sources do not identify which state body this generic term denotes.

agencies.name: the board
agencies.explanation: The bill directs the board to adopt rules for the pilot, but the supplied sources do not identify which state body this generic term denotes.

HB911.summary: The bill would let a qualified voter vote by mail if the voter will be in the second or third trimester of pregnancy on election day. It would also expand the existing expected-childbirth eligibility window from three to four weeks before or after election day.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill changes eligibility for early voting by mail.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The bill amends Texas Election Code provisions governing qualified voters' eligibility for early voting by mail.

affected_groups.group: Qualified voters who will be in the second or third trimester of pregnancy on election day
affected_groups.explanation: They would become eligible to vote by mail under the bill.

affected_groups.group: Qualified voters expecting to give birth shortly before or after election day
affected_groups.explanation: The bill would extend their existing mail-voting eligibility window to four weeks before or after election day.

major_effects.label: Pregnancy-based mail-voting eligibility
major_effects.explanation: A qualified voter in the second or third trimester on election day would be eligible for early voting by mail.

major_effects.label: Expanded expected-childbirth window
major_effects.explanation: The expected-childbirth eligibility window would increase from three to four weeks before or after election day.

HB912.summary: Beginning with the 2028–2029 school year, the bill would require at least four hours of voter-registration and civic-engagement instruction for public school district students who are or will be 18 during the school year. The State Board of Education and the Secretary of State’s Elections Division would develop the instruction and related resources; public and private high school principals would also certify annually that they complied with existing requirements and that students have access to voter registration forms.

policy_tags.explanation: Adds required curriculum and educator-training development for certain high school students.
The required instruction covers voter registration, voting rights, elections, and voting systems, and students must have an opportunity to complete a registration application during instruction.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The requirements apply to qualifying students enrolled in school districts and to public and private high schools, without a narrower geographic limitation.

affected_groups.group: Public school district high school students who are or will be 18 during the school year
affected_groups.explanation: They would receive the required voter-registration and civic-engagement instruction.

affected_groups.group: Public and private high school principals
affected_groups.explanation: Each principal would make an annual certification concerning compliance with existing requirements and student access to registration application forms.

affected_groups.group: Educators involved in delivering the instruction
affected_groups.explanation: They would have educator training modules and related instructional resources available.

major_effects.label: Required voter-registration and civic-engagement instruction
major_effects.explanation: Requires at least four hours of instruction for the specified district-enrolled students, including an in-class opportunity to complete a voter registration application.

major_effects.label: Instruction and training development
major_effects.explanation: Requires the State Board of Education and Elections Division to coordinate development of instruction and training, with public comment before the board finalizes instruction.

major_effects.label: Annual school-principal certification
major_effects.explanation: Requires each public and private high school principal to certify annually to the Secretary of State compliance with existing subsection (d) and student access to registration application forms.

agencies.name: State Board of Education
agencies.explanation: The board is expressly defined as the State Board of Education and is assigned rulemaking and instruction-development responsibilities.

agencies.name: Texas Secretary of State
agencies.explanation: The bill defines the Elections Division as part of the Office of the Secretary of State and assigns it joint instruction-development responsibilities; principals must also submit annual certifications to the secretary of state.

agencies.name: the agency
agencies.explanation: The bill assigns an agency a duty to develop and make additional instructional resources available, but does not identify which agency.

HB913.summary: The bill would require a governmental body of a political subdivision to hold meetings at a designated location within that subdivision. It would allow meetings by telephone or video conference under existing law, provided the physical location requirements still comply with the within-the-subdivision rule.

policy_tags.explanation: Imposes a meeting-location requirement on governmental bodies of political subdivisions.
Changes where covered governmental bodies may conduct their meetings.

locations.name: Statewide in Texas
locations.explanation: The requirement applies to political-subdivision governmental bodies across the state.

affected_groups.group: Governmental bodies of political subdivisions
affected_groups.explanation: These bodies would have to designate a meeting location within the boundaries of their political subdivision. They may conduct telephone or video conference meetings, provided the physical location requirements comply with that rule.

major_effects.label: Meeting-location requirement
major_effects.explanation: Requires covered meetings to be held at a designated location within the political subdivision; telephone or video meetings remain permitted if their physical location requirements comply.

HB914.summary: The bill replaces “governmental agency” with “person” in the consumer AI disclosure requirement, broadening who must comply. A covered person must tell each consumer, before or when interaction begins, that the consumer is interacting with an artificial intelligence system.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill broadens a consumer disclosure duty to persons making consumer-interactive AI systems available.
The requirement concerns disclosure when a consumer interacts with an artificial intelligence system.

locations.name: Texas
locations.explanation: This is a Texas enactment with statewide reach.

affected_groups.group: Persons making artificial intelligence systems available for consumer interaction
affected_groups.explanation: They would be subject to the disclosure requirement when their system is intended to interact with consumers.

affected_groups.group: Consumers interacting with artificial intelligence systems
affected_groups.explanation: They must be told that they are interacting with an AI system before or when the interaction occurs.

major_effects.label: Broadened AI interaction disclosure duty
major_effects.explanation: A person making a consumer-interactive AI system available must disclose the AI interaction before or at the time it occurs.

HB916.summary: HB 916 would add a condition for private schools seeking approval to participate in the education savings account program: they must disclose whether they accept students whose medical conditions make attendance infeasible and what accommodations, if any, they provide. The requirement would apply beginning with the 2027-2028 school year.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes eligibility requirements for private schools participating in an education savings account program.
Adds a disclosure condition to private-school participation in the education savings account program.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The change governs eligibility for participation in the state education savings account program, without a geographic limitation.

affected_groups.group: Private schools seeking approval to participate in the education savings account program
affected_groups.explanation: These schools would have to disclose their acceptance policy and any accommodations for students whose medical conditions make attendance infeasible.

affected_groups.group: Students with medical conditions that make school attendance infeasible, and their families
affected_groups.explanation: The bill requires schools to disclose whether they accept these students and what accommodations, if any, they offer; it does not require a school to accept them or provide accommodations.

major_effects.label: Private-school participation disclosure condition
major_effects.explanation: Adds disclosure of acceptance policies and any accommodations for medically related absences as a condition for private-school approval; it does not itself guarantee acceptance or accommodations.

agencies.name: Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts
agencies.explanation: The comptroller approves providers for program participation, and the bill adds a private-school condition to that approval.

HB917.summary: For appraisal districts that use a computer-assisted mass appraisal system, the bill requires the chief appraiser to establish and maintain an online portal, on the district’s website if it has one, allowing public access to and use of the system’s available functions and information except information confidential under law. It also adds a link to that portal, when applicable, to the appraisal district’s property-tax database.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill changes public access to a system appraisal districts use to determine appraised property values and adds a portal link to a property-tax database.
It assigns portal-establishment and maintenance duties to appraisal districts, which are local entities.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The requirement applies to any appraisal district in Texas that uses the specified system.

affected_groups.group: Appraisal districts that use a computer-assisted mass appraisal system and their chief appraisers
affected_groups.explanation: They must establish and maintain the public portal, subject to the bill’s stated conditions.

affected_groups.group: People seeking access to appraisal-system information
affected_groups.explanation: The portal must let a person use the system’s available functions and access its information, except information confidential under law.

major_effects.label: Public appraisal-system portal
major_effects.explanation: Requires a covered district’s chief appraiser to establish and maintain a portal; it must be on the district website if the district maintains one, and confidential information is excluded from public access.

major_effects.label: Link in property-tax database
major_effects.explanation: Requires the database to link to the Section 6.18 portal when applicable.

HB918.summary: The bill would prohibit peace officers from motorcycle profiling, including actions based on a person operating a motorcycle or wearing motorcycle-related or motorcycle club-related paraphernalia rather than the person’s behavior or information indicating criminal activity. Each law enforcement agency in Texas would have to adopt a written policy with a complaint process and corrective action after a substantiated violation by December 1, 2027.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill regulates peace officers’ conduct and requires law enforcement agency policies addressing motorcycle profiling.
The bill changes rules governing peace officers’ profiling and motor vehicle stops.
The bill prohibits profiling on the specified motorcycle-related basis and requires a process for individuals to complain.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The policy requirement applies to each law enforcement agency in the state.

affected_groups.group: Motorcycle operators and people wearing motorcycle-related or motorcycle club-related paraphernalia
affected_groups.explanation: They are the individuals whose interactions with law enforcement are covered by the bill’s definition and prohibition on motorcycle profiling.

affected_groups.group: Peace officers
affected_groups.explanation: The bill prohibits peace officers from motorcycle profiling and requires corrective action after an investigation establishes a policy violation.

affected_groups.group: Law enforcement agencies
affected_groups.explanation: Each agency must adopt a detailed written policy and provide a complaint process.

major_effects.label: Prohibition on motorcycle profiling
major_effects.explanation: Bars peace officers from profiling based wholly or partly on motorcycle operation or related paraphernalia rather than behavior or information identifying criminal activity; the definition includes certain stops extended beyond their purpose.

major_effects.label: Agency policies, complaints, and corrective action
major_effects.explanation: Each law enforcement agency must adopt a written policy that prohibits profiling, establishes a complaint process, and requires appropriate corrective action after an investigation finds a violation. The policy must be adopted by December 1, 2027.

agencies.name: law enforcement agency
agencies.explanation: The bill directly requires each law enforcement agency in the state to adopt a policy. The term is defined by reference to Article 2B.0053, whose definition is not included in the supplied sources, so specific state bodies covered cannot be identified.

HB919.summary: HB 919 would require the department to notify people within 60 days after adding their information to its intelligence database, explain how to dispute inclusion or seek removal after renouncing membership, and prohibit use of the information in employment-eligibility decisions or to limit constitutional rights or access to licenses, permits, or benefits. It would require annual audits, removal of information retained more than 10 years when the department cannot reestablish sufficient evidence, and public summaries of database counts. It would also strengthen administrative and judicial review, and require removal on the second anniversary of a person's renunciation of membership in a combination, criminal street gang, or foreign terrorist organization.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes how criminal information is reviewed, retained, and challenged in intelligence databases.
Adds protections against use of database information to limit constitutional rights and permits review of alleged constitutional violations.
Restricts use of personal information in a government intelligence database and requires review and possible removal of records.
Prohibits the database information from being used in employment-eligibility determinations.
Assigns annual audit and public-summary duties and requires the department to establish rules and forms for renunciation-based removal.

affected_groups.group: People whose information is included in the department's intelligence database
affected_groups.explanation: They would receive notice, have expanded ways to dispute information, and receive protections on how the information may be used.

affected_groups.group: Former members of combinations, criminal street gangs, or foreign terrorist organizations
affected_groups.explanation: A person who renounces membership would have a process for seeking removal of their information, with removal required on the second anniversary of renunciation.

affected_groups.group: People or parents and guardians requesting review of information, including information about a child
affected_groups.explanation: The bill expands the grounds for requesting review and changes the review standards and procedures.

affected_groups.group: Law enforcement agencies that collected the information
affected_groups.explanation: An agency would have to destroy records when review determines that the information fails the stated accuracy, submission, or legal-compliance tests.

major_effects.label: Notice and information about dispute and removal processes
major_effects.explanation: The department would have to notify a person within 60 days of adding their information and describe the dispute and renunciation-based removal processes; process information must also be posted online.

major_effects.label: Limits on use of database information
major_effects.explanation: Information in the database could not be used in employment-eligibility decisions or to limit constitutional rights or access to federal or state licenses, permits, or benefits.

major_effects.label: Annual audit, retention review, and public summary
major_effects.explanation: The state auditor would annually audit the database and publish a demographic summary, including counts of information retained more than five and 10 years; when information has been retained more than 10 years and sufficient evidence cannot be reestablished, it must be removed.

major_effects.label: Expanded administrative and judicial review
major_effects.explanation: Review would apply a probable-cause accuracy standard and consider submission criteria and specified legal violations. Judicial review would proceed by hearing, with the relevant information made available to the person's counsel under Article 39.14.

major_effects.label: Removal following renunciation
major_effects.explanation: The department would establish rules and forms for renunciation and removal; covered information must be removed on the second anniversary of renunciation.

agencies.name: the department
agencies.explanation: The bill assigns the department duties to notify people, publish information, destroy or remove records, and adopt rules. The supplied text does not identify the department by name.

agencies.name: state auditor
agencies.explanation: The bill assigns the state auditor annual database-audit and summary duties; the supplied text does not establish a canonical registry identity.

HB920.summary: HB 920 would require the Texas A&M AgriLife Extension Service to study each plant disease or pest outbreak in Texas annually and publish a report on the prior year’s study. By January 1, 2030, it would also publish a summary of the annual reports with policy recommendations for addressing outbreaks and provide that report to specified state officials; the requirement expires January 31, 2030.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill creates study and reporting requirements concerning plant disease and pest outbreaks.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The required studies cover outbreaks in Texas.

affected_groups.group: Agricultural producers and plant growers
affected_groups.explanation: They are among the populations materially affected by plant disease and pest outbreaks addressed by the required studies and recommendations.

affected_groups.group: State officials receiving the summary report
affected_groups.explanation: The Extension Service must provide the final summary and recommendations report to the listed state officials.

major_effects.label: Recurring outbreak studies and reports
major_effects.explanation: Requires annual studies of plant disease and pest outbreaks, annual public reports, and a summary report with policy recommendations by January 1, 2030; the section expires January 31, 2030.

agencies.name: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension Service
agencies.explanation: The bill assigns the Extension Service recurring study and publication duties. The supplied registry does not contain a matching canonical entry, so no registry ID is assigned.

HB921.summary: The bill would make an application for low-income housing tax credits ineligible if the development is in a school district to which Education Code Section 48.257(a) applied at any time during the five years before the application round begins. The change would apply only to application cycles based on the 2028 qualified allocation plan or a later plan; earlier-plan cycles would remain governed by prior law.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes eligibility for the low-income housing tax credit program based on where a housing development is located.
Changes which applications may be considered for an allocation of housing tax credits.

locations.name: School districts to which Education Code Section 48.257(a) applied during the five-year lookback period
locations.explanation: The eligibility restriction is limited to developments in districts meeting this statutory condition.

affected_groups.group: Applicants proposing low-income housing tax credit developments in qualifying school districts
affected_groups.explanation: Their applications would be ineligible for consideration under the specified geographic and lookback condition.

major_effects.label: Housing tax-credit eligibility
major_effects.explanation: Adds a location-based ineligibility condition for developments in qualifying school districts, subject to the application-plan transition rule.

agencies.name: Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs
agencies.explanation: The bill changes eligibility in the housing tax credit program, and identifies the department as the recipient of covered applications.

HB922.summary: HB 922 would repeal Property Code Section 202.024, which the bill describes as prohibiting property owners' associations from restricting rentals based on a person's method of payment. The repeal would remove that statutory prohibition.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill removes a statutory restriction on property owners' associations' rental policies.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The bill repeals a provision of the Texas Property Code, with statewide relevance.

affected_groups.group: Property owners' associations
affected_groups.explanation: The repeal removes a statutory prohibition concerning their rental restrictions based on payment method.

affected_groups.group: People seeking to rent property whose method of payment is relevant
affected_groups.explanation: The repealed prohibition concerned rental restrictions based on a person's method of payment.

major_effects.label: Remove payment-method rental restriction
major_effects.explanation: Repeals the statutory prohibition on property owners' associations imposing rental restrictions based on a person's method of payment.

HB925.summary: For residential-property appraisal protests concerning tax years beginning on or after January 1, 2028, an appraisal review board would have to adopt the value supported by the property owner’s appraisal if the appraisal meets the bill’s filing, certification, timing, and validity conditions, subject to an existing exception. The bill would also extend the Class B misdemeanor provision to appraisals filed under this new procedure when the appraiser had a contingency interest in the hearing outcome.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes the process for determining appraised or market value in certain residential property tax protests.
Imposes a new decision-making duty on appraisal review boards and requires delivery of the appraisal to the chief appraiser.
Expands the appraisals covered by an existing Class B misdemeanor provision involving appraisers with a contingency interest.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The bill sets a generally applicable rule for qualifying residential property protests, without specifying a narrower geographic area.

affected_groups.group: Owners of residential real property who protest an appraisal
affected_groups.explanation: Except as provided by Subsection (d), qualifying owners would receive the value supported by their appraisal if they satisfy the bill’s conditions.

affected_groups.group: Appraisal review boards and appraisal districts
affected_groups.explanation: Except as provided by Subsection (d), boards must issue the specified decision and written order in qualifying protests; the chief appraiser receives a copy of the owner’s appraisal.

affected_groups.group: Certified appraisers with a contingency interest in an appraisal review board hearing
affected_groups.explanation: Their appraisals filed under the new procedure would be included in the records covered by the specified Class B misdemeanor provision.

major_effects.label: Required adoption of a qualifying owner appraisal
major_effects.explanation: In a qualifying residential-property protest, the board must favor the owner and change the recorded value to the value supported by the owner’s appraisal, subject to Subsection (d) and the bill’s conditions.

major_effects.label: Expanded coverage of Class B misdemeanor provision
major_effects.explanation: The provision would cover an appraisal filed under the new subsection when the appraisal was performed by a person with a contingency interest in the hearing outcome.

HB927.summary: HB 927 would designate the specified segment of State Highway 31 in Henderson County as part of Texas’s portion of the national Purple Heart Trail. It would also provide that all designations listed under subsection (a), rather than only the prior item (a)(8), are in addition to any other designation.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill adds a defined segment of a state highway to a statutory trail designation.

locations.name: Part of State Highway 31 in Henderson County between the Navarro County line and the eastern municipal boundary of Athens
locations.explanation: The bill defines the designated highway segment by its county-line and municipal-boundary endpoints.

major_effects.label: Purple Heart Trail designation
major_effects.explanation: Adds the specified State Highway 31 segment to the Texas portion of the national Purple Heart Trail and makes the listed designations additional to any other designation.

HB928.summary: The bill would prohibit construction of a data center within a municipality or an unincorporated county area unless the relevant municipal governing body or county commissioners court approves it at a public hearing. The requirement would apply only when the first application for a building permit or other required local construction authorization is submitted on or after the Act’s effective date.

policy_tags.explanation: Creates a local approval requirement for construction of a defined data center.
Assigns municipal governing bodies and county commissioners courts approval authority over covered construction.

locations.name: Boundaries of a municipality
locations.explanation: The approval requirement applies to data center construction within municipal boundaries.

locations.name: Unincorporated area of a county
locations.explanation: The approval requirement separately applies to data center construction in a county's unincorporated area.

affected_groups.group: People or entities seeking to construct data centers
affected_groups.explanation: Covered construction would require approval at a public hearing by the relevant local governing body.

affected_groups.group: Municipal governing bodies and county commissioners courts
affected_groups.explanation: These local bodies would vote on approval of covered data center construction at public hearings.

major_effects.label: Local approval before data center construction
major_effects.explanation: Requires a public-hearing vote approving construction by the municipality or county, depending on the location. It applies only when the first required building-permit or other local construction-authorization application is submitted on or after the Act's effective date.

HB930.summary: HB 930 would define coercive control as a pattern of specified acts and include it in family violence for conservatorship and possession decisions. After notice and a hearing, a preponderance finding of family violence would create a rebuttable presumption against specified custody and access arrangements; the bill sets different proof and safety requirements for supervised versus other arrangements. It would also require written findings in qualifying contested proceedings and apply to suits filed on or after its effective date, leaving earlier-filed suits under prior law.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes custody and access standards and requires safety conditions in certain family-violence cases to protect the child and victim.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The amendments concern suits under the Texas Family Code and apply to qualifying suits filed on or after the Act's effective date.

affected_groups.group: Parents involved in conservatorship or possession proceedings where family violence is alleged or found
affected_groups.explanation: The bill defines relevant conduct and changes the standards for conservatorship, possession, and access after a family-violence finding.

affected_groups.group: Children and victims of family violence
affected_groups.explanation: The court must consider effects on their safety and may impose protective terms for possession and access.

affected_groups.group: Qualified neutral persons or entities supervising parent-child contact
affected_groups.explanation: When supervised possession or access is ordered, the court must designate a qualified neutral supervisor; the victim may not serve in that role.

major_effects.label: Coercive control included in family violence
major_effects.explanation: Defines coercive control as a contextual pattern of threatening, intimidating, or controlling acts and includes it in family violence for the specified custody determinations.

major_effects.label: Rebuttable presumption on custody and access
major_effects.explanation: After notice and an opportunity to be heard, a preponderance finding of family violence triggers a presumption against the listed conservatorship, residence, possession, or access arrangements. The bill requires clear and convincing evidence for the specified appointment, right, or unsupervised contact, while supervised contact requires a preponderance showing and appropriate safety conditions.

major_effects.label: Safety conditions for supervised contact
major_effects.explanation: If supervised possession or access is ordered, the court must set its terms and designate a qualified neutral supervisor; the victim cannot be the supervisor. A later change to unsupervised contact requires another order and the required findings.

major_effects.label: Written findings in qualifying contested proceedings
major_effects.explanation: When a contested proceeding admits evidence concerning alleged family violence, the court must make written findings addressing whether violence occurred, the applicable presumption and proof, and why the terms and safeguards serve the child's best interest.

agencies.name: court
agencies.explanation: The bill assigns decision-making and written-finding duties to a court, but does not identify a particular court or establish its canonical agency identity.

HB933.summary: The bill would prohibit employers from collecting or receiving any part of a gratuity paid or left for a tipped employee, including to cover a credit or debit card issuer’s financial-service costs. It declares the gratuity to be the tipped employee’s property and applies the prohibition only to gratuities paid or left on or after the Act’s effective date.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill changes employers’ treatment of gratuities paid or left for tipped employees.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The bill amends the Texas Labor Code and establishes a rule for covered employers and employees under that state law.

affected_groups.group: Tipped employees
affected_groups.explanation: Their gratuities would be protected from collection or receipt by an employer.

affected_groups.group: Employers of tipped employees
affected_groups.explanation: They would be prohibited from collecting or receiving any portion of a covered gratuity.

major_effects.label: Protects tipped employees’ gratuities
major_effects.explanation: Would bar employers from taking any portion of a covered gratuity, including to compensate a card issuer for financial services, and makes the gratuity the employee’s property.

HB935.summary: HB 935 adds an abusive work environment to the statutory definition of sexual harassment and expressly applies existing anti-retaliation protections to acts relating to sexual harassment. It allows a civil action over a sexual-harassment-based employment practice whether or not a commission complaint was filed, and regardless of whether a filed complaint is pending or a right-to-sue notice has been received; it also changes the limitations period for actions filed without a complaint and removes the Labor Code damages cap for covered actions, subject to Civil Practice and Remedies Code Section 41.008. The changes apply only to conduct occurring on or after the Act’s effective date.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill expands sexual-harassment protections and access to civil remedies for unlawful employment practices.
The bill changes employment-practice protections and civil claims involving employers, labor unions, and employment agencies.

locations.name: Texas (statewide)
locations.explanation: The bill amends the Texas Labor Code and changes the rules for covered claims under that state law.

affected_groups.group: Individuals affected by sexual harassment, including complainants and people participating in related proceedings
affected_groups.explanation: They receive express anti-retaliation protection and may bring covered civil actions without first filing a commission complaint or waiting for a right-to-sue notice.

affected_groups.group: Employers, labor unions, and employment agencies
affected_groups.explanation: These entities are identified as subject to the unlawful-practice provision, and respondents in covered sexual-harassment actions are affected by the damages-cap change.

major_effects.label: Sexual-harassment protections
major_effects.explanation: The definition includes an abusive working environment, and anti-retaliation protections expressly cover acts relating to sexual-harassment practices.

major_effects.label: Access to civil actions
major_effects.explanation: An individual may sue over a sexual-harassment-based employment practice whether or not a commission complaint was filed, including while a complaint is pending or before receipt of a right-to-sue notice.

major_effects.label: Limitations period for suits filed without a complaint
major_effects.explanation: For a covered action filed without a commission complaint, the two-year period runs from the date the conduct occurred rather than the date a complaint was filed.

major_effects.label: Damages-cap exception
major_effects.explanation: The Labor Code cap in Section 21.2585(d) does not apply to covered sexual-harassment damages actions, which remain subject to Civil Practice and Remedies Code Section 41.008.

agencies.name: commission
agencies.explanation: The bill makes sexual-harassment civil actions independent of whether a complaint has been filed with the commission or remains pending, affecting the relationship between the commission complaint process and court access. The bill does not identify the commission by its full name.

HB936.summary: HB 936 would make equal, meaningful opportunity for every student’s academic and professional development part of the stated mission of public higher-education governing boards. The restrictions on institutional DEI offices and activities would not apply when required by federal law or for purposes of fulfilling that mission; the mission exception qualifies the restrictions.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes the stated mission and governance requirements for public institutions of higher education.
Changes the scope of restrictions concerning DEI activities, preferences, and training that reference protected characteristics.

locations.name: Texas
locations.explanation: The provisions apply to the described public higher-education governing boards statewide.

affected_groups.group: Students at public institutions of higher education
affected_groups.explanation: The stated board mission would expressly include ensuring each student's equal, meaningful opportunity for academic and professional development.

affected_groups.group: Public institutions of higher education and their governing boards
affected_groups.explanation: Boards would have a revised mission and would ensure institutional units comply with the qualified DEI restrictions.

affected_groups.group: Institution employees, contractors, applicants, and institutional participants
affected_groups.explanation: The existing restrictions cover institutional DEI-related employment, statements, preferences, and required training, subject to the bill's added mission-related qualification.

major_effects.label: Higher-education board mission
major_effects.explanation: Adds ensuring each student's equal, meaningful opportunity for academic and professional development to the stated mission of governing boards.

major_effects.label: Qualification to institutional DEI restrictions
major_effects.explanation: Adds fulfillment of the board's revised mission as a qualification to the listed restrictions; the text also retains its federal-law qualification.

agencies.name: governing boards of institutions of higher education
agencies.explanation: The bill directly changes the stated mission of these boards and the requirements they must ensure each institutional unit follows. The source identifies a category of boards, not a specific board with a canonical registry identity.

HB937.summary: The bill would require school districts to give parents or legal guardians of students with an intellectual disability or developmental delay information about services and public benefits from the local intellectual and developmental disability authority at each admission, review, and dismissal committee meeting, rather than only at the first individualized education program meeting. The requirement would apply beginning with the 2027-2028 school year.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes the information school districts must provide to parents or guardians in connection with students' admission, review, and dismissal committee meetings.
Imposes an expanded information-providing duty on school districts.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The requirement applies to school districts statewide.

affected_groups.group: Parents and legal guardians of students with an intellectual disability or developmental delay
affected_groups.explanation: They would receive information at each admission, review, and dismissal committee meeting.

affected_groups.group: Students with an intellectual disability or developmental delay
affected_groups.explanation: Their families would receive the specified local-authority service and public-benefit information at each committee meeting.

affected_groups.group: School districts
affected_groups.explanation: They would provide the information at each relevant committee meeting instead of only at the first individualized education program meeting.

major_effects.label: Information at each committee meeting
major_effects.explanation: Expands the school district information requirement from the first individualized education program meeting to each admission, review, and dismissal committee meeting; the information concerns services and public benefits from the local authority serving the student's county.

HB938.summary: The bill removes operation of a motor vehicle on a public highway from the Family Code chapter’s definition of “license” and prohibits a court or the Title IV-D agency from ordering a driver’s license or motor vehicle registration suspended, or an order that would cause either not to be renewed. These changes apply only to orders rendered on or after the Act’s effective date; earlier orders remain governed by prior law.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes whether driver’s licenses and motor vehicle registrations may be suspended or not renewed through child-support enforcement orders.
Restricts the order-making authority of courts and the Title IV-D agency under Family Code Chapter 232.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The bill amends Texas Family Code provisions without limiting the changes to a particular place.

affected_groups.group: Individuals delinquent in child support whose driver’s licenses or motor vehicle registrations could be targeted by an order
affected_groups.explanation: They would be protected from the specified license and registration orders for orders rendered on or after the effective date.

major_effects.label: Limits child-support license and registration orders
major_effects.explanation: Removes motor-vehicle operation from the chapter’s “license” definition and prohibits courts and the Title IV-D agency from ordering driver’s-license or motor-vehicle-registration suspension or nonrenewal. The restriction applies to orders rendered on or after the effective date.

agencies.name: Title IV-D agency
agencies.explanation: The bill directly bars this agency from rendering the specified orders. The supplied text does not identify which Texas entity is the Title IV-D agency.

agencies.name: Court
agencies.explanation: The bill directly bars a court from rendering the specified orders but does not identify a particular court.

HB939.summary: HB 939 would establish the Texas Southern University College of Medicine as a college of Texas Southern University, managed by its board of regents. The board could set courses and operating rules, arrange affiliations and facilities, and solicit gifts and grants; a teaching hospital could be provided by a public or private entity but could not be constructed, maintained, or operated with state funds. The bill would also add the college to education-law definitions and lists, including one governing eligibility for appropriations from a fund for medical research, health education, or treatment programs.

policy_tags.explanation: Creates a university college of medicine and authorizes its courses, degrees, and operating rules.
Adds the college to medical-school and health-related institution provisions, including medical education and health-related fund eligibility.

Adds the college to the institutions whose medical research, health education, or treatment programs may benefit from appropriations from the specified fund; it does not make a specific appropriation.

affected_groups.group: Texas Southern University medical students and professional staff
affected_groups.explanation: The college is created within the university, and the bill includes its staff members and students in provisions concerning health care liability self-insurance funds.

affected_groups.group: Public and private entities providing facilities or hospital services
affected_groups.explanation: Such entities may provide additional teaching and research facilities or a teaching hospital for the college; the hospital may not use state funds for construction, maintenance, or operation.

affected_groups.group: Medical research, health education, and treatment programs at the college
affected_groups.explanation: These programs become eligible to benefit from appropriations from the specified fund through the college's addition to the eligible institution list.

major_effects.label: Creates the College of Medicine
major_effects.explanation: Establishes the Texas Southern University College of Medicine as a college of the university under the board's management and control.

major_effects.label: Authorizes college operations and facilities
major_effects.explanation: Authorizes the board to prescribe courses and rules, enter affiliation or coordinating agreements, arrange additional facilities, and solicit and administer gifts and grants.

major_effects.label: Limits state funding for a teaching hospital
major_effects.explanation: A suitable teaching hospital may be provided by a public or private entity, but state funds may not be used to construct, maintain, or operate it.

major_effects.label: Adds the college to medical-institution provisions
major_effects.explanation: Adds the college to statutory medical-school and health-related institution lists, including the list whose programs may benefit from appropriations from the specified fund.

major_effects.label: Extends self-insurance provisions to the college
major_effects.explanation: Adds the college to provisions allowing a board to establish a self-insurance fund for specified health care liability claims and applies the related restriction on use of appropriated funds.

agencies.name: board of regents of Texas Southern University
agencies.explanation: The bill assigns this board management and control of the college and authority over its courses, rules, agreements, facilities, and gifts and grants. No canonical registry entry is supplied for this named board.

agencies.name: Texas Southern University
agencies.explanation: The bill establishes the college as part of the university and permits degrees to be offered under the university's name and authority. No canonical registry entry is supplied for the university.

HB941.summary: The bill would add social workers, as defined by Section 505.002, Occupations Code, to the occupations eligible for low-interest home mortgage loans under the Homes for Texas Heroes program. Applicants would still have to meet the program’s residency and income limits, and proceeds from program-issued obligations could fund loans to eligible social workers.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill expands access to a low-interest home mortgage loan program.

locations.name: Texas
locations.explanation: The eligibility requirements include Texas residency, and the home must be in the state.

affected_groups.group: Social workers seeking program home loans
affected_groups.explanation: The bill adds them to the eligible occupations, subject to the program’s residency and income requirements.

major_effects.label: Expand home-loan eligibility
major_effects.explanation: Adds social workers, as defined by the Occupations Code, to the eligible occupations; existing residency and income limits remain applicable.

major_effects.label: Allow program proceeds to fund social-worker loans
major_effects.explanation: Includes eligible social workers among the borrowers whose loans may be funded with proceeds from obligations issued under the program; this does not itself provide a new appropriation.

agencies.name: the corporation
agencies.explanation: The corporation administers the affected home-loan program, and the bill adds social workers to its eligible borrower group. Its identity and status as a state body are not established in the supplied text.

HB942.summary: The bill revises which municipalities are covered by the local-option provisions in Alcoholic Beverage Code Section 251.742, including a separate qualification for municipalities with at least 240,000 residents that span two or more counties and border a man-made lake of at least 20,000 acres. In a zone designated under that section, a municipality’s governing body may adopt zoning and land-use regulations for premises selling alcoholic beverages, subject to Chapter 211 of the Local Government Code.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill revises the municipality criteria for coverage by a provision concerning local-option elections.
It changes which municipalities are covered and authorizes their governing bodies to regulate qualifying premises in designated zones.
It authorizes local zoning and land-use regulation of premises that sell alcoholic beverages in designated zones.

locations.name: Municipalities meeting the Section 251.742(b) criteria and zones designated under that section
locations.explanation: The bill concerns municipalities meeting specified population and geographic criteria, and designated zones within those municipalities.

affected_groups.group: Governing bodies of municipalities meeting the statutory criteria
affected_groups.explanation: These municipalities are covered by the revised criteria, and their governing bodies may adopt zoning and land-use regulations for qualifying premises in designated zones.

affected_groups.group: Operators of premises selling alcoholic beverages in designated zones
affected_groups.explanation: Their premises may be subject to municipal zoning and land-use regulations under the bill.

major_effects.label: Revises municipalities covered
major_effects.explanation: The bill specifies a Gulf-coast county qualification for municipalities with at least 15,000 residents and adds an alternative qualification for municipalities with at least 240,000 residents that span two or more counties and border a qualifying man-made lake.

major_effects.label: Municipal zoning authority
major_effects.explanation: A qualifying municipality may adopt zoning and land-use regulations for premises selling alcoholic beverages in a zone designated under the section, subject to Chapter 211 of the Local Government Code.

HB943.summary: HB 943 would expand the cancers covered by Government Code Section 607.055(b) for firefighters’ and emergency medical technicians’ benefit or compensation claims to include other cancers linked to specified exposures or carcinogens identified by the International Agency for Research on Cancer. The change would apply only to claims brought on or after the Act’s effective date.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill expands cancer coverage relevant to firefighters’ and emergency medical technicians’ benefit or compensation claims.
The changed claim coverage applies to firefighters and emergency medical technicians.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The amendment is to the Texas Government Code and applies to qualifying claims under that state law.

affected_groups.group: Firefighters and emergency medical technicians bringing cancer-related benefit or compensation claims
affected_groups.explanation: Their claims could cover additional cancers, subject to the bill’s exposure and carcinogen criteria and its application-date limitation.

major_effects.label: Expanded covered cancer claims
major_effects.explanation: Adds other cancers meeting the specified exposure or carcinogen criterion to the cancers covered by the section; the change applies only to claims brought on or after the Act’s effective date.

HB944.summary: HB 944 would establish training on pregnancy fraud for health care practitioners and law enforcement officers, require covered health care facilities to adopt procedures for addressing credible threats and submit procedure summaries to their licensing agency, and allow up to two hours of continuing education credit for practitioners. It would also require a public-awareness campaign and create a Class B misdemeanor for knowingly presenting false pregnancy-related medical records to deceive someone in order to facilitate a felony, when the person knows they are not pregnant.

policy_tags.explanation: Creates health care practitioner training and facility procedures concerning pregnancy fraud.
Training and facility procedures address credible threats to public health or safety and de-escalation.
Adds a criminal offense and requires pregnancy-fraud training for officers.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The provisions concern health-care services authorized in Texas and statewide agency programs.

affected_groups.group: Health care practitioners who provide care to pregnant women
affected_groups.explanation: They are the intended participants in the training program and may claim continuing education credit.

affected_groups.group: Health care facilities and their personnel
affected_groups.explanation: Facilities must adopt threat-response procedures and submit summaries; personnel receive guidance on evaluating and responding to suspected pregnancy fraud.

affected_groups.group: Law enforcement officers
affected_groups.explanation: Officers are included in a required training program on recognizing pregnancy fraud and responding to related safety threats.

affected_groups.group: Potential victims of pregnancy fraud and their families
affected_groups.explanation: Training must include resources available to potential victims and their families.

major_effects.label: Pregnancy-fraud training
major_effects.explanation: Requires evidence-based training programs for relevant health care practitioners and officers; each program must include at least two hours of training.

major_effects.label: Facility procedures and oversight
major_effects.explanation: Requires facilities to adopt procedures for evaluating credible threats and submit written summaries to their licensing agency; violations are subject to agency disciplinary action.

major_effects.label: Public-awareness campaign
major_effects.explanation: Requires a public campaign and online educational materials about identifying and reporting suspected pregnancy fraud and related safety threats.

major_effects.label: Pregnancy-record offense
major_effects.explanation: Creates a Class B misdemeanor for knowingly presenting a false, fraudulent, or fictitious medical record to deceive someone into believing the actor is pregnant, when done to facilitate a felony and with knowledge the actor is not pregnant.

agencies.name: Health and Human Services Commission
agencies.explanation: The executive commissioner must adopt implementing rules, and the Commission must collaborate on a public-awareness campaign and post educational materials.

agencies.name: Texas Commission on Law Enforcement
agencies.explanation: The bill assigns the Commission rulemaking responsibilities for the officer training program; the bill expressly identifies it as the commission responsible for implementing Section 1701.275.

agencies.name: the department
agencies.explanation: The bill assigns this body responsibility for establishing and maintaining practitioner training, but does not identify it by name in the supplied text.

agencies.name: the state agency that issues the facility's license, certification, or other authorization
agencies.explanation: The relevant agency must receive facility procedure summaries and may take disciplinary action only against a health care facility that violates this chapter, as if it had violated the applicable licensing or regulatory law. The bill does not identify the agencies or specify which facility licensing regimes apply.

agencies.name: a regulatory authority that licenses or regulates a health care practitioner
agencies.explanation: Covered authorities must allow eligible practitioners to claim continuing education credit, but the bill does not name the authorities or identify the licenses involved.

HB946.summary: The bill would raise salary-schedule factors and require specified 2025–2026 compensation increases: covered teachers, librarians, counselors, and nurses would receive at least their prior-year schedule salary, including applicable supplements, plus $1,500; other covered full-time district employees would receive a 25 percent wage increase, except administrators and employees on the minimum salary schedule. It would preserve specified salary or wage levels in later years for employees who remain with the same district or in the same position, and provide school districts annual state aid for these increases, restricted to salary and wage increases.

policy_tags.explanation: Amends public-school salary schedules and compensation requirements for school district employees.
Sets compensation increases and continuing pay floors for public school employees.
Requires school districts to increase employee compensation and provides aid to districts for those increases.
Creates annual state aid for districts' specified salary and wage increases.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The requirements apply to school districts as a statewide class; no particular locality is specified.

affected_groups.group: Classroom teachers, full-time librarians, certified full-time school counselors, and full-time school nurses
affected_groups.explanation: Receive the specified 2025–2026 salary increase and a continuing salary floor while employed by the same district.

affected_groups.group: Other full-time school district employees covered by the wage provision
affected_groups.explanation: Receive a 25 percent wage increase for 2025–2026, excluding administrators and employees subject to the minimum salary schedule; later wages have a floor if they remain in the same position.

affected_groups.group: School districts
affected_groups.explanation: Must fund the required compensation increases and are entitled to annual state aid for the specified increases, including districts otherwise ineligible for aid under the chapter.

major_effects.label: Higher salary-schedule factors
major_effects.explanation: Raises the salary factors used for the statutory public-school salary schedule.

major_effects.label: Required compensation increases and continuing pay floors
major_effects.explanation: Sets 2025–2026 minimum salary or wage increases for specified employees and maintains salary or wage floors in later years subject to the same-district or same-position conditions.

major_effects.label: Annual state aid for compensation increases
major_effects.explanation: Entitles districts, including otherwise aid-ineligible districts, to annual aid calculated in part from covered staff counts and required wage increases; the aid must be used for the specified salary and wage increases.

agencies.name: Texas Education Agency
agencies.explanation: The new Chapter 48 state-aid entitlement likely affects the state education funding administrator, but the bill does not name an administering agency.

HB947.summary: When a party to a divorce suit discloses pregnancy, the suit must include a parent-child suit concerning the unborn child, and the court may not delay the divorce solely because of the pregnancy. If the court knows a party is pregnant, it may sever the child-related suit or a marital-estate matter for good cause; the bill also gives a party to the divorce standing to file the parent-child suit and sets requirements for petitions concerning an unborn child. These changes apply to suits filed on or after the Act’s effective date.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes court procedures and authority in covered divorce and parent-child cases.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The changes apply to covered suits under the Texas Family Code filed on or after the effective date.

affected_groups.group: Parties to a divorce suit when either party is pregnant
affected_groups.explanation: Their divorce proceedings must include a parent-child suit concerning the unborn child, and a party to the divorce may file that suit.

affected_groups.group: Unborn children and children born after a covered petition is filed
affected_groups.explanation: The parent-child suit concerns the unborn child, and the petition must be updated with the child’s name and date of birth after birth.

major_effects.label: Court handling of divorce and related cases
major_effects.explanation: A pregnancy disclosure requires inclusion of a parent-child suit concerning the unborn child. A court may not delay the divorce solely because of pregnancy, and may sever the related suit or a marital-estate matter only when the pregnancy is known to the court and good cause is shown.

major_effects.label: Standing to file a parent-child suit
major_effects.explanation: A party to a divorce suit in which either party is pregnant is added as a person who may file an original suit.

major_effects.label: Petition information for an unborn child
major_effects.explanation: A petition filed under the new standing provision must state that the child has not been born and provide the expected birth date, then be amended after birth with the child’s name and date of birth.

major_effects.label: Protections when a related matter is severed
major_effects.explanation: When a matter is severed, the court must provide relief it considers necessary to protect the parties, child or unborn child, and marital estate until final adjudication; claims are not waived and no additional fees may be required for the severed matter.

agencies.name: court
agencies.explanation: The bill directly assigns courts new requirements and authority in covered cases, but does not identify a particular court or court system.

HB948.summary: The bill would repeal several specified Texas laws regulating abortion, including Health and Safety Code Chapter 170A and Subchapter H of Chapter 171, along with other cited provisions. It also removes Chapter 171’s exception to the commission’s enforcement mandate, but repeals Subchapter H in the same bill, so the text does not establish a surviving Subchapter H enforcement regime.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill repeals specified laws regulating abortion, a healthcare-related subject.

locations.name: Statewide (Texas)
locations.explanation: The bill changes Texas statutes and applies statewide.

affected_groups.group: People seeking or providing abortion-related care
affected_groups.explanation: They are among the people affected by the repeal of specified laws regulating abortion.

affected_groups.group: People or entities involved in private civil enforcement actions under the repealed provisions
affected_groups.explanation: The bill repeals Subchapter H, which the existing text describes as providing for private civil enforcement actions.

major_effects.label: Repeal of specified abortion-related provisions
major_effects.explanation: Repeals the listed statutory provisions, including Health and Safety Code Chapter 170A and Subchapter H of Chapter 171. The bill text does not describe the full content or legal consequences of every repealed provision.

HB949.summary: HB 949 would require procuring entities to require U.S.-produced construction materials in covered public infrastructure contracts estimated at $1 million or more; entities could also impose the requirement on projects estimated at $1 million or less, so the ranges overlap at $1 million. The mandatory requirement could be waived by written determination for specified availability, quality, delay, or cost reasons, and the subchapter would not apply to disaster-response or federally funded contracts. State agencies would add a Texas-purchase contract provision under existing law, while political subdivisions could choose to do so; the Comptroller would adopt rules, collect annual purchase and exemption information, and report to the Legislature.

policy_tags.explanation: Creates domestic-material procurement requirements and implementation and reporting duties for public infrastructure contracts.
Applies procurement requirements to political subdivisions and allows them to add a Texas-purchase contract provision.

locations.name: Texas (statewide)
locations.explanation: The procurement provisions apply to qualifying projects of state agencies and political subdivisions across the state.

affected_groups.group: Public procuring entities, including state agencies and political subdivisions
affected_groups.explanation: They must apply the sourcing requirement to covered projects, subject to the bill's exceptions; political subdivisions may elect to include the Texas-purchase provision.

affected_groups.group: Contractors and bidders on covered public infrastructure projects
affected_groups.explanation: Bid documents and resulting contracts must require covered construction materials to be produced in the United States, except as provided by Section 2252.235.

major_effects.label: Domestic sourcing for infrastructure projects
major_effects.explanation: Requires U.S.-produced construction materials in covered projects estimated at $1 million or more and permits the requirement for projects estimated at $1 million or less; the mandatory rule is subject to written exemptions and specified disaster-related and federal-funding exclusions.

major_effects.label: Texas-purchase contract provision
major_effects.explanation: State agencies must include the provision specified by existing law when they include a domestic-materials provision; political subdivisions may include it.

major_effects.label: Implementation rules
major_effects.explanation: Directs the Comptroller to adopt rules to administer the new subchapter, including rules to ensure contractor compliance.

major_effects.label: Annual procurement reporting
major_effects.explanation: Requires the Comptroller to collect information on material purchase sources and the reasoning for specified exemptions, then report a summary to the Legislature.

agencies.name: Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts
agencies.explanation: The Comptroller is assigned rulemaking, information-collection, and legislative reporting duties.

agencies.name: state agency
agencies.explanation: State agencies are directly affected when acting as procuring entities; the bill refers to the statutory definition rather than naming individual agencies.

HB950.summary: The bill would prohibit selling algorithmic products or services used to set or recommend residential rent, and would separately bar providers advising landlords from using nonpublic competitor data in their calculations. The chapter would not apply to a covered device when the nonpublic competitor data includes executed lease data also made publicly available in aggregated, anonymous form for no more than a reasonable charge; violations of the prohibitions would be actionable as deceptive trade practices.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill regulates algorithmic tools used to determine or recommend rent for residential premises.
It prohibits specified commercial sales and data-use practices and makes violations actionable as deceptive trade practices.
The bill restricts the use of defined nonpublic competitor data in algorithmic rent calculations.

locations.name: Texas
locations.explanation: The data-use restriction expressly concerns residential properties in this state.

affected_groups.group: Businesses selling algorithmic rent-setting or rent-recommending products or services
affected_groups.explanation: Their sales for the specified rent-setting purposes would be prohibited, subject to the chapter's applicability exception.

affected_groups.group: Providers of algorithmic services or products that advise landlords
affected_groups.explanation: Providers advising landlords about rent could not use nonpublic competitor data in algorithmic calculations, subject to the chapter's applicability exception.

affected_groups.group: Landlords and residential tenants
affected_groups.explanation: The regulated tools are used to advise landlords on rent amounts that may be charged to tenants.

major_effects.label: Prohibition on selling rent-setting tools
major_effects.explanation: Prohibits selling algorithmic services or products for setting or recommending residential rent; the chapter's applicability exception may exclude a device using qualifying publicly available aggregated data.

major_effects.label: Restriction on competitor-data use
major_effects.explanation: Providers advising landlords may not use nonpublic competitor data about Texas residential properties in algorithmic calculations, subject to the chapter's applicability exception.

major_effects.label: Deceptive-trade-practice claims
major_effects.explanation: A violation of the specified prohibitions would be actionable as a deceptive trade practice under the cited existing law.

HB951.summary: HB 951 would add the part of Interstate Highway 20 in Kaufman County to the Texas portion of the national Purple Heart Trail. It also clarifies that the highway designations under subsection (a) are additional to any other designation.
