policy_tags.explanation: The bill changes the statutory designation of a specific interstate highway segment.

locations.name: Kaufman County
locations.explanation: The newly designated highway segment is located in Kaufman County.

affected_groups.group: Highway users in Kaufman County
affected_groups.explanation: The bill changes the designation applying to a segment of Interstate Highway 20 in the county.

affected_groups.group: Veterans and Purple Heart recipients
affected_groups.explanation: The newly included highway segment would be part of a trail named in recognition of Purple Heart recipients.

major_effects.label: Adds an Interstate 20 segment to the Purple Heart Trail
major_effects.explanation: The part of Interstate Highway 20 in Kaufman County would join the listed highways designated as the Texas portion of the national Purple Heart Trail; the bill also states those designations are additional to any other designation.

HB952.summary: HB 952 would establish a supported independent living program for young adults interested in voluntarily entering extended foster care, with independent placements, case management, limited supervision, and support toward self-sufficiency. It would update related housing and criminal-history provisions to refer to supported rather than supervised independent living; youth in the program could cosign a lease only if the property owner does not object.

policy_tags.explanation: Establishes independent living placements and updates foster-care transition and rental-history provisions for supported independent living.
Assigns a state department responsibility to establish and administer a new program.
Updates criminal-history information provisions to cover people connected with supported independent living services and host homes.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The program is established under Texas law without a specified local or regional limit.

affected_groups.group: Young adults interested in voluntarily entering extended foster care
affected_groups.explanation: They are the intended participants in the new supported independent living program.

affected_groups.group: Youth transitioning from foster care
affected_groups.explanation: Their transition plans and housing arrangements reference supported independent living.

affected_groups.group: Supported independent living providers, their workers and volunteers, and people regularly working or staying in host homes
affected_groups.explanation: The bill updates criminal-history information provisions for people connected with these services and settings.

major_effects.label: Supported independent living program
major_effects.explanation: Requires the department to establish placements with case management and limited supervision, and support young adults in pursuing goals, accessing resources, learning life skills, and building relationships.

major_effects.label: Housing-transition provisions updated
major_effects.explanation: Updates existing transition planning, housing preparation, placement-capacity, and lease-history provisions to refer to supported independent living; lease cosigning remains conditional on the property owner's nonobjection.

major_effects.label: Criminal-history information for supported living settings
major_effects.explanation: Updates the covered provider and host-home categories in the provision allowing DFPS or HHSC to obtain criminal-history information.

agencies.name: Texas Department of Family and Protective Services
agencies.explanation: Expressly included in the criminal-history information provision for people connected with supported independent living services.

agencies.name: Health and Human Services Commission
agencies.explanation: Expressly included in the criminal-history information provision for people connected with supported independent living services.

agencies.name: the department
agencies.explanation: The bill directly assigns this body the program-establishment duty, but the supplied text does not identify which state agency the generic term denotes.

HB954.summary: The bill would create an Office of Youth Health and Safety within the Health and Human Services Commission and establish a board to govern it. The office would develop and submit a plan for juvenile justice system changes, including strategies for alternatives to secure commitment, county-based services, and reducing racial and disability disparities; these are planning requirements, not an order to implement the changes or close facilities.

policy_tags.explanation: Creates an office and governing board within the Health and Human Services Commission.
Requires a plan for changes to the juvenile justice system, including alternatives to post-adjudication secure commitment.
The required plan must include strategies to end racial and disability disparities in the juvenile justice system.
The plan must address county-level infrastructure and local delinquency-prevention and intervention services.
The plan must include strategies to increase evidence-based delinquency responses and interventions in schools.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The plan must address infrastructure in every Texas county.

affected_groups.group: Children ages 10 through 17 under juvenile court jurisdiction
affected_groups.explanation: These children are the defined population addressed by the office's goals and juvenile justice plan.

affected_groups.group: Counties and juvenile probation departments
affected_groups.explanation: The plan must address county-level alternatives and services, and the office must consult juvenile probation departments.

affected_groups.group: Children affected by racial or disability disparities in the juvenile justice system
affected_groups.explanation: The required plan must include strategies directed at ending these disparities.

major_effects.label: Youth health and safety office and governing board
major_effects.explanation: Creates the office within the commission and establishes a board to govern it.

major_effects.label: Juvenile justice improvement plan
major_effects.explanation: Requires a plan with strategies for alternatives to secure commitment, county-based services, and disparity reduction; the plan requirement does not itself implement those strategies or close facilities.

major_effects.label: Plan submission
major_effects.explanation: Requires the office to submit its plan to state leadership and legislators.

agencies.name: Health and Human Services Commission
agencies.explanation: The commission's executive commissioner must maintain the new office and appoint the board's initial members.

agencies.name: Office of Youth Health and Safety
agencies.explanation: The bill creates the office and assigns it responsibility for developing the juvenile justice improvement plan.

agencies.name: Board of Youth Health and Safety
agencies.explanation: The bill creates the board as the office's governing body and sets its membership.

agencies.name: Texas Education Agency
agencies.explanation: The director of the agency's Early Childhood Education Division is included on the new board.

agencies.name: Texas Juvenile Justice Department
agencies.explanation: The required plan sets strategies concerning commitments to, and possible closure of, the department's post-adjudication secure facilities; it does not itself order those changes.

HB955.summary: HB 955 would define a lactation room and extend the invasive visual recording offense to recording, broadcasting, or transmitting a visual image of another person in such a room without consent and with intent to invade that person's privacy. The existing offense provision covering promotion of images described by the statute would also encompass images from lactation rooms; the change would apply only to offenses committed on or after the Act's effective date.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill expands the settings covered by an existing Penal Code offense.
The change covers electronic visual recording and related conduct that invades another person's privacy in a lactation room.

locations.name: Texas statewide
locations.explanation: The bill amends the Texas Penal Code and states no local geographic limitation.

affected_groups.group: People using lactation rooms
affected_groups.explanation: They would be covered by the expanded offense when someone records or transmits their image there without consent and with intent to invade their privacy.

affected_groups.group: People who record, transmit, or promote covered images
affected_groups.explanation: Their conduct may fall within the expanded offense when it meets the statute's existing conditions.

major_effects.label: Expands invasive visual recording offense
major_effects.explanation: Adds a lactation room to the settings covered by the offense, subject to its existing consent and intent requirements; promotion of images described by the offense is also covered.

HB956.summary: HB 956 would revise the expressly listed uses of school safety allotment funds, including adding threat detection and reporting systems and removing several specified mental-health, restorative-practice, and suicide-prevention uses. It would create an annual Foundation School Program mental-health allotment—$100,000 for districts with 1,000 or fewer students or $100 per enrolled student for larger districts—and require the funds to support a comprehensive school mental-health system, with annual district and commissioner reporting.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes school-district funding and requirements for school safety and mental-health supports.
Creates a new annual allotment through the Foundation School Program.
Funds school mental-health supports, including services for students with or at risk of mental-health or substance-use conditions.
Revises the permissible uses of school safety allotment funds, including for threat detection and reporting systems.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The provisions apply to school districts generally, without limiting them to a specified place.

affected_groups.group: Texas school districts
affected_groups.explanation: Districts receive the new allotment, implement the required system, and report outcomes and expenditures; the allotment amount varies by enrollment.

affected_groups.group: Students, including students with or at risk of mental-health or substance-use conditions
affected_groups.explanation: The allotment is directed toward school supports intended to contribute to student learning and well-being.

affected_groups.group: School personnel
affected_groups.explanation: Allotment funds may support personnel who plan, coordinate, deliver, or monitor services and training for school personnel.

major_effects.label: New school mental-health allotment
major_effects.explanation: Provides an annual allotment of $100,000 for districts with 1,000 or fewer students, or $100 per enrolled student for larger districts. The funds may not supplant other funds for the same purpose.

major_effects.label: Comprehensive school mental-health systems
major_effects.explanation: Requires allotment funds to develop or enhance a comprehensive system of tiered supports and services; specified costs may include personnel, training, partnerships, and restorative-justice programs.

major_effects.label: Revised school safety allotment uses
major_effects.explanation: Makes threat detection and reporting systems an expressly listed use and removes several previously enumerated uses. This revises the list of express uses; it does not itself state that all related activities are prohibited under other permissible uses.

major_effects.label: Annual allotment reporting
major_effects.explanation: Requires districts to provide information on outcomes and expenditures and requires the commissioner to publish an annual report on use of the allotment.

agencies.name: commissioner
agencies.explanation: The bill assigns the commissioner a role in setting district reporting requirements and publishing an annual report, but does not identify the commissioner’s agency by name.

HB959.summary: The bill would create an annual fine arts allotment for school districts for each student in average daily attendance in grades 6–12 enrolled in an approved fine arts course. The agency would approve qualifying courses and publish the approved-course list annually; qualifying courses must provide at least 225 minutes of fine arts instruction per week for a full-time student.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill changes public school finance and establishes course approval criteria for fine arts education.
The bill creates a school-district funding allotment calculated from the basic allotment.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The allotment is added to the statewide public school finance system and applies to school districts meeting its criteria.

affected_groups.group: School districts
affected_groups.explanation: Eligible districts would receive the new annual allotment for qualifying students.

affected_groups.group: Students in grades 6 through 12 enrolled in approved fine arts courses
affected_groups.explanation: Their enrollment in a qualifying course determines the district’s allotment eligibility.

major_effects.label: Fine arts allotment
major_effects.explanation: Creates an annual district allotment per eligible student, calculated as 0.8% of the basic allotment, or of the basic allotment plus the applicable Section 48.101 allotment.

major_effects.label: Fine arts course approval
major_effects.explanation: Directs the agency to approve qualifying courses and annually publish the approved-course list; eligibility includes the specified weekly instructional minimum.

agencies.name: Texas Education Agency
agencies.explanation: The bill directly assigns course-approval and annual publication duties to an entity called “the agency,” but the supplied text does not establish its canonical identity.

HB961.summary: The bill revises the affidavit requirements for claiming a local-option property-tax exemption on leased real property used for a child-care facility and defines “net lease.” The affidavit clause requires certification that the property is subject to a net lease under which the lessee is directly responsible for ad valorem taxes. A later “either” condition includes a monthly or annual rent credit; the supplied text does not establish that this credit replaces the certification.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes affidavit criteria related to a local-option ad valorem property-tax exemption.
The exemption is granted by a county or municipality, and the revised affidavit is submitted to the chief appraiser for the appraisal district.

locations.name: Texas
locations.explanation: The bill amends the statewide Tax Code framework for exemptions granted by counties or municipalities.

affected_groups.group: People claiming the exemption for leased property
affected_groups.explanation: Claimants must include an affidavit addressing disclosure of the tax reduction and how it is reflected in rent.

affected_groups.group: Lessee operators of child-care facilities
affected_groups.explanation: The affidavit provisions address whether the lessee is responsible for property taxes or receives the tax reduction through a rent credit.

affected_groups.group: Counties, municipalities, and appraisal districts
affected_groups.explanation: Local governments grant the exemption, and the affidavit is provided to the chief appraiser for the appraisal district.

major_effects.label: Affidavit conditions for leased-property exemption claims
major_effects.explanation: Revises the affidavit conditions for claimants and defines “net lease.” The affidavit clause requires certification that the property is subject to a net lease under which the lessee is directly responsible for ad valorem taxes. A later “either” condition includes a monthly or annual rent-credit option.

HB962.summary: The bill would require each school district campus to report every overdose occurring there as soon as practicable to the district and the executive commissioner of the Health and Human Services Commission. The commissioner and the HHSC executive commissioner would jointly adopt rules for implementing the reporting requirement in compliance with federal and state student-privacy laws.

policy_tags.explanation: Creates a reporting requirement for school district campuses.
Places a new reporting duty on school district campuses.
Requires reporting of overdose incidents to the Health and Human Services Commission.

locations.name: Statewide school district campuses
locations.explanation: The reporting duty applies to each school district campus.

affected_groups.group: School districts and their campuses
affected_groups.explanation: Campuses must report overdoses to their district and HHSC's executive commissioner.

affected_groups.group: People experiencing an overdose on a school district campus
affected_groups.explanation: An overdose occurring on campus triggers the reporting requirement; the bill does not limit the reported person to a student.

major_effects.label: Campus overdose reporting
major_effects.explanation: Requires each school district campus to report each overdose occurring there as soon as practicable to the district and HHSC's executive commissioner.

major_effects.label: Joint implementation rules
major_effects.explanation: Requires the commissioner and HHSC executive commissioner to adopt rules that comply with applicable federal and state student-privacy laws.

agencies.name: Health and Human Services Commission
agencies.explanation: Its executive commissioner is a recipient of overdose reports and shares responsibility for adopting implementing rules.

agencies.name: commissioner
agencies.explanation: The bill assigns this official joint rulemaking responsibility, but does not specify the commissioner's agency in the text.

HB963.summary: The bill would expressly allow school safety allotment funds to support educator professional development in classroom behavioral management and programs involving restorative justice practices, culturally relevant instruction, and mental health support. Other listed security and school-safety uses of the allotment remain in place.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill changes the statutorily permitted uses of a school safety allotment under the Foundation School Program, including educator training and school programs.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The provision concerns school districts under a statewide Education Code funding program and names no particular locality.

affected_groups.group: School districts
affected_groups.explanation: Districts could use school safety allotment funds for the added training and program purposes.

affected_groups.group: Educators
affected_groups.explanation: Educators could receive professional development in classroom behavioral management funded through the allotment.

affected_groups.group: Students
affected_groups.explanation: Students in districts using the funds for the added programs may be affected by restorative-practice and mental-health supports.

major_effects.label: Expanded permitted uses of school safety allotment funds
major_effects.explanation: Adds educator professional development in classroom behavioral management and specified restorative-practice, culturally relevant instruction, and mental-health-support programs as permitted uses.

HB965.summary: The bill expands the dog-fighting offense to cover additional dealings in dog-fighting equipment and selling a dog when the person intends the dog to be used in an exhibition of dog fighting. It classifies offenses under the section as state jail felonies except spectator attendance, which remains a Class A misdemeanor.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill expands criminal conduct and changes the felony classification for most offenses under the dog-fighting statute.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The bill amends a Penal Code provision, making the criminal-law change statewide in scope.

affected_groups.group: People who engage in dog-fighting-related conduct, including equipment suppliers and people who sell dogs for intended use in dog fighting
affected_groups.explanation: The bill adds specified equipment-related conduct and selling a dog with the stated intent to the offense.

major_effects.label: Expanded dog-fighting offense
major_effects.explanation: Adds specified manufacture, sale, exchange, advertising, and offering of dog-fighting equipment, and selling a dog for intended use in an exhibition, subject to the statute's intent requirements.

major_effects.label: State jail felony classification for most offenses
major_effects.explanation: Makes offenses under the section state jail felonies except spectator attendance, which remains a Class A misdemeanor.

HB966.summary: The bill extends retaliation protections to people acting in relation to sexual-harassment practices, adds “abusive” to the working-environment definition of sexual harassment, and permits a harassment-based civil action without first filing a commission complaint or waiting for a right-to-sue notice. If the action is filed without a complaint, the two-year filing period runs from the conduct; harassment damages actions are exempt from the specified Labor Code damages cap but remain subject to Civil Practice and Remedies Code Section 41.008. The changes apply only to conduct occurring on or after the Act’s effective date.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes employment-practice protections and the procedures and remedies for sexual-harassment claims.
Expands protections and civil remedies relating to sexual harassment and retaliation in employment.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The bill amends Texas Labor Code provisions with statewide application.

affected_groups.group: Individuals affected by sexual harassment or retaliation in employment
affected_groups.explanation: They receive expanded retaliation protections and access to civil actions for harassment-based claims.

affected_groups.group: Employers, labor unions, and employment agencies
affected_groups.explanation: They are among the entities covered by the amended prohibition on retaliation or discrimination.

major_effects.label: Sexual-harassment retaliation protection
major_effects.explanation: Extends the section’s retaliation and discrimination protections to acts taken in relation to a sexual-harassment practice.

major_effects.label: Direct civil action access
major_effects.explanation: Allows an individual to bring a sexual-harassment-based civil action regardless of whether a commission complaint was filed, and, if one was filed, whether it remains pending or a right-to-sue notice was received.

major_effects.label: Claim deadline and damages cap
major_effects.explanation: For a sexual-harassment civil action filed without a commission complaint, the two-year deadline runs from the conduct. The specified Labor Code damages cap does not apply to harassment damages actions, which remain subject to Section 41.008.

HB967.summary: The bill would require voter-registration applicants to provide an accepted form of proof of citizenship. In-person applicants would present it to the county registrar; mail or fax applicants would present it to a Department of Public Safety employee, and the registrar would send those applicants a notice with instructions. The requirements would apply only to applications submitted on or after the Act’s effective date.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes the documentation required to submit a voter-registration application and the process for presenting it.
Assigns county registrars duties to receive proof for in-person applications and notify applicants who apply by mail or fax.

locations.name: Texas
locations.explanation: The voter-registration changes apply in Texas.

affected_groups.group: People applying to register to vote
affected_groups.explanation: Applicants must provide an accepted form of proof of citizenship; the presentation process differs for in-person and mail or fax applications.

affected_groups.group: County voter registrars
affected_groups.explanation: Registrars receive proof from in-person applicants and must notify mail or fax applicants of the requirements and how to satisfy them.

affected_groups.group: Department of Public Safety employees
affected_groups.explanation: Employees at a department office are designated to receive proof from mail or fax applicants.

major_effects.label: Citizenship documentation for registration
major_effects.explanation: Requires proof of citizenship with a voter-registration application and lists documents that count as proof.

major_effects.label: Notice and presentation process
major_effects.explanation: Requires mail or fax applicants to present proof at a Department of Public Safety office and requires the registrar to send them notice and instructions.

agencies.name: Texas Department of Public Safety
agencies.explanation: A Department of Public Safety employee at the department's office is designated to receive proof of citizenship from applicants who submit registration applications by mail or fax.

HB969.summary: The bill would remove certain driver's licenses—those with an expiration provided by specified Transportation Code provisions—from the photo identification accepted for voting. Election identification certificates and personal identification cards remain among the listed acceptable forms.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes which photo identification documents are acceptable for voting.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The amendment applies to the Texas Election Code provision governing acceptable identification for voting.

affected_groups.group: Voters presenting driver's licenses with expirations provided by the cited Transportation Code provisions
affected_groups.explanation: Those licenses would no longer qualify as acceptable photo identification under the amended provision.

major_effects.label: Voting photo-identification rules
major_effects.explanation: Excludes driver's licenses with expirations provided by the specified Transportation Code provisions from the listed acceptable photo identification.

agencies.name: Texas Department of Public Safety
agencies.explanation: The bill changes whether certain driver's licenses issued by the Department are accepted as voting identification; it does not assign the Department a new administrative duty.

HB970.summary: The bill would require the Texas Department of Criminal Justice to ensure that pregnant inmates and inmates who gave birth in the preceding year are screened for depression during pregnancy and at specified times after birth. It would also require the Commission on Jail Standards to adopt county-jail rules requiring health services plans to address the same screenings.

policy_tags.explanation: Creates depression-screening requirements for pregnant inmates and inmates who recently gave birth.
Changes health-care requirements for people held in state custody and county jails.
Requires county-jail standards to address depression screening through jail health services plans.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The requirements apply to the covered state inmates and county jails throughout Texas.

affected_groups.group: Pregnant inmates and inmates who have given birth in the preceding year
affected_groups.explanation: They would be subject to the new depression-screening requirements while in TDCJ custody or county jail.

affected_groups.group: County jail operators
affected_groups.explanation: County-jail health services plans would be covered by the screening requirements in rules the Commission must adopt.

major_effects.label: Depression screening
major_effects.explanation: Requires TDCJ to ensure screenings for pregnant inmates and inmates who gave birth in the preceding year, including screenings once each trimester, during the six weeks after birth, and at six and 12 months after birth.

major_effects.label: County-jail screening standards
major_effects.explanation: Requires the Commission on Jail Standards to adopt rules requiring county-jail health services plans to address the same depression screenings.

agencies.name: Texas Department of Criminal Justice
agencies.explanation: The bill title identifies the department, and the new provision assigns it the duty to ensure the specified inmates are screened.

agencies.name: Commission on Jail Standards
agencies.explanation: The bill requires the Commission to adopt the rules and procedures governing county-jail health-plan requirements. The supplied registry does not include a canonical ID for this named body.

HB971.summary: HB 971 would designate the specified portion of State Highway 121 in Collin County as the Officer D. Weston “Wes” Hardy Memorial Highway, in addition to any other designation. Subject to Transportation Code Section 225.021(c), it would require “the department” to design and erect markers for the designation.

policy_tags.explanation: Designates a highway segment and requires markers identifying it.

locations.name: State Highway 121 in Collin County, between State Highway 289 and Farm-to-Market Road 2478
locations.explanation: This is the highway segment covered by the designation.

affected_groups.group: Motorists and other road users on the designated segment
affected_groups.explanation: They would encounter the memorial highway designation and its markers.

major_effects.label: Memorial highway designation
major_effects.explanation: Adds the memorial designation to the specified State Highway 121 segment without displacing any other designation.

major_effects.label: Designation markers
major_effects.explanation: Subject to Section 225.021(c), requires the department to design and construct markers and place them at the highway ends and appropriate intermediate sites.

agencies.name: Texas Department of Transportation
agencies.explanation: The bill directly assigns marker-related duties to “the department,” but the supplied text and reviewed definitions do not establish its canonical identity.

HB972.summary: The bill would require employers, except as provided by Labor Code Section 62.057, to pay employees at least the greater of $15 an hour or the federal minimum wage. It also repeals Labor Code Section 62.151; the supplied text does not show what that section provides.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill changes the minimum wage employers must pay employees.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The bill amends the Texas Labor Code minimum-wage provision.

affected_groups.group: Employees covered by the Texas minimum-wage requirement
affected_groups.explanation: Their statutory wage floor would be at least the greater of $15 an hour or the federal minimum wage, subject to the stated exception.

affected_groups.group: Employers subject to the Texas minimum-wage requirement
affected_groups.explanation: They would be required to meet the revised minimum-wage floor, subject to the stated exception.

major_effects.label: Raises the statutory minimum-wage floor
major_effects.explanation: Except as provided by Section 62.057, the required wage would be the greater of $15 an hour or the federal minimum wage.

major_effects.label: Repeals Labor Code Section 62.151
major_effects.explanation: The bill repeals the section, but the supplied text does not establish the provision's subject or the repeal's substantive consequences.

HB973.summary: HB973 would bar charter holders from using money received for an open-enrollment charter school to support a school outside Texas, except under a contract to provide goods or services to the charter school that received the money. If the commissioner finds a violation, the bill requires withholding three times the amount spent from that school year's entitlement, allows adjustments to later-year entitlements to recover any balance, and requires charter revocation if the holder spent at least $100,000 in violation.

policy_tags.explanation: Creates restrictions and sanctions concerning funds for open-enrollment charter schools.
Changes charter-school funding entitlements by requiring a withholding tied to the amount spent in violation.

locations.name: Schools located outside Texas
locations.explanation: The bill restricts use of the specified charter-school money to support schools in this area.

affected_groups.group: Charter holders of open-enrollment charter schools
affected_groups.explanation: They would face a new restriction on use of specified funds and financial and charter-revocation consequences for violations.

affected_groups.group: Schools located outside Texas
affected_groups.explanation: They could not be supported with the specified open-enrollment charter school money, subject to the bill's contract exception.

major_effects.label: Restriction on use of charter-school funds
major_effects.explanation: Bars using money received for an open-enrollment charter school to support a school outside Texas, except money spent under a contract for goods or services to the charter school that received it.

major_effects.label: Funding withholding for violations
major_effects.explanation: Requires withholding three times the amount spent in violation from the entitlement for the school year of the violation; later-year entitlements may be adjusted to recover any remaining amount.

major_effects.label: Charter revocation for violations of at least $100,000
major_effects.explanation: Requires revocation if the charter holder spent at least $100,000 in violation of the new restriction.

agencies.name: commissioner
agencies.explanation: The bill assigns the commissioner enforcement and revocation duties, but the supplied text does not identify the office or establish its canonical agency identity.

HB974.summary: Beginning with qualifying stores opened on or after January 1, 2028, the bill would create a franchise tax credit for taxable entities that open a grocery store or healthy corner store in a food desert and meet the income-area or customer-base, nutrition-benefit acceptance, and year-round operation requirements. The credit would equal 5% of specified establishment costs, subject to a limit of 50% of franchise tax due and a carryforward of up to five reports; the bill also requires eligibility certification and supporting documentation.

policy_tags.explanation: Creates a franchise tax credit for specified store establishment costs, with limits and a carryforward.
The tax incentive is targeted at establishing qualifying food retailers in areas with limited healthy-food access.

locations.name: Food deserts in Texas
locations.explanation: The bill makes location in a department-determined food desert a condition for the credit.

affected_groups.group: Taxable entities establishing grocery stores or healthy corner stores
affected_groups.explanation: Eligible entities may claim the new credit if their stores meet the bill's location and operating conditions.

affected_groups.group: Consumers in food deserts and qualifying low- or moderate-income areas
affected_groups.explanation: The incentive is intended to support stores offering greater access to healthy food in these areas; it does not guarantee that a store will open.

major_effects.label: Franchise tax credit for establishment costs
major_effects.explanation: Provides a credit equal to 5% of specified costs for each qualifying store. The credit is limited to 50% of franchise tax due on a report, and unused credit may be carried forward for up to five reports; inventory costs are excluded.

major_effects.label: Conditions for qualifying stores
major_effects.explanation: The store must be in a food desert and meet the low- or moderate-income location/customer-base alternative, accept WIC and SNAP benefits within 90 days after opening, and remain open year-round.

major_effects.label: Certification and claim documentation
major_effects.explanation: Before claiming the credit, an entity must obtain a department eligibility certificate and submit it with an audited cost report, evidence of the store's opening date, and an expenditure attestation to the comptroller.

major_effects.label: Implementation rules
major_effects.explanation: Authorizes the department to adopt rules on qualification, including which stores and areas qualify, and the comptroller to adopt other necessary administration rules.

agencies.name: Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs
agencies.explanation: The bill expressly identifies the department as TDHCA and assigns it food-desert determinations, eligibility certification, and related rulemaking.

agencies.name: Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts
agencies.explanation: The bill assigns the comptroller a role in receiving credit documentation, administering credit applications, and adopting related rules.

HB975.summary: Beginning with the 2027–2028 school year, school districts and open-enrollment charter schools may adopt paid parental-leave policies for full-time employees after a qualifying birth or adoption. If a school adopts a policy, it must provide eight weeks for a primary caregiver or four weeks for the caregiver’s spouse; employees must have at least 12 months of full-time service, use the leave within six months of the birth or placement, and take it concurrently with qualifying FMLA leave. The bill provides school districts an annual allotment equal to covered employees’ compensation during leave and requires the agency to report on participation, costs, projections, and recommendations.

policy_tags.explanation: Creates an optional paid parental-leave policy framework for school districts and open-enrollment charter schools and adds an allotment in the Education Code.
Establishes required paid-leave terms for eligible full-time school employees when an employer adopts the policy.
Creates an annual state-funded allotment for school districts based on compensation paid during parental leave.
School districts may adopt the policy and receive the new allotment.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The provisions apply to school districts and open-enrollment charter schools under Texas law, without limiting the policy to a particular geographic area.

affected_groups.group: Full-time employees of school districts and open-enrollment charter schools
affected_groups.explanation: Eligible employees may receive paid leave following specified births or an adoption, subject to the policy’s service and timing requirements.

affected_groups.group: School districts
affected_groups.explanation: Districts may adopt the policy and, for each employee who received leave under it, are entitled to an annual allotment equal to that employee’s compensation for the leave period.

affected_groups.group: Open-enrollment charter schools
affected_groups.explanation: Charter schools may adopt the policy and are included in the agency’s participation reporting; the new allotment is expressly for school districts.

major_effects.label: Optional paid parental-leave policies
major_effects.explanation: Districts and open-enrollment charter schools may adopt a policy; if adopted, it must provide eight consecutive weeks for a primary caregiver or four for the caregiver’s spouse. Eligibility requires 12 months of full-time employment, expires six months after birth or placement, and leave runs concurrently with FMLA leave when the employee is eligible.

major_effects.label: Annual allotment for school districts
major_effects.explanation: For each employee who received leave under an adopted policy during the preceding school year, a district is entitled to an annual allotment equal to the employee’s compensation for the leave period.

major_effects.label: Biennial legislative report
major_effects.explanation: The agency must report on leave participation by district and charter school, costs, future projections, and recommendations.

agencies.name: Texas Education Agency
agencies.explanation: The bill assigns the agency responsibility for preparing and submitting a legislative report, but does not identify the agency by name in this provision.

HB977.summary: HB 977 would extend expunction eligibility to people placed on deferred adjudication community supervision for unlawful carrying of a handgun. The offense must have been committed before September 1, 2021, under former Penal Code Section 46.02(a).

policy_tags.explanation: The bill changes eligibility for expunction of arrest records and files following a criminal case.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The bill amends a provision of the Texas Code of Criminal Procedure, changing the expunction rule statewide.

affected_groups.group: People placed on deferred adjudication community supervision for qualifying unlawful carrying of a handgun offenses
affected_groups.explanation: They would become eligible for expunction when the offense meets the bill's historical date and statutory-section limits.

major_effects.label: Expunction eligibility
major_effects.explanation: Adds deferred adjudication community supervision as a qualifying case outcome for expunction, subject to the existing offense and arrest-record requirements and the stated date and former-law limits.

HB978.summary: HB 978 would make arson a first-degree felony if, at trial, it is shown that bodily injury or death was suffered by any person because of the offense, or that the intended property was a government building. The change would apply only to offenses committed on or after the Act’s effective date.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill increases the felony degree for arson involving a government building.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: This amendment to the Penal Code applies generally statewide and does not identify a narrower geographic area.

affected_groups.group: People accused of arson involving a government building
affected_groups.explanation: They may face first-degree felony classification if the government-building condition is shown at trial.

major_effects.label: First-degree felony classification
major_effects.explanation: Arson is elevated to a first-degree felony if it is shown at trial that the property the actor intended to damage or destroy was a government building.

HB979.summary: HB 979 would redefine exploitation and add definitions of coercion, deception, and isolation for the offense involving a child, elderly individual, or disabled individual. It would replace the current offense test with knowing appropriation of the person’s resources through exploitation, deception, coercion, or isolation for the actor’s or another person’s benefit, but not the protected person’s benefit. The changes apply only to offenses committed on or after the Act’s effective date.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes the elements and culpability standard for a Penal Code offense involving exploitation of a child, elderly individual, or disabled individual.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The bill amends a Texas Penal Code offense without limiting its application to a particular area.

affected_groups.group: Children, elderly individuals, and disabled individuals whose resources may be appropriated
affected_groups.explanation: The offense concerns appropriation of resources belonging to these protected individuals.

affected_groups.group: People accused of the exploitation offense
affected_groups.explanation: The bill changes the conduct and culpability required for the offense.

major_effects.label: Revises offense elements and culpability
major_effects.explanation: Replaces the prior test of intentionally, knowingly, or recklessly causing exploitation with knowing appropriation of resources through exploitation, deception, coercion, or isolation for the actor’s or another person’s benefit, excluding the protected individual.

major_effects.label: Defines means of exploitation
major_effects.explanation: Adds statutory definitions of coercion, deception, and isolation relevant to the offense.

HB980.summary: The bill would require the Department of Family and Protective Services (DFPS) or a foster-care services contractor, upon request, to share relevant information with a state or local juvenile justice agency as soon as practicable, extending the covered youth to include a child whose parental rights have been terminated. It would also require DFPS, as soon as practicable after a request, to provide foster-care history and prior placement counts for a child in a juvenile justice agency’s custody; these changes apply only to requests made on or after the Act’s effective date.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill changes information-sharing arrangements for state and local juvenile justice agencies.
The bill changes duties for DFPS and foster-care services contractors to respond to juvenile justice agency requests for information.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The provisions apply to requests involving state or local juvenile justice agencies, without specifying a narrower geographic area.

affected_groups.group: Children and youth with the specified child-welfare history who are involved with juvenile justice agencies
affected_groups.explanation: These young people are the subjects of requested information sharing, including children whose parental rights have been terminated.

affected_groups.group: Children in the custody of a juvenile justice agency who have a foster-care history
affected_groups.explanation: DFPS must provide information about whether these children have been in foster care and, if applicable, their prior placement count.

affected_groups.group: Foster-care services contractors
affected_groups.explanation: A single source continuum contractor that contracts with DFPS to provide foster-care services must share covered information when requested.

major_effects.label: Expanded child-welfare information sharing
major_effects.explanation: On request, DFPS or a covered foster-care services contractor must share relevant information with juvenile justice agencies as soon as practicable; the covered youth include children for whom parental rights have been terminated.

major_effects.label: Foster-care history responses
major_effects.explanation: DFPS must respond as soon as practicable to a qualifying request with whether a child in juvenile justice agency custody is or has been in foster care and, if applicable, the number of prior foster-care placements.

agencies.name: Department of Family and Protective Services
agencies.explanation: DFPS must share requested information under Section 58.0052 and provide foster-care history information under Section 243.008. The supplied registry has no matching entry.

agencies.name: State or local juvenile justice agency
agencies.explanation: These agencies are expressly identified as requesters and recipients of information; the precise entities included depend on the referenced statutory definition.

HB983.summary: HB 983 would require juvenile probation department staff and, at case closeout, specified probation department or Texas Juvenile Justice Department officials to provide written and oral information about sealing juvenile records, answer questions, and share local assistance resources. It would also require the Texas Juvenile Justice Department to publish an online brochure and the State Bar of Texas to create a public directory of low- or no-cost attorneys organized by administrative judicial region.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill changes information and assistance procedures for children navigating the sealing of juvenile records.
Juvenile probation department employees and officials would have new duties to provide sealing information and resources.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The attorney directory covers attorneys in Texas and is to be made available on the State Bar's website.

locations.name: Administrative judicial regions
locations.explanation: The directory is organized to describe these regions and list attorneys offering representation in them.

affected_groups.group: Children referred to juvenile probation departments and their parents, guardians, or custodians
affected_groups.explanation: When a child is referred to a juvenile probation department, the child and their parent, guardian, or custodian receive written and oral information about record sealing.

affected_groups.group: Juvenile probation department employees and Texas Juvenile Justice Department officials
affected_groups.explanation: Specified employees and officials would have new information-provision responsibilities.

affected_groups.group: Attorneys who represent people applying to seal juvenile records at low or no cost
affected_groups.explanation: Their services would be listed in local resource information and a statewide online directory.

major_effects.label: Expanded sealing information and referral assistance
major_effects.explanation: At referral and case closeout, specified staff would provide written explanations and local resource lists; oral explanations and opportunities to ask questions are also required.

major_effects.label: Texas Juvenile Justice Department online brochure
major_effects.explanation: The department would publish a brochure describing the sealing process and listing assistance resources.

major_effects.label: State Bar attorney directory
major_effects.explanation: The State Bar would create and maintain a public online directory of low- or no-cost attorneys, organized by administrative judicial region.

agencies.name: Texas Juvenile Justice Department
agencies.explanation: The department is assigned to publish an online brochure, and its officials are among those who must provide information at case closeout.

HB987.summary: HB 987 would repeal specified abortion-related provisions, including Health and Safety Code Chapter 170A, and revise abortion-complication reporting, including adding an infant born alive after an abortion to the listed complications. It would change medication-abortion protocol rules, including a dosage exception based on the cited 2013 ACOG guidelines, and specify a follow-up deadline after administration or use of the drug.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill changes abortion-related reporting and requirements for providing abortion-inducing drugs.

locations.name: Statewide, Texas
locations.explanation: The bill amends Texas statutes and applies statewide.

affected_groups.group: Pregnant people receiving abortion-inducing drugs
affected_groups.explanation: The bill changes the protocol and dosage rules for providing abortion-inducing drugs and specifies follow-up timing.

affected_groups.group: Physicians who provide abortion-inducing drugs or diagnose and treat abortion complications
affected_groups.explanation: The bill changes medication-abortion requirements and specifies which physician conduct falls within complication reporting.

affected_groups.group: Hospitals, abortion facilities, and emergency medical care facilities
affected_groups.explanation: The bill identifies these types of facilities as subject to the complication-reporting section.

major_effects.label: Repeal of specified abortion-related provisions
major_effects.explanation: Repeals the listed provisions, including Chapter 170A. The unchanged text states that other laws regulating or prohibiting abortion are not repealed or made unenforceable by the subchapter.

major_effects.label: Abortion-complication reporting scope
major_effects.explanation: Adds an infant born alive after an abortion to the listed complications and limits physician reporting to specified facility-related circumstances; covered health care facilities are also identified.

major_effects.label: Medication-abortion protocol and follow-up
major_effects.explanation: Generally requires compliance with the FDA-authorized final-label protocol, except that a person may provide the dosage amount prescribed by the specified ACOG Practice Bulletin guidelines as they existed on January 1, 2013. Separately, requires a follow-up visit within 14 days after administration or use.

HB988.summary: The bill would add a basis for expunging arrest records and files for a person covered by the applicable subchapter when no indictment or information was presented and presentment did not occur solely because the grand jury failed to find probable cause that the person committed the offense. The change would apply to offenses occurring before, on, or after its effective date.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes eligibility for expunction of arrest records and files.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The change applies under the statewide Code of Criminal Procedure.

affected_groups.group: People arrested for criminal offenses who are covered by the expunction subchapter
affected_groups.explanation: They may qualify for expunction under the added ground when presentment did not occur solely because the grand jury failed to find probable cause.

affected_groups.group: Custodians of records and files relating to qualifying arrests
affected_groups.explanation: The added eligibility ground concerns expunction of all records and files relating to the arrest.

major_effects.label: Adds an expunction eligibility ground
major_effects.explanation: A person otherwise covered by the subchapter may qualify when no charging instrument was presented and the grand jury’s failure to find probable cause was the sole reason presentment did not occur.

major_effects.label: Applies to offenses from before or after the effective date
major_effects.explanation: The added rule applies to offenses occurring before, on, or after the effective date.

HB989.summary: The bill would require covered health benefit plans delivered, issued, or renewed on or after January 1, 2028, to include at least one epinephrine auto-injector on the plan’s formulary and cap cost-sharing at $25 per prescription for a 30-day supply when the injector is on the formulary. It expressly applies to specified private and public coverage, including Medicaid, the child health plan program, and school-district group health coverage. If a state agency determines federal authorization is necessary to implement a provision, it must request that authorization and may delay implementing that provision until it is granted.

policy_tags.explanation: Establishes formulary and cost-sharing requirements for epinephrine auto-injectors in covered health benefit plans.
The new requirements expressly apply to the state Medicaid program, including Medicaid managed care.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The requirements apply statewide to health benefit plans within the bill's specified coverage categories.

affected_groups.group: Enrollees who need an epinephrine auto-injector
affected_groups.explanation: Their covered auto-injector prescriptions would be subject to the cost-sharing cap.

affected_groups.group: Issuers and sponsors of covered health benefit plans
affected_groups.explanation: Covered plans would have to include an auto-injector on their formularies and comply with the cost-sharing limit.

affected_groups.group: People covered by Medicaid, the child health plan program, and school-district group health coverage
affected_groups.explanation: These public or school-district coverage categories are expressly included in the bill's applicability provision.

major_effects.label: Formulary coverage
major_effects.explanation: Each covered plan must include at least one epinephrine auto-injector within its respective therapeutic class on its drug formulary.

major_effects.label: Cost-sharing limit
major_effects.explanation: For an auto-injector included on the formulary, cost-sharing may not exceed $25 per prescription for a 30-day supply, regardless of the amount or type needed.

major_effects.label: Conditional federal authorization process
major_effects.explanation: If an affected state agency determines a waiver or authorization is necessary before implementing a provision, it must request it and may delay that provision until it is granted.

HB990.summary: The bill directs the Texas Department of Transportation to study flooding’s transportation impacts in the Rio Grande Valley, prepare a written report with possible recommendations, and submit it to the Legislature. The Act expires January 1, 2030.

policy_tags.explanation: Requires a study of flooding’s impacts on transportation in the Rio Grande Valley.

locations.name: Rio Grande Valley
locations.explanation: The study is focused on transportation impacts of flooding in this region.

affected_groups.group: Transportation users and communities in the Rio Grande Valley
affected_groups.explanation: The required study concerns flooding’s transportation impacts in their region; the bill does not itself provide a direct service or benefit to them.

major_effects.label: Transportation study and report to the Legislature
major_effects.explanation: Requires TxDOT to study flooding-related transportation impacts, prepare a report with possible recommendations, and submit it to the Legislature.

agencies.name: Texas Department of Transportation
agencies.explanation: The bill defines the department as the Texas Department of Transportation and assigns it the study and reporting duties.

HB991.summary: The bill would allow a county that offers a deferred compensation plan to elect automatic enrollment for its employees, with a default contribution of 1% of compensation or a higher rate set by the county up to 3%; employees could opt out or change their contribution and investment choices. The requirements would apply only to an employee of a county subject to Section 609.1026 who initially begins employment on or after January 1, 2028, and an electing county would have to provide enrollment information and keep a record of each new employee’s acknowledgment.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill gives county commissioners courts authority to elect automatic enrollment and requires electing counties to provide information and maintain acknowledgment records.
The bill changes how eligible county employees participate and contribute to county deferred compensation plans.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The bill establishes an option available to qualifying counties across Texas; a county must offer a deferred compensation plan and elect to use automatic participation.

affected_groups.group: Employees of counties subject to Section 609.1026 who initially begin employment on or after January 1, 2028
affected_groups.explanation: For employees of a county subject to Section 609.1026 who initially begin employment on or after January 1, 2028, the county’s automatic enrollment applies if the county elects it. Employees are automatically enrolled unless they affirmatively opt out, with a default contribution and options to change participation and investment choices.

affected_groups.group: Counties that offer deferred compensation plans and elect automatic participation
affected_groups.explanation: These counties would set the applicable requirements and provide enrollment information and acknowledgment records.

major_effects.label: County election of automatic enrollment
major_effects.explanation: A qualifying county commissioners court could elect by order to require automatic participation in its deferred compensation plan.

major_effects.label: Default enrollment and contributions
major_effects.explanation: Employees in an electing county would be enrolled by default and contribute 1% of compensation, or a higher rate set by the county up to 3%, unless they opt out; they could also change their contribution or investment choices.

major_effects.label: Employee notice and acknowledgment records
major_effects.explanation: An electing county would inform new employees of automatic enrollment and the right to opt out and maintain records acknowledging receipt of that information.

HB992.summary: The bill directs the commissioner to develop training resources for school administrators about bilingual education and dual language immersion programs. It also requires agency rules for monitoring bilingual and special language programs, including district engagement and technical assistance, and expands program-related information that districts may be required to report through PEIMS.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill changes training, monitoring, and reporting requirements for public school bilingual and special language programs.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The bill amends Texas Education Code provisions applying to school districts and does not limit the changes to a particular place.

affected_groups.group: School administrators
affected_groups.explanation: They are the intended audience for the new training resources.

affected_groups.group: School districts offering bilingual education or special language programs
affected_groups.explanation: They may face additional PEIMS reporting requirements and are subject to agency engagement, identification of program deficiencies, and technical assistance.

affected_groups.group: Emergent bilingual students
affected_groups.explanation: The bill directs program review and agency engagement toward meeting their needs, closing learning gaps, and improving outcomes.

major_effects.label: Administrator training resources
major_effects.explanation: Requires development and availability of training resources covering bilingual education and dual language immersion programs.

major_effects.label: Program monitoring and district assistance
major_effects.explanation: Requires rules for monitoring bilingual and special language programs, including review of requirements and direct engagement with districts to address deficiencies and improve student outcomes.

major_effects.label: Additional PEIMS program information
major_effects.explanation: Adds agency-required program information to the list of information districts must include in PEIMS reporting.

agencies.name: the commissioner
agencies.explanation: The bill assigns this role responsibility for developing and making training resources available; its canonical state-body identity is not verified by the supplied definitions.

agencies.name: Texas Education Agency
agencies.explanation: The bill assigns this entity rulemaking and monitoring responsibilities and makes its program-related information requirements relevant to district reporting; its canonical identity is not verified by the supplied definitions.

HB993.summary: The bill directs the Texas Workforce Commission, in consultation with the Texas Higher Education Coordinating Board, to establish and administer a geothermal energy workforce education and training initiative. It provides for customized curricula, support for training and employer partnerships, and identification of opportunities to use existing workforce development funds subject to their restrictions; degree or certificate programs remain subject to coordinating board approval. The commission must also report annually to relevant legislative committees.

policy_tags.explanation: Creates education and training programs and curriculum requirements for geothermal energy careers.
The initiative specifically supports workforce preparation for the geothermal energy industry.
Establishes a workforce education and training initiative and supports industry apprenticeships and employment opportunities.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The initiative concerns geothermal workforce training and jobs in Texas.

affected_groups.group: Students and graduates pursuing geothermal energy careers
affected_groups.explanation: They may benefit from customized education, training, apprenticeship, and employment opportunities.

affected_groups.group: Higher education institutions, public technical institutes, public junior colleges, and career schools or colleges
affected_groups.explanation: The commission must consult representatives of these education providers and develop curriculum requirements for programs they may offer. Degree or certificate programs offered by institutions of higher education are subject to coordinating board approval; the source states no such condition for programs offered by career schools or colleges.

affected_groups.group: Geothermal energy industry employers
affected_groups.explanation: Employers are consulted on curriculum development and may partner with higher education institutions to offer apprenticeships and employment opportunities.

major_effects.label: Geothermal workforce initiative
major_effects.explanation: Requires the commission, in consultation with the coordinating board, to establish and administer an initiative by rule for geothermal energy education and workforce training.

major_effects.label: Curricula, training support, and partnerships
major_effects.explanation: Directs development of customized curriculum requirements and support for education and employer partnerships; degree or certificate programs at institutions of higher education are subject to coordinating board approval.

major_effects.label: Identify existing funding opportunities
major_effects.explanation: Requires the commission to identify opportunities to use its administered workforce development funding for geothermal training assistance, subject to existing distribution requirements and restrictions; it does not itself provide a new appropriation.

major_effects.label: Annual legislative report
major_effects.explanation: Requires an annual report to standing committees with primary jurisdiction over workforce development, higher education, or energy industry matters.

agencies.name: Texas Workforce Commission
agencies.explanation: The bill identifies the commission as the Texas Workforce Commission and assigns it responsibility for establishing and administering the initiative, developing curriculum requirements, identifying funding opportunities, supporting partnerships, and reporting.

agencies.name: Texas Higher Education Coordinating Board
agencies.explanation: The bill defines the coordinating board as the Texas Higher Education Coordinating Board and requires consultation with it on the initiative and curriculum development.

HB994.summary: The bill would establish a temporary Texas Geothermal Energy Production Policy Council within the commission, including the commission chair or designee, the Bureau of Economic Geology director or designee, and commission appointees. The council would study geothermal development and possible incentives or federal cooperation, develop a state plan for commission oversight, and recommend legislative changes; it would be abolished on January 1, 2034.

policy_tags.explanation: Creates a state council to study geothermal energy production, transportation, storage, and oversight policy.
The council's assigned work includes studying development of the geothermal industry and ways to encourage geothermal projects.
Establishes a temporary state policy council and assigns it study and recommendation functions.

locations.name: Texas
locations.explanation: The council's studies and recommendations concern geothermal development and projects in this state.

affected_groups.group: Geothermal energy industry representatives
affected_groups.explanation: The commission would appoint council members to represent different participants, including a specified number of industry representatives.

affected_groups.group: Geothermal energy project and facility developers
affected_groups.explanation: The council would study development of geothermal projects and facilities for production, pipeline transportation, and storage.

major_effects.label: Temporary geothermal policy council
major_effects.explanation: Creates a council within the commission and provides that it will be abolished on January 1, 2034.

major_effects.label: Geothermal policy study and recommendations
major_effects.explanation: Assigns the council research, state-plan development, and legislative recommendation functions; it does not itself enact new geothermal regulations or tax incentives.

agencies.name: Texas geothermal energy production policy council
agencies.explanation: The bill creates the council and assigns it study, planning, and recommendation functions.

agencies.name: the commission
agencies.explanation: The bill places the council within this commission, gives it appointment and chair roles, and refers to its future oversight plan; the supplied text does not identify the commission's canonical name.

agencies.name: Bureau of Economic Geology of The University of Texas at Austin
agencies.explanation: Its director or designee is specified as a member of the newly created council; the registry does not provide a matching entry for this named university bureau.

HB996.summary: The bill would require Medicaid reimbursement for abortion, FDA-approved contraception, and voluntary sterilization even when federal matching funds are unavailable, subject to applicable state and federal law. It would require health benefit plans to cover those services, including counseling and pain and anxiety management for contraceptive-device insertion or removal, and would bar cost-sharing and other coverage barriers; these plan requirements apply to plans issued or renewed on or after January 1, 2028. If a state agency determines that a federal waiver or authorization is needed to implement a provision, it must request it and may delay implementation until it is granted.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes coverage and access rules for abortion, contraception, and sterilization services.
Requires medical assistance reimbursement for specified reproductive health services and removes coverage barriers in the program.
Requires reimbursement even when federal matching funds are unavailable, potentially leaving the state responsible for costs.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The bill amends Texas Medicaid and insurance law with no narrower geographic limitation.

affected_groups.group: Medicaid recipients seeking abortion, contraception, or voluntary sterilization services
affected_groups.explanation: The bill requires reimbursement for these services for medical assistance recipients and removes specified coverage barriers.

affected_groups.group: Health benefit plan enrollees seeking reproductive health services
affected_groups.explanation: Plans must provide coverage for specified services and associated care for contraceptive-device insertion or removal.

affected_groups.group: Health benefit plans and their issuers
affected_groups.explanation: Health benefit plans must cover abortion services, all FDA-approved forms of contraception (including device insertion and removal and related counseling and pain and anxiety management), and voluntary sterilization, including vasectomies, in accordance with applicable state and federal law.

major_effects.label: Medicaid reimbursement
major_effects.explanation: Requires Medicaid reimbursement for specified reproductive health services even if federal matching funds are unavailable.

major_effects.label: Required health-plan coverage
major_effects.explanation: Requires health benefit plans to cover abortion, FDA-approved contraception, including specified device-related care, and voluntary sterilization, subject to applicable law; applies to plans issued or renewed on or after January 1, 2028.

major_effects.label: Limits on cost-sharing and coverage barriers
major_effects.explanation: Bars cost-sharing, utilization review, prior authorization, step therapy, and restrictions or delays for the covered services under Medicaid and health benefit plans.

agencies.name: the commission
agencies.explanation: The bill assigns the commission responsibility for ensuring Medicaid reimbursement and provision of the specified services. Its canonical identity is not established in the supplied bill text or definitions.

HB997.summary: HB997 would let a county donate surplus or salvage property to a civic or charitable organization located in the county without first determining that selling it would likely produce no bids or a bid price below the county’s sale-process expenses. The donation would still need to serve a public purpose, remain subject to sufficient county control to accomplish that purpose, and provide adequate consideration to the county.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill changes the conditions under which a county commissioners court may donate county surplus or salvage property.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The amendment applies to counties generally and does not identify a particular county.

affected_groups.group: Texas counties
affected_groups.explanation: County commissioners courts would have broader authority to donate surplus or salvage property under the specified conditions.

affected_groups.group: Civic or charitable organizations located in a county
affected_groups.explanation: These organizations may receive county surplus or salvage property if the donation meets the stated conditions.

major_effects.label: Broader county donation authority
major_effects.explanation: Removes the condition that the county determine a sale would likely produce no bids or a bid below the county’s sale-process expenses; the public-purpose, county-control, and adequate-consideration conditions remain.

HB998.summary: HB 998 would let a county commissioners court regulate specified roadside vendor activities and solicitation if the county has a population over 600,000, replacing the narrower population and adjacency criteria. The authority would apply in the county’s unincorporated area when the activities occur on a public highway or road, its right-of-way, or in a parking lot.

policy_tags.explanation: Expands which counties may exercise regulatory authority by order.
Authorizes qualifying counties to regulate roadside vendor sales, vendor structures, and solicitation of money.
The expanded county regulatory authority is expressly framed as promoting public safety.

locations.name: Unincorporated areas of Texas counties with a population over 600,000
locations.explanation: The authority applies in the unincorporated area of a qualifying county and only when the covered conduct occurs on a public highway or road, its right-of-way, or in a parking lot.

affected_groups.group: Commissioners courts of counties with a population over 600,000
affected_groups.explanation: These county bodies could use an order to regulate the specified conduct in the defined locations.

affected_groups.group: Food and merchandise vendors, including live-animal vendors
affected_groups.explanation: Their sales and placement or maintenance of structures could be regulated by qualifying counties.

affected_groups.group: People soliciting money
affected_groups.explanation: Solicitation of money is among the activities qualifying counties could regulate.

major_effects.label: Expanded county authority over roadside activity
major_effects.explanation: Qualifying counties could regulate vendor sales and structures, and solicitation of money, by order in the specified unincorporated locations.

HB999.summary: The bill would let qualifying political subdivisions establish a civil-service system for certified emergency medical services personnel employed outside police or fire departments, through a voter-adoption election; municipalities subject to Subchapter K of Chapter 143 are excluded. If adopted, qualifying employees would receive civil-service status, and applicable Chapter 143 provisions would apply; voters could later repeal the system by election.

policy_tags.explanation: Creates an optional civil-service framework that qualifying local political subdivisions may adopt and administer.
Changes civil-service status and applicable employment rules for qualifying emergency medical services personnel.
The employment framework applies specifically to certified emergency medical services personnel.
Provides for voter-initiated elections to adopt or repeal the local civil-service framework.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The framework is available to qualifying political subdivisions across Texas, subject to the bill's applicability limits and local voter adoption.

affected_groups.group: Certified emergency medical services personnel employed outside a political subdivision's police or fire department
affected_groups.explanation: If the subdivision adopts the chapter, qualifying incumbent employees with more than six months of service who are entitled to civil-service classification receive civil-service status; applicable Chapter 143 provisions also apply to covered personnel.

affected_groups.group: Qualifying political subdivisions
affected_groups.explanation: Their governing bodies may be required to order adoption or repeal elections and must implement the chapter if voters approve adoption.

affected_groups.group: Registered voters residing in qualifying political subdivisions
affected_groups.explanation: Voters may petition for adoption or repeal elections and decide the propositions.

major_effects.label: Local-option adoption and repeal
major_effects.explanation: A qualifying subdivision may adopt the framework by election after a qualifying voter petition; after operating under it for at least one year, it may also be repealed by election following a qualifying petition.

major_effects.label: Civil-service status and employment provisions
major_effects.explanation: Upon local adoption, qualifying incumbents receive civil-service status without a competitive examination to remain in their current positions; Chapter 143 provisions apply to covered EMS personnel only to the extent they can be made applicable.

HCR10.summary: HCR 10 would designate March as Endometriosis Awareness Month in Texas. Under the resolution’s cited Government Code provision, the designation would remain in effect until the 10th anniversary of the date the resolution is finally passed.

locations.name: Texas
locations.explanation: The designation is made by the Texas Legislature and applies as a Texas observance.

affected_groups.group: People affected by endometriosis
affected_groups.explanation: The awareness-month designation is intended to raise awareness of the condition and those living with it.

major_effects.label: Awareness-month designation
major_effects.explanation: Would formally designate March as Endometriosis Awareness Month, with the designation lasting until the 10th anniversary of final passage.

HCR11.summary: The resolution designates April as Promise Month in Texas. The designation remains in effect until the 10th anniversary of the resolution’s final passage.

locations.name: Texas
locations.explanation: The designation is made by the Texas Legislature for Promise Month.

major_effects.label: Ceremonial designation
major_effects.explanation: Designates April as Promise Month, with the designation lasting until the 10th anniversary of final passage.

HCR12.summary: The resolution would designate October 14 as Charlie Kirk Day in Texas. Texans are encouraged to reflect on the principles he championed and participate in educational events promoting civic engagement; the designation would remain in effect until the 10th anniversary of the resolution’s final passage.

locations.name: Texas
locations.explanation: The designation is made by the Texas Legislature and applies statewide.

affected_groups.group: Texans
affected_groups.explanation: Texans are encouraged to observe the day through reflection and civic-engagement educational events.
