major_effects.label: Commemorative day designation
major_effects.explanation: Designates October 14 as Charlie Kirk Day, with the designation lasting until the 10th anniversary of final passage.

HCR13.summary: The resolution authorizes Guy Herman’s burial in the State Cemetery only if the State Cemetery Committee approves his application under existing law. It does not guarantee burial space or bypass the committee’s approval.

policy_tags.explanation: The resolution makes a specific authorization concerning eligibility for burial in the State Cemetery, subject to the committee’s approval.

locations.name: State Cemetery
locations.explanation: The State Cemetery is the location specified for the authorized burial.

affected_groups.group: Guy Herman
affected_groups.explanation: The resolution specifically authorizes his burial in the State Cemetery, contingent on committee approval of his application.

major_effects.label: Conditional burial authorization
major_effects.explanation: Authorizes Guy Herman’s burial in the State Cemetery only if the State Cemetery Committee approves his application as required by law.

agencies.name: State Cemetery Committee
agencies.explanation: The resolution makes the committee’s approval of Herman’s burial-space application a condition of the authorization; it does not require the committee to approve it. The source does not identify the committee’s parent agency or a matching registry identity.

HCR14.summary: The resolution urges Congress to pass legislation making daylight saving time permanent. It also asks the Texas secretary of state to send official copies of the resolution to federal officials and the Texas congressional delegation.

locations.name: United States
locations.explanation: The requested congressional action concerns permanent daylight saving time at the national level.

affected_groups.group: United States Congress
affected_groups.explanation: Congress is asked to enact legislation adopting permanent daylight saving time.

major_effects.label: Request for federal legislation
major_effects.explanation: The resolution expresses the Texas Legislature's request that Congress adopt permanent daylight saving time; it does not itself change timekeeping.

major_effects.label: Transmission of resolution
major_effects.explanation: The Texas secretary of state is asked to send official copies to designated federal officials and the Texas congressional delegation.

agencies.name: Texas Secretary of State
agencies.explanation: The resolution asks the secretary to transmit official copies to federal officials and members of the Texas delegation.

HCR15.summary: The resolution honors Vaibhav Duggal and expresses sympathy to those mourning him. It directs that an official copy be prepared for his family and that the House and Senate adjourn in his memory.

affected_groups.group: Vaibhav Duggal's family
affected_groups.explanation: The resolution directs that an official copy be prepared for his family.

affected_groups.group: People mourning Vaibhav Duggal
affected_groups.explanation: The resolution expresses sympathy to those mourning his death.

major_effects.label: Memorial recognition
major_effects.explanation: The Legislature pays tribute to Vaibhav Duggal, expresses sympathy to those mourning him, and directs a family copy and adjournment in his memory.

HCR16.summary: The resolution designates the Texas sabal palm as the official State Palm of Texas. It recognizes the species as a statewide symbol without establishing an implementation program.

locations.name: Texas
locations.explanation: The designation applies to the state as a whole.

major_effects.label: State symbol designation
major_effects.explanation: Designates the Texas sabal palm as the official state palm.

HCR17.summary: The resolution designates the Texas two-step as the official State Dance of Texas. It separately notes that square dance is the official folk dance; the resolution does not change that designation.

locations.name: Texas
locations.explanation: The designation is for the State of Texas.

major_effects.label: State designation
major_effects.explanation: Recognizes the Texas two-step as the official State Dance of Texas.

HCR18.summary: HCR 18 expresses the Texas Legislature’s support for a proposed federally owned transcontinental pipeline running from the western coast of the Mexico–United States border to refineries on the Gulf Coast of Texas and Louisiana. It is an expression of support, not an authorization to build the pipeline or a change to state law, funding, or regulatory authority.

locations.name: Western coast of the Mexico-United States border
locations.explanation: The resolution identifies this as the proposed pipeline system’s western starting area.

locations.name: Gulf Coast of Texas and Louisiana
locations.explanation: The resolution identifies this as the area where the pipeline would reach refineries.

major_effects.label: Legislative expression of support
major_effects.explanation: The resolution formally expresses support for the proposed federally owned pipeline; it does not itself authorize or fund construction.

HCR19.summary: HCR 19 urges Congress to propose and send to the states for ratification a constitutional amendment allowing Congress and the states to reasonably regulate and limit spending to influence campaigns, elections, or ballot measures, including by distinguishing natural persons from corporations, unions, and artificial intelligences. It also asks the Texas secretary of state to forward the resolution to specified federal officials and Texas’s congressional delegation; the resolution itself does not change campaign-finance law.

policy_tags.explanation: The resolution concerns regulation of spending to influence campaigns, elections, and ballot measures.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The resolution is an action of the Texas Legislature.

affected_groups.group: Campaign, election, and ballot-measure spenders
affected_groups.explanation: The amendment Congress is urged to propose could permit spending limits and distinctions among natural persons and artificial entities; the resolution itself does not impose those rules.

major_effects.label: Urges a constitutional amendment on election spending
major_effects.explanation: Calls on Congress to propose an amendment for state ratification that would permit reasonable regulation and limits on spending to influence campaigns, elections, or ballot measures.

major_effects.label: Forwards the resolution to federal officials
major_effects.explanation: Asks the Texas secretary of state to distribute official copies to specified federal officials and the Texas congressional delegation.

agencies.name: Texas Secretary of State
agencies.explanation: The resolution assigns the secretary of state the task of forwarding official copies to specified federal officials and members of the Texas congressional delegation.

HCR6.summary: The resolution urges the U.S. Congress to require a citizenship checkbox for each household member on questionnaires used in the decennial census. It also directs the Texas Secretary of State to send official copies of the resolution to federal officials and Texas’s congressional delegation; it does not itself change the federal census questionnaire.

policy_tags.explanation: The resolution requests a change to the content of the federal decennial census questionnaire and directs a state official to transmit the request; it does not itself change federal census requirements.

locations.name: United States
locations.explanation: The requested census-question change is directed to the U.S. Congress and concerns the decennial census.

affected_groups.group: Households and individuals responding to the decennial census
affected_groups.explanation: If Congress adopts the request, respondents would be asked to indicate whether each household member is a U.S. citizen.

major_effects.label: Request for a census questionnaire change
major_effects.explanation: Urges Congress to require a citizenship checkbox for each household member on decennial census questionnaires; the resolution does not itself impose that federal requirement.

major_effects.label: Transmit the resolution
major_effects.explanation: Directs the Texas Secretary of State to send official copies to the named federal recipients and Texas’s congressional delegation.

agencies.name: Texas Secretary of State
agencies.explanation: The resolution directs the Secretary of State to forward official copies to federal officials and members of the Texas congressional delegation.

HCR7.summary: HCR 7 would have the Legislature affirm the importance of engaged fatherhood, recognize barriers it attributes to state welfare programs, and express support for research and policies encouraging fathers’ involvement. It also supports employment-related programs for incarcerated people and mentoring or foster-parenting initiatives, but does not itself establish or fund those programs or amend law.

locations.name: Texas
locations.explanation: The resolution is a statement by the Texas Legislature concerning fatherhood and families across the state.

affected_groups.group: Children and families, including children in fatherless or single-parent homes
affected_groups.explanation: The resolution focuses on children’s development and the role of fathers and families; it does not create eligibility or legal rights.

affected_groups.group: Fathers
affected_groups.explanation: The resolution expresses support for engaged fatherhood and policies intended to encourage fathers’ involvement.

affected_groups.group: Incarcerated individuals
affected_groups.explanation: The resolution supports programs to help incarcerated people seek employment after detention, without creating such a program.

major_effects.label: Legislative policy statements
major_effects.explanation: Expresses the Legislature’s views and support for fatherhood-related research and initiatives; it does not itself enact or fund a program.

HCR8.summary: HCR 8 would have the 90th Texas Legislature officially recognize the Green Star Service Banner as a symbol honoring veterans who died by suicide and their surviving families. The resolution is a symbolic recognition and does not establish a program or benefit.

locations.name: Texas
locations.explanation: The resolution proposes official recognition by the Texas Legislature.

affected_groups.group: Veterans who died by suicide
affected_groups.explanation: Their service and memory would be honored through recognition of the banner.

affected_groups.group: Families of veterans who died by suicide
affected_groups.explanation: The resolution would recognize the families left behind.

major_effects.label: Symbolic recognition
major_effects.explanation: Officially recognizes the Green Star Service Banner as a symbol honoring veterans who died by suicide and their families.

HCR9.summary: The resolution would direct the Texas Facilities Commission to name the building planned for Phase Two of the Texas Capitol Complex Master Plan the Irma Rangel Building. It would also direct the secretary of state to send an official copy of the resolution to the commission’s chair and executive director.

policy_tags.explanation: The resolution directs a state commission to designate a state building and requires transmission of an official copy.

locations.name: Northwest corner of Congress Avenue and 15th Street
locations.explanation: The resolution identifies the building site by its location at this intersection corner.

major_effects.label: Designation of a state building
major_effects.explanation: Directs the Texas Facilities Commission to name the specified building the Irma Rangel Building.

agencies.name: Texas Facilities Commission
agencies.explanation: The resolution directs the commission to name the specified building.

agencies.name: Texas Secretary of State
agencies.explanation: The resolution directs the secretary of state to forward an official copy to the commission’s chair and executive director.

HJR21.summary: HJR 21 proposes a Texas constitutional amendment requiring the state to provide medical assistance to everyone who applies when federal ACA matching funds are available for that assistance. The amendment would be submitted to voters on November 2, 2027, and, if approved, would take effect January 1, 2028.

policy_tags.explanation: The proposal would require medical assistance for an expanded group of applicants, subject to federal matching funds being available.
The proposed amendment expressly requires expansion of Medicaid eligibility under the stated federal-funding condition.
The proposal would impose a state obligation to provide medical assistance for covered applicants, while limiting the obligation to cases for which federal matching funds are available.

locations.name: Statewide (Texas)
locations.explanation: The proposed constitutional provision applies to the state, rather than to a specified locality.

affected_groups.group: Individuals who apply for medical assistance and for whom federal ACA matching funds are available
affected_groups.explanation: These applicants would be covered by the proposed state obligation.

affected_groups.group: Texas voters
affected_groups.explanation: Voters would decide whether to approve the proposed constitutional amendment.

major_effects.label: Medicaid coverage expansion
major_effects.explanation: Would require medical assistance for all applicants for whom federal matching funds are available; the requirement depends on voter approval of the constitutional amendment.

agencies.name: Health and Human Services Commission
agencies.explanation: The bill does not name an administering agency. HHSC is listed as an inferred potential implementer of the proposed Medicaid coverage requirement; the assignment is not established by the bill text.

HJR23.summary: If voters approve the proposed constitutional amendment, political subdivisions generally could not impose ad valorem taxes on or after January 1, 2032. They would still have to impose taxes as necessary to repay qualifying bonds or other obligations issued before that date and secured wholly or partly by ad valorem tax revenue, until those obligations are paid in full.

policy_tags.explanation: The amendment would prohibit political subdivisions from imposing ad valorem taxes after the specified date, subject to a debt-repayment exception.
The amendment would restrict the taxing authority of political subdivisions.

locations.name: Statewide, Texas
locations.explanation: The proposed restriction applies to political subdivisions throughout the state.

affected_groups.group: Political subdivisions of Texas
affected_groups.explanation: Their authority to impose ad valorem taxes would generally end on or after January 1, 2032, except they must impose taxes as necessary to repay preexisting bonds or other obligations secured wholly or partly by ad valorem tax revenue.

affected_groups.group: Owners of taxable property in political subdivisions
affected_groups.explanation: They would generally no longer be subject to political-subdivision ad valorem taxes after the specified date, except as needed to repay qualifying obligations.

affected_groups.group: Holders of qualifying pre-2032 bonds or other obligations
affected_groups.explanation: Taxes could continue as necessary to repay principal and interest on qualifying obligations until they are paid in full.

major_effects.label: Prohibition on political-subdivision ad valorem taxes
major_effects.explanation: Beginning January 1, 2032, political subdivisions generally could not impose ad valorem taxes.

major_effects.label: Limited tax authority for repayment of existing obligations
major_effects.explanation: Political subdivisions would have to impose taxes as necessary to repay qualifying pre-2032 obligations, and revenue under this exception could be used only for that repayment.

HJR24.summary: HJR 24 proposes a Texas constitutional right to personal reproductive autonomy, including abortion on or before 24 weeks post-fertilization, certain abortions after that point, contraception, and assisted reproductive technology. The amendment would be submitted to voters on November 2, 2027, and would take effect only if voters approve it.

policy_tags.explanation: The proposal addresses abortion, contraception, and assisted reproductive technology.
The proposed amendment would establish a constitutional individual right and limit state restrictions on its exercise.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The proposed right applies to each individual residing in Texas and limits the state.

affected_groups.group: Individuals residing in Texas
affected_groups.explanation: The proposed right to reproductive autonomy would apply to each individual residing in the state.

affected_groups.group: Pregnant individuals
affected_groups.explanation: The proposal expressly addresses abortion access, including specified circumstances after 24 weeks post-fertilization.

affected_groups.group: People seeking contraception or assisted reproductive technology
affected_groups.explanation: The proposed right expressly includes contraception and in vitro fertilization or similar treatments and procedures.

major_effects.label: Proposed constitutional reproductive-autonomy right
major_effects.explanation: If approved by voters, the amendment would establish a right to personal reproductive autonomy and bar state restrictions, including the specified abortion protections, contraception, and assisted reproductive technology.

HJR25.summary: HJR 25 proposes a Texas constitutional amendment allowing retroactive laws for civil causes of action arising out of child sexual abuse. The amendment would take effect only if approved by voters at the November 2, 2027 election; it does not itself enact a specific retroactive law.

policy_tags.explanation: The proposal changes constitutional protections by creating an exception that would allow retroactive laws for this category of civil claim.

locations.name: Texas
locations.explanation: The proposal amends the Texas Constitution and is submitted to voters statewide.

affected_groups.group: People pursuing civil claims arising out of child sexual abuse
affected_groups.explanation: If the amendment is approved, retroactive laws could be made concerning their category of civil action.

affected_groups.group: People or entities facing civil claims arising out of child sexual abuse
affected_groups.explanation: The proposed exception could permit retroactive laws affecting this category of civil claims.

major_effects.label: Constitutional exception for retroactive civil claims
major_effects.explanation: If voters approve the amendment, the Constitution would retain its general prohibition on retroactive laws, except that retroactive laws may be made as to a civil cause of action arising out of child sexual abuse. The proposal does not itself enact a particular retroactive law.

HJR26.summary: HJR 26 proposes a Texas constitutional amendment authorizing the legislature to enact a general law allowing courts to commute punishment for certain people serving prison terms. The amendment would take effect only if voters approve it; the proposed amendment is to be submitted to voters on November 2, 2027.

policy_tags.explanation: The proposal would allow future legislation to authorize courts to commute punishment for certain people serving prison terms.
The proposal requires submission of the constitutional amendment to voters and specifies the ballot proposition.

locations.name: Texas statewide
locations.explanation: The proposal amends the Texas Constitution and submits the amendment to voters.

affected_groups.group: People serving a term of imprisonment who may qualify under future law
affected_groups.explanation: They could be eligible for a court-ordered commutation if voters approve the amendment and the legislature enacts a law providing for it.

major_effects.label: Conditional authorization for court commutations
major_effects.explanation: If voters approve the amendment, the legislature may enact a general law allowing courts to commute punishment for certain people serving prison terms.

major_effects.label: Voter submission
major_effects.explanation: The proposed amendment must be submitted to voters on November 2, 2027, with the stated proposition on the ballot.

HJR27.summary: If voters approve the proposed constitutional amendment at the November 2, 2027 election, a Texas Redistricting Commission would receive authority to adopt plans for U.S. House districts in Texas and for the Texas House and Senate; the Legislature would provide by general law for the commission’s composition and operation. The commission provisions would take effect January 1, 2030, when the Legislative Redistricting Board would be abolished, and the commission would first convene in 2031. If the Judicial Districts Board misses its existing deadline to reapportion judicial districts, the commission would convene on September 1 and have 90 days to complete that reapportionment.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes which body adopts electoral district plans for congressional and state legislative elections.
Creates a constitutional commission, assigns it authority, and requires the Legislature to provide for its composition and operation.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The proposed commission’s plans cover Texas congressional and legislative districts, and its conditional judicial reapportionment is statewide.

affected_groups.group: Texas voters
affected_groups.explanation: Voters would elect representatives from districts drawn under the commission’s plans and would vote on the proposed amendment.

affected_groups.group: People in Texas judicial districts
affected_groups.explanation: Their district boundaries may be reapportioned by the commission if the Judicial Districts Board misses its deadline.

major_effects.label: Redistricting authority assigned to a commission
major_effects.explanation: The commission would adopt U.S. House and Texas legislative district plans; districts may be established or changed only as provided by this section.

major_effects.label: Legislative Redistricting Board abolished
major_effects.explanation: The board would be abolished January 1, 2030, with the commission taking its place under the proposed provisions.

major_effects.label: Conditional judicial-district reapportionment fallback changed
major_effects.explanation: If the Judicial Districts Board misses its deadline, the commission would convene on September 1 and complete statewide reapportionment within 90 days.

agencies.name: Texas Redistricting Commission
agencies.explanation: The proposed amendment assigns the commission redistricting authority and a conditional role in judicial-district reapportionment.

agencies.name: Legislative Redistricting Board
agencies.explanation: The amendment abolishes the board effective January 1, 2030, and provides that references to the commission temporarily mean this board until that date.

agencies.name: Texas Legislature
agencies.explanation: The amendment directs the Legislature to provide by general law for the commission’s composition and operation.

HJR28.summary: If voters approve the amendment on November 2, 2027, it would bar election to the House after eight full regular sessions there, to the Senate after eight there, or to either chamber after 12 combined sessions, subject to stated four-year Senate exceptions. It would also limit eligibility for statewide elected executive offices to people with fewer than 16 years of credited service and require a general law prohibiting state employees from more than 24 years of service in the legislative or executive departments; specified service before 2029 would not count.

policy_tags.explanation: The amendment changes eligibility to run for legislative and statewide elected executive offices.
The amendment sets service limits for state elected officials and requires a state-employee service cap to be established by general law.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The amendment governs eligibility for state offices and service in state government.

affected_groups.group: People seeking election to the Texas House or Senate
affected_groups.explanation: Candidates would be subject to chamber-specific and combined legislative-service eligibility limits, with stated Senate-term exceptions.

affected_groups.group: Candidates for statewide elected executive offices
affected_groups.explanation: Eligibility would be limited based on credited service in covered executive and legislative offices.

affected_groups.group: State employees in the legislative or executive departments
affected_groups.explanation: A general law would be required to prohibit more than 24 total years of service in those departments.

major_effects.label: Legislative service limits
major_effects.explanation: Sets limits based on service in each chamber and across both chambers; specified four-year Senate terms remain permitted under the stated exceptions.

major_effects.label: Statewide executive-office service limit
major_effects.explanation: Bars election to covered statewide executive offices when credited service reaches 16 years; legislative service is credited, and the constitutional holdover allowance remains.

major_effects.label: Service-credit and transition rules
major_effects.explanation: Certain statewide executive service counts toward legislative limits, while specified service before 2029 is excluded from the legislative and executive eligibility calculations.

major_effects.label: Required state-employee service cap
major_effects.explanation: Requires the Legislature to enact a general law prohibiting state employees from serving more than 24 total years in the legislative or executive departments.

HJR29.summary: HJR 29 asks voters to amend the Texas Constitution to authorize the Legislature to define “farm products” and “in the hands of the producer” for the farm-products tax exemption, and to allow that definition to include livestock, poultry, timber, and farming-operation supplies. If voters approve the amendment on November 2, 2027, the exemption would apply to farm products in producers’ hands and family supplies, but the resolution itself does not enact statutory definitions or automatically add each listed category.

policy_tags.explanation: The proposal changes the constitutional framework for the tax exemption of farm products by authorizing the Legislature to define its terms.

locations.name: Texas statewide
locations.explanation: The proposal amends the Texas Constitution and submits the amendment to voters at an election.

affected_groups.group: Agricultural producers holding farm products
affected_groups.explanation: The Legislature could define which farm products and producer-held property qualify for the exemption.

affected_groups.group: Owners of livestock, poultry, timber, or farming-operation supplies
affected_groups.explanation: These categories could be included in the statutory definition, but the proposal does not automatically add them to the exemption.

major_effects.label: Legislative authority to define exemption terms
major_effects.explanation: If approved by voters, the amendment would authorize the Legislature by general law to define “farm products” and “in the hands of the producer,” including the option to include specified categories.

major_effects.label: Constitutional farm-products exemption framework
major_effects.explanation: The proposal revises the constitutional provision governing the exemption; the amendment would not itself enact statutory definitions or guarantee exemption for every category that the Legislature may include.

HJR30.summary: If voters approve the proposed constitutional amendment, a school district’s ad valorem tax for paying principal and interest on its bonds would require approval by three-fifths of the qualified voters voting in the election. The amendment would be submitted to voters on November 2, 2027.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes the voter-approval requirement for school district bond-related taxes.
Raises the voter-approval threshold for the specified school district ad valorem taxes used to pay bond principal and interest.

locations.name: Texas school districts
locations.explanation: The proposed requirement applies to the specified bond-related taxes in all school districts.

affected_groups.group: Qualified voters in school districts
affected_groups.explanation: Voters would need to meet a three-fifths approval threshold for the specified school district bond-related tax.

affected_groups.group: School districts issuing bonds
affected_groups.explanation: The higher approval threshold would apply to an ad valorem tax used to pay principal and interest on district-issued bonds.

major_effects.label: Higher approval threshold for school bond-related taxes
major_effects.explanation: If the proposed amendment is approved, the tax approval rule in Subsection (e) is subject to Subsection (e-1): a tax for paying principal and interest on district-issued bonds requires approval by three-fifths of voters, rather than the general majority required under Subsection (e).

HJR31.summary: HJR 31 proposes a constitutional amendment creating an independent commission to draw districts for Texas’s U.S. House, Senate, and House elections, with specified appointment, mapping, and public-participation rules. The commission would also take over judicial-district reapportionment if the Judicial Districts Board misses its deadline. If voters approve the amendment at the November 2, 2027 election, the new provisions take effect January 1, 2029.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes who draws congressional and state legislative districts and establishes procedures for adopting those plans.
Creates a commission and related selection and oversight processes, and assigns duties to a nonpartisan agency and select committee.
Sets redistricting standards requiring equal opportunity for racial, ethnic, and language minorities to participate and elect candidates of choice.
Requires collection and public posting of applicant and political-activity information, with limited authority to redact sensitive application information.

locations.name: Texas
locations.explanation: The proposed commission draws districts for elections from this state, and its public process and mapping duties operate statewide.

affected_groups.group: Texas voters
affected_groups.explanation: Voters in the affected congressional and state legislative districts would vote under plans developed under the new process.

affected_groups.group: Racial, ethnic, and language minorities
affected_groups.explanation: The commission’s selection and map-drawing standards specifically address meaningful participation and the ability to elect candidates of choice.

affected_groups.group: Commission applicants, employees, and vendors
affected_groups.explanation: Applicants face eligibility and information-reporting requirements, and employees and vendors have recurring political-activity reporting obligations.

major_effects.label: Redistricting authority
major_effects.explanation: Assigns congressional and state legislative plan adoption to the commission; an approved plan becomes law after 45 days if it receives the required majority and category votes. If the Judicial Districts Board misses its reapportionment deadline, the commission must convene on September 1 and complete that reapportionment within 90 days after the board’s deadline.

major_effects.label: Commission and selection process
major_effects.explanation: Creates a 15-member commission and a process involving an agency-developed selection pool, public input, and legislative committee review.

major_effects.label: Mapping standards
major_effects.explanation: Requires plans to meet specified legal and population criteria, protect minority electoral opportunity, avoid unfairly favoring or disfavoring any political party when considered on a statewide basis, and respect communities of interest to the extent practicable.

major_effects.label: Public process and disclosures
major_effects.explanation: Requires open commission meetings, public access to plans and records, and political-activity reports from commission employee applicants, employees, and vendor applicants and vendors.

major_effects.label: Agency procedures
major_effects.explanation: Requires the nonpartisan agency to adopt and publish rules, after notice and opportunity for comment, for carrying out its duties.

agencies.name: independent redistricting commission
agencies.explanation: The proposed amendment creates the commission and assigns it authority to adopt covered redistricting plans; it also assigns it judicial-district reapportionment if the Judicial Districts Board misses its deadline.

agencies.name: nonpartisan agency
agencies.explanation: The proposed amendment assigns this agency duties to establish and appoint the commission, develop selection pools, train members, and adopt procedural rules. The bill leaves the agency’s identity to later legislation.

agencies.name: select committee on redistricting
agencies.explanation: The proposed amendment creates this legislative committee and assigns it approval or rejection of selection pools for commission membership.

HJR32.summary: If voters approve the proposed constitutional amendment at the November 2, 2027 election, the Governor would have to convene the Legislature when proposing a renewal or new order for the same disaster or emergency that meets specified geographic or population thresholds. The Legislature could renew or extend the declaration. A declaration subject to Subsection (c) could not continue beyond 30 days without legislative renewal or extension, except that a declaration subject to Subsection (c) related to a nuclear or radiological event recognized by the federal agency with primary authority for federal response could not continue beyond 90 days without legislative renewal or extension. The amendment would also give a legislator standing to participate as a party in a suit against the Governor for failing to convene the Legislature, with the Supreme Court having original jurisdiction.

policy_tags.explanation: The proposal changes the constitutional powers and duties of the Governor, Legislature, and Supreme Court in connection with qualifying disaster or emergency declarations.

locations.name: Texas
locations.explanation: The proposal applies to qualifying disasters or emergencies in the state.

locations.name: Trauma service areas in Texas
locations.explanation: For a public health emergency or disaster, the proposal includes a trigger based on affected counties in trauma service areas.

affected_groups.group: Governor of Texas
affected_groups.explanation: The Governor would have a duty to convene the Legislature when the proposal's conditions are met and would be subject to the specified suit.

affected_groups.group: Texas legislators
affected_groups.explanation: The Legislature would gain specified authority over qualifying declarations, and an individual member could participate as a party in a suit alleging the Governor failed to convene it as required.

affected_groups.group: People affected by gubernatorial disaster or emergency declarations subject to Subsection (c)
affected_groups.explanation: For declarations subject to Subsection (c), the duration is limited to 30 days unless the Legislature renews or extends the declaration. The limit is 90 days for declarations related to a nuclear or radiological event recognized by the federal agency with primary response authority, unless the Legislature renews or extends the declaration.

major_effects.label: Special sessions and legislative authority
major_effects.explanation: When the Governor proposes a renewal or new order for the same qualifying disaster or emergency, the Governor must convene a special session; the Legislature may renew or extend the declaration and respond to the emergency.

major_effects.label: Limits on qualifying declarations
major_effects.explanation: A qualifying declaration generally may not continue beyond 30 days without legislative renewal or extension; the limit is 90 days for a related nuclear or radiological event recognized by the federal agency with primary authority for federal response.

major_effects.label: Legislator suit and Supreme Court jurisdiction
major_effects.explanation: A legislator would have standing to participate as a party in a suit against the Governor for violating the duty to convene the Legislature, and the Supreme Court would hear that suit in the first instance.

agencies.name: Texas Judicial Branch
agencies.explanation: The Supreme Court would receive original jurisdiction over the specified suit against the Governor; the court's role is to hear that suit in the first instance.

HJR33.summary: HJR 33 proposes a Texas constitutional amendment allowing the legislature, by general law, to permit a person to vote in a primary election if the person will be at least 18 on the date of the subsequent general election for state and county officers and meets the other applicable voting requirements. The amendment would take effect only if approved by voters at the November 2, 2027 election.

policy_tags.explanation: The amendment would authorize the legislature to permit eligible people under 18 to vote in a primary election.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The proposal amends the Texas Constitution and submits the amendment to voters; its scope is statewide.

affected_groups.group: People under 18 who will be at least 18 by the subsequent general election for state and county officers
affected_groups.explanation: They could be permitted to vote in the preceding primary if they also satisfy other applicable eligibility requirements and the legislature provides for it by general law.

affected_groups.group: Texas voters
affected_groups.explanation: Voters would decide whether to approve the proposed constitutional amendment.

major_effects.label: Potential primary voting by eligible people under 18
major_effects.explanation: If the amendment is approved, the legislature may provide by general law for primary voting by people who will be at least 18 by the subsequent general election and meet other applicable eligibility requirements.

major_effects.label: Constitutional amendment submitted for voter approval
major_effects.explanation: The proposal is submitted to voters on November 2, 2027; it is not itself an enacted constitutional change.

HJR35.summary: If approved by voters on November 2, 2027, HJR 35 would amend the Texas Constitution to authorize the Legislature to set ad valorem appraisal limits by general law. It would lower the homestead limit’s percentage benchmark from 110% to 102.5% and authorize a separate limit for other real property; qualifying limits could continue after ownership changes when eligibility remains continuous.

policy_tags.explanation: The proposal changes constitutional rules for limiting property appraised values used for ad valorem taxation.

locations.name: Texas
locations.explanation: The proposal would amend the Texas Constitution and submit the amendment to voters statewide.

affected_groups.group: Owners of residence homesteads qualifying for the exemption
affected_groups.explanation: The proposal changes the homestead appraisal-limit benchmark and permits qualification based on a predecessor in title if the property continuously qualifies.

affected_groups.group: Owners of non-homestead real property that qualifies for a limitation under future law
affected_groups.explanation: The amendment would authorize appraisal limits for other real property and allow a qualifying limitation to continue across ownership changes while qualification is continuous.

major_effects.label: Homestead appraisal-limit benchmark
major_effects.explanation: Changes the homestead percentage benchmark from 110% to 102.5% of the prior tax year's appraised value, while allowing a greater percentage by general law and retaining the market-value comparison.

major_effects.label: Appraisal limits for other real property
major_effects.explanation: Would authorize the Legislature by general law to set appraisal limits for real property outside the homestead limitation, with additional eligibility requirements permitted. The amendment itself would not impose a limit.

major_effects.label: Qualification can continue across ownership changes
major_effects.explanation: For both categories, a predecessor's qualification may support the limitation after a change in ownership if eligibility has remained continuous; the limitation expires when the property ceases to qualify.

HJR36.summary: HJR 36 proposes a constitutional amendment allowing eligible political subdivisions—excluding school districts, counties, cities or towns, and junior college districts—to limit increases in ad valorem taxes on qualifying homesteads of limited-means disabled or elderly people, with specified protections for surviving spouses. The surviving-spouse protection is subject to exceptions provided by general law. If voters approve the amendment at the November 2, 2027 election, the provision would take effect January 1, 2028.

policy_tags.explanation: The amendment would authorize limits on increases in local ad valorem taxes on qualifying residence homesteads.
The amendment would give certain political subdivisions authority to establish the tax limitation and require an election under the specified petition process.

locations.name: Texas statewide
locations.explanation: The proposal amends the Texas Constitution and would apply statewide if approved by voters.

affected_groups.group: Limited-means disabled or elderly people with qualifying residence homesteads
affected_groups.explanation: They could benefit from a tax limitation if an eligible political subdivision establishes one and they receive a qualifying homestead exemption.

affected_groups.group: Qualifying surviving spouses
affected_groups.explanation: A surviving spouse may retain the limitation if the deceased person received a homestead exemption in the year of death and the spouse meets the specified financial, age, and homestead conditions.

affected_groups.group: Eligible political subdivisions and their registered voters
affected_groups.explanation: Subdivision governing bodies could establish the limitation; a petition signed by five percent of registered voters would require an election on whether to establish it.

major_effects.label: Optional homestead tax limitation
major_effects.explanation: An eligible political subdivision could limit increases in its total ad valorem taxes on qualifying homesteads while they remain the residence homestead of the qualifying person or spouse. Taxes may be increased to reflect value added by improvements other than repairs or improvements required by government; the subsection also excepts increases consistent with a transfer of the limitation under a law authorized by the subsection.

major_effects.label: Local adoption and petition-triggered election
major_effects.explanation: A governing body could establish the limitation by official action; alternatively, a petition signed by five percent of the subdivision's registered voters would require an election, with establishment determined by majority vote.

HJR37.summary: HJR 37 proposes a constitutional amendment allowing certain revenue transferred to the state highway fund to be used for public transportation, public bicycle paths, and public sidewalks, as well as public roadways other than toll roads. These expanded uses would be allowed only if voters approve the amendment at the November 2, 2027 election.

policy_tags.explanation: The amendment would expand the transportation purposes eligible for certain state highway fund revenue.
The proposal would broaden the uses for which dedicated state revenue transferred to the state highway fund may be spent.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The proposal amends the Texas Constitution and governs revenue transferred to the state highway fund.

affected_groups.group: Public transportation providers and users
affected_groups.explanation: They could benefit from state highway fund revenue being eligible for public transportation uses if voters approve the amendment.

affected_groups.group: People who use public bicycle paths or sidewalks
affected_groups.explanation: The amendment would make these public facilities eligible uses of the specified revenue if approved.

major_effects.label: Expanded eligible uses of highway-fund revenue
major_effects.explanation: If voters approve the amendment, certain revenue transferred to the state highway fund could be used for public transportation, public bicycle paths, and public sidewalks, in addition to public roadways other than toll roads.

HJR38.summary: If approved by voters, the amendment would change the constitutional percentage in the residence-homestead appraisal limit from 110% to 103% of the prior tax year's appraised value, while allowing the Legislature to set a greater percentage by general law; the limit would still be capped at the homestead's most recent market value. The change is conditional on voter approval.

policy_tags.explanation: The proposal changes the constitutional percentage used to limit the appraised value of a residence homestead for ad valorem taxation.

locations.name: Texas statewide
locations.explanation: The resolution proposes an amendment to the Texas Constitution for submission to voters.

affected_groups.group: Owners of residence homesteads who qualify for the applicable exemption
affected_groups.explanation: Their qualifying homesteads are subject to the appraisal-value limit if the amendment is approved and a limitation applies.

major_effects.label: Proposed change to the homestead appraisal-value limit
major_effects.explanation: If voters approve the amendment, the constitutional percentage would change from 110% to 103% of the preceding tax year's appraised value, or a greater percentage set by general law. The limit remains subject to the lesser-of-market-value rule.

HJR39.summary: If voters approve the proposed amendment, it would take effect September 1, 2029 and redirect 12% of the comptroller’s baseline allocation to the economic stabilization fund to a new Grow Texas fund, subject to a $250 million per-biennium cap. The Legislature could appropriate the fund only for infrastructure needs in oil- and gas-producing areas it determines are significantly affected by production; general law could provide for grants to state agencies and political subdivisions. A new commission would administer appropriated money and advise the Legislature.

policy_tags.explanation: Redirects general revenue to a new fund and establishes limits on how its money may be appropriated.
General law may authorize grants from the fund to political subdivisions for eligible infrastructure purposes.
Creates a dedicated fund for infrastructure needs in areas significantly affected by oil and gas production.
Creates a commission to administer fund appropriations and advise the Legislature.

locations.name: Areas of the state where oil and gas are produced and that the Legislature determines are significantly affected by production
locations.explanation: These are the only areas in which the fund may be appropriated for eligible infrastructure needs.

affected_groups.group: Political subdivisions in eligible oil- and gas-producing areas
affected_groups.explanation: They may be eligible for grants if general law provides for them.

affected_groups.group: Communities in areas significantly affected by oil and gas production
affected_groups.explanation: The fund is restricted to infrastructure needs in these areas.

major_effects.label: Redirects a portion of revenue to the Grow Texas fund
major_effects.explanation: The comptroller would redirect 12% of the amount otherwise allocated to the economic stabilization fund under Subsection (c-1), capped at $250 million per state fiscal biennium. Amounts added to the economic stabilization fund under Subsection (c-2) are excluded from this calculation.

major_effects.label: Creates a restricted-purpose fund
major_effects.explanation: The fund may be appropriated only for infrastructure needs in qualifying production-affected areas. General law may provide for grants to state agencies and political subdivisions; remaining unobligated and unappropriated money transfers to the economic stabilization fund at the end of each biennium.

major_effects.label: Creates the Grow Texas fund commission
major_effects.explanation: The commission would administer money appropriated from the fund and advise the Legislature on appropriations.

agencies.name: Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts
agencies.explanation: The comptroller is assigned the revenue-transfer duties, including the reduction and transfer to the Grow Texas fund.

agencies.name: Grow Texas fund commission
agencies.explanation: The bill creates this commission and assigns it fund-administration and advisory functions; no canonical registry identity is established by the supplied sources.

HJR40.summary: If voters approve the proposed constitutional amendment, beginning with the tax year starting January 1, 2028, a county commissioners court may—but is not required to—exempt up to $140,000 of an individual’s residence homestead appraised value from county property taxation; other applicable exemptions remain available. A county may continue taxing the otherwise exempt value until pledged debt is discharged if ending the levy would impair the debt contract.

policy_tags.explanation: The amendment would authorize an optional county ad valorem tax exemption for a portion of a residence homestead’s appraised value.
The proposed exemption applies to an individual’s residence homestead.
The amendment would give county commissioners courts discretion to adopt the exemption and would allow continued county tax collection in a specified debt circumstance.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The proposed constitutional authority is available to a county generally and is not limited to a named place.

affected_groups.group: Individuals with residence homesteads in counties that adopt the exemption
affected_groups.explanation: Their county-taxable homestead value could be reduced if their county adopts the exemption.

affected_groups.group: County governments
affected_groups.explanation: County commissioners courts would decide whether to adopt the exemption, subject to the proposed limit and debt-related qualification.

major_effects.label: Optional county homestead tax exemption
major_effects.explanation: If voters approve the amendment, a county may choose to exempt up to $140,000 of an individual’s residence homestead appraised value from county ad valorem taxation. The exemption is not automatic, and pledged taxes may continue to be collected until debt is discharged when ending the levy would impair the debt contract.

major_effects.label: County authority to adopt the exemption
major_effects.explanation: The proposed constitutional amendment would authorize county commissioners courts to adopt the exemption by official action, subject to voter approval.

HJR41.summary: HJR 41 proposes a Texas constitutional amendment allowing the Legislature, by general law, to authorize a court to commute punishment for certain people serving prison terms. The amendment would authorize this only if approved by voters, and the proposition is to be submitted at the November 2, 2027 election.

policy_tags.explanation: The proposed amendment would allow the Legislature to authorize a court to commute punishment for certain incarcerated people.
The resolution directs that the proposed constitutional amendment be submitted to voters at a specified election.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The proposal amends the Texas Constitution.

affected_groups.group: Certain individuals serving a term of imprisonment
affected_groups.explanation: They could be eligible for a court-ordered commutation under a future general law.

affected_groups.group: Texas voters
affected_groups.explanation: Voters would decide whether to approve the proposed constitutional amendment.

major_effects.label: Authority for court commutations
major_effects.explanation: If voters approve the amendment, the Legislature may enact a general law allowing a court to commute punishment for certain people serving prison terms.

major_effects.label: Constitutional amendment ballot
major_effects.explanation: The proposed amendment must be submitted to voters at the November 2, 2027 election.

agencies.name: a court
agencies.explanation: A court could receive authority to grant commutations if the Legislature enacts a general law; the amendment does not identify a particular court or itself assign it a duty.

HJR43.summary: HJR 43 proposes a constitutional amendment lowering the population threshold for a city to adopt or amend a charter from more than 5,000 to more than 500 inhabitants. A city that previously adopted or amended a charter under this provision could still amend it if its population later falls to 500 or fewer; the amendment would take effect only if approved by voters at the November 2, 2027 election.

policy_tags.explanation: The proposal changes which cities may adopt or amend municipal charters.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The proposed change is to the Texas Constitution and applies to cities meeting the population criteria.

affected_groups.group: Cities with more than 500 and no more than 5,000 inhabitants
affected_groups.explanation: These cities would be able to adopt or amend a charter under the proposed lower threshold.

affected_groups.group: Cities with an existing charter under this provision whose population falls to 500 or fewer
affected_groups.explanation: These cities would retain the ability to amend their charters.

affected_groups.group: Texas voters
affected_groups.explanation: Voters would decide whether to approve the proposed constitutional amendment.

major_effects.label: Municipal charter authority
major_effects.explanation: Lowers the population threshold for cities to adopt or amend charters and allows cities covered by the provision to continue amending charters if their population later falls to 500 or fewer.

HJR44.summary: If voters approve the proposed constitutional amendment, the Governor must convene a special legislative session when at least two-thirds of the members of each house petition for one, with the petition specifying the date and purposes. The amendment is to be submitted to voters on November 2, 2027.

policy_tags.explanation: The proposal changes the process for convening the Legislature in special session.
The proposed constitutional amendment must be submitted to voters at an election.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The proposed constitutional amendment governs the Texas Legislature and is submitted to voters statewide.

affected_groups.group: Members of each house of the Texas Legislature
affected_groups.explanation: At least two-thirds of the members of each house may petition to trigger a special session.

affected_groups.group: Texas voters
affected_groups.explanation: Voters decide whether to approve the proposed constitutional amendment.

major_effects.label: Petition-triggered special sessions
major_effects.explanation: If the amendment is approved, a petition signed by at least two-thirds of each house requires the Governor to convene a special session on the date specified, for the purposes specified.

major_effects.label: Voter approval
major_effects.explanation: The proposed constitutional change is submitted to voters on November 2, 2027; it does not itself amend the Constitution.

agencies.name: Governor
agencies.explanation: The proposal directly assigns the Governor the duty to convene a special session after a qualifying petition.

agencies.name: Legislature
agencies.explanation: The proposal changes the conditions under which the Legislature is convened and limits the session to the purposes stated in the petition.

HJR45.summary: HJR 45 proposes a constitutional amendment allowing the Legislature, at any time during a regular session, to introduce bills and resolutions, hold committee hearings, and otherwise act on them. It replaces the existing staged schedule in Article III, Section 5(c)—first 30 days for introduction and specified emergency and confirmation matters, succeeding 30 days for committee hearings, and the remainder for action on pending matters—and repeals that subsection. The amendment is to be submitted to voters on November 2, 2027, and is contingent on voter approval.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes the constitutional rules governing legislative activity during a regular session.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The proposal amends the Texas Constitution and changes procedures for the Texas Legislature.

affected_groups.group: Texas legislators
affected_groups.explanation: Legislators would be able to introduce, hear, and act on bills and resolutions at any time during a regular session.

affected_groups.group: Texas voters
affected_groups.explanation: Voters are asked to decide whether to adopt the proposed constitutional amendment.

major_effects.label: Regular-session legislative procedure
major_effects.explanation: Would replace the existing staged schedule for bill introduction, committee hearings, and legislative action with authority to introduce, hold hearings on, and otherwise act on bills and resolutions at any time during a regular session; the resolution also repeals Article III, Section 5(c).

HJR47.summary: HJR 47 proposes a constitutional amendment barring state and political-subdivision agencies from regulating the educational program of a private school, including a home school. It would be submitted to voters on November 2, 2027, and the proposed protection would take effect only if voters approve it.

policy_tags.explanation: The proposal would limit regulation of private-school and home-school educational programs.
The proposed restriction also applies to agencies of political subdivisions.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The proposed restriction applies to private schools in Texas and to state and political-subdivision agencies.

affected_groups.group: Private schools, including home schools
affected_groups.explanation: Their educational programs would be protected from the specified state and local regulation if voters approve the amendment.

affected_groups.group: State agencies
affected_groups.explanation: They would be barred from regulating private-school educational programs under the proposed amendment.

affected_groups.group: Political subdivisions and their agencies
affected_groups.explanation: Their agencies would also be subject to the proposed restriction.

major_effects.label: Limits state and local regulatory authority
major_effects.explanation: If approved by voters, the amendment would bar state and political-subdivision agencies from regulating private-school educational programs, including home schools.

agencies.name: An agency of the state government
agencies.explanation: The proposed amendment directly bars this general class of state bodies from regulating the specified educational programs; the text does not identify individual agencies.

HJR48.summary: HJR 48 proposes a Texas constitutional amendment recognizing a right to use generally accepted practices to explore for, produce, and export minerals, including oil and gas. If voters approve it at the November 2, 2027 election, it would limit legislative authorization of state and local regulation of those practices, while preserving specified regulation to protect public health and safety from imminent danger only when clear and convincing evidence shows it is necessary, regulation to conserve natural resources, and authority to acquire property for public use.

policy_tags.explanation: The proposed right specifically covers exploration for, production, and export of oil, gas, and other minerals.
The proposal changes the constitutional framework for regulating mineral practices, while retaining authority to regulate for natural-resource conservation.
The proposal limits legislative authorization of political subdivisions to regulate covered mineral practices, subject to specified exceptions.

locations.name: Statewide (Texas)
locations.explanation: The proposed amendment would add a section to the Texas Constitution and apply statewide if approved.

affected_groups.group: People and businesses engaged in mineral exploration, production, or export
affected_groups.explanation: They would receive the proposed constitutional protection for generally accepted practices in those activities.

affected_groups.group: State agencies and political subdivisions that regulate mineral practices
affected_groups.explanation: Their ability to regulate covered mineral practices under laws authorized by the legislature would be subject to the amendment’s limits. Regulation to protect public health and safety from imminent danger is preserved only when clear and convincing evidence shows it is necessary; regulation to preserve or conserve the state’s natural resources is also preserved.

major_effects.label: Constitutional right to engage in mineral practices
major_effects.explanation: If approved by voters, the amendment would protect generally accepted practices concerning mineral exploration, production, and export.

major_effects.label: Limits on regulation of mineral practices
major_effects.explanation: It would limit legislative authority to authorize regulation of covered mineral practices, while preserving regulation to protect public health and safety from imminent danger only when clear and convincing evidence shows it is necessary, regulation to preserve or conserve natural resources, and the stated public-use property authority.

major_effects.label: Voter approval condition
major_effects.explanation: The proposed constitutional amendment is to be submitted to voters; the proposed changes depend on approval.

agencies.name: state agency
agencies.explanation: The proposed amendment would affect state agencies that regulate covered mineral practices. It preserves such regulation to protect public health and safety from imminent danger only when clear and convincing evidence shows it is necessary, as well as regulation to preserve or conserve the state’s natural resources.

HJR49.summary: The proposed amendment would provide ordinary pay to officers suspended during impeachment and allow the Governor to make a provisional appointment for a suspended officer other than the Governor. These changes take effect January 1, 2028, and apply only when impeachment articles are preferred on or after that date.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes constitutional procedures and legislative authority concerning impeachment, suspension, removal, and disqualification of state officers.
Requires officers suspended during impeachment to continue receiving ordinary pay.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The proposal concerns officers of the State and constitutional procedures applicable statewide.

affected_groups.group: State officers subject to impeachment
affected_groups.explanation: The proposal addresses their suspension and pay during impeachment and the appointment of a provisional replacement for suspended officers other than the Governor.

affected_groups.group: The Governor
affected_groups.explanation: The Governor may make specified provisional appointments, while a separate provision addresses a vacancy caused by the Governor's suspension or removal.

affected_groups.group: Texas Legislature
affected_groups.explanation: The Legislature would be authorized to enact general laws implementing constitutional impeachment and related provisions.

affected_groups.group: Texas voters
affected_groups.explanation: Voters would decide whether to approve the proposed constitutional amendment.

major_effects.label: Ordinary pay during impeachment suspension
major_effects.explanation: Would provide ordinary pay to officers while they are suspended during pending impeachment; this change applies to articles preferred on or after January 1, 2028.

major_effects.label: Provisional appointments and gubernatorial vacancy procedure
major_effects.explanation: Would permit provisional appointments for suspended officers other than the Governor and apply the constitutional gubernatorial-vacancy provision to the Governor's impeachment suspension or removal.

major_effects.label: Legislative authority to implement constitutional provisions
major_effects.explanation: Would authorize the Legislature to enact general laws consistent with the Constitution to implement specified impeachment, trial, removal, and disqualification provisions.

HJR50.summary: If voters approve the proposed amendment, the Texas Constitution would authorize the legislature to provide a residence-homestead property-tax exemption for a partially disabled veteran equal to the veteran’s disability percentage; the legislature could add eligibility requirements, and the amendment itself would not automatically grant an exemption. It would also allow the legislature to provide the veteran’s surviving spouse the same portion of the exemption, subject to existing conditions including not remarrying and continuing to use the property as a homestead.

policy_tags.explanation: The proposed constitutional amendment would authorize the legislature to provide a partial residence-homestead property-tax exemption for partially disabled veterans and their qualifying surviving spouses, if voters approve it.

locations.name: Texas
locations.explanation: The proposed change is to the Texas Constitution and would authorize a statewide homestead-tax exemption if voters approve it and the legislature provides for it.

affected_groups.group: Partially disabled veterans with disability ratings of at least 10 percent but less than 100 percent
affected_groups.explanation: If voters approve the amendment and the legislature provides for the exemption, this group could qualify for a homestead exemption based on the veteran’s disability percentage.

affected_groups.group: Surviving spouses of veterans who qualified for an exemption under the proposed provision
affected_groups.explanation: The legislature could provide the surviving spouse the same portion of the homestead exemption if the spouse has not remarried and the property remains the spouse’s residence homestead.

major_effects.label: Authorize a potential partial homestead property-tax exemption
major_effects.explanation: If voters approve the amendment, the legislature may provide an exemption for a partially disabled veteran equal to the disability percentage and may set additional eligibility requirements; it would also be authorized to provide the same portion to a qualifying surviving spouse. The amendment does not itself grant the exemption.

HJR51.summary: HJR 51 proposes a Texas constitutional amendment that would allow the Legislature, by general law, to authorize county commissioners courts to exempt from ad valorem taxation the part of a property's assessed value attributable to an installed rainwater harvesting or graywater system. The amendment would take effect only if voters approve it, and an exemption would still require subsequent general-law authorization and could have additional eligibility requirements.

policy_tags.explanation: The proposed amendment would enable a property-tax exemption for the portion of assessed value attributable to specified water systems, subject to voter approval and enabling legislation.
It would permit the Legislature to authorize county commissioners courts to grant the specified exemption from taxes imposed by taxing political subdivisions.
The proposed tax incentive specifically targets installation of rainwater harvesting and graywater systems.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The proposed amendment to the Texas Constitution would provide authority applicable to county commissioners courts across the state.

affected_groups.group: Property owners with rainwater harvesting or graywater systems
affected_groups.explanation: Their property's assessed value attributable to installation of such a system could qualify for an exemption if voters approve the amendment and enabling law authorizes it.

affected_groups.group: County commissioners courts
affected_groups.explanation: The amendment would allow the Legislature to authorize them to grant the specified exemption.

affected_groups.group: Political subdivisions that tax property
affected_groups.explanation: The authorized exemption could apply to ad valorem taxes imposed by each political subdivision that taxes the property.

major_effects.label: Potential county authority to grant a limited property-tax exemption
major_effects.explanation: If voters approve the amendment, the Legislature could authorize county commissioners courts by general law to exempt the assessed-value portion attributable to a rainwater harvesting or graywater system. The amendment itself does not grant an exemption.

HJR53.summary: HJR 53 proposes a constitutional amendment, to be submitted to voters, limiting when the Legislature may enact or modify districts for the U.S. House: during the census-release year or, for a census released after September 1, within 120 days of release. If voters approve it, the timing limit would not prevent the Legislature from acting in response to a finding that districts are invalid or an action that prevents elections in them.

policy_tags.explanation: The proposal changes when Texas may enact or modify districts used to elect members of the U.S. House.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The proposed constitutional rule applies to the Texas Legislature and congressional districts in the state.

affected_groups.group: Texas voters in U.S. House elections
affected_groups.explanation: The proposal governs when the districts used for their elections may be enacted or modified.

major_effects.label: Limits timing of congressional redistricting
major_effects.explanation: If approved by voters, the amendment would confine enactment or modification of U.S. House districts to specified periods tied to the decennial census, while allowing action in response to specified invalidity or election-prohibition findings.

HJR54.summary: HJR 54 proposes a constitutional amendment for a November 2, 2027, voter decision that would reserve initiative powers to propose statutory or constitutional measures and referendum powers to repeal entire legislative bills, subject to petition, signature, election, and approval requirements. If voters approve the amendment, voter-approved statutory initiatives could be amended or repealed within five years only by a two-thirds vote of each house, and a successful referendum repeal would take effect upon official declaration of the election result.

policy_tags.explanation: Creates petition, signature verification, ballot, and voter-approval processes for initiatives and referendums.
Changes the constitutional allocation of legislative power and assigns related duties to state bodies.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The proposed initiative and referendum processes submit measures to voters statewide.

locations.name: Texas Senate districts
locations.explanation: Signature thresholds for initiatives and referendums are measured statewide and in each Texas Senate district.

affected_groups.group: Registered voters
affected_groups.explanation: Registered voters could sign initiative and referendum petitions and vote on qualifying measures.

affected_groups.group: Initiative and referendum petitioners
affected_groups.explanation: Petitioners would propose measures or seek repeal of bills and would be subject to filing and signature requirements.

affected_groups.group: Texas Legislature
affected_groups.explanation: The Legislature's authority would be subject to reserved initiative and referendum powers; initiative statutes could be amended or repealed within five years only by a two-thirds vote of each house.

major_effects.label: Reserve initiative and referendum powers
major_effects.explanation: The proposed amendment would reserve to the people the power to propose measures and repeal statutes, subject to the procedures in the new constitutional sections.

major_effects.label: Create initiative election process
major_effects.explanation: Initiatives would require qualifying petitions and voter approval; statutory measures require a majority, while constitutional measures require 60 percent approval.

major_effects.label: Create referendum election process
major_effects.explanation: A referendum could target an enacted bill in its entirety, and an approved repeal would take effect upon official declaration of the election result.

agencies.name: Texas Secretary of State
agencies.explanation: The secretary of state would issue and review petitions, certify them, and submit qualifying measures to voters.

agencies.name: Texas Legislative Council
agencies.explanation: The Council would advise on and review initiative measures and route measures with state-fund implications for fiscal analysis.

agencies.name: Legislative Budget Board
agencies.explanation: The Board would prepare and sign a fiscal note when the Council determines a proposed measure authorizes or requires expenditure or diversion of state funds.

HJR55.summary: If voters approve the proposed amendment, the Legislature generally could enact or modify Texas legislative districts only at the time it is required to apportion them. It could act in response to a court or governmental agency finding that districts are invalid or action that prevents elections in them, except while the Legislative Redistricting Board has exclusive jurisdiction; voters would decide the amendment on November 2, 2027.

policy_tags.explanation: The proposal changes when the Legislature may enact or modify districts used to elect its members.

locations.name: Statewide, Texas
locations.explanation: The proposed constitutional amendment concerns districts for the Texas Legislature.

affected_groups.group: Texas legislators
affected_groups.explanation: The proposal would generally limit when the Legislature may enact or modify districts for its members, but would allow a response to qualifying court or agency findings or actions, except while the Legislative Redistricting Board has exclusive jurisdiction.

affected_groups.group: Texas voters
affected_groups.explanation: Voters would decide whether to adopt the proposed amendment, and the proposal concerns districts used to elect legislative members.

major_effects.label: Limits timing of legislative redistricting
major_effects.explanation: If approved, the amendment would generally restrict legislative redistricting to the required apportionment period, with a response exception for certain court or agency findings or actions affecting districts or elections; that exception would not apply while the Legislative Redistricting Board has exclusive jurisdiction.

HJR60.summary: HJR 60 proposes a constitutional amendment that would direct to a tax-reduction and education fund an amount of general revenue matching the increase in general revenue when the comptroller limits transfers to the Economic Stabilization Fund to stay within its biennial cap. Money in that fund could be appropriated only to reduce school district maintenance-and-operations ad valorem taxes under general law; the amendment would take effect only if voters approve it, and its amendments would take effect January 1, 2028.

policy_tags.explanation: The dedicated funds are restricted to reducing school district maintenance-and-operations taxes.
The amendment dedicates revenue to the purpose of reducing school district ad valorem taxes, though it does not itself prescribe the tax-reduction mechanism.
The amendment redirects general revenue to a dedicated fund and restricts the purpose for which that money may be appropriated.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The proposed amendment changes the Texas Constitution and contains no geographic limitation on the school district tax relief purpose.

affected_groups.group: Property taxpayers subject to school district maintenance-and-operations ad valorem taxes
affected_groups.explanation: The dedicated funds may be appropriated only to reduce these taxes; the bill does not specify the amount or mechanism of any reduction.

major_effects.label: Dedicated revenue for school tax relief
major_effects.explanation: When specified revenue is kept from the Economic Stabilization Fund to comply with its biennial limit, an equal amount of general revenue must be transferred to the designated fund or successor account. Appropriations from that fund are limited to reducing school district maintenance-and-operations ad valorem taxes under general law.

agencies.name: Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts
agencies.explanation: The bill names the comptroller of public accounts and assigns the office the transfer duty when specified actions are taken to keep the Economic Stabilization Fund within its limit.

HJR61.summary: HJR 61 proposes a constitutional amendment concerning ad valorem homestead exemptions. Under subsection (b), the optional local exemption appears to cover a homestead owner who is disabled and is also the parent or guardian of a disabled person residing with them. Separately, subsection (c) authorizes the Legislature by general law to provide a school-purpose homestead exemption of up to $60,000 for a parent or guardian living with a disabled person, without stating that the parent or guardian must personally be disabled.

policy_tags.explanation: The proposal changes eligibility for optional local and school-purpose homestead property-tax exemptions.
Counties, cities, school districts, and other political subdivisions may choose whether to provide the subsection (b) exemption.
The amendment adds a parent or guardian to the class for which the Legislature may authorize an additional exemption from taxes for public school purposes.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The proposed constitutional changes apply to political subdivisions throughout Texas.

affected_groups.group: Disabled homestead owners who are also parents or guardians of a disabled person residing with them; separately, parents or guardians living with a disabled person may be eligible for a school-purpose
affected_groups.explanation: Subsection (b) places the parent-or-guardian phrase after the description of persons who are disabled, so the owner appears to have to meet the disability test for the optional local exemption. Subsection (c) separately identifies a parent or guardian living with a disabled person for a possible school-purpose exemption.

affected_groups.group: Counties, cities, school districts, and other local taxing subdivisions
affected_groups.explanation: These entities may choose whether to adopt the local homestead exemption; school districts are also affected by the potential school-purpose exemption.

affected_groups.group: People eligible for multiple disability, parent-or-guardian, or age-based exemptions
