The conversion takes effect only after the relevant bonds are paid or sufficient funds are set aside to pay them; the converted tax rate replaces or matches the corresponding reduction in the venue tax, without changing the combined local sales-tax rate. Certain qualifying elections held before September 1, 2027, can satisfy the voter-approval requirement without another election.

policy_tags.explanation: Authorizes conversion of all or part of an existing municipal sales and use tax to a different municipal sales and use tax.
Changes the tax authority and election-related duties of eligible municipalities.
Requires majority voter approval for a conversion, while recognizing certain qualifying earlier elections.
Redirects tax authority from venue purposes to economic-development purposes.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The provisions are available to qualifying municipalities in Texas; the bill names no particular municipality or geographic area.

affected_groups.group: Municipalities with a Chapter 334 venue tax and qualifying outstanding bond debt
affected_groups.explanation: These municipalities may seek voter approval to convert all or part of the tax, subject to the bond-payment timing condition.

affected_groups.group: Voters in eligible municipalities
affected_groups.explanation: Their majority approval at an election authorizes the conversion, subject to the provision recognizing certain earlier elections.

major_effects.label: Voter-approved conversion authority
major_effects.explanation: Qualifying municipalities may convert all or part of a Chapter 334 venue tax to a tax under Chapter 504 or 505 after majority voter approval; the conversion takes effect only after the specified bonds are paid or fully provided for.

major_effects.label: Corresponding tax-rate conversion
major_effects.explanation: The new tax rate matches the venue-tax rate if that tax is abolished, or equals the amount of any rate reduction; the combined rate of political-subdivision sales taxes may not change.

major_effects.label: Advance notice to the Comptroller
major_effects.explanation: A municipality must notify the Comptroller of the conversion at least 60 days before it takes effect.

agencies.name: Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts
agencies.explanation: The municipality must notify the Comptroller in advance of a conversion.

SB79.summary: If voters approve the proposed constitutional amendment, SB 79 would establish a nine-member Texas Redistricting Commission with sole responsibility for drawing districts for the U.S. House of Representatives and the Texas Legislature. It sets membership rules, plan standards and public reporting requirements, and provides for Texas Supreme Court action in specified circumstances, including if the commission does not adopt a plan on time.

policy_tags.explanation: Creates a commission to draw congressional and Texas legislative election districts.
Creates and establishes the membership, procedures, and duties of a state commission.
Requires legislative appropriations for commission compensation, expenses, and staff.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The commission draws districts for Texas's congressional delegation and both chambers of the Texas Legislature.

affected_groups.group: Texas voters and residents represented by congressional and state legislative districts
affected_groups.explanation: The commission's plans establish the districts in which these residents are represented.

affected_groups.group: Texas voters applying for commission membership
affected_groups.explanation: Except as otherwise provided by the subchapter, a Texas voter older than 25 is eligible for membership; appointment-specific political-primary requirements also apply.

affected_groups.group: People aggrieved by a redistricting plan
affected_groups.explanation: They may petition the Texas Supreme Court to challenge an adopted plan.

major_effects.label: Establishes the redistricting commission
major_effects.explanation: Creates a nine-member commission and assigns it responsibility for drawing specified congressional and state legislative districts.

major_effects.label: Sets membership and appointment rules
major_effects.explanation: Sets applicant qualifications and restrictions and provides for legislative-party appointments and selection of an independent presiding member.

major_effects.label: Provides court fallback and plan review
major_effects.explanation: The Texas Supreme Court adopts a plan if the commission misses the specified deadline and may hear challenges to adopted plans.

major_effects.label: Funds commission operations and support
major_effects.explanation: Requires sufficient appropriations for commission compensation and expenses, and assigns technical and clerical support to the Texas Legislative Council.

major_effects.label: Requires plan reports and public access
major_effects.explanation: Each adopted plan must include a report with specified population, criteria, map, expenditure, and other information, and the Secretary of State must make a copy available to the public.

major_effects.label: Sets district-plan standards
major_effects.explanation: To the extent practicable to comply with federal law, plans must use contiguous, nearly equal-population districts that are compact and convenient and separated by specified boundaries.

agencies.name: Texas Redistricting Commission
agencies.explanation: The bill establishes the commission and assigns it responsibility for creating the specified districts.

agencies.name: Texas Legislative Council
agencies.explanation: The bill assigns it responsibility for providing technical staff and clerical services to the commission.

agencies.name: Texas Secretary of State
agencies.explanation: The Secretary of State receives applications, plans, and reports; makes reports public; and becomes custodian of the commission's records after it suspends operations.

agencies.name: Texas Judicial Branch
agencies.explanation: The Texas Supreme Court must adopt a plan if the commission misses the specified deadline and may hear challenges to adopted plans.

SB80.summary: The bill would make it an offense for a person younger than 21 to knowingly purchase or possess a defined assault weapon. It would also prohibit offering or transferring assault weapons to people under 21 and classify that transfer offense as a state jail felony.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill restricts purchase, possession, and transfer of defined assault weapons by people under 21.
The bill creates a new offense and assigns misdemeanor and felony classifications to specified conduct.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The bill amends the Penal Code and establishes statewide criminal rules.

affected_groups.group: People younger than 21
affected_groups.explanation: They may not knowingly purchase or possess an assault weapon under the new offense, subject to stated defenses.

affected_groups.group: People who transfer or offer to transfer weapons to minors
affected_groups.explanation: The bill revises restrictions for transfers to people under 18 and separately restricts assault-weapon transfers to people under 21.

affected_groups.group: People who lawfully possessed an assault weapon on August 31, 2027
affected_groups.explanation: The bill provides a defense to the possession offense for such possession.

affected_groups.group: Peace officers and members of the armed forces or state military forces
affected_groups.explanation: The bill provides specified defenses relating to official duties and qualifying transfers.

major_effects.label: Under-21 purchase and possession offense
major_effects.explanation: Creates an offense for a person younger than 21 who knowingly purchases or possesses an assault weapon.

major_effects.label: Defenses to the new offense
major_effects.explanation: Provides official-duty defenses for specified purchases and possession, and a separate defense for possession lawfully held on August 31, 2027.

major_effects.label: Age-based transfer restrictions
major_effects.explanation: Revises the under-18 transfer rule to cover firearms other than assault weapons, restricts assault-weapon transfers to people under 21, and provides a defense when the recipient supplies evidence of qualifying status.

major_effects.label: Misdemeanor and felony classifications
major_effects.explanation: The purchase-or-possession offense is a Class A misdemeanor; the assault-weapon transfer offense under Subsection (a)(2)(B) is a state jail felony.

SB81.summary: SB 81 changes the immunization registry from consent-based inclusion to default inclusion with a right to request exclusion. An exclusion request need be made only once, and the information stays out unless the individual or legally authorized representative later submits a written request for inclusion; the bill also sets rules for registry notices, data use, and research access. For an adult whose information was not in the registry on or before January 1, 2029, inclusion is not authorized unless a provider elects to submit post-date immunization information and gives the individual the required advance notice.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes the operation of the state immunization registry and the handling of immunization records.
Changes confidentiality, research-use and release conditions for individually identifying registry information and prohibits its sale.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The bill concerns the state-administered immunization registry, rather than a particular locality.

affected_groups.group: Individuals whose immunization information is in or submitted to the registry, and their legally authorized representatives
affected_groups.explanation: Their information is included by default subject to exclusion requests, and they receive notice and have specified choices about continued inclusion and research release.

affected_groups.group: Health care providers who administer immunizations
affected_groups.explanation: Providers submitting immunization data must notify the individual or representative about inclusion and how to request exclusion; providers may use the department's printable form.

affected_groups.group: Public health researchers
affected_groups.explanation: Researchers may receive registry information through the applicable external-research pathways. For individually identifiable information, the institutional review board may approve release only if the proposal requires researchers to obtain informed consent from each individual or their legally authorized representative before the department releases that individual's data.

major_effects.label: Default registry inclusion with an exclusion option
major_effects.explanation: The bill replaces consent-based inclusion with inclusion unless exclusion is requested. One exclusion request is sufficient, and information may be included again only after a subsequent written request for inclusion.

major_effects.label: Research access and registry data protections
major_effects.explanation: Allows internal and external public health research subject to review, authorization or de-identification conditions; identifiable external research release through board approval requires informed consent. Registry information may not be sold.

major_effects.label: Protection against disaster-related service exclusion
major_effects.explanation: Registry information may not be used to exclude an individual from a service during a natural or man-made disaster, except when the service is withheld because of a medical contraindication.

major_effects.label: Provider and public notice procedures
major_effects.explanation: Requires providers submitting data to notify individuals or their legally authorized representatives that immunization information will be included in the registry unless exclusion is requested under adopted guidelines, and to explain how to request exclusion. Also requires the department to post a printable notice form and conduct a public awareness campaign.

major_effects.label: Transition limit for adults not already in the registry
major_effects.explanation: For adults 18 or older whose information was not included on or before January 1, 2029, the bill does not authorize inclusion unless a provider elects to submit later immunization data and gives the individual the specified notice before submission.

major_effects.label: Privacy-compliance rules
major_effects.explanation: Requires the executive commissioner to adopt rules ensuring registry use and release comply with state and federal health-information privacy, protection, confidentiality, and transmission laws.

agencies.name: Department of State Health Services
agencies.explanation: The department administers the immunization registry and is assigned registry, notice, research-use, and public-awareness duties; the bill explicitly identifies the Department of State Health Services in the transition provision.

agencies.name: Health and Human Services Commission
agencies.explanation: The executive commissioner of the Commission is expressly required to adopt rules for privacy-compliant use and release of registry information.

SB82.summary: The bill would require the department to establish a veteran discount program for electronic toll collection customers using State Highway 130. It would direct toll revenue from the specified 2007 development agreement to fund free or discounted use, prioritizing Segments 5 and 6 between U.S. Highway 183 and Interstate Highway 10 before allowing remaining revenue to support other portions of State Highway 130.

policy_tags.explanation: Creates a discount program for customers using State Highway 130 toll facilities.
Directs toll revenue to fund free or discounted toll use through the program.

locations.name: State Highway 130
locations.explanation: The program applies to electronic toll collection customers using State Highway 130.

locations.name: State Highway 130 from U.S. Highway 183 to Interstate Highway 10 (Segments 5 and 6)
locations.explanation: The bill prioritizes funding discounts on this portion of the route.

affected_groups.group: Veterans
affected_groups.explanation: The bill creates a veteran discount program for State Highway 130 use.

affected_groups.group: Electronic toll collection customers using State Highway 130
affected_groups.explanation: These customers are the stated users covered by the program.

major_effects.label: Veteran toll discount program
major_effects.explanation: Requires the department to establish and implement the program for electronic toll collection customers using State Highway 130.

major_effects.label: Toll revenue for discounts
major_effects.explanation: Requires specified toll revenue to fund free or discounted use, prioritizing Segments 5 and 6; remaining revenue may fund discounts on other portions of State Highway 130.

agencies.name: Texas Department of Transportation
agencies.explanation: The bill directly assigns the department duties to establish the program and use toll revenue. The supplied text does not identify the department by its canonical name.

SB83.summary: The bill would enact the Cosmetology Licensure Compact and name the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation as Texas’s compact administrator, allowing qualifying cosmetologists to seek licenses recognized in other member states. The compact would take effect only after its statute is enacted in a seventh member state; Texas would not be a member if the Commission finds its enactment materially different from the model. The compact also establishes shared licensing and investigative information, interstate regulatory powers, Commission rulemaking, and potential assessments and fees.

policy_tags.explanation: Creates an interstate framework for cosmetology professional licensing, practice, and regulation.
The multistate license is designed to facilitate cosmetologists’ practice across member states and workforce mobility.
Requires member states to submit licensing and investigative information to a coordinated data system and limits some information’s availability.
If Texas participates, the compact permits annual assessments on member states and fees on licensees to support the Commission.
Creates an interstate compact commission, assigns Texas an administrator, and changes the means by which Texas may withdraw from the compact.

locations.name: Texas
locations.explanation: The bill establishes statewide administration of the compact in Texas.

affected_groups.group: Cosmetologists seeking to practice in multiple member states
affected_groups.explanation: Qualifying licensees may apply for a multistate license recognized by member states, subject to compact requirements.

affected_groups.group: Cosmetology licensing and regulatory authorities in member states
affected_groups.explanation: They would receive complaints, share investigative and adverse-action information, and enforce compact-related licensing rules.

affected_groups.group: Active military members and their spouses who hold cosmetology licenses
affected_groups.explanation: They may retain their designated Home State during an active-duty assignment.

affected_groups.group: Consumers of cosmetology services in member states
affected_groups.explanation: The compact is intended to facilitate access to cosmetology services while supporting public protection.

major_effects.label: Interstate cosmetology licensure compact
major_effects.explanation: Enacts the compact, which becomes operative only when its statute is enacted in a seventh member state; Texas membership also depends on its enactment not being found materially different from the model.

major_effects.label: Multistate cosmetology license
major_effects.explanation: A licensee may qualify for a multistate license if the licensee holds an active, unencumbered home-state single-state license and meets compact requirements; the license is recognized by member states subject to the compact.

major_effects.label: Shared licensing and investigative data
major_effects.explanation: Member states must submit a uniform data set to the compact system, including licensing, adverse-action, and investigative information; some investigative information is restricted to member states.

major_effects.label: Interstate licensing and disciplinary authority
major_effects.explanation: The compact allocates discipline to the state where services are provided and gives remote states specified authority over a licensee’s authorization to practice, while reserving action against the multistate license to the home state.

major_effects.label: Compact Commission rulemaking
major_effects.explanation: Commission rules have force of law in member states, except where a court finds a conflict with a member state’s cosmetology scope-of-practice laws; the Texas commission named in the bill may also adopt rules to implement the chapter.

major_effects.label: Compact assessments and fees
major_effects.explanation: The compact permits annual assessments on member states and fees on licensees to fund Commission operations; these charges apply subject to Texas becoming a member.

major_effects.label: Texas withdrawal authority
major_effects.explanation: Texas may withdraw on a governor’s proclamation or other executive action rescinding consent, subject to compact notice and temporary license-recognition requirements.

agencies.name: Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation
agencies.explanation: Named as Texas’s administrator of the compact.

agencies.name: Texas Commission of Licensing and Regulation
agencies.explanation: The bill authorizes this named body to adopt rules to implement the chapter; the supplied sources do not establish its registry mapping or relationship to TDLR.

agencies.name: Cosmetology Licensure Compact Commission
agencies.explanation: The Commission is not a single Texas state body; the Compact creates it as a joint government agency of the Member States. It administers Compact functions, including the coordinated data system.

agencies.name: Texas State Licensing Authority (identity not specified in the bill)
agencies.explanation: The compact assigns duties to each member state’s State Licensing Authority, but the bill does not identify which Texas body holds that role. TDLR is named as compact administrator, which does not itself establish that it is the licensing authority for all compact duties.

SB84.summary: The bill allows an initial recount of paperless electronic voting system results without stating a specific ground, subject to the candidate eligibility limits in subsection (b). A candidate shown by the election returns not to be nominated or elected may seek a recount; a candidate shown to have won may do so only if an opposing candidate has an approved recount under Section 212.131(c) that omits some voting-system precincts. The Secretary of State must prescribe procedures.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes eligibility for initial recounts of paperless electronic voting system results and requires procedures to accommodate them.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The bill amends generally applicable Election Code provisions governing recounts in elections.

affected_groups.group: Candidates in elections using paperless electronic voting systems
affected_groups.explanation: The bill changes when candidates may obtain an initial recount of those election results.

major_effects.label: Initial recount access
major_effects.explanation: Removes the specific-ground requirement for initial recounts of paperless electronic results, subject to the candidate eligibility limits and exception stated in the bill.

major_effects.label: Recount procedures
major_effects.explanation: Directs the Secretary of State to prescribe procedures needed to accommodate recounts without a specific ground.

agencies.name: Texas Secretary of State
agencies.explanation: The bill directly assigns the Secretary of State responsibility for prescribing procedures to accommodate the recount authorization.

SB85.summary: The bill expands the uses of the economically distressed areas account to include costs of platting or replatting an area to prepare it for connection to public water or sewer. This applies only if the area was developed before the board adopted its model rules; the account's existing assistance for water and sewer services remains.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill expands account funding for work preparing areas for connection to public water or sewer systems.
The bill broadens the purposes for which money in a state account may be used.
The account provides assistance to political subdivisions, and the bill adds a qualifying use for that assistance.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The bill changes a Texas Water Development Board account used to assist political subdivisions, rather than limiting the change to a named place.

affected_groups.group: Political subdivisions seeking assistance from the economically distressed areas account
affected_groups.explanation: They may receive financial assistance for the newly authorized qualifying platting or replatting costs.

affected_groups.group: Areas developed before the board adopted its model rules that are being prepared for water or sewer connection
affected_groups.explanation: Only qualifying areas of this kind may have platting or replatting costs supported under the new use.

major_effects.label: Adds a qualifying account funding use
major_effects.explanation: The board may use account money for platting or replatting costs when the work prepares an area for public water or sewer connection and the area was developed before adoption of the board's model rules.

agencies.name: Texas Water Development Board
agencies.explanation: The bill amends the permitted uses of the account administered by the board; the bill's title identifies the board as the Texas Water Development Board.

SB86.summary: SB 86 would revise the membership categories for the lottery advisory committee, including specifying individual representatives and adding people with law-enforcement, legal, or financial expertise. It would also repeal Occupations Code § 51.217(b), whose contents are not included in the supplied bill text.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill changes membership categories for a state lottery advisory committee.

affected_groups.group: Members and prospective members of the lottery advisory committee
affected_groups.explanation: The bill revises the categories of people to be represented, including members of the public and people with specified expertise.

affected_groups.group: Licensed lottery sales agents
affected_groups.explanation: Licensed sales agents remain an identified interest category in the committee's composition.

affected_groups.group: People with divergent views on lottery operations or ties to lottery contributions
affected_groups.explanation: The bill specifies that individuals, rather than interest groups or entities, represent these perspectives.

major_effects.label: Revises lottery advisory committee composition
major_effects.explanation: The commission's appointments would reflect revised individual membership categories, including newly specified law-enforcement, legal, or financial expertise.

major_effects.label: Repeals subsection (b)
major_effects.explanation: The bill repeals Occupations Code § 51.217(b), but the supplied text does not state what that subsection provides.

agencies.name: the commission
agencies.explanation: The commission is responsible for establishing the committee and appointing its members under the revised composition criteria; the bill text does not identify the commission by its full name.

SB87.summary: SB 87 would make Section 481.125 inapplicable to specified conduct involving testing equipment that identifies a substance in Penalty Group 1-B. The change would apply only to offenses committed on or after the Act’s effective date; earlier offenses would remain governed by prior law.

policy_tags.explanation: Creates an exception to the application of a criminal statute for specified conduct involving qualifying testing equipment.

locations.name: Texas
locations.explanation: The bill amends Texas law and has statewide scope.

affected_groups.group: People who use, possess, deliver, or manufacture qualifying testing equipment
affected_groups.explanation: The exception applies to people engaging in the specified conduct involving equipment that identifies a Penalty Group 1-B substance.

major_effects.label: Exception from Section 481.125
major_effects.explanation: Section 481.125 would not apply to the specified use, possession, delivery, or manufacture of qualifying testing equipment.

SB88.summary: SB 88 would add congenital cytomegalovirus testing to the existing hearing-screening requirements for newborns and infants born at a birthing facility, generally before discharge and subject to listed exceptions, including parental declination, transfer, prior completion, and certain early-discharge referrals. It would require notice that parents may decline both procedures, expand department-maintained data to include CMV tests, and repeal Health and Safety Code Section 47.0032(b); the repealed text is not included in the supplied bill.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill adds congenital CMV testing to newborn and infant screening requirements and includes those tests in department-maintained data.

locations.name: Texas
locations.explanation: The bill amends a Texas Health and Safety Code requirement applying to birthing facilities.

affected_groups.group: Newborns and infants born at birthing facilities
affected_groups.explanation: They would be subject to the added CMV test requirement, subject to the bill's exceptions.

affected_groups.group: Parents of newborns and infants
affected_groups.explanation: Parents must be informed of the screening and test and may decline both.

affected_groups.group: Birthing facilities and certified screening programs
affected_groups.explanation: Facilities must arrange for the added CMV test, directly or through a certified program, subject to the listed exceptions.

major_effects.label: Adds congenital CMV testing
major_effects.explanation: Requires a CMV test alongside hearing screening for each newborn or infant born at a birthing facility, generally before discharge and subject to the listed exceptions.

major_effects.label: Parent notice and option to decline
major_effects.explanation: Requires facilities to inform parents about both procedures and that parents may decline both.

major_effects.label: Expands screening data maintained
major_effects.explanation: Adds infants who receive a congenital CMV test to the group for which the department maintains data and information.

agencies.name: the department
agencies.explanation: Subject to Section 47.008, the bill expressly requires the department to maintain data and information for newborns or infants receiving a congenital CMV test. The supplied text does not identify which state agency “the department” denotes.

SB89.summary: The bill would require each public school district campus to report every overdose occurring there to the district and the Health and Human Services Commission’s executive commissioner as soon as practicable. It would also require joint rules to keep reports free of personally identifying information and to protect student information under applicable federal and state privacy law.

policy_tags.explanation: Creates overdose reporting and related privacy-rule requirements for public school campuses.
Imposes a reporting duty on school districts, which are local governmental entities.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The reporting requirement applies to each school district campus in Texas.

affected_groups.group: Public school districts and campus operators
affected_groups.explanation: District campuses must report each overdose occurring on campus to the district and the designated state official.

affected_groups.group: Students whose overdose information is reported
affected_groups.explanation: Rules must ensure reports exclude personally identifying information and comply with student-information privacy law.

major_effects.label: Campus overdose reporting
major_effects.explanation: Requires each school district campus to report every overdose occurring there to the district and the Health and Human Services Commission’s executive commissioner as soon as practicable.

major_effects.label: Privacy safeguards for reports
major_effects.explanation: Requires the commissioner and the Health and Human Services Commission’s executive commissioner to jointly adopt necessary rules ensuring reports exclude personally identifying information and comply with applicable student-information privacy law.

agencies.name: Health and Human Services Commission
agencies.explanation: Its executive commissioner would receive reports and jointly adopt rules governing reporting and privacy.

agencies.name: the commissioner
agencies.explanation: The bill assigns this commissioner a joint rulemaking duty, but does not identify the office by name in the supplied text.

SB90.summary: The bill would limit when a day-care center, group day-care home, or registered family home may deny services to a child with a disability: only after meeting with the child and family and determining under the ADA that accommodating the child would satisfy a specified condition, including posing an undue burden. It would require standards promoting inclusion and access for certified childhood intervention providers, add parent-provided records for children with special needs to required records, and require written information for parents about early intervention and the provider’s disability-care policies.

policy_tags.explanation: Adds disability-related limits on denying child-care services and requires inclusive practices.
Requires integration into general activities and access to childhood intervention services in an educational or instructional area.
Imposes new standards, recordkeeping, and parent-disclosure requirements on covered child-care providers.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The requirements apply to covered child-care facilities and registered family homes under the statewide Human Resources Code chapter.

affected_groups.group: Children with disabilities or special needs who attend covered child-care providers
affected_groups.explanation: Children with disabilities who attend covered child-care providers would receive stronger protections against service denials: a provider may deny services only after meeting with the child and family and determining under the ADA that accommodating the child would satisfy a specified condition, including posing an undue burden. The bill also provides for inclusion and access to certified childhood intervention services.

affected_groups.group: Day-care centers, group day-care homes, and registered family homes
affected_groups.explanation: These providers would be subject to new standards, recordkeeping, and written-disclosure requirements.

affected_groups.group: Parents and guardians of children attending covered providers
affected_groups.explanation: They would receive written information about early intervention access and the provider’s disability-care policies.

affected_groups.group: Certified childhood intervention service providers
affected_groups.explanation: They would be allowed access to child clients at covered providers to deliver services under an individualized family service plan in an educational or instructional area.

major_effects.label: Limits disability-based service denials
major_effects.explanation: A covered provider may deny services to a child with a disability only after meeting with the child and family and determining that an ADA-listed condition applies, such as undue burden, a direct threat, fundamental alteration, or difficulty or expense removing architectural barriers.

major_effects.label: Requires inclusive-care standards and intervention-provider access
major_effects.explanation: The standards must promote inclusive practices and integration into general activities, and allow certified childhood intervention providers to deliver services under an individualized family service plan while the child is integrated in an educational or instructional area.

major_effects.label: Adds special-needs records
major_effects.explanation: Operators of licensed or certified facilities must maintain records provided by parents for children with special needs.

major_effects.label: Requires written parent disclosures
major_effects.explanation: Providers must give each child’s parent or guardian the Commission’s developmental checklist, available information on accessing early childhood intervention in the area served, and the provider’s disability-care policies.

agencies.name: Health and Human Services Commission
agencies.explanation: The executive commissioner of the Commission must adopt rules necessary to implement the bill’s changes.

SB91.summary: SB 91 would require cameras covered by Education Code §29.022, subject to subsection (c-1), to record audio across covered areas and generally extend retention from three to 12 months, with additional holds for certain requests and reported incidents. It would expand access to recordings, including repeat viewing or listening by involved employees and parents and release to their attorneys within one week, while requiring FERPA-compliant release and retaining limits on monitoring and use. It would change the trigger for notifying the Department of Family and Protective Services about possible abuse or neglect and permit certain school-safety allocations to cover audio surveillance when the district has already installed security cameras.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes requirements and record-access rules for surveillance in special education settings.
Expands audio recording while changing access, retention, confidentiality, and permitted-use safeguards.
Changes school-safety surveillance requirements and recognizes video and audio surveillance as a safety-related equipment use.
Imposes recording-retention and access duties on school districts, alongside open-enrollment charter schools.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The requirements apply to school districts and open-enrollment charter schools under statewide law.

affected_groups.group: Students receiving special education services
affected_groups.explanation: Their special education settings are subject to the camera and audio-recording requirements, and recordings remain protected.

affected_groups.group: Parents of students involved in alleged incidents
affected_groups.explanation: They may access recordings, and the bill bars limits on repeat viewing or listening for recordings documenting an incident.

affected_groups.group: Employees involved in alleged incidents
affected_groups.explanation: The bill provides access rights and requires retention of available recordings involving an employee in a reported incident, even if a recording does not document the incident.

affected_groups.group: School districts and open-enrollment charter schools
affected_groups.explanation: They must meet the recording, retention, and access requirements. The 12-month retention period is subject to exceptions; for a requested recording, retention continues through viewing and the determination, and if it documents an alleged incident, until the incident is resolved, including exhaustion of appeals. Certain safety-allocation uses are also specified for districts.

major_effects.label: Audio recording in special education settings
major_effects.explanation: Subject to subsection (c-1), cameras must cover all areas of the setting, including an attached time-out room, and record audio from those areas.

major_effects.label: Longer retention and incident holds
major_effects.explanation: The general retention period becomes at least 12 months. Recordings subject to a viewing or listening request, and available recordings involving an employee in a reported incident, must be retained through the applicable review or incident resolution, including appeals.

major_effects.label: Expanded access with privacy limits
major_effects.explanation: Involved employees and parents may not be limited in the number of times they view or listen to a recording documenting an incident; their attorneys must receive access within one week. Release must comply with FERPA, and a student's face may be obscured as necessary.

major_effects.label: Limits on monitoring and use
major_effects.explanation: The restrictions on regular or continual monitoring and non-safety uses extend to audio recordings as well as video.

major_effects.label: Abuse-or-neglect notification trigger
major_effects.explanation: A person described in subsection (i)(4) or (5) who believes a recording documents possible abuse or neglect as defined by the Family Code must notify the Department of Family and Protective Services for investigation.

major_effects.label: School-safety equipment eligibility
major_effects.explanation: The specified school-safety allocation may cover video and audio surveillance as other security equipment when the district has already installed security cameras.

agencies.name: State Board for Educator Certification
agencies.explanation: Its personnel or agents are authorized recipients of recordings, and the bill extends the viewing provision to listening.

agencies.name: the agency
agencies.explanation: The agency conducts expedited review of certain district determinations; the amended provision includes determinations not to release a recording.

agencies.name: appropriate agency
agencies.explanation: Its personnel or agents are among those authorized to view or listen to recordings as part of an investigation; the bill does not identify the entity.

SB92.summary: Beginning with the 2027–2028 school year, SB 92 would require school districts to give parents or legal guardians of students with an intellectual disability or developmental delay information about services and public benefits from the local intellectual and developmental disability authority serving the student’s county. The information would be provided at each admission, review, and dismissal committee meeting and would include services under federal waiver programs.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes the information school districts must provide to parents or guardians through student admission, review, and dismissal committee meetings.
Imposes an expanded information-provision duty on school districts, which are local public entities.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The duty is assigned to school districts generally, without limiting it to a particular locality.

locations.name: County in which the student resides
locations.explanation: The information concerns the local authority serving the county where the student resides.

affected_groups.group: Parents or legal guardians of students with an intellectual disability or developmental delay
affected_groups.explanation: Would receive information about services and public benefits at each relevant committee meeting.

affected_groups.group: Students with an intellectual disability or developmental delay
affected_groups.explanation: Their parents or guardians would receive information about local authority services and benefits.

affected_groups.group: School districts
affected_groups.explanation: Would provide the information at each admission, review, and dismissal committee meeting.

major_effects.label: Expanded parent information duty
major_effects.explanation: Requires information about local intellectual and developmental disability authority services and public benefits at each relevant committee meeting.

SB93.summary: The bill would require the Department of State Health Services School Health Advisory Committee to develop model policies encouraging age-appropriate outdoor recess and effective outdoor activity facilities. Each school district would have to adopt a recess policy specifying weekly minutes of unstructured playtime, review it at least every five years, and have covered campuses implement it.

policy_tags.explanation: Creates recess policy requirements for public school districts and campuses.
Assigns school districts duties to adopt and periodically review recess policies, and requires covered campuses to implement them.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The requirements apply to each school district and its covered campuses in Texas.

affected_groups.group: School district boards and campuses subject to the recess policy
affected_groups.explanation: District boards must adopt and review recess policies, and covered campuses must implement them.

affected_groups.group: Public school students
affected_groups.explanation: Students would be covered by district policies specifying weekly unstructured playtime during the school day.

major_effects.label: Model recess policies
major_effects.explanation: Requires the Department of State Health Services School Health Advisory Committee to develop model policies covering constructive, age-appropriate outdoor play and outdoor activity facilities.

major_effects.label: District recess policies and campus implementation
major_effects.explanation: Districts must adopt policies specifying weekly unstructured-play minutes, review them at least every five years, and ensure covered campuses implement them.

agencies.name: Department of State Health Services
agencies.explanation: The department's School Health Advisory Committee is assigned to develop model recess policies.

SB94.summary: SB 94 would add educator professional development, including classroom behavioral-management training, to the permissible uses of school safety allotment funds under the Foundation School Program. It does not specify an increase to the allotment amount.

policy_tags.explanation: Changes the permissible use of funds in a school funding program for educator professional development.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The change concerns the state Foundation School Program's school safety allotment.

affected_groups.group: School districts receiving school safety allotment funds
affected_groups.explanation: The bill expands the permissible uses of funds allocated under the school safety allotment.

affected_groups.group: Educators
affected_groups.explanation: Professional development for educators, including classroom behavioral-management training, would become a permissible use of the funds.

major_effects.label: Expanded permissible use of school safety allotment funds
major_effects.explanation: Would allow the funds to pay for educator professional development that includes classroom behavioral-management training.

SB95.summary: The bill would add lactation rooms to the places where a person is considered to have a reasonable expectation of privacy when disrobing, as described in the definition concerning photographing, visually recording, broadcasting, or transmitting images. It would define a lactation room as a room or portioned area provided for or primarily used for specified purposes, including addressing other needs related to breast-feeding.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill expands the locations covered by a definition relevant to prosecuting invasive visual recording.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The bill amends the Texas Penal Code, so the change applies statewide.

affected_groups.group: People using lactation rooms
affected_groups.explanation: Their use of a qualifying lactation room would fall within the places covered by the privacy definition.

affected_groups.group: People prosecuted for invasive visual recording in a lactation room
affected_groups.explanation: The expanded definition would make a qualifying lactation room relevant to prosecution under the offense.

major_effects.label: Expands places covered by the privacy definition
major_effects.explanation: Adds lactation rooms to the locations included in the definition of a place where a person has a reasonable expectation of privacy for the invasive visual recording offense.

SB96.summary: SB 96 would direct the Texas Higher Education Coordinating Board to establish a grant program under which it may award grants to eligible higher education institutions for regenerative agriculture research, education, and producer assistance, beginning with the 2028–2029 academic year. It also sets grant priorities and uses, requires progress and program reporting, and permits the board to accept gifts and grants; the bill does not specify a grant appropriation amount.

policy_tags.explanation: Creates a higher education grant program that supports research, student projects, and education and training for producers and rural communities.
Funds research and assistance intended to help agricultural producers adopt regenerative practices.
The program supports soil health and conservation practices, including research aligned with soil and water conservation programs.
Creates a grant program and permits grant awards from available program funds, without specifying an appropriation amount.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The program provides for statewide distribution of funds and a statewide online resource hub.

affected_groups.group: Eligible institutions of higher education
affected_groups.explanation: May apply for grants and would be subject to program criteria, reporting, and grant-use requirements.

affected_groups.group: Agricultural producers and rural communities
affected_groups.explanation: Are intended recipients of education, technical assistance, and research-supported methods; resources are prioritized for small and mid-sized farms.

affected_groups.group: Students
affected_groups.explanation: May benefit from student-led projects, internships, and research initiatives supported by grant funds.

affected_groups.group: Nonprofit organizations
affected_groups.explanation: May participate as research partners, and partnerships with nonprofits are a grant-award priority.

major_effects.label: Regenerative agriculture grant program
major_effects.explanation: Requires the coordinating board to establish and administer a program under which it may award grants to eligible institutions for research, education, and producer assistance; the subchapter applies beginning in the 2028–2029 academic year.

major_effects.label: Grant allocation and uses
major_effects.explanation: Limits the share any one institution may receive, sets priority and statewide distribution requirements, and restricts grant money to specified program purposes.

major_effects.label: Grant and program reporting
major_effects.explanation: Requires annual progress reports from recipients and an annual report to the legislature summarizing outcomes, challenges, and recommendations.

major_effects.label: Program rules and application materials
major_effects.explanation: Requires the coordinating board to adopt administrative rules and make application forms, report templates, and guidelines available by January 1, 2028.

major_effects.label: Consequences for misuse or noncompliance
major_effects.explanation: Allows grant funding to be suspended or terminated, future awards to be barred, and misused funds to be repaid when an institution misuses funds or fails to meet program requirements.

agencies.name: Texas Higher Education Coordinating Board
agencies.explanation: The board must establish and administer the grant program, make grant awards, adopt rules, and participate in program reporting.

agencies.name: Texas State Soil and Water Conservation Board
agencies.explanation: The board must collaborate with the coordinating board on program alignment and the annual report to the legislature.

SB97.summary: If enacted, SB97 would expand the civic knowledge required in public school curriculum, including more detailed coverage of government organization and the federal and Texas court systems. It would also add specified source material to the foundation curriculum; the changes would apply beginning with the 2027–2028 school year.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill revises required civic knowledge and source material for public school foundation and social studies curricula.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The curriculum requirements apply to the statewide public school curriculum.

affected_groups.group: Public school students
affected_groups.explanation: Students would be taught the expanded civic knowledge and social studies content required by the revised standards.

affected_groups.group: Public school curriculum planners and educators
affected_groups.explanation: Curriculum planning and instruction would need to reflect the revised essential knowledge and skills adopted by the State Board of Education.

major_effects.label: Expanded civic curriculum requirements
major_effects.explanation: Revises the required civic knowledge content, including greater emphasis on court systems and the judiciary in K–12 social studies. For the foundation curriculum, the Board is to adopt civic knowledge content as appropriate, with additions to the specified source material.

agencies.name: State Board of Education
agencies.explanation: The bill directly assigns the State Board of Education duties to adopt the revised essential knowledge and skills.

SB99.summary: SB 99 would repeal Chapter 753, including requirements for certain sheriffs to enter agreements with ICE to enforce federal immigration law and the related grant program. From the effective date, affected sheriffs could terminate existing agreements with written notice, and the comptroller could not award new grants; previously awarded grants would remain subject to existing requirements. Pending attorney general enforcement actions would be dismissed, and equitable relief granted to enforce the chapter would be void.

policy_tags.explanation: The bill repeals requirements for certain sheriffs to enter agreements with federal immigration authorities to enforce federal immigration law.
The bill removes agreement requirements affecting sheriffs and permits sheriffs with existing agreements to terminate them.
The bill ends new awards under the state grant program while keeping existing awards subject to the program's requirements.

locations.name: Texas
locations.explanation: The changes apply to sheriffs and state officials under Texas law without limiting the provisions to a particular locality.

affected_groups.group: Sheriffs and counties with agreements under Chapter 753
affected_groups.explanation: The agreement requirements are repealed, and sheriffs with existing agreements may terminate them under the bill's notice provision.

affected_groups.group: Recipients of grants awarded before the effective date
affected_groups.explanation: Existing grants remain subject to the requirements of the repealed subchapter and related administration rules or procedures.

major_effects.label: Repeals sheriff agreement requirements
major_effects.explanation: Repeals Chapter 753, including the requirements for certain sheriffs to enter agreements with ICE to enforce federal immigration law.

major_effects.label: Allows termination of existing agreements
major_effects.explanation: A sheriff with an agreement required by the repealed chapter may terminate it by written notice within a reasonable period before the stated termination date.

major_effects.label: Ends new grant awards
major_effects.explanation: No new grants may be awarded under the repealed program after the effective date, but awards made earlier remain subject to the program's requirements.

major_effects.label: Resolves pending enforcement actions
major_effects.explanation: Pending attorney general actions to enforce Chapter 753 would be dismissed on the effective date, and equitable relief granted to enforce the chapter would be void.

agencies.name: Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts
agencies.explanation: The bill prohibits the comptroller from awarding new grants under the repealed program and preserves administration requirements for grants awarded before the effective date.

agencies.name: Office of the Attorney General
agencies.explanation: The bill provides for dismissal of pending actions brought by the attorney general to enforce Chapter 753 and voids equitable relief granted for that purpose.

SCR1.summary: The resolution designates October 15 as Lobular Breast Cancer Awareness Day in Texas. The designation remains in effect until the 10th anniversary of the date the resolution is finally passed.

locations.name: Texas
locations.explanation: The designation is made by the Texas Legislature for an awareness day in the state.

affected_groups.group: People affected by lobular breast cancer
affected_groups.explanation: The awareness-day designation recognizes lobular breast cancer and the people who need care for it.

major_effects.label: Awareness-day designation
major_effects.explanation: Designates October 15 as Lobular Breast Cancer Awareness Day, with the designation lasting until the 10th anniversary of final passage.

SCR2.summary: SCR 2 urges Congress to propose and send to the states a constitutional amendment allowing Congress and the states to reasonably regulate and limit spending to influence campaigns, elections, or ballot measures, including by distinguishing natural persons from artificial entities. It also directs the Texas secretary of state to send official copies to specified federal officials and Texas's congressional delegation; the resolution itself does not impose campaign-spending limits.

policy_tags.explanation: The resolution asks Congress to propose a constitutional amendment concerning regulation of spending to influence campaigns, elections, and ballot measures.

affected_groups.group: People and entities engaging in political spending
affected_groups.explanation: The amendment Congress is urged to propose could permit regulation of their spending and distinctions between natural persons and artificial entities; the resolution itself creates no such limits.

major_effects.label: Request for constitutional amendment
major_effects.explanation: Urges Congress to propose and send to the states an amendment concerning regulation of spending to influence campaigns, elections, or ballot measures.

major_effects.label: Forwarding resolution copies
major_effects.explanation: Directs the Texas secretary of state to send official copies to specified federal officials and the Texas congressional delegation.

agencies.name: Texas Secretary of State
agencies.explanation: The resolution directs the secretary of state to forward official copies to specified federal officials and members of the Texas congressional delegation.

SJR10.summary: SJR 10 proposes a Texas constitutional amendment allowing retroactive laws for civil causes of action arising out of child sexual abuse. Voters would decide the amendment on November 2, 2027; if approved, it would permit—but would not itself enact—a retroactive law or revive a claim.

policy_tags.explanation: The proposal changes a constitutional limit on retroactive laws for a specified category of civil claims.

locations.name: Texas
locations.explanation: The proposed amendment concerns the Texas Constitution and would apply statewide if approved.

affected_groups.group: People who experienced child sexual abuse and seek civil remedies
affected_groups.explanation: They may be affected by future retroactive laws concerning civil causes of action arising from child sexual abuse.

affected_groups.group: People subject to civil claims arising out of child sexual abuse
affected_groups.explanation: They may face claims affected by a future retroactive law within the category permitted by the amendment.

affected_groups.group: Texas voters
affected_groups.explanation: Voters would decide whether to adopt the proposed constitutional amendment.

major_effects.label: Constitutional exception for specified retroactive civil laws
major_effects.explanation: If voters approve, the constitutional prohibition on retroactive laws would have an exception for civil causes of action arising out of child sexual abuse. The amendment itself does not enact a retroactive law.

major_effects.label: Voter approval required
major_effects.explanation: The proposed constitutional amendment is submitted to voters; it would change the Constitution only if approved.

SJR11.summary: The proposed amendment would go to Texas voters on November 2, 2027; only if approved would it authorize the Legislature to permit and strictly regulate casino gaming and sports wagering by general law. It would require a state commission, operator licenses and fees, on-site casino gaming at no more than 10 facilities, a gaming tax capped at 15 percent, and a good-faith Tribal-State compact process when a tribe requests one.

policy_tags.explanation: Would establish licensing and strict regulatory requirements for casino gaming and sports wagering operators.
Would require a tax on casino gaming and sports wagering revenue, capped at 15 percent, and limit additional taxes and fees on operators.
Would provide specified state revenue sources to fund the proposed commission.

Would restrict political subdivisions from imposing additional taxes or fees on specified gaming-related revenue or license-holder operations, subject to an exception for generally applicable business taxes or fees.
Would require establishment of a state commission with regulatory, licensing, investigative, enforcement, and audit responsibilities.

locations.name: Texas
locations.explanation: The proposed authorization and casino facility limit concern gaming conducted at locations in this state.

locations.name: Existing lands in Texas of the three federally recognized Indian tribes with Indian lands in the state
locations.explanation: The proposed compact process concerns Class III Indian gaming on a tribe's existing lands in Texas, if the tribe requests it.

affected_groups.group: Casino gaming and sports wagering operators and applicants
affected_groups.explanation: Would be subject to licensing, application fees, operating limits, and the gaming tax.

affected_groups.group: Political subdivisions of Texas
affected_groups.explanation: Would be restricted from imposing certain additional taxes or fees on gaming revenue and license-holder operations.

affected_groups.group: Federally recognized Indian tribes with Indian lands in Texas
affected_groups.explanation: Would be eligible to request a good-faith process to negotiate and execute a Tribal-State gaming compact for Class III gaming on existing lands.

major_effects.label: Conditional authority to authorize gaming
major_effects.explanation: If voters approve the amendment, the Legislature may authorize and strictly regulate casino gaming and sports wagering by general law.

major_effects.label: State gaming and lottery commission
major_effects.explanation: Would require a state agency funded from specified proceeds, taxes, and fees to regulate authorized lotteries and gift enterprises and enforce prohibitions on unauthorized ones.

major_effects.label: Operator licensing and application fees
major_effects.explanation: Would require licenses and application fees for casino gaming and sports wagering operators.

major_effects.label: Limits on casino locations and operation
major_effects.explanation: Would confine casino gaming to licensed operators' physical premises in Texas, cap the number of facilities at 10, and require license terms of at least 40 years.

major_effects.label: Gaming tax and limits on additional levies
major_effects.explanation: Would cap the gaming-revenue tax at 15 percent and bar additional state or local taxes or fees on specified gaming and license-holder revenues, except taxes or fees generally applicable to businesses in Texas.

major_effects.label: Tribal-State gaming compact process
major_effects.explanation: Would require a good-faith, timely process to negotiate and execute a compact for Class III gaming on a requesting tribe's existing lands in Texas.

agencies.name: commission
agencies.explanation: The proposed amendment would require the implementing law to establish this commission as a state agency and assign it regulatory and enforcement duties. The bill does not specify the commission's formal name or identify it as an existing agency.

SJR12.summary: If voters approve the proposed amendment, the Kickapoo Traditional Tribe of Texas could execute the specified gaming compact; the compact would take effect only under its federal approval or operation-of-law and Federal Register publication terms. The compact authorizes covered gaming on tribal Indian lands and allows additional forms at a tribal-owned or -leased site outside the reservation only if Texas authorizes additional gaming after January 1, 2027. It also establishes state and tribal oversight, licensing and patron safeguards, limits certain taxes and fees, and provides for a conditional payment to the state.

policy_tags.explanation: Creates a legal framework for tribal gaming operations and specifies licensing and operational requirements.
Limits state and local tax rates or fees on certain tribal gaming and bars state taxes and fees on the Tribe or its enterprises under the compact.
The amendment expressly limits local as well as state tax rates or fees on the specified tribal gaming operations.
Assigns state gaming oversight and rulemaking responsibilities, with the possibility that the Legislature authorizes another agency to administer the section.
Requires gaming-facility safeguards addressing underage gambling, intoxication, security, and patron safety.

locations.name: Texas
locations.explanation: The gaming framework applies within Texas, including to mobile wagers by players physically located in the state.

locations.name: Kickapoo Traditional Tribe of Texas Indian lands
locations.explanation: The compact authorizes covered games on the Tribe's Indian lands.

locations.name: Tribal-owned or -leased land in Texas outside the reservation
locations.explanation: An eligible site for additional gaming only if Texas authorizes additional gaming after January 1, 2027.

locations.name: Area within 200 miles of the Tribe's reservation boundary
locations.explanation: The absence of specified additional gaming authorization in this area is part of the condition for the Tribe's state revenue payment.

affected_groups.group: Kickapoo Traditional Tribe of Texas and its gaming operations
affected_groups.explanation: The Tribe receives gaming authority under the compact and assumes operational, regulatory, and conditional payment responsibilities.

affected_groups.group: Gaming patrons and gaming employees
affected_groups.explanation: Employees are subject to compact licensing and training requirements, while patrons receive specified safeguards and dispute procedures.

affected_groups.group: State and local governments
affected_groups.explanation: State bodies receive oversight or payment responsibilities, while state and local tax or fee authority is limited for specified gaming operations.

major_effects.label: Tribal gaming authorization
major_effects.explanation: Authorizes covered games on the Tribe's Indian lands under the compact; additional forms of gaming at a qualifying off-reservation site are allowed only if Texas authorizes additional gaming after January 1, 2027.

major_effects.label: State oversight and rules
major_effects.explanation: Names the Secretary of State as a regulator and authorizes state rules for the state's responsibilities unless the Legislature assigns administration to another agency; the compact also establishes monitoring duties.

major_effects.label: Conditional state revenue share
major_effects.explanation: The Tribe must pay the state 3 percent of annual net win from Class III covered games only while the state does not authorize or allow the specified additional forms of gaming within 200 miles after January 1, 2027.

major_effects.label: Limits on gaming taxes and fees
major_effects.explanation: For the additional gaming authorized under the stated condition, state and local tax or fee rates may not exceed comparable rates; the compact separately bars state taxes and fees on the Tribe or its enterprises.

major_effects.label: Licensing, operating safeguards, and patron procedures
major_effects.explanation: Requires compliance with specified federal and tribal licensing requirements, establishes gaming-facility safeguards, and provides patron dispute and tort-claim procedures subject to the compact's limits.

agencies.name: Texas Secretary of State
agencies.explanation: The Secretary of State is expressly named as a regulator and may adopt rules for the state's responsibilities, unless the Legislature authorizes another state agency to administer the section. The compact identifies the Secretary's office as the default state compliance agency.

agencies.name: Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts
agencies.explanation: The compact directs that any required revenue-share payments be made to the state comptroller.

SJR13.summary: This resolution would submit a proposed constitutional amendment to Texas voters on November 2, 2027; the amendment would take effect only if voters approve it. If approved, and only if Texas after January 1, 2027, authorizes video lottery terminals, slot machines, or other gaming not previously authorized, the Kickapoo Traditional Tribe of Texas could offer gaming, including mobile gaming, at a designated site on its Texas land outside its reservation, subject to a device-count limit tied to other gaming locations. The Tribe and the Secretary of State would regulate that gaming, state rules could be no more restrictive than rules for comparable state-licensed gaming, and state or local taxes and fees could not exceed those imposed on other gaming operators.

policy_tags.explanation: The amendment would authorize conditional tribal gaming and establish how that gaming is regulated.
It would cap taxes and fees on the Tribe's gaming operations relative to those imposed on other gaming locations or facilities.
The tax and fee cap applies to local as well as state taxes and fees.

locations.name: Texas land owned or leased by the Kickapoo Traditional Tribe of Texas outside the Tribe's reservation
locations.explanation: The designated gaming location must be on the Tribe's land in Texas and outside the reservation boundary.

affected_groups.group: Kickapoo Traditional Tribe of Texas
affected_groups.explanation: If the amendment is approved and the state gaming-authorization condition is met, the Tribe could conduct specified gaming at a designated location and would be subject to the stated regulatory and tax limits.

affected_groups.group: State and local taxing authorities
affected_groups.explanation: The amendment would limit the tax rates and fees that state and local authorities may impose on the Tribe's gaming operations.

major_effects.label: Conditional tribal gaming authorization and regulation
major_effects.explanation: If voters approve the amendment and Texas later authorizes previously unauthorized gaming after January 1, 2027, the Tribe could offer authorized gaming at a qualifying location. The Tribe and Secretary of State would regulate it, and state rules could not be more restrictive than rules for comparable state-licensed gaming.

major_effects.label: Cap on taxes and fees for tribal gaming
major_effects.explanation: State and local tax rates and fees on the Tribe's gaming operations could not exceed those imposed on operators of other gaming locations or facilities in Texas.

agencies.name: Texas Secretary of State
agencies.explanation: The amendment names the Secretary of State as a regulator of the Tribe's gaming, if the amendment is approved and its gaming-authorization condition is met.

SJR14.summary: If voters approve it, the proposed constitutional amendment would let the Legislature set by general law a residence-homestead appraisal limit using a 103% rather than 110% benchmark (or a greater percentage), while retaining the lesser-of-market-value rule. A limit would begin no earlier than the later of the law’s effective date or January 1 after the owner first qualifies for the homestead exemption, and would end when neither that owner nor a spouse or surviving spouse qualifies; the amendment is scheduled for a November 2, 2027, election.

policy_tags.explanation: The amendment would change the constitutional benchmark for a potential statutory limit on residence-homestead appraised values for ad valorem taxation; it does not itself impose a new tax rate or set a new limit by statute.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The proposed constitutional rule concerns residence homesteads for ad valorem tax purposes across Texas.

affected_groups.group: Owners of residence homesteads qualifying for the Section 1-b exemption, and their spouses or surviving spouses
affected_groups.explanation: The potential appraisal limit would take effect based on the owner’s qualification for the homestead exemption and would expire when neither the owner nor a spouse or surviving spouse qualifies.

major_effects.label: Authorization for a lower homestead appraisal limit
major_effects.explanation: If approved, the amendment would permit the Legislature to set a statutory limit using a 103% benchmark instead of 110%; the amendment does not itself enact that statutory limit.

SJR15.summary: SJR 15 proposes a constitutional amendment to expand the uses of certain revenue transferred to the state highway fund, allowing it to support public transportation, public bicycle paths, and public sidewalks as well as public roadways other than toll roads. The proposal would change the Constitution only if approved by voters at the November 2, 2027 election.

policy_tags.explanation: Adds public transportation, bicycle paths, and sidewalks to the eligible uses of the specified state highway fund revenue.
Expands the permitted uses of dedicated public revenue transferred to the state highway fund.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The proposal concerns a Texas constitutional amendment and revenue transferred to the state highway fund.

affected_groups.group: Public transportation providers and project sponsors
affected_groups.explanation: Public transportation projects would become eligible for the specified highway fund revenue, subject to the listed construction, maintenance, and right-of-way purposes.

affected_groups.group: Bicycle and pedestrian infrastructure project sponsors and users
affected_groups.explanation: Public bicycle paths and public sidewalks would become eligible infrastructure uses.

major_effects.label: Expanded eligible highway-fund uses
major_effects.explanation: If voters approve the amendment, the specified state highway fund revenue could be used for constructing, maintaining, and acquiring rights-of-way for public transportation, public bicycle paths, and public sidewalks, in addition to public roadways other than toll roads.

SJR6.summary: SJR 6 proposes a constitutional amendment requiring Texas to provide medical assistance to every applicant for whom federal matching funds are available under the Affordable Care Act. If voters approve the proposition at the November 2, 2027 election, the provision would take effect January 1, 2028.

policy_tags.explanation: The proposal expands the state's Medicaid assistance obligation to applicants for whom federal matching funds are available.
The amendment would require the state to provide medical assistance to the specified applicants.
The state would have a new obligation to provide assistance, limited to individuals for whom federal matching funds are available.

locations.name: State of Texas
locations.explanation: The proposed constitutional duty applies to the state statewide.

affected_groups.group: Individuals who apply for medical assistance and for whom federal matching funds are available
affected_groups.explanation: These applicants would be covered by the proposed state assistance requirement.

major_effects.label: Federal-match-linked Medicaid assistance
major_effects.explanation: If approved by voters, the amendment would require medical assistance for all applicants for whom federal matching funds are available; it does not extend the mandate beyond that condition.

agencies.name: Health and Human Services Commission
agencies.explanation: The amendment assigns the assistance obligation to the state rather than naming an agency. HHSC is identified as an inferred potential implementer because the mandate concerns Medicaid.

SJR7.summary: The proposed constitutional amendment would devote the first 30 days of a regular session to introducing bills and resolutions and holding committee hearings, while allowing lawmakers to continue introducing bills during the rest of the session. It would also change the vote threshold for either house to set its order of business from four-fifths to two-thirds; these changes would take effect only if voters approve the amendment at the November 2, 2027 election.

policy_tags.explanation: The proposal changes the Legislature’s regular-session procedures and the vote threshold for determining each house’s order of business.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The proposed change concerns the Texas Constitution and the procedures of the state Legislature.

affected_groups.group: Texas legislators and legislative committees
affected_groups.explanation: The proposal changes when legislators may introduce bills and how committees consider pending matters during a regular session.

affected_groups.group: Texas voters
affected_groups.explanation: Voters would decide whether to approve the proposed constitutional amendment at the specified election.

major_effects.label: Regular-session procedures
major_effects.explanation: If ratified, the amendment would revise bill-introduction and committee-hearing procedures and lower the vote threshold for either house to determine its order of business.

major_effects.label: Voter approval required
major_effects.explanation: The proposed constitutional changes are submitted to voters and would take effect only if approved.

SJR8.summary: If voters approve the amendment on November 2, 2027, it would establish the Texas Redistricting Commission to adopt congressional and Texas House and Senate district plans, with the Legislature setting the commission’s composition and operation by law. The change takes effect January 1, 2030, when the Legislative Redistricting Board is abolished; until then, references to the commission in the judicial-redistricting provision mean the existing board, and the new commission is to convene for the first time in 2031. If the Judicial Districts Board misses its reapportionment deadline, the applicable commission would convene on September 1 and have 90 days after that deadline to complete the reapportionment.

policy_tags.explanation: The amendment changes who adopts the district plans used for elections to the U.S. House from Texas and the Texas Legislature.
It creates a constitutional commission, assigns it redistricting authority, and abolishes the existing Legislative Redistricting Board in 2030.

locations.name: Statewide
locations.explanation: The amendment concerns statewide congressional and legislative district plans and statewide judicial reapportionment.

affected_groups.group: Texas voters
affected_groups.explanation: The commission’s plans would determine the districts used in elections for Texas’s U.S. House seats and the Texas House and Senate.

affected_groups.group: Candidates and officeholders for Texas’s U.S. House seats, Texas House, and Texas Senate
affected_groups.explanation: Their electoral districts would be adopted by the commission under the proposed constitutional process.

affected_groups.group: Residents of Texas judicial districts
affected_groups.explanation: If the Judicial Districts Board misses its reapportionment deadline, the fallback commission process and completion period would change.

major_effects.label: Establishes a redistricting commission
major_effects.explanation: If approved by voters, the commission would adopt plans for Texas’s U.S. House districts and the Texas House and Senate; the Legislature would provide for its composition and operation by general law.

major_effects.label: Transfers legislative redistricting authority
major_effects.explanation: The commission would exercise the state’s redistricting authority for the covered legislative bodies, and districts could not be established or changed except as provided by the new constitutional section.

major_effects.label: Abolishes the Legislative Redistricting Board in 2030
major_effects.explanation: The board would be abolished when the new constitutional section takes effect on January 1, 2030.

major_effects.label: Changes the fallback for judicial reapportionment
major_effects.explanation: If the Judicial Districts Board misses its deadline, the commission would convene on September 1 and complete the reapportionment within 90 days after the board’s deadline, rather than 150 days.

agencies.name: Texas Redistricting Commission
